questions.q: The physical separation of racial or ethnic groups into different neighborhoods within the same metropolitan area is called:
o: Residential segregation
Correct: groups are spatially separated across neighborhoods.
Gentrification
Gentrification is higher-income newcomers displacing existing residents.
Suburbanization
Suburbanization is population movement from cities to suburbs.
Urban renewal
Urban renewal is redevelopment of city areas, often by clearing old housing.
questions.x: Residential segregation is the spatial separation of groups into different neighborhoods of the same area, produced historically by discriminatory lending, zoning, and housing choices. It describes a lasting pattern of where groups live. Gentrification is tempting because it also reshapes neighborhoods, but it is a process of affluent newcomers displacing existing residents, not the separation pattern itself.

questions.q: A study finds that hazardous waste facilities are disproportionately located in low-income, majority-minority neighborhoods. This pattern is a central concern of which movement?
o: Anti-gentrification organizing
That movement targets displacement by rising rents, not pollution siting.
Environmental justice
Correct: it addresses unequal exposure to environmental hazards by race and class.
Meritocracy advocacy
Meritocracy concerns allocating positions by talent, not hazard siting.
Deinstitutionalization
That refers to moving psychiatric patients out of institutions.
questions.note: Environmental justice = fair distribution of environmental burdens and benefits.
questions.x: Environmental justice focuses on how environmental hazards such as waste sites, highways, and polluting plants are distributed, and finds they fall disproportionately on poor and minority communities. The concern is fair sharing of environmental burdens and benefits. Anti-gentrification organizing also concerns poor neighborhoods, but its issue is displacement by rising costs, not exposure to pollution.

questions.q: Families randomly offered housing vouchers to move to low-poverty neighborhoods have children who later earn more as adults than children in control families. This most directly supports:
o: Social reproduction through cultural capital
Cultural capital transmitted by parents was not what was manipulated.
Intragenerational mobility of the parents
The outcome measured was the children's adult earnings, not parents' careers.
Neighborhood effects on life chances
Correct: randomly changing the neighborhood changed outcomes, so place itself matters.
Reverse causation between income and residence
Random assignment rules out reverse causation.
questions.x: Because families were randomly offered vouchers, the only systematic difference between groups was the neighborhood they could move to, so better adult earnings can be attributed to place itself. This is a neighborhood effect on life chances. Random assignment is exactly what rules out reverse causation, and the outcome measured was the children's earnings, not the parents' careers.

questions.q: As higher-income professionals move into a historically working-class urban district, property values and rents climb and many longtime residents are forced out. This process is:
o: Urban sprawl
Sprawl is low-density expansion at a city's edge.
Suburbanization
Suburbanization is movement out of the city, not into it.
Residential segregation
Segregation is separation of groups, not this specific displacement process.
Gentrification
Correct: affluent in-migration raises costs and displaces existing residents.
questions.x: Gentrification occurs when higher-income residents move into a lower-income urban area, renovating housing and raising property values and rents until longtime residents are priced out. Its hallmark is inward affluent migration plus displacement. Suburbanization is the opposite direction of movement, out of the city toward the suburbs.

questions.q: A society's hierarchical ranking of groups according to unequal access to wealth, power, and prestige is called:
o: Social stratification
Correct: stratification is the layered ranking of groups by valued resources.
Social mobility
Mobility is movement between strata, not the ranking itself.
Social exclusion
Exclusion is being shut out of participation in society.
Social capital
Social capital is the value of one's networks and relationships.
questions.x: Social stratification is the structured, hierarchical ranking of groups by unequal access to valued resources like wealth, power, and prestige; it persists across generations and is supported by beliefs that justify it. Social mobility is the tempting distractor, but mobility describes movement between those layers, not the layered system itself.

questions.q: In which type of stratification system is a person's position ascribed at birth, with movement between strata essentially prohibited?
o: Class system
Class systems allow some movement based on achievement.
Caste system
Correct: caste is ascribed, closed, and often enforced by endogamy.
Meritocracy
Meritocracy allocates position by talent and effort, the opposite of ascription.
Open system
An open system permits mobility between strata.
questions.x: A caste system is a closed stratification system: position is ascribed at birth, often tied to occupation and enforced by endogamy, so movement between strata is essentially prohibited. Class systems are the tempting alternative because they also rank people, but they are open systems in which achievement allows some mobility.

questions.q: Socioeconomic status (SES) is most commonly measured by combining which three indicators?
o: Income, age, and religion
Age and religion are not standard SES components.
Wealth, race, and gender
Race and gender are social categories, not SES measures.
Income, education, and occupation
Correct: these three form the classic SES composite.
Occupation, marital status, and family size
Marital status and family size are not standard SES indicators.
questions.x: Socioeconomic status is a composite measure of social position, classically built from income, educational attainment, and occupational prestige. Each captures a different resource: money, knowledge and credentials, and standing at work. Race and gender strongly correlate with SES but are social identity categories, not components of the SES measure.

questions.q: Two families each earn 80,000 dollars per year. One owns a paid-off home and a stock portfolio; the other rents and carries large debts. The families differ primarily in:
o: Income
Their annual incomes are identical.
Occupational prestige
Nothing in the stem describes their jobs.
Educational attainment
Education is not described.
Wealth
Correct: wealth is net assets (what you own minus what you owe).
questions.note: Income is a flow; wealth is a stock of accumulated assets.
questions.x: Income is a flow of money received over a period, while wealth is a stock: total assets minus debts. Two households with identical incomes can differ enormously in wealth, and wealth better reflects security and the ability to pass advantage to children. Since both families earn the same, income cannot be the difference, and nothing is said about their jobs or schooling.

questions.q: In Marxist theory, workers' awareness of their shared exploitation and common interests as a class is termed:
o: Class consciousness
Correct: recognizing a shared class position and interests.
False consciousness
False consciousness is adopting beliefs that work against one's class interests.
Anomie
Anomie is Durkheim's concept of normlessness.
Alienation
Alienation is estrangement from one's labor and its products.
questions.x: For Marx, class consciousness is the workers' recognition that they share a position of exploitation and common interests opposed to the bourgeoisie, a precondition for collective action. False consciousness is the tempting opposite: holding beliefs, often from dominant ideology, that work against one's own class interests.

questions.q: A low-wage worker opposes a minimum wage increase because she believes business owners have earned their wealth and should not be burdened. A Marxist would most likely label her view:
o: Class consciousness
She is not recognizing shared interests with other workers.
False consciousness
Correct: she holds beliefs that serve the dominant class against her own interests.
Relative deprivation
Relative deprivation is dissatisfaction from comparison with others.
Status inconsistency
That is having mismatched ranks on different stratification dimensions.
questions.x: Marx used false consciousness for beliefs held by subordinate groups that serve the ruling class, often absorbed through dominant ideology. A low-wage worker defending owners' interests over a raise for herself fits this. It is not class consciousness, which would mean recognizing her shared interests with other workers and opposing the owning class.

questions.q: According to Marx, which development is most necessary for the proletariat to move from a 'class in itself' to a 'class for itself'?
o: Workers gaining ownership of capital through higher wages
Wage gains do not transfer ownership of the means of production.
Upward intragenerational mobility of individual workers
Individual mobility does not create collective awareness.
Recognition of shared interests in opposition to the bourgeoisie
Correct: a class for itself has developed class consciousness and acts collectively.
Adoption of bourgeois cultural tastes and manners
Adopting elite culture is closer to false consciousness.
questions.note: Class in itself = objective position; class for itself = conscious, organized class.
questions.x: Marx distinguished a class in itself, people who objectively share a relation to the means of production, from a class for itself, which recognizes its shared interests and organizes to pursue them. The transition requires collective class consciousness. Individual gains like higher wages or personal mobility do not create this shared awareness and can even weaken it.

questions.q: A first-generation college student feels unsure how to approach professors during office hours, while peers from professional families do so with ease. The peers' advantage best illustrates:
o: Social capital
Social capital is network ties; the advantage here is know-how and comfort.
Economic capital
Money is not what makes office hours easier to navigate.
Status inconsistency
That refers to mismatched ranks across stratification dimensions.
Cultural capital
Correct: familiarity with institutional norms is embodied cultural capital.
questions.x: Bourdieu's cultural capital includes the knowledge, skills, and comfort with institutional norms that children absorb at home; this embodied form helps students navigate settings like office hours. The peers' advantage is know-how, not money. Social capital is tempting, but it refers to useful relationships, and no connections are being used here.

questions.q: A job seeker gets an interview because her former neighbor works at the company and recommends her. She is benefiting from:
o: Social capital
Correct: resources gained through social relationships and networks.
Cultural capital
Cultural capital is knowledge, tastes, and credentials, not connections.
Economic capital
No money or assets are involved.
Meritocracy
She got the interview through a connection, not purely merit.
questions.x: Social capital is the set of resources available through one's relationships and networks, such as referrals, information, and trust. A neighbor's recommendation opening a door is a textbook case. Cultural capital is the common mix-up, but it refers to knowledge, tastes, and credentials held by the person, not to who they know.

questions.q: Research shows people more often learn about new jobs through casual acquaintances than through close friends. This finding emphasizes the value of:
o: Strong ties within a dense network
Close friends tend to share the same information as the job seeker.
Weak ties that bridge separate networks
Correct: acquaintances connect people to new, non-redundant information.
Embodied cultural capital
This finding concerns networks, not personal dispositions.
Institutionalized cultural capital
Credentials are not what the finding describes.
questions.note: Granovetter: 'the strength of weak ties.'
questions.x: Granovetter's strength of weak ties finding is that acquaintances bridge to other social circles and so carry new, non-redundant information, such as job openings. Close friends usually move in the same circles as the job seeker and already share what they know. Strong ties offer support, but weak ties are better for information spread.

questions.q: In Bourdieu's framework, a medical degree from a prestigious university is an example of:
o: Embodied cultural capital
Embodied capital is internalized: accent, manners, dispositions.
Objectified cultural capital
Objectified capital is physical cultural goods like art or books.
Institutionalized cultural capital
Correct: formal credentials recognized by institutions.
Bonding social capital
Bonding capital is ties within a close-knit group.
questions.x: Bourdieu described three forms of cultural capital: embodied (internalized dispositions and skills), objectified (cultural goods such as books and art), and institutionalized (credentials such as degrees that institutions formally recognize). A medical degree is institutionalized. Embodied capital is tempting because training builds skills, but the degree itself is the official certification of them.

questions.q: A family owns a large collection of rare books and original paintings that can be passed physically to heirs. In Bourdieu's terms, this represents:
o: Embodied cultural capital
Embodied capital lives in the person and cannot be handed over directly.
Institutionalized cultural capital
That is credentials such as degrees.
Bridging social capital
These are objects, not relationships.
Objectified cultural capital
Correct: cultural goods in material form.
questions.note: Objectified capital needs embodied capital to be fully appreciated.
questions.x: Objectified cultural capital is culture in material form, such as books, paintings, and instruments, which can be transferred like property. Embodied cultural capital is the tempting choice, but it exists inside the person as tastes and skills and cannot be handed over directly; it is what lets someone appreciate the objects.

questions.q: Children of affluent parents tend to attend well-funded schools, earn advanced degrees, and enter high-status jobs, keeping the family's class position across generations. This is best described as:
o: Social reproduction
Correct: social structures transmit class position from one generation to the next.
Structural mobility
Structural mobility is movement caused by changes in the economy.
Horizontal mobility
Horizontal mobility is a change of position at the same rank.
Exchange mobility
Exchange mobility is offsetting rises and falls in a fixed structure.
questions.x: Social reproduction is the process by which social structures, such as unequal schools, inheritance, and transmitted cultural capital, pass class position from one generation to the next. The family's status stays the same across generations. Structural mobility is the tempting distractor, but it describes change in position driven by economic shifts, not persistence.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that schools reward the speech patterns and behaviors of upper-middle-class children, so grades partly reflect home background rather than ability. This argument is most consistent with:
o: The functionalist view of schools as meritocratic sorting
Functionalists see schools as sorting by merit, which this argument denies.
Bourdieu's theory of social reproduction
Correct: schools treat class-based cultural capital as merit, reproducing inequality.
Weber's theory of bureaucracy
Bureaucracy concerns formal organizational structure.
Durkheim's concept of mechanical solidarity
That describes cohesion based on similarity in simple societies.
questions.x: Bourdieu argued schools reward the cultural capital of dominant classes, such as their speech and behavior, while presenting the results as merit, which reproduces inequality. The functionalist view is tempting because it also discusses schools sorting students, but it claims schools sort by ability, which this argument explicitly denies.

questions.q: Which finding would most strongly challenge the claim that a society is a meritocracy?
o: High-achieving students earn more as adults than low-achieving students
This is what a meritocracy would predict.
Occupations requiring longer training tend to pay more
This is consistent with rewards following effort and skill.
Parental income predicts children's adult earnings better than their test scores do
Correct: inherited position outweighing ability contradicts meritocracy.
Most citizens believe that hard work leads to success
A belief in meritocracy is not evidence about actual allocation.
questions.x: A meritocracy allocates rewards by talent and effort, so ability measures should predict outcomes better than inherited background. If parental income beats test scores in predicting adult earnings, ascribed advantage is driving outcomes. Widespread belief in hard work is tempting, but beliefs about meritocracy say nothing about how rewards are actually distributed.

questions.q: Unearned advantages that members of a dominant group receive simply by belonging to that group are called:
o: Prestige
Prestige is social esteem attached to a position, often earned.
Achieved status
Achieved status is earned through one's own actions.
Cultural capital
Cultural capital is knowledge and tastes that can be acquired.
Privilege
Correct: privilege is unearned advantage from group membership.
questions.x: Privilege refers to unearned advantages that come automatically from membership in a dominant group, often invisible to those who hold them. Cultural capital is the tempting choice because it also confers advantage, but it consists of knowledge and tastes that can be acquired, whereas privilege attaches to group membership itself.

questions.q: Surveys consistently rank physicians and scientists above many higher-paid occupations in respect and esteem. This dimension of stratification is:
o: Prestige
Correct: prestige is the social honor attached to a position.
Power
Power is the ability to impose one's will despite resistance.
Wealth
These occupations rank high despite earning less than some others.
Privilege
Privilege is unearned group advantage, not occupational esteem.
questions.x: Prestige is the social honor or respect attached to a position, and it can diverge from pay: scientists and physicians are esteemed above some better-paid occupations. This shows prestige is a separate stratification dimension. Wealth cannot explain the ranking because the respected jobs rank above others that earn more.

questions.q: Max Weber argued that stratification has three distinct dimensions. Which choice lists them?
o: Income, education, and occupation
These are the components of SES, not Weber's dimensions.
Class, status, and party (power)
Correct: economic position, social honor, and political power.
Bourgeoisie, proletariat, and petite bourgeoisie
These are Marx's class categories.
Economic, cultural, and social capital
These are Bourdieu's forms of capital.
questions.x: Weber rejected Marx's purely economic model and described three dimensions: class (economic position and market life chances), status (social honor or prestige), and party (power, the ability to influence collective action). Income, education, and occupation is tempting, but that is the modern SES composite, not Weber's framework.

questions.q: A respected member of the clergy has high prestige but a low income. In Weber's multidimensional model, this is an example of:
o: Downward mobility
No change in position over time is described.
False consciousness
That is a Marxist concept about beliefs against class interests.
Status inconsistency
Correct: ranking high on one dimension and low on another.
Horizontal mobility
Horizontal mobility is moving between positions of similar rank.
questions.x: Because Weber treated class, status, and power as separate dimensions, a person can rank high on one and low on another; this mismatch is status inconsistency. A clergy member with high prestige and low income fits. Downward mobility is tempting, but mobility requires a change in position over time, which is not described.

questions.q: The framework that examines how overlapping identities such as race, gender, and class combine to produce distinct experiences of advantage or disadvantage is:
o: Meritocracy
Meritocracy concerns allocation by talent and effort.
Social reproduction
Social reproduction concerns transmission of class across generations.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is judging a culture by its own standards.
Intersectionality
Correct: identities interact rather than simply adding up.
questions.x: Intersectionality, from Kimberlé Crenshaw, holds that identities such as race, gender, and class interact, so a person's experience at their intersection cannot be understood by examining each identity separately. Social reproduction is tempting because it also concerns inequality, but it concerns transmission of class position across generations.

questions.q: A study finds that Black women earn less than both white women and Black men, and the gap is larger than predicted by simply adding separate race and gender effects. This finding supports:
o: Intersectionality
Correct: combined identities produce effects beyond the sum of each.
Meritocracy
Group-based pay gaps contradict merit-only allocation.
Horizontal mobility
No movement between positions is described.
Exchange mobility
Exchange mobility concerns rises and falls within a fixed structure.
questions.x: Intersectionality predicts that combined identities produce effects that are not simply the sum of each identity's effect. Here the pay gap for Black women exceeds the additive prediction of separate race and gender penalties, which is exactly that non-additive pattern. Meritocracy is ruled out because group-based gaps contradict merit-only allocation rather than supporting it.

questions.q: Researchers studying maternal health outcomes want to test an intersectional hypothesis about race and income. Which analysis is most appropriate?
o: Comparing outcomes by race alone
This ignores how income modifies race effects.
Testing for a statistical interaction between race and income
Correct: an interaction tests whether the effect of one depends on the other.
Comparing outcomes by income while controlling for race
Controlling treats race as additive, not interacting.
Reporting only the overall national outcome rate
An aggregate rate hides all group differences.
questions.note: Intersectionality maps onto interaction effects, not simple main effects.
questions.x: An intersectional hypothesis claims that the effect of race depends on income level and vice versa, which is a statistical interaction. Testing an interaction term asks whether combined categories differ beyond what separate effects predict. Controlling for race while examining income is tempting, but it assumes the effects are additive, the very assumption intersectionality challenges.

questions.q: Comparing a person's adult social class with the class of his or her parents measures which type of mobility?
o: Intragenerational mobility
Intragenerational mobility is change within one person's lifetime.
Horizontal mobility
Horizontal mobility is a change in position without a change in rank.
Intergenerational mobility
Correct: mobility measured across generations.
Structural mobility
Structural mobility is caused by changes in the economy's structure.
questions.x: Intergenerational mobility compares a person's position with that of their parents, showing how much class persists across generations. Intragenerational mobility is the tempting confusion: it tracks changes within one person's own lifetime, such as rising through a career. The prefix inter- means between generations; intra- means within one life.

questions.q: A woman starts her career as a bank teller and retires as the bank's regional vice president. This is an example of:
o: Upward intergenerational mobility
No comparison with her parents is made.
Horizontal intragenerational mobility
Her rank rose, so the move was vertical.
Downward intergenerational mobility
She rose, and no parental comparison is given.
Upward intragenerational mobility
Correct: she rose in rank within her own lifetime.
questions.x: Mobility is classified by direction (upward, downward, or horizontal) and time frame (within a lifetime or across generations). Rising from teller to vice president is a vertical, upward move within one career, so it is upward intragenerational mobility. Intergenerational choices are wrong because no comparison with her parents is made.

questions.q: A registered nurse leaves hospital work to become a public school teacher with similar income and prestige. This change is an example of:
o: Horizontal mobility
Correct: a change of occupation without a change in rank.
Upward vertical mobility
Her income and prestige did not rise.
Downward vertical mobility
Her income and prestige did not fall.
Intergenerational mobility
No comparison with her parents is made.
questions.x: Horizontal mobility is a change of occupation or position without a change in social rank, such as switching between jobs of similar income and prestige. Vertical mobility requires moving up or down the hierarchy. Intergenerational mobility is ruled out because it requires comparing the person with their parents, which the stem does not do.

questions.q: After a factory closes, a skilled machinist takes a lower-paying job as a retail cashier. This is best described as:
o: Horizontal mobility
Pay and skill level dropped, so the move was not lateral.
Downward intragenerational vertical mobility
Correct: he moved down in rank within his own career.
Upward structural mobility
He moved down, not up.
Downward intergenerational mobility
The comparison is within his own career, not with his parents.
questions.x: Moving from skilled machinist to lower-paid cashier is a drop in rank, so it is vertical, downward mobility, and since it occurs within his own career it is intragenerational. Horizontal mobility is tempting because he simply changed jobs, but horizontal moves keep rank roughly constant, and here pay and skill fell.

questions.q: Between 1900 and 1960, many children of farmers moved into factory and office jobs because farm employment shrank while industrial jobs expanded. This is primarily:
o: Exchange mobility
Exchange mobility assumes a fixed structure with offsetting moves.
Horizontal mobility
The shift changed income and occupational rank for many.
Structural mobility
Correct: changes in the economy itself drove large-scale movement.
Social reproduction
Social reproduction is the persistence of class position, not change.
questions.x: Structural mobility is movement caused by changes in the economy's structure, such as shrinking farm jobs and expanding industrial ones, which pushes large numbers into new positions regardless of individual effort. Exchange mobility is tempting, but it assumes the number of positions at each level stays fixed, while here the occupational structure itself changed.

questions.q: In a society with a fixed number of positions at each class level, some individuals rise while an equal number fall. This pattern is called:
o: Structural mobility
Structural mobility requires the distribution of positions to change.
Horizontal mobility
These moves change rank, so they are vertical.
Social reproduction
People are changing positions, so class is not simply reproduced.
Exchange mobility
Correct: offsetting upward and downward moves within a stable structure.
questions.x: Exchange mobility occurs when the distribution of positions stays fixed, so every person who rises is offset by someone who falls; it measures openness rather than overall growth. Structural mobility is the tempting alternative, but it requires the structure itself to change, such as more professional jobs becoming available.

questions.q: A system in which social positions are allocated on the basis of individual talent and effort rather than inherited status is called:
o: A meritocracy
Correct: rewards follow merit rather than birth.
A caste system
Caste positions are ascribed at birth.
An aristocracy
Aristocracy is rule by a hereditary elite.
A plutocracy
Plutocracy is rule by the wealthy.
questions.x: A meritocracy allocates social positions by individual achievement, talent and effort, rather than by ascribed traits like family background. Functionalists often describe modern societies this way, while conflict theorists question it. A caste system is the opposite case: position is ascribed at birth and movement is essentially prohibited.

questions.q: Cross-national data show that countries with greater income inequality tend to have stronger correlations between parents' and children's earnings. Higher inequality is therefore associated with:
o: Greater intergenerational mobility
A stronger parent-child earnings link means less mobility.
Lower intergenerational mobility
Correct: earnings persist more strongly across generations.
No relationship to intergenerational mobility
The data show a clear association.
Greater horizontal mobility
Earnings correlations measure vertical, not lateral, movement.
questions.note: A stronger parent-child correlation means less mobility.
questions.x: A strong correlation between parents' and children's earnings means children's outcomes are largely predicted by their parents', which is low intergenerational mobility. The cross-national pattern linking higher inequality with lower mobility is often called the Great Gatsby curve. Choosing greater mobility comes from misreading a strong parent-child link as more movement rather than less.

questions.q: Lacking the resources needed to meet basic survival needs such as food, shelter, and clean water is called:
o: Relative poverty
Relative poverty is falling below a society's typical living standard.
Social exclusion
Social exclusion is being shut out of participation in society.
Absolute poverty
Correct: inability to meet basic needs, regardless of others' living standards.
Status inconsistency
That is mismatched ranks across stratification dimensions.
questions.x: Absolute poverty is the inability to meet basic survival needs such as food, shelter, and clean water, judged against a fixed standard regardless of how others live. Relative poverty is tempting, but it is defined by comparison to a society's typical living standard, so someone can be relatively poor while having basic needs met.

questions.q: A family in a wealthy nation has adequate food and shelter but cannot afford internet access, a car, or school trips that most families consider standard. They are experiencing:
o: Absolute poverty
Their basic survival needs are met.
Social reproduction
No transmission across generations is described.
Downward mobility
No change in position over time is described.
Relative poverty
Correct: they fall below their society's typical standard of living.
questions.x: Relative poverty means having significantly less than a society's typical standard of living, even if survival needs are met; it shifts with the norms of that society. This family has food and shelter, so absolute poverty is ruled out, but cannot afford things most families treat as standard, which is the defining feature of relative poverty.

questions.q: Long-term unemployed residents of an isolated housing estate lack transportation, political voice, and access to services, so they cannot participate fully in society. Sociologists call this:
o: Social exclusion
Correct: multiple barriers cut people off from mainstream social life.
Absolute poverty
The stem stresses lack of participation, not inability to survive.
Gentrification
No affluent in-migration or displacement is described.
Horizontal mobility
No change in position is described.
questions.x: Social exclusion is a multidimensional disadvantage in which people are cut off from full participation in economic, political, and social life through barriers like isolation, lack of transport, and no political voice. Absolute poverty is tempting, but it concerns inability to meet survival needs, while the stem emphasizes exclusion from participation.

questions.q: The official U.S. poverty threshold was originally set at roughly three times the cost of a minimal food budget. This threshold is primarily a measure of:
o: Relative poverty
It does not depend on the society's median income.
Absolute poverty
Correct: it is a fixed basic-needs standard adjusted only for inflation.
Social exclusion
It measures income only, not participation in society.
Subjective poverty
It is not based on how people feel about their situation.
questions.x: The U.S. official poverty threshold was built from a minimal food budget multiplied by three and since adjusted only for inflation, so it is a fixed basic-needs cutoff, an absolute measure. Relative poverty is tempting because poverty lines seem comparative, but a relative measure would move with median income, which this threshold does not.

questions.q: A researcher argues that persistent poverty results mainly from a lack of local jobs, underfunded schools, and discriminatory lending rather than from values held by the poor. This view rejects:
o: Structural explanations of poverty
Her view is itself a structural explanation.
Conflict theory
Conflict theory is consistent with emphasizing structural barriers.
The culture of poverty thesis
Correct: that thesis blames poverty on self-perpetuating values of the poor.
The concept of relative poverty
Her argument concerns causes, not how poverty is defined.
questions.x: The culture of poverty thesis claims that poverty persists because the poor develop values and behaviors, such as fatalism, that are passed to children. Structural explanations instead point to job loss, underfunded schools, and discrimination. The researcher's view is itself structural, so the tempting choice of structural explanations is the position she holds, not rejects.

questions.q: A full-time employee earning minimum wage whose household income still falls below the poverty line is classified as part of the:
o: Structurally unemployed
She is employed full-time.
Underclass
The underclass is defined by long-term joblessness and isolation.
Upper-middle class
Her income is below the poverty line.
Working poor
Correct: employed people whose income remains below the poverty line.
questions.x: The working poor are people who are employed, often full-time, yet whose household income still falls below the poverty line, typically because of low wages. The underclass is a tempting alternative, but it refers to people marked by long-term joblessness and social isolation, while this worker holds a full-time job.

questions.q: The conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age that shape health outcomes are called:
o: Social determinants of health
Correct: nonmedical social and economic factors that drive health.
Biomedical risk factors
These are biological traits like blood pressure or genotype.
Health behaviors
Behaviors are individual actions, partly shaped by these conditions.
Healthcare disparities
Those are differences in access to or quality of care.
questions.x: Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age, such as income, education, housing, and neighborhood, which shape health outcomes. Health behaviors are tempting, but they are individual actions like smoking or exercise that are themselves shaped by these broader conditions.

questions.q: A study of British civil servants found that mortality rose steadily at each lower employment grade, even though none of the workers were poor. This pattern is best described as:
o: A threshold effect limited to the poorest
Risk rose at every step, not just at the bottom.
A social gradient in health
Correct: health worsens incrementally with each step down the hierarchy.
Evidence that only access to care matters
All civil servants had access to national health care.
An effect of absolute poverty
None of the workers lived in absolute poverty.
questions.x: The Whitehall studies of British civil servants showed mortality rising at every step down the employment hierarchy, even though all workers were employed and had national health coverage. This stepwise pattern is the social gradient in health. A threshold effect at the bottom is ruled out because risk rose at each grade, not only among the poorest.

questions.q: A study finds that low income predicts poor health. A critic argues instead that chronic illness causes people to lose jobs and fall into lower income brackets. The critic is proposing:
o: The social causation hypothesis
Social causation says low SES causes poor health, the original claim.
Intersectionality
The argument is not about overlapping identities.
The health selection (social drift) hypothesis
Correct: poor health leads to downward mobility.
Fundamental cause theory
That theory holds SES causes health through flexible resources.
questions.x: Social causation says low SES causes poor health; health selection (social drift) reverses the arrow, saying illness causes job loss and downward mobility. The critic's argument that chronic illness pushes people into lower incomes is the selection view. Fundamental cause theory is tempting, but it is a social causation account explaining why SES keeps shaping health.

questions.q: Researchers want to test whether low income causes poor health rather than the reverse. Which design provides the strongest causal evidence?
o: A cross-sectional survey of income and health
Measures both at one time, so direction cannot be determined.
A case-control study of hospitalized patients
Cannot rule out illness causing income loss.
Correlating county income with county mortality
Ecological correlations cannot establish individual causation.
Randomly assigning families to receive an income supplement and tracking health
Correct: random assignment of income isolates its causal effect.
questions.x: Establishing causal direction requires manipulating the proposed cause while balancing other factors, which random assignment of an income supplement does. Any later health difference can then be attributed to income. Observational designs such as cross-sectional surveys or case-control studies cannot rule out illness lowering income or other confounders.

questions.q: Even after controlling for insurance and income, Black patients in the U.S. are less likely than white patients to receive adequate pain medication for the same injuries. This is best classified as:
o: A racial disparity in healthcare treatment
Correct: unequal care for the same clinical need, independent of SES.
A difference fully explained by SES
Income and insurance were controlled.
A genetic difference in pain sensitivity
No such difference justifies unequal treatment; this is a known false belief.
An example of relative poverty
Relative poverty concerns income relative to others.
questions.x: A healthcare disparity is a difference in access to or quality of care across groups with the same clinical need. Because insurance and income were controlled, the gap in pain treatment cannot be attributed to SES, pointing to factors such as provider bias. The genetic explanation is a documented false belief about racial differences in pain, not a valid justification.

questions.q: Women in the U.S. live longer on average than men yet report more chronic illness and disability. This pattern is often called:
o: The healthy immigrant effect
That concerns immigrants' initial health advantage.
The morbidity-mortality paradox
Correct: women have higher morbidity but lower mortality.
The social gradient in health
The gradient refers to health declining with SES.
The Hispanic paradox
That concerns Hispanic Americans' favorable mortality despite lower SES.
questions.x: The morbidity-mortality paradox, also called the gender paradox, describes women living longer than men while reporting more chronic illness and disability. Explanations include men's higher rates of fatal conditions and risk behaviors and women's greater use of care. The Hispanic paradox is tempting because it is also a paradox, but it concerns ethnicity and SES, not gender.

questions.q: Despite lower average SES, Hispanic Americans have life expectancy similar to or higher than that of non-Hispanic white Americans. This finding is known as:
o: The gender health paradox
That concerns women's higher morbidity but lower mortality.
The social gradient in health
The gradient predicts the opposite of this finding.
The Hispanic (Latino) paradox
Correct: better-than-expected outcomes given SES.
Reverse causation
No causal direction is in question here.
questions.x: The Hispanic or Latino paradox refers to Hispanic Americans having mortality and life expectancy similar to or better than non-Hispanic white Americans despite lower average SES. Proposed explanations include strong family networks and selective migration. The social gradient is tempting but would predict worse outcomes for lower-SES groups, the opposite of this finding.

questions.q: Women having heart attacks more often present with fatigue, nausea, or back pain and are more likely than men to be misdiagnosed. This contributes to:
o: A class-based health disparity
The difference is by gender, not class.
Social exclusion
No exclusion from social participation is described.
Residential segregation
No spatial separation is described.
A gender disparity in healthcare quality
Correct: care differs by gender for the same condition.
questions.x: When patients with the same condition receive different quality of care by gender, that is a gender disparity in healthcare. Women's heart attacks more often present with atypical symptoms, contributing to misdiagnosis and delays. A class-based disparity is ruled out because the stem compares men and women, not income groups.

questions.q: A low-income urban neighborhood has no supermarket or grocery store selling fresh produce within a mile, and few residents own cars. Such an area is called a:
o: Food desert
Correct: limited access to affordable, nutritious food.
Ethnic enclave
An enclave is a cluster of one ethnic group with its own institutions.
Gated community
A gated community is a walled, often affluent, residential area.
Central business district
That is a city's commercial core.
questions.x: A food desert is an area, often low-income, where residents lack nearby access to affordable, nutritious food such as fresh produce, especially when they also lack cars. It is linked to poorer diets and diet-related disease. An ethnic enclave is tempting because it is also a neighborhood type, but it is defined by ethnic clustering, not food access.

questions.q: Mid-20th-century federal maps rated minority neighborhoods as high-risk, denying residents mortgages. Today those neighborhoods still have lower home values and more heat-related illness. This illustrates:
o: Individual prejudice that ended with the policy
Effects persisted long after the maps stopped being used.
Institutional discrimination with long-term spatial effects
Correct: redlining was policy-based and its harms persist in place.
Voluntary self-segregation by residents
Residents were denied credit, not choosing freely.
Horizontal mobility of homeowners
No lateral movement between positions is described.
questions.note: Redlining shows how past policy shapes present health by place.
questions.x: Redlining was federally backed mapping that rated minority neighborhoods as hazardous, denying them mortgage credit; this is institutional discrimination because it operated through official policy rather than individual attitudes. Its effects persist in lower home values and hotter, less green environments. Individual prejudice is ruled out because the harm came from policy and outlasted the maps.

questions.q: William Julius Wilson argued that the loss of manufacturing jobs and the departure of middle-class families from inner-city neighborhoods produced:
o: Rapid gentrification of those neighborhoods
Wilson described abandonment, not affluent in-migration.
Increased exchange mobility
Wilson described blocked mobility, not offsetting moves.
Concentrated poverty and social isolation
Correct: jobless, isolated neighborhoods with few institutional supports.
The end of residential segregation
Segregation persisted and poverty became more concentrated.
questions.x: In The Truly Disadvantaged, Wilson argued that deindustrialization removed stable jobs from inner cities while middle-class families moved out, leaving neighborhoods of concentrated joblessness and poverty, cut off from institutions and role models. This structural account explains social isolation. Gentrification is ruled out because Wilson described abandonment and decline, not affluent in-migration.

questions.q: After controlling for household income, researchers find that majority-Black neighborhoods have higher levels of airborne pollutants than majority-white neighborhoods. This result suggests that:
o: Pollution exposure differs by race even at similar incomes
Correct: the racial gap remains once income is held constant.
Income fully explains the racial difference in exposure
Income was controlled, yet the gap remained.
Pollution exposure is randomly distributed
A systematic racial pattern is not random.
Only individual prejudice could produce the pattern
Institutional processes like zoning can produce it without individual prejudice.
questions.note: Environmental racism: race predicts exposure beyond class.
questions.x: Controlling for a variable holds it constant, so any remaining difference cannot be explained by it. Since majority-Black neighborhoods still have more pollution at similar incomes, race predicts exposure beyond class, a pattern called environmental racism. Claiming that only individual prejudice could cause this is wrong because institutional practices like zoning and siting decisions can produce it.

questions.q: Residents of high-poverty neighborhoods have higher asthma rates. A researcher wants to show that the neighborhood itself, not individual income, drives this. Which comparison is most useful?
o: High- and low-income residents within a single neighborhood
This varies individual income while holding neighborhood constant, the opposite test.
Residents' beliefs about the causes of asthma
Beliefs do not isolate a neighborhood effect.
Asthma rates measured only in high-poverty areas
Without a comparison group, no effect can be isolated.
People of similar income living in neighborhoods with different poverty levels
Correct: holding individual income constant isolates the neighborhood effect.
questions.x: To isolate a neighborhood effect, individual income must be held constant while neighborhood poverty varies, so comparing similar-income people in different neighborhoods is the right test. Comparing rich and poor residents within one neighborhood is tempting because it is a comparison, but it holds neighborhood constant and varies income, testing the opposite factor.

questions.q: A neighborhood where immigrants of one ethnicity cluster together and maintain their own businesses and institutions is called:
o: A ghetto
A ghetto implies involuntary segregation, often with concentrated poverty.
An ethnic enclave
Correct: a clustered ethnic community with its own economy and institutions.
A food desert
A food desert is an area lacking access to healthy food.
A gated community
A gated community is a walled residential area, often affluent.
questions.x: An ethnic enclave is a neighborhood where members of one ethnic group, often immigrants, cluster voluntarily and build their own businesses, institutions, and networks, which can aid economic adaptation. A ghetto is the tempting alternative, but the term implies involuntary segregation, often with concentrated poverty, rather than a self-sustaining community economy.

questions.q: In Marx's theory, the class defined by its ownership of the means of production is the:
o: Bourgeoisie
Correct: capitalists who own factories, land, and capital.
Proletariat
The proletariat sells its labor and owns no means of production.
Lumpenproletariat
This is Marx's term for the marginal underclass outside regular labor.
Petite bourgeoisie
They own small businesses but are not the defining capitalist class.
questions.x: Marx defined classes by their relationship to the means of production: the bourgeoisie own factories, land, and capital, while the proletariat must sell their labor to survive. The petite bourgeoisie is tempting because they also own something, but they are small owners such as shopkeepers who often work alongside any employees, not the defining capitalist class.

questions.q: The Davis-Moore thesis holds that social stratification is:
o: A tool the ruling class uses to exploit workers
That is a conflict-theory view.
Created through everyday symbolic interactions
That reflects symbolic interactionism, not Davis-Moore.
Eliminated in modern industrial societies
Davis and Moore argued stratification is universal.
Functional, because unequal rewards motivate talented people to fill vital roles
Correct: this is the functionalist account of inequality.
questions.x: Davis and Moore offered a functionalist account: stratification is universal and useful because societies must attach larger rewards to important, demanding positions to motivate the most talented people to train for and fill them. The exploitation view is the tempting contrast, but that is conflict theory, which sees inequality as serving the powerful.

questions.q: Which observation most directly undermines the Davis-Moore thesis?
o: Surgeons earn more than cashiers
This fits Davis-Moore, since surgery is important and demanding.
Many essential jobs pay little, while heirs gain wealth without filling any role
Correct: rewards do not track functional importance or talent.
Jobs requiring longer training tend to pay more
This supports the thesis.
Wages for scarce skills rise when demand increases
This is consistent with the thesis.
questions.x: The Davis-Moore thesis predicts that rewards track a position's functional importance and the scarcity of talent needed to fill it. Essential workers earning little, and heirs gaining wealth without filling any role, show rewards that do not follow importance or talent. Surgeons out-earning cashiers is tempting as a challenge but actually fits the thesis.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that health inequality persists because powerful groups shape policy to protect their own advantages. This reflects which perspective?
o: Functionalism
Functionalism stresses how structures maintain stability.
Symbolic interactionism
That micro view focuses on meaning in interaction.
Conflict theory
Correct: inequality reflects competition and domination by powerful groups.
Social exchange theory
That explains relationships as cost-benefit exchanges.
questions.x: Conflict theory views society as an arena of competition over scarce resources, where powerful groups use institutions and policy to protect their advantages, perpetuating inequality, including in health. Functionalism is the tempting contrast: it explains social arrangements by how they maintain stability, not by who benefits from them.

questions.q: A researcher observes how affluent and working-class shoppers interpret brand logos as signals of who 'belongs' in certain stores. This study best reflects which approach?
o: Symbolic interactionism
Correct: it examines shared meanings of symbols in everyday interaction.
Functionalism
Functionalism looks at how structures serve society as a whole.
Macro-level conflict theory
The focus is micro-level meaning, not class struggle over resources.
Rational choice theory
That models decisions as cost-benefit calculations.
questions.x: Symbolic interactionism is a micro-level perspective that studies how people create and interpret shared meanings of symbols, like brand logos, in everyday interactions. Here shoppers read logos as signals of belonging. Conflict theory is tempting because class is involved, but the study focuses on interpretation of symbols, not macro-level struggle over resources.

questions.q: Buying luxury watches and cars primarily to display wealth and signal social status is called:
o: Cultural relativism
That is judging a culture by its own standards.
Social reproduction
That is transmission of class across generations.
Relative deprivation
That is dissatisfaction from comparing oneself to others.
Conspicuous consumption
Correct: Veblen's term for consumption meant to display status.
questions.x: Conspicuous consumption, Thorstein Veblen's term, is buying expensive goods mainly to display wealth and signal social status rather than for their practical use. Relative deprivation is tempting because both involve comparison with others, but it describes the discontent felt when people see themselves as worse off than a reference group.

questions.q: Despite rising average incomes, workers report greater dissatisfaction after learning that executive pay has grown much faster than their own. This is best explained by:
o: Absolute poverty
The workers' incomes are rising, and basic needs are met.
Relative deprivation
Correct: discontent arises from comparison with a reference group.
False consciousness
They recognize the inequality, so they are not misperceiving their interests.
Downward mobility
Their incomes rose, so they did not move down.
questions.x: Relative deprivation is discontent arising from comparing one's situation with a reference group, not from absolute hardship. Workers whose pay is rising can still feel deprived when executive pay grows much faster. Absolute poverty is ruled out because their incomes are rising and their basic needs are met.

questions.q: Bourdieu's term for the deeply ingrained dispositions, tastes, and habits that people acquire from their class background is:
o: Field
A field is a social arena in which people compete for capital.
Doxa
Doxa is the taken-for-granted beliefs of a society.
Habitus
Correct: internalized class-based dispositions that guide behavior.
Anomie
Anomie is Durkheim's concept of normlessness.
questions.x: Habitus, in Bourdieu's theory, is the system of durable dispositions, tastes, and habits people internalize from their class background, which guides behavior largely without conscious thought. Field is tempting because it is also Bourdieu's term, but a field is the social arena, such as education, in which people compete for capital.

questions.q: An immigrant community's tight mutual-aid networks help members survive hardship but rarely connect them to jobs outside the community. This describes:
o: Strong bonding social capital with limited bridging social capital
Correct: inward ties support members but do not link outward.
Strong bridging social capital
Bridging capital links people across groups, which is lacking here.
Institutionalized cultural capital
That is formal credentials, not networks.
Objectified cultural capital
That is material cultural goods.
questions.x: Bonding social capital consists of strong ties within a close-knit group that provide support and solidarity, while bridging social capital links people to different groups and outside opportunities. This community has abundant mutual aid but few links outward, so bonding is strong and bridging weak. Bridging capital is tempting, but outward connections are exactly what is missing.

questions.q: Which of the following is an achieved status?
o: Being female
Sex is ascribed at birth.
Being born into nobility
Noble birth is ascribed.
Being 65 years old
Age is ascribed, not earned.
Being a licensed physician
Correct: earned through one's own effort and training.
questions.x: An achieved status is gained through one's own actions, such as earning a medical license, while an ascribed status is assigned involuntarily, by birth or stage of life, such as sex, noble birth, or age. Being 65 is tempting because it takes time to reach, but age is not earned by effort, so it is ascribed.

questions.q: At a large company, women hold many middle-management jobs but few executive positions, despite qualifications similar to those of male executives. This barrier is called:
o: The glass escalator
That is men's rapid advancement in female-dominated fields.
The glass ceiling
Correct: an invisible barrier to advancement into top positions.
Horizontal mobility
Horizontal mobility is a lateral move, not a blocked one.
Status inconsistency
That is mismatched ranks across different dimensions.
questions.x: The glass ceiling is an invisible barrier that limits advancement of women and minorities into top leadership positions despite comparable qualifications. Women filling middle management but not executive ranks is the classic pattern. The glass escalator is tempting because the terms sound alike, but it describes men's faster advancement in female-dominated occupations.

questions.q: Men entering female-dominated professions such as nursing tend to be promoted faster than their female colleagues. This phenomenon is called:
o: The glass ceiling
The glass ceiling blocks advancement; here men are advanced.
Status inconsistency
That is mismatched ranks across stratification dimensions.
The glass escalator
Correct: men are carried upward in female-dominated occupations.
Exchange mobility
Exchange mobility is offsetting moves in a fixed structure.
questions.x: The glass escalator describes men in female-dominated fields, such as nursing or teaching, being promoted faster than their female peers, as though carried upward. It shows gender advantage persisting even when men are the numerical minority. The glass ceiling is the opposite situation, a barrier blocking women's advancement into top positions.

questions.q: A study finds that women earn less than men on average, but the gap shrinks substantially after controlling for occupation. This suggests that part of the gap reflects:
o: Occupational segregation by gender
Correct: men and women are concentrated in differently paid occupations.
Differences in intelligence
The data say nothing about intelligence, and controlling occupation explains the shrinkage.
Purely random variation
A gap that changes with a control variable is systematic.
Women's higher educational attainment
Higher education would predict higher, not lower, pay.
questions.x: When controlling for a variable shrinks a gap, that variable accounts for part of it. The pay gap narrowing after controlling for occupation means men and women are concentrated in differently paid jobs, called occupational segregation. Random variation is ruled out because a gap that changes systematically with a control is not noise, and part of the gap remains unexplained.

questions.q: Preventable differences in disease burden or health outcomes between socially defined groups are called:
o: Healthcare rationing
Rationing is the deliberate allocation of limited care.
The epidemiological transition
That is a shift from infectious to chronic disease.
Morbidity rates
Morbidity is illness frequency, not group differences.
Health disparities
Correct: avoidable differences in health between groups.
questions.x: Health disparities are preventable differences in disease burden, injury, or outcomes between socially defined groups, such as those based on race, income, or gender. Morbidity rates are tempting because they measure illness, but a rate by itself is just frequency in a population; a disparity is the avoidable gap between groups.

questions.q: Which example describes a healthcare disparity rather than a broader health disparity?
o: Higher infant mortality among low-income families
That is a difference in health outcomes.
Rural patients waiting longer than urban patients for specialist care
Correct: a difference in access to medical care itself.
Higher obesity rates in neighborhoods with limited healthy food
That is a difference in a health outcome.
Shorter average life expectancy among men than women
That is a difference in a health outcome.
questions.note: Health disparity = outcomes; healthcare disparity = access or quality of care.
questions.x: A health disparity is a difference in health outcomes between groups, while a healthcare disparity is a difference in access to or quality of medical care. Longer waits for specialists among rural patients reflect unequal access to care itself. Infant mortality and obesity differences are tempting, but they are outcome measures, so they are health disparities.

questions.q: Sociologists note that SES stays linked to mortality even as the leading causes of death change, because money, knowledge, and connections help people avoid whatever risks are current. This idea is:
o: The health selection hypothesis
That says illness causes low SES.
The culture of poverty thesis
That blames poverty on the values of the poor.
Fundamental cause theory
Correct: SES is a fundamental cause acting through flexible resources.
The demographic transition model
That describes changes in birth and death rates with development.
questions.x: Fundamental cause theory, from Link and Phelan, holds that SES persists as a cause of mortality because money, knowledge, power, and connections are flexible resources that let advantaged people avoid whatever risks dominate at a given time. The health selection hypothesis is tempting, but it reverses causation, saying illness causes low SES.

questions.q: Chronic stress from repeated experiences of discrimination is proposed to accelerate biological aging and early health decline in Black Americans. This is the:
o: Weathering hypothesis
Correct: cumulative social adversity wears down health early.
Healthy immigrant effect
That concerns immigrants arriving healthier than natives.
Social drift hypothesis
That says illness causes downward mobility.
Hispanic paradox
That concerns Hispanic Americans' favorable mortality.
questions.x: The weathering hypothesis, from Arline Geronimus, proposes that cumulative stress from racism and social adversity causes early health deterioration and accelerated biological aging in Black Americans. Social drift is tempting because it links health and social position, but it says illness causes downward mobility, not that social stress erodes health.

questions.q: Researchers find that low-SES adults score higher on an index combining cortisol, blood pressure, and inflammatory markers. This index most directly measures:
o: Social capital
Social capital is network resources, not physiology.
Relative poverty
Relative poverty is measured by income compared with others.
Cultural capital
Cultural capital is knowledge and tastes.
Allostatic load
Correct: cumulative physiological wear from chronic stress.
questions.x: Allostatic load is the cumulative wear on the body from chronic stress, measured by combining markers such as cortisol, blood pressure, and inflammation. Higher allostatic load in low-SES groups is one pathway linking social disadvantage to disease. Relative poverty is tempting because SES is involved, but it is an income-based measure, not a physiological one.

questions.q: Recent immigrants often arrive healthier than native-born residents of similar SES, but their health declines with longer residence. The initial advantage is called the:
o: Morbidity-mortality paradox
That describes women's higher illness but lower mortality.
Healthy immigrant effect
Correct: immigrants are initially healthier, partly due to selection.
Social gradient in health
The gradient links health to SES rank.
Inverse care law
That concerns care availability varying inversely with need.
questions.x: The healthy immigrant effect is the finding that recent immigrants are often healthier than native-born people of similar SES, partly because healthier people are more likely to migrate, with the advantage fading over time through acculturation and stress. The morbidity-mortality paradox is tempting as another health paradox, but it describes gender differences.

questions.q: In the U.S., infant mortality among Black infants is about twice that of white infants, and the gap persists even among college-educated mothers. This suggests that:
o: Maternal education fully explains the gap
The gap remains among college-educated mothers.
The gap results solely from genetic differences
Race is a social category; no evidence points to genetics alone.
The disparity is not explained by maternal education alone
Correct: the gap persists when education is high.
College-educated Black mothers have the lowest infant mortality of any group
The gap persists, so their rate exceeds that of college-educated white mothers.
questions.x: If a racial gap in infant mortality persists among college-educated mothers, maternal education cannot fully explain it; other factors such as discrimination-related stress and differences in care likely contribute. Genetic explanations are tempting but unsupported, because race is a social category and the gap tracks social conditions rather than ancestry alone.

questions.q: Which of the following is a social determinant of health rather than a biological one?
o: Neighborhood safety
Correct: a feature of the social and built environment.
Genotype
Genotype is biological.
Age
Age is a biological factor.
Sex chromosomes
Sex chromosomes are biological.
questions.x: Social determinants of health are features of the social, economic, and physical environment, such as neighborhood safety, income, and housing, that shape health. Genotype, age, and sex chromosomes are biological determinants rooted in the body. Age is tempting because it has social meaning, but as a determinant of health it is a biological factor.

questions.q: In the U.S., Medicaid primarily provides health coverage for:
o: All adults aged 65 and older
That describes Medicare.
Military veterans
Veterans are covered through the VA system.
Federal employees
They have a separate employer-based program.
Low-income individuals and families
Correct: Medicaid is means-tested public insurance.
questions.note: Medicare = age 65+; Medicaid = low income.
questions.x: Medicaid is a means-tested program jointly funded by federal and state governments that covers low-income people. Medicare is the federal program for people 65 and older and some people with disabilities. Confusing the two is the classic trap; remember Medicare is for the elderly, Medicaid is for those with low income.

questions.q: A state expands public health insurance. Researchers compare health outcomes before and after the expansion with those in a similar neighboring state that did not expand. This design is best described as a:
o: Randomized controlled trial
No one was randomly assigned.
Natural (quasi-) experiment
Correct: a policy change creates comparison groups without randomization.
Case study
A case study examines one case in depth without this comparison.
Cross-sectional survey
Data are compared across time, not at a single point.
questions.x: A natural or quasi-experiment uses a real-world event, such as a policy change, to create comparison groups without random assignment. Comparing before and after in an expanding state against a similar non-expanding state is this design. It is not a randomized controlled trial because no one was randomly assigned, so unmeasured differences between states remain possible.

questions.q: A study finds that residents of racially segregated neighborhoods have higher rates of hypertension. Which unmeasured variable would most threaten the conclusion that segregation causes hypertension?
o: The total number of neighborhoods studied
This affects precision, not confounding.
Whether all blood pressures were measured in the morning
Measuring everyone the same way does not bias the comparison.
Residents' individual household income
Correct: income could drive both where people live and their blood pressure.
The sex of the interviewers, held constant across sites
A constant factor cannot confound the comparison.
questions.note: A confounder must relate to both the exposure and the outcome.
questions.x: A confounder is a third variable related to both the exposure and the outcome, creating an apparent causal link. Household income influences where people can live and also affects blood pressure through stress, diet, and care. Factors held constant across all groups, like interviewer sex or measurement timing, cannot confound a comparison because they do not differ between groups.

questions.q: Patients with limited English proficiency who receive professional interpreters experience fewer medical errors. This finding highlights which source of healthcare disparities?
o: Language barriers in patient-provider communication
Correct: interpretation improves communication and safety.
Genetic differences among patient groups
Interpreters do not change genetics.
Residential segregation
The finding concerns communication, not where patients live.
Status inconsistency
That is mismatched ranks across stratification dimensions.
questions.x: Language barriers between patients and providers are a major source of healthcare disparities, causing misunderstandings, medication errors, and poorer outcomes. Professional interpreters reduce these errors by improving communication. Genetic differences are ruled out because providing an interpreter changes only communication, so the improvement must come from that channel.

questions.q: Physicians shown identical case vignettes that differed only by patient race recommended cardiac catheterization less often for Black patients. This most directly demonstrates:
o: Differences in patient treatment preferences
The patients were fictional and expressed no preferences.
Unequal insurance coverage
Insurance was identical across vignettes.
Genetic differences in heart disease
The clinical details were identical.
Provider bias affecting treatment decisions
Correct: only race varied, and recommendations changed.
questions.x: In an audit or vignette study, everything is held identical except one variable; any systematic change in decisions can then be attributed to that variable. Since only patient race varied, lower catheterization recommendations for Black patients point to provider bias. Patient preferences are ruled out because the patients were hypothetical and expressed none.

questions.q: In a study, physicians receive identical clinical vignettes that differ only in the patient's stated race. Why does this design support a causal claim about race's effect on recommendations?
o: It uses a large national sample of real patients
The vignettes are hypothetical, not real patients.
Patient race is varied while all clinical details are held constant
Correct: manipulating one variable isolates its effect.
It measures actual long-term patient outcomes
It measures recommendations, not outcomes.
Physicians report their own biases directly
Self-report is not what supports causal inference here.
questions.x: Causal inference requires manipulating one variable while holding everything else constant, which isolates that variable's effect. Varying only stated race across otherwise identical vignettes does this. A large sample of real patients is tempting, but size alone cannot remove confounding; it is control over the other variables that supports a causal conclusion.

questions.q: Historically, many clinical trials enrolled mostly men, leaving drug dosing and side effects in women less studied. This has contributed to:
o: Class consciousness among patients
Class consciousness is a Marxist concept about workers.
Residential segregation
This is about research participation, not housing.
A gender-based healthcare disparity
Correct: women receive care based on evidence drawn mostly from men.
Upward social mobility
No movement between social positions is involved.
questions.x: Excluding or underrepresenting women in clinical trials means dosing and side-effect data come mainly from men, so women receive care based on less applicable evidence. This produces a gender-based healthcare disparity in the quality of care. Distractors such as residential segregation do not fit because the problem lies in research participation, not place.

questions.q: Adults who grew up poor but became affluent have better health than those who stayed poor, but worse health than those affluent throughout life. This pattern suggests that:
o: Health reflects cumulative SES exposure across the life course
Correct: both childhood and adult SES contribute.
Only childhood SES affects adult health
Upward movers would then match those who stayed poor.
Only current SES affects adult health
Upward movers would then match the always-affluent.
Upward mobility itself damages health
Upward movers were healthier than those who stayed poor.
questions.x: The life course perspective holds that health reflects cumulative exposure to advantage and disadvantage over a lifetime. Upward movers fall between the always-poor and the always-affluent, showing both childhood and adult SES matter. If only current SES mattered, upward movers would match the always-affluent; if only childhood SES mattered, they would match the always-poor.

questions.q: In the U.S., the median white household holds several times the wealth of the median Black household, a gap much larger than the income gap. What best explains why the wealth gap exceeds the income gap?
o: Differences in current hourly wages alone
Wage differences would produce a gap similar to the income gap.
Differences in average household size
Household size does not explain asset accumulation.
Historical exclusion from homeownership, compounded by inheritance across generations
Correct: wealth accumulates and is transmitted, so past barriers persist.
Differences in educational attainment alone
Education affects income more than accumulated wealth.
questions.x: Wealth accumulates over time and is passed between generations through inheritance and gifts, so past exclusion, such as redlining and denial of home loans, keeps compounding. Income reflects only current earnings. Differences in current wages are tempting but would produce a wealth gap similar to the income gap, not a much larger one.

questions.q: Max Weber defined the ability to achieve one's goals despite resistance from others as:
o: Prestige
Prestige is social honor or esteem.
Power
Correct: Weber's definition of power.
Status
Status is social standing or honor, not imposing one's will.
Privilege
Privilege is unearned advantage from group membership.
questions.x: Weber defined power as the ability to realize one's will even against the resistance of others, and he treated it as a separate dimension of stratification from class and status. Status or prestige is tempting because high-status people often have power, but status refers to social honor and esteem, not the ability to impose one's will.

questions.q: Children of college graduates are more likely to finish college than other children, even when comparing children with equal test scores and equal family income. This persistence most likely reflects transmission of:
o: Economic capital
Family income was held equal.
Absolute poverty
No deprivation of basic needs is described.
Horizontal mobility
Horizontal mobility is lateral movement, not inherited advantage.
Cultural capital
Correct: parents' educational know-how passes to children beyond money.
questions.x: When income and test scores are equal and the advantage persists, money and measured ability cannot explain it. Parents who attended college pass on cultural capital: knowledge about applications, expectations, and how to navigate institutions. Economic capital is tempting because it often accompanies education, but family income was held equal.

questions.q: In world-systems theory, nations that mainly supply raw materials and low-wage labor to wealthy industrialized nations are classified as:
o: Periphery nations
Correct: the periphery is exploited for resources and cheap labor.
Core nations
Core nations are wealthy and industrialized.
Semi-periphery nations
The semi-periphery is intermediate, partly industrialized.
Postindustrial nations
These have service-based economies, typically in the core.
questions.x: Wallerstein's world-systems theory divides nations into core (wealthy, industrialized, capital-intensive), semi-periphery (intermediate, partly industrialized), and periphery (supplying raw materials and cheap labor to the core). The semi-periphery is tempting as a middle answer, but the stem describes the role of the exploited periphery.

questions.q: A country's Gini coefficient rises from 0.30 to 0.45. This indicates:
o: Lower income inequality
A higher Gini means more inequality.
Greater income inequality
Correct: the Gini runs from 0 (equality) to 1 (maximal inequality).
Necessarily higher absolute poverty
Inequality can rise while absolute poverty falls.
An increase in average income
The Gini measures distribution, not average level.
questions.x: The Gini coefficient measures income distribution, from 0 (everyone has equal income) to 1 (one person has everything), so a rise from 0.30 to 0.45 means greater inequality. It says nothing about average income or absolute poverty: inequality can rise while everyone's income grows, so higher absolute poverty does not necessarily follow.

questions.q: Over 20 years, a country's GDP doubles and the share of people below a fixed subsistence income falls, while the gap between rich and poor widens. Which statement is correct?
o: Both absolute and relative poverty decreased
A widening gap means relative poverty did not necessarily fall.
Absolute poverty rose while relative poverty fell
Fewer people fall below the fixed line, so absolute poverty fell.
Absolute poverty fell while relative poverty may have risen
Correct: fixed-line poverty dropped, but the distance from typical living standards grew.
Neither form of poverty changed
Fewer people fall below the fixed line, so absolute poverty did change.
questions.x: Absolute poverty is measured against a fixed subsistence line, so fewer people below that line means absolute poverty fell. Relative poverty is measured against the society's typical living standard, so a widening gap between rich and poor means relative poverty may have increased. Saying both fell is tempting because the economy grew, but growth does not shrink relative distance.

questions.q: The trend in which women, especially single mothers, make up a growing share of the poor is called:
o: The glass ceiling
That is a barrier to top positions.
The second shift
That is unpaid domestic work after paid work.
Gender socialization
That is learning gender roles.
The feminization of poverty
Correct: poverty increasingly concentrated among women.
questions.x: The feminization of poverty is the trend of women, especially single mothers and their children, making up a growing share of the poor, driven by wage gaps, caregiving burdens, and single-earner households. The glass ceiling is tempting because it is also a gender inequality concept, but it concerns barriers to top positions, not poverty.
