questions.q: A metropolitan measure shows that 70% of Black residents would need to move to different neighborhoods for Black and white residents to be evenly distributed. This statistic is the:
o: Gini coefficient
The Gini measures income inequality.
Index of dissimilarity
Correct: the share of a group that would need to move to achieve evenness.
Poverty threshold
That is an income cutoff for poverty.
Social distance scale
That measures willingness to interact with other groups.
questions.x: The index of dissimilarity measures residential segregation as the percentage of one group that would need to move to make each neighborhood's composition match the metropolitan area's. A value of 70% indicates high segregation. The Gini coefficient is tempting because both range from even to uneven distribution, but the Gini measures income inequality.

questions.q: The mid-20th-century movement of white middle-class families from cities to suburbs, often in response to racial integration, is termed:
o: White flight
Correct: white out-migration that deepened urban segregation.
Gentrification
Gentrification is affluent movement into cities, the reverse direction.
Urban renewal
Urban renewal is government redevelopment of city areas.
Chain migration
Chain migration is migrants following kin to a destination.
questions.x: White flight refers to the mid-20th-century movement of white middle-class families from cities to suburbs, often as neighborhoods and schools racially integrated, which deepened segregation and shrank the urban tax base. Gentrification is tempting because it concerns urban demographic change, but it describes affluent movement into cities, the reverse direction.

questions.q: Many U.S. public schools are funded largely by local property taxes. As a result, residential segregation by income tends to:
o: Equalize school resources across districts
Wealthier districts raise more revenue, so resources diverge.
Have no effect on school quality
Funding differences affect resources and quality.
Reinforce educational inequality across neighborhoods
Correct: richer areas fund better schools, sustaining advantage.
Increase funding in low-income districts
Low property values yield less tax revenue.
questions.x: When school budgets depend on local property taxes, wealthier areas with high property values raise more revenue for their schools than poorer areas. Combined with residential segregation by income, this reinforces educational inequality and passes advantage to the next generation. Low-income districts do not gain funding because lower property values yield less tax revenue.

questions.q: Neighborhoods with high levels of mutual trust and civic participation have lower mortality, even after adjusting for residents' income. This supports the role of:
o: Community social capital as a determinant of health
Correct: networks and trust benefit health beyond income.
Objectified cultural capital
That refers to cultural goods, not trust or participation.
Absolute poverty
Income was adjusted for, and trust is not poverty.
Health selection
Health selection says illness lowers SES.
questions.x: Community social capital includes trust, mutual support, and civic participation, which can improve health by spreading information, enforcing healthy norms, and providing aid. Because the mortality difference remains after adjusting for income, it is not just poverty. Health selection is ruled out because it describes illness lowering SES, not community ties affecting health.

questions.q: Weber's term for the opportunities a person has to improve his or her quality of life, which depend on class position, is:
o: Habitus
Habitus is Bourdieu's term for ingrained dispositions.
Social capital
Social capital is network resources.
Status
Status is social honor or prestige.
Life chances
Correct: class shapes access to education, health, and income.
questions.x: Weber's life chances are the opportunities a person has to improve their quality of life, such as access to education, health care, and income, which depend largely on class position. Status is tempting because it is also a Weberian term, but status refers to social honor and prestige rather than material opportunities.

questions.q: A researcher reports that the health penalty of being low-income is larger for women than for men. Statistically, this is best described as:
o: A main effect of gender only
The income effect itself differs by gender.
An interaction between income and gender
Correct: the effect of income depends on gender.
A confounding variable
Nothing is distorting the income-health link here.
Reverse causation
No causal direction is in question.
questions.x: An interaction effect occurs when the effect of one variable depends on the level of another. A health penalty of low income that is larger for women than for men means the income effect depends on gender. A main effect of gender is tempting, but it would describe an overall gender difference regardless of income, not a change in the income effect.

questions.q: The observation that the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the needs of the population served is known as the:
o: Social gradient in health
The gradient links health outcomes to SES rank.
Hispanic paradox
That concerns Hispanic Americans' favorable mortality.
Inverse care law
Correct: those who need care most often get the least.
Fundamental cause theory
That links SES to health through flexible resources.
questions.x: The inverse care law, described by Julian Tudor Hart, states that the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need of the population served, so the sickest communities often have the least access. The social gradient is tempting because it also links disadvantage and health, but it describes outcomes rather than care availability.

questions.q: How does social exclusion differ from poverty as it is usually measured?
o: Social exclusion includes being shut out of social, political, and civic participation, not just low income
Correct: exclusion is multidimensional.
Social exclusion applies only in low-income countries
It is used widely in wealthy nations.
Social exclusion is measured by a fixed income cutoff
That describes absolute poverty measures.
Social exclusion refers only to racial segregation
It covers many forms of marginalization.
questions.x: Poverty is usually measured by income alone, while social exclusion is multidimensional: it includes being shut out of social, political, economic, and civic participation. Someone could be excluded without being income-poor. Measuring by a fixed income cutoff is tempting but describes absolute poverty measures, not the broader concept of exclusion.

questions.q: Research shows the richest 1% of American men live about 15 years longer than the poorest 1%. This is an example of:
o: A healthcare rationing policy
No deliberate allocation of care is described.
A socioeconomic health disparity
Correct: health outcomes differ by income.
The Hispanic paradox
That concerns ethnicity, not income.
A gender health disparity
Only men are being compared.
questions.x: A socioeconomic health disparity is a difference in health outcomes between groups defined by income, wealth, or other SES measures. A roughly 15-year life expectancy gap between the richest and poorest men shows health following the income ladder. A gender disparity is ruled out because only men are being compared, so the difference is by income.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that believing success depends only on hard work leads people to blame the poor for their poverty, which legitimizes inequality. This argument treats meritocratic belief as:
o: A functional source of social solidarity
That is a functionalist framing, not this critique.
Evidence of high actual mobility
Beliefs about mobility are not measures of mobility.
An ideology that legitimizes existing inequality
Correct: a conflict view of meritocracy as justification.
A form of institutionalized cultural capital
Institutionalized capital is credentials, not beliefs.
questions.x: From a conflict perspective, ideology consists of beliefs that legitimize the existing distribution of power and resources. Belief that success depends only on effort leads people to blame the poor and accept inequality as deserved. The functionalist framing is tempting, but it would treat shared beliefs as promoting cohesion rather than as justifying domination.

questions.q: What is the absolute threshold of a sensory system?
o: The smallest change in intensity that can be noticed
That defines the difference threshold (JND), not the absolute threshold.
The intensity at which a stimulus becomes painful
That is the pain threshold, a separate concept.
The minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time
Correct: absolute threshold is defined statistically as detection on half of trials.
The stimulus intensity detected on 100% of trials
Thresholds are set at 50% because detection varies trial to trial.
questions.note: Absolute threshold = 50% detection of a stimulus vs. no stimulus.
questions.x: Detection is probabilistic: near threshold, the same faint stimulus is noticed on some trials and missed on others because neural noise fluctuates. Psychophysicists therefore define the absolute threshold as the intensity detected on 50% of trials. Do not confuse it with the difference threshold (JND), which is the smallest detectable change between two stimuli rather than the minimum detectable stimulus.

questions.q: A listener can just tell apart tones of 400 Hz and 408 Hz. By Weber's law, which frequency difference should be just noticeable at 1600 Hz?
o: 32 Hz
Correct: the Weber fraction is 8/400 = 0.02, and 0.02 × 1600 = 32 Hz.
8 Hz
Assumes the JND is a constant amount rather than a constant proportion.
16 Hz
Doubles rather than quadruples the JND when the base quadruples.
64 Hz
Overshoots: 0.02 × 1600 is 32, not 64.
questions.note: Weber's law: ΔI/I = k, so the JND scales with the base stimulus.
questions.x: Weber's law says the JND is a fixed fraction of the baseline: ΔI/I = k. Here k = 8/400 = 0.02, so at 1600 Hz the JND is 0.02 × 1600 = 32 Hz. The tempting answer of 8 Hz treats the JND as a fixed absolute amount, which is exactly what Weber's law rejects.

questions.q: Weber's law predicts that the just-noticeable difference for a stimulus:
o: Is a constant absolute amount regardless of intensity
That ignores the proportional relationship central to Weber's law.
Decreases as the original stimulus becomes stronger
The JND rises, not falls, with stronger baselines.
Equals the absolute threshold for that sense
The JND concerns change detection, not minimal detection.
Is a constant proportion of the original stimulus intensity
Correct: ΔI/I = k, so the JND grows in proportion to the baseline.
questions.x: Weber's law states ΔI/I = k: the change needed to notice a difference grows in proportion to the starting intensity. Adding 1 candle to a room with 10 is noticeable, but adding 1 to a room with 100 is not. The JND therefore increases, not decreases, with stronger baselines, and it is unrelated to the absolute threshold, which concerns detecting a stimulus at all.

questions.q: Weight discrimination has a Weber fraction of about 0.02, and brightness about 0.08. What does this imply?
o: Brightness is discriminated more precisely than weight
A larger fraction means a bigger relative change is needed, so it is less precise.
People detect proportionally smaller changes in weight than in brightness
Correct: a smaller Weber fraction means finer relative discrimination.
Weight has a lower absolute threshold than brightness
Weber fractions describe difference thresholds, not absolute thresholds.
Brightness adapts more slowly than weight
Weber fractions say nothing about adaptation rate.
questions.note: Smaller Weber fraction = more sensitive to relative change.
questions.x: A Weber fraction is the proportional change needed to notice a difference. A fraction of 0.02 for weight means a 2% change is detectable, while brightness needs about 8%, so weight discrimination is relatively finer. The trap is reading a bigger number as better; a larger Weber fraction means poorer relative sensitivity, and it says nothing about absolute thresholds.

questions.q: In signal detection theory, a 'hit' occurs when:
o: No signal is present and the observer reports none
That is a correct rejection.
A signal is present and the observer reports it
Correct: hits are correct detections of a present signal.
A signal is present and the observer misses it
That is a miss.
No signal is present but the observer reports one
That is a false alarm.
questions.x: Signal detection theory crosses two facts (signal present or absent) with two responses (yes or no), giving four outcomes. Signal present + yes = hit; present + no = miss; absent + yes = false alarm; absent + no = correct rejection. Keeping this 2×2 grid in mind prevents mixing up hits with false alarms, which are both 'yes' responses.

questions.q: A radiologist is told that missing a tumor will lead to a lawsuit, so she flags more ambiguous scans. In signal detection terms, what changed?
o: Her sensitivity (d′) increased
Sensitivity reflects perceptual discriminability, which incentives do not improve.
Her absolute threshold for light decreased
No change in sensory detection of light occurred.
Her criterion became more conservative
A conservative criterion would reduce, not increase, positive reports.
Her response criterion became more liberal
Correct: motivation shifts the decision criterion, increasing hits and false alarms.
questions.note: Payoffs move the criterion (β); stimulus clarity and skill move d′.
questions.x: Signal detection theory separates sensitivity (d′, how well signal is distinguished from noise) from the response criterion (how much evidence is needed to say 'yes'). Payoffs and consequences shift the criterion: penalizing misses makes the observer more liberal, raising both hits and false alarms. Her actual ability to see tumors (d′) has not changed, which rules out a sensitivity explanation.

questions.q: Two observers have identical hit rates of 80%, but observer X has a 10% false-alarm rate and observer Y has a 40% false-alarm rate. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: X has greater sensitivity (d′) than Y
Correct: same hits with fewer false alarms means better signal–noise discrimination.
Y has greater sensitivity than X
More false alarms at the same hit rate indicates poorer discrimination.
X and Y have equal sensitivity because hit rates match
Sensitivity depends on both hits and false alarms, not hits alone.
X uses a more liberal criterion than Y
X makes fewer false alarms, which suggests a stricter, not looser, criterion.
questions.note: Always compare hits against false alarms; hits alone are meaningless.
questions.x: Sensitivity (d′) reflects the separation between hit rate and false-alarm rate. With equal 80% hit rates, X achieves them with only 10% false alarms, while Y must say 'yes' to 40% of noise trials, so X discriminates signal from noise better. Hit rate alone cannot show sensitivity, because anyone can raise hits by simply saying 'yes' more often.

questions.q: On a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, an observer performing at chance would produce:
o: A curve bowed sharply toward the upper-left corner
That shape indicates high sensitivity.
A horizontal line at a 100% hit rate
That would require perfect detection regardless of criterion.
A diagonal line where hit rate equals false-alarm rate
Correct: with no discrimination, saying 'yes' more raises hits and false alarms equally.
A single point at the origin
Chance performance spans all criteria, not a single point.
questions.note: The farther the ROC bows from the diagonal, the higher d′.
questions.x: An ROC curve plots hit rate against false-alarm rate as the criterion shifts. If an observer cannot tell signal from noise, any increase in 'yes' responses raises hits and false alarms equally, tracing the diagonal. The more the curve bows toward the upper-left corner, the greater the sensitivity, so a strongly bowed curve indicates good discrimination, not chance.

questions.q: Researchers add more background static to an auditory detection task while keeping payoffs constant. What is the most likely effect?
o: The response criterion becomes more liberal
Payoffs, not noise level, mainly drive criterion shifts.
Hit rate increases while false alarms decrease
That pattern reflects improved, not worsened, discrimination.
The Weber fraction for loudness changes
Weber fractions are properties of the sense, not of this task's noise.
Sensitivity (d′) decreases
Correct: more noise overlaps the signal distribution, reducing discriminability.
questions.x: Sensitivity (d′) depends on how far apart the noise and signal-plus-noise distributions are. Adding background static increases noise and makes the distributions overlap more, so discriminability drops. Because payoffs were held constant, there is no reason to expect a criterion shift; the change is in sensitivity, not bias.

questions.q: Sensory adaptation refers to:
o: A decrease in attention to a stimulus judged unimportant
That is habituation, a learning/attention process rather than receptor change.
An increase in sensitivity after repeated exposure
That describes sensitization.
A decrease in receptor responsiveness to a constant stimulus
Correct: receptors fire less with sustained, unchanging input.
Conversion of a stimulus into neural signals
That is transduction.
questions.note: Adaptation = receptor level; habituation = behavioral/central level.
questions.x: Sensory adaptation is a decrease in receptor responsiveness when a stimulus stays constant, which frees the nervous system to signal change. It happens at the receptor or early neural level. Habituation looks similar but is a learned, central decrease in behavioral response to a repeated, unimportant stimulus, so it is not the best definition here.

questions.q: A swimmer finds the pool water cold at first but comfortable after a few minutes, even though the temperature is unchanged. This best illustrates:
o: Signal detection with a liberal criterion
No decision under uncertainty is involved here.
Sensory adaptation of thermoreceptors
Correct: thermoreceptor firing declines with a constant temperature.
Weber's law for temperature
Weber's law concerns detecting changes, not reduced response to a constant one.
Top-down perceptual processing
The change arises in the receptors, not from expectations.
questions.x: Thermoreceptors fire strongly to a change in temperature and then reduce firing when the temperature stays constant. The water has not warmed; the receptors adapted, so the sensation of cold fades. Weber's law is a tempting distractor, but it describes how big a change must be to be noticed, not the fading response to an unchanging stimulus.

questions.q: Which receptor type is the best example of a rapidly adapting (phasic) mechanoreceptor?
o: Pacinian corpuscle
Correct: Pacinian corpuscles respond to onset and offset of pressure and vibration, then quiet.
Merkel disc
Merkel discs are slowly adapting and signal sustained pressure.
Ruffini ending
Ruffini endings are slowly adapting stretch receptors.
Nociceptor
Nociceptors adapt little, which keeps pain signaling.
questions.x: Mechanoreceptors differ in adaptation speed. Rapidly adapting (phasic) receptors like Pacinian corpuscles fire at stimulus onset and offset, making them ideal for vibration, while slowly adapting (tonic) receptors like Merkel discs and Ruffini endings keep firing to sustained pressure or stretch. Nociceptors adapt little, which keeps warning signals going.

questions.q: Transduction in sensory systems is best defined as:
o: Relay of sensory signals through the thalamus
That is part of sensory transmission, not transduction.
Interpretation of signals in association cortex
That is perception.
Conversion of physical energy into electrical signals by receptors
Correct: receptors turn light, sound, chemicals or pressure into receptor potentials.
Reduction in firing to a constant stimulus
That is adaptation.
questions.x: Transduction is the first step of sensation: a receptor converts a physical or chemical stimulus into a change in membrane potential (a receptor potential). Photoreceptors transduce light, hair cells transduce mechanical motion, and taste and olfactory cells transduce chemicals. Relaying signals through the thalamus or interpreting them in cortex happens later and is transmission and perception, not transduction.

questions.q: The doctrine of specific nerve energies explains why pressing on a closed eye produces a flash of light. Which statement captures this idea?
o: The sensation depends on which nerve is activated, not on the stimulus type
Correct: optic nerve activation is experienced as light regardless of cause.
Each receptor responds equally to all forms of energy
Receptors have an adequate stimulus they respond to best.
Pressure is converted into light inside the eye
No light is generated; the signal is neural.
The brain ignores mechanical input to the eye
The mechanical input does activate the visual pathway.
questions.note: Labeled lines: where a signal goes determines what it feels like.
questions.x: The doctrine of specific nerve energies (labeled lines) holds that the quality of a sensation depends on which pathway is activated, not on what activated it. Pressure on the eye mechanically stimulates retinal neurons, and because their signals travel the visual pathway, the brain interprets them as light. No light is actually produced, so the experience is neural in origin.

questions.q: Which sense does NOT have its primary pathway relayed through the thalamus before reaching cortex?
o: Gustation
Taste relays through the VPM nucleus of the thalamus.
Audition
Hearing relays through the medial geniculate nucleus.
Vision
Vision relays through the lateral geniculate nucleus.
Olfaction
Correct: olfactory bulb output reaches piriform cortex directly, bypassing the thalamus.
questions.note: Smell is the thalamic exception.
questions.x: Vision (LGN), hearing (MGN), taste (VPM) and body touch (VPL) all relay through thalamic nuclei before reaching cortex. Olfaction is the exception: olfactory bulb neurons project directly to piriform cortex and limbic areas such as the amygdala. This direct access is one reason smells are tightly linked to emotion and memory.

questions.q: In a psychophysics study, subjects detect a faint light on 20%, 50% and 85% of trials at intensities of 2, 4 and 6 units. When subjects are offered a bonus for every correct detection, detection at 4 units rises to 70%. The best interpretation is that:
o: The bonus increased retinal sensitivity to light
Payoffs do not alter photoreceptor physiology.
The bonus shifted the response criterion, so the measured threshold is not purely sensory
Correct: payoff-driven changes show threshold measures include decision bias.
The true absolute threshold is now 2 units
The 2-unit condition was not retested; and bias, not sensitivity, changed.
Weber's law does not apply to vision
The study does not test difference thresholds at all.
questions.note: Classical thresholds mix sensitivity and bias; SDT separates them.
questions.x: Classical threshold measurement assumes detection reflects only sensory ability, but an observer's willingness to say 'yes' also matters. Rewarding correct detections without penalizing false alarms makes people more liberal, so measured detection rises even though the retina is unchanged. Signal detection theory was developed to separate this decision bias from true sensitivity.

questions.q: Light first passes through which structure as it enters the eye?
o: Lens
The lens lies behind the cornea, aqueous humor and pupil.
Cornea
Correct: the cornea is the clear outer surface and provides most of the eye's refraction.
Pupil
Light reaches the pupil only after crossing the cornea and aqueous humor.
Vitreous humor
Vitreous humor fills the posterior chamber behind the lens.
questions.x: Light travels through the eye in this order: cornea, aqueous humor, pupil (an opening in the iris), lens, vitreous humor, and finally the retina. The cornea also does most of the eye's focusing, because the largest change in refractive index is at the air–cornea boundary. The lens provides the smaller, adjustable portion of focusing power.

questions.q: When a person shifts focus from a distant mountain to a book held close, what happens in the eye?
o: The ciliary muscle relaxes and the lens flattens
That is accommodation for distant objects.
The iris dilator contracts and the pupil widens
Near viewing is accompanied by pupil constriction, not dilation.
The cornea changes curvature to focus near objects
Corneal shape is fixed; the lens provides adjustable focusing.
The ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes rounder
Correct: contraction slackens the zonule fibers, letting the lens thicken for near focus.
questions.note: Near = ciliary contracts, lens rounds, pupil constricts.
questions.x: Accommodation for near vision works by contraction of the ciliary muscle, a ring that narrows when it contracts and so slackens the zonule fibers. Freed from tension, the elastic lens rounds up and increases its refractive power. The tempting reversal, ciliary relaxation with a flattened lens, is the configuration for distant viewing.

questions.q: Which part of the retina provides the sharpest visual acuity in bright light?
o: Fovea
Correct: the fovea is packed with cones and has minimal convergence.
Optic disc
The optic disc has no photoreceptors and creates the blind spot.
Peripheral retina
The periphery is rod-dominated with high convergence and low acuity.
Ciliary body
The ciliary body controls the lens and is not part of the neural retina.
questions.x: Acuity depends on receptor density and how many receptors share a ganglion cell. The fovea is packed with cones and has nearly one-to-one connections to ganglion cells, preserving fine detail in bright light. The peripheral retina is rod-dominated with heavy convergence, which helps in dim light but blurs detail.

questions.q: Why does each person have a blind spot in each eye?
o: The fovea contains only cones that fail in dim light
The fovea is not the blind spot; it gives the sharpest vision.
The lens cannot focus light onto the retinal periphery
The blind spot is a gap in receptors, not a focusing problem.
The optic nerve exits where there are no photoreceptors
Correct: the optic disc lacks rods and cones.
Blood vessels block all light reaching the macula
Vessels cast minor shadows but do not create the blind spot.
questions.x: The blind spot is the optic disc, where retinal ganglion cell axons gather and exit the eye as the optic nerve along with blood vessels. Because no rods or cones occupy this spot, light falling there cannot be detected. The brain normally fills in the gap, and the other eye covers the missing region, so we rarely notice it.

questions.q: Compared with cones, rods are:
o: Responsible for color vision
Color vision depends on three cone types.
Concentrated in the fovea
The fovea is cone-dominated; rods are peripheral.
Less numerous across the retina
Rods (~120 million) far outnumber cones (~6 million).
More sensitive to dim light but poorer at fine detail
Correct: high sensitivity and high convergence trade off against acuity.
questions.x: Rods contain rhodopsin, are extremely sensitive and dominate the peripheral retina, so they support night (scotopic) vision. Many rods converge onto each ganglion cell, trading acuity for sensitivity, and having one pigment they cannot signal color. Cones are fewer, concentrated in the fovea, and provide color and fine detail in bright light.

questions.q: Why does visual acuity from rods tend to be lower than from foveal cones?
o: Rods contain no photopigment
Rods contain rhodopsin.
Rods are located behind the choroid
Rods are in the retina, not behind the choroid.
Many rods converge onto each ganglion cell
Correct: convergence pools signals, boosting sensitivity but blurring spatial detail.
Rods respond only to long wavelengths
Rods are most sensitive near 500 nm, not to long wavelengths.
questions.note: Convergence: sensitivity up, acuity down.
questions.x: Convergence means many photoreceptors feed into one ganglion cell. Summing many rods lets weak light signals add up, increasing sensitivity, but the brain cannot tell which rod was stimulated, so spatial detail is lost. Foveal cones have nearly private lines to ganglion cells, which preserves detail; rods do contain photopigment, so absence of pigment is not the reason.

questions.q: In darkness, a rod photoreceptor is depolarized. Which event directly causes it to hyperpolarize when light arrives?
o: Opening of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Photoreceptors hyperpolarize, so Na⁺ influx does not increase.
Closure of cGMP-gated Na⁺ channels after cGMP is hydrolyzed
Correct: activated transducin stimulates phosphodiesterase, cGMP falls and the dark current stops.
Increased glutamate release onto bipolar cells
Glutamate release falls when rods hyperpolarize.
Conversion of all-trans-retinal to 11-cis-retinal
Light does the reverse: 11-cis becomes all-trans.
questions.note: Light → less cGMP → channels close → hyperpolarize → less glutamate.
questions.x: In darkness, high cGMP keeps cation channels open, producing a depolarizing 'dark current' and steady glutamate release. Light activates rhodopsin, which activates transducin, which activates phosphodiesterase; PDE breaks down cGMP, the channels close and the rod hyperpolarizes. Photoreceptors are unusual in that light causes hyperpolarization and reduced, not increased, transmitter release.

questions.q: Absorption of a photon by rhodopsin directly causes:
o: Isomerization of 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal
Correct: this shape change activates opsin and starts the cascade.
Phosphorylation of cGMP
cGMP is hydrolyzed by phosphodiesterase, not phosphorylated.
Release of glutamate from the rod
Light decreases glutamate release.
Depolarization of the ganglion cell
Ganglion cell effects come later and depend on the bipolar cell type.
questions.x: Rhodopsin is opsin bound to 11-cis-retinal. Absorbing a photon isomerizes retinal to all-trans, changing opsin's shape and activating it; this is the only light-dependent step. Everything after, including transducin activation, cGMP hydrolysis by phosphodiesterase and reduced glutamate release, is a downstream cascade rather than the direct effect of the photon.

questions.q: Photoreceptors release less glutamate in light. How does an ON-center bipolar cell respond to light in its receptive field center?
o: It hyperpolarizes because glutamate release decreases
That describes OFF bipolar cells.
It fires action potentials directly to the thalamus
Bipolar cells use graded potentials and project to ganglion cells, not thalamus.
It depolarizes because glutamate had been inhibiting it
Correct: ON bipolar cells use mGluR6, so glutamate hyperpolarizes them and its removal excites them.
It is unaffected because only ganglion cells sense glutamate
Bipolar cells are the direct targets of photoreceptor glutamate.
questions.note: ON bipolars are inverted by glutamate (sign-inverting synapse).
questions.x: Photoreceptors release glutamate in the dark and less in light. ON bipolar cells express mGluR6, a metabotropic receptor whose activation closes cation channels, so glutamate hyperpolarizes them; when light reduces glutamate, they depolarize. OFF bipolar cells use ionotropic receptors, so they depolarize to glutamate and hyperpolarize in light, which is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: What is the correct order of cells in the direct retinal pathway?
o: Photoreceptor → bipolar cell → ganglion cell
Correct: signals flow from receptors to bipolar cells to ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve.
Ganglion cell → bipolar cell → photoreceptor
This reverses the direction of signal flow.
Photoreceptor → ganglion cell → bipolar cell
Bipolar cells are between receptors and ganglion cells.
Bipolar cell → photoreceptor → amacrine cell
Photoreceptors are the first cells to respond to light.
questions.x: The retina's direct (vertical) pathway runs photoreceptor → bipolar cell → ganglion cell, and ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve. Horizontal and amacrine cells act as lateral interneurons that modify signals. Light physically passes through the ganglion and bipolar layers to reach photoreceptors at the back, but signals flow in the opposite direction.

questions.q: Horizontal cells in the retina mainly contribute to:
o: Carrying signals from the retina to the thalamus
Ganglion cell axons do that.
Producing the photopigment rhodopsin
Rhodopsin is made by rods.
Controlling pupil diameter
Pupil size is controlled by iris muscles via autonomic nerves.
Lateral inhibition that sharpens contrast at edges
Correct: horizontal cells connect neighboring photoreceptors and create center–surround antagonism.
questions.x: Horizontal cells link neighboring photoreceptors and feed inhibitory signals back onto them. This lateral inhibition creates the antagonistic surround of bipolar and ganglion cell receptive fields, so edges and contrast are exaggerated. Signals to the thalamus are carried by ganglion cell axons, not horizontal cells.

questions.q: Which cells' axons form the optic nerve?
o: Bipolar cells
Bipolar cells stay within the retina and use graded potentials.
Retinal ganglion cells
Correct: ganglion cells are the retina's output neurons and fire action potentials.
Amacrine cells
Amacrine cells are retinal interneurons.
Cones
Cones are photoreceptors and do not leave the eye.
questions.x: Retinal ganglion cells are the retina's output neurons and the first in the pathway to fire action potentials; their axons bundle into the optic nerve. Photoreceptors and bipolar cells use graded potentials over short distances within the retina. Amacrine cells are interneurons, so they do not leave the eye.

questions.q: A patient has a lesion of the optic chiasm that destroys fibers crossing the midline. What visual field loss is expected?
o: Complete blindness in one eye
That results from an optic nerve lesion before the chiasm.
Loss of the temporal (outer) half of both visual fields
Correct: crossing fibers come from nasal retinas, which see temporal fields (bitemporal hemianopia).
Loss of the left visual field in both eyes
That is homonymous hemianopia from a right optic tract or cortex lesion.
Loss of the nasal half of both visual fields
Nasal fields are seen by temporal retinas, whose fibers do not cross.
questions.note: Nasal retina fibers cross; they see the temporal field.
questions.x: At the optic chiasm, only fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross. Because the lens inverts images, the nasal retina receives light from the temporal (outer) visual field. Destroying the crossing fibers therefore removes both temporal fields, a bitemporal hemianopia often caused by pituitary tumors. Nasal-field loss would require damage to uncrossed temporal-retina fibers.

questions.q: Damage to the left optic tract would cause loss of vision in:
o: The entire left eye
Single-eye loss implies an optic nerve lesion.
The left visual field of both eyes
The left hemisphere processes the right visual field.
The temporal fields of both eyes
That results from a chiasm lesion.
The right visual field of both eyes
Correct: the left tract carries left temporal and right nasal retina fibers, which view the right field.
questions.x: After the chiasm, each optic tract carries ipsilateral temporal-retina fibers and contralateral nasal-retina fibers, which together view the opposite visual field. The left tract therefore carries information about the right visual field from both eyes. Its damage causes right homonymous hemianopia, not loss of one whole eye, which requires a lesion before the chiasm.

questions.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays visual information to the primary visual cortex?
o: Lateral geniculate nucleus
Correct: the LGN receives optic tract input and projects to V1.
Medial geniculate nucleus
The MGN relays auditory information.
Ventral posterolateral nucleus
The VPL relays body somatosensation.
Suprachiasmatic nucleus
The SCN receives retinal input for circadian rhythms, not conscious vision.
questions.note: Lateral = Light, Medial = Music.
questions.x: Sensory signals except smell pass through specific thalamic nuclei. The lateral geniculate nucleus receives optic tract axons and projects via the optic radiations to primary visual cortex (V1). The medial geniculate nucleus is its auditory counterpart, which is the most tempting confusion; the mnemonic 'lateral = light, medial = music' helps.

questions.q: The primary visual cortex is located in which lobe?
o: Temporal
Temporal cortex holds primary auditory cortex and the 'what' stream.
Parietal
Parietal cortex holds somatosensory cortex and the 'where' stream.
Occipital
Correct: V1 lies along the calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe.
Frontal
Frontal cortex is involved in motor and executive function.
questions.x: Primary visual cortex (V1, striate cortex) lies in the occipital lobe along the calcarine sulcus. From V1, information flows into two streams: a ventral 'what' stream into the temporal lobe and a dorsal 'where/how' stream into the parietal lobe. These streams explain why temporal and parietal lobes handle vision too, but neither contains V1.

questions.q: Hubel and Wiesel found that certain cells in primary visual cortex fire maximally to a bar of light at a specific orientation. These cells are best described as:
o: Photoreceptors
Photoreceptors are in the retina and respond to light, not orientation.
Ganglion cells with center–surround fields
Ganglion cells have circular fields and are not orientation-tuned.
Place cells
Place cells are hippocampal neurons that encode location.
Feature detectors
Correct: neurons tuned to specific features like edges, orientation and movement.
questions.x: Hubel and Wiesel discovered that V1 neurons respond selectively to specific stimulus features such as bars at a particular orientation, which is why they are called feature detectors. This contrasts with retinal ganglion and LGN cells, whose circular center–surround fields respond to spots of light but not orientation. Feature detection builds complex perception from simple elements.

questions.q: A V1 neuron fires strongly to a vertical bar anywhere within a broad region and fires most when the bar moves rightward. This neuron is best classified as a:
o: Simple cell
Simple cells require the bar in a specific position within distinct ON/OFF subregions.
Rod bipolar cell
Bipolar cells are retinal and not orientation-tuned.
Complex cell
Correct: complex cells are orientation-selective, position-tolerant and often direction-selective.
Hair cell
Hair cells are auditory and vestibular receptors.
questions.x: V1 contains simple and complex cells. Simple cells respond to a bar of one orientation only in a specific location within ON and OFF subregions. Complex cells keep orientation selectivity but respond wherever the bar falls in a larger field, and many prefer one direction of motion. Position tolerance plus direction preference identifies a complex cell rather than a simple cell.

questions.q: Parallel processing in vision refers to:
o: Processing each feature one at a time in sequence
That is serial processing.
Simultaneous analysis of features such as color, motion and form by separate pathways
Correct: different attributes are processed at the same time by specialized streams.
Both eyes sending identical signals to one hemisphere
Each hemisphere receives input from both eyes about the opposite visual field.
Rods and cones taking turns depending on light level
That concerns photopic vs. scotopic vision, not parallel processing.
questions.x: Parallel processing means the visual system analyzes color, form, motion and depth simultaneously in separate pathways, such as magnocellular vs. parvocellular and dorsal vs. ventral streams. This is much faster than handling features one at a time. Serial processing, the tempting alternative, would handle each attribute in sequence.

questions.q: A patient after a stroke can identify objects by sight but cannot judge whether a car is moving toward or away from her; she sees the world as a series of still frames. Damage to which pathway is most likely?
o: The dorsal 'where/how' stream toward parietal cortex
Correct: motion analysis (e.g., area MT) is part of the dorsal stream.
The ventral 'what' stream toward temporal cortex
Ventral damage would impair object recognition, which is intact.
The parvocellular layers of the LGN
Parvocellular pathways carry color and fine detail, not motion.
The olfactory tract
Olfaction is unrelated to motion vision.
questions.note: Dorsal = where/how/motion; ventral = what/form/color.
questions.x: From V1, the dorsal stream runs to parietal cortex and processes motion and spatial location, with area MT/V5 central to motion perception. Damage there causes akinetopsia, in which motion is not perceived smoothly. The ventral stream to temporal cortex handles object identity, which explains why her object recognition is preserved.

questions.q: Parvocellular ganglion cells, compared with magnocellular cells, are specialized for:
o: Fast motion and low-contrast detection
That describes magnocellular cells.
Depth from vestibular cues
Vestibular cues are not processed by retinal ganglion cells.
Color and fine spatial detail
Correct: parvo cells have small receptive fields and color opponency.
Circadian light detection
That is the role of melanopsin-containing ganglion cells.
questions.note: Parvo = particular details and color; Magno = motion.
questions.x: Parvocellular ganglion cells have small receptive fields, color opponency and sustained responses, so they carry fine detail and color mainly to the ventral stream. Magnocellular cells have large receptive fields, fast transient responses and high contrast sensitivity, suiting motion and low-contrast detection. The mnemonic: parvo for particulars and color, magno for motion.

questions.q: A patient with damage to the fusiform face area of the temporal lobe can recognize a friend's voice but not her face. This deficit is called:
o: Prosopagnosia
Correct: prosopagnosia is a selective inability to recognize faces.
Akinetopsia
Akinetopsia is motion blindness.
Hemineglect
Hemineglect is inattention to one side of space, usually after parietal damage.
Anosmia
Anosmia is loss of smell.
questions.x: Prosopagnosia, or face blindness, results from damage to the fusiform face area in the ventral temporal lobe, part of the 'what' stream. Patients can see faces and recognize people by voice or gait but cannot identify them by face. Akinetopsia is the tempting distractor, but it is motion blindness from dorsal-stream damage.

questions.q: After staring at a red square for 60 seconds and then looking at a white wall, a person sees a green square. Which theory best explains this?
o: Trichromatic theory
Trichromatic theory explains color via three cone types but not complementary afterimages.
Place theory
Place theory concerns pitch perception along the basilar membrane.
Gate control theory
Gate control theory concerns pain modulation.
Opponent-process theory
Correct: fatiguing red channels lets the opposing green response dominate briefly.
questions.note: Afterimages = opponent process (red–green, blue–yellow, black–white).
questions.x: Opponent-process theory proposes that color is coded in paired channels (red vs. green, blue vs. yellow, black vs. white) beyond the cones. Staring at red fatigues the red side of the channel, so a neutral white surface produces a relative green signal and a green afterimage. Trichromatic theory explains color via three cone types but cannot account for complementary afterimages.

questions.q: The trichromatic (Young–Helmholtz) theory proposes that color vision depends on:
o: Opposing pairs of color channels in the retina and thalamus
That is opponent-process theory.
Three cone types maximally sensitive to short, medium and long wavelengths
Correct: color is coded by the relative activity of S, M and L cones.
Rods that respond differently to each wavelength
Rods have a single pigment and cannot distinguish wavelengths.
Different firing rates of a single cone type
One receptor type cannot disambiguate wavelength from intensity.
questions.x: The Young–Helmholtz theory states that three cone types, maximally sensitive to short, medium and long wavelengths, together code color by their relative activity. One receptor type alone could not separate wavelength from intensity, which is why rods give colorless vision. Opponent processing is a later stage that complements, rather than replaces, trichromacy.

questions.q: A man cannot distinguish red from green, and genetic testing shows a defect in his M-cone opsin. Why is this condition far more common in males?
o: The S-cone opsin gene is on the Y chromosome
The S opsin gene is autosomal (chromosome 7), and red–green defects involve M/L genes.
The M and L opsin genes are on the X chromosome
Correct: males have one X, so a single defective allele is expressed.
Testosterone damages cones in the fovea
Red–green color blindness is genetic, not hormonal.
Males have fewer rods than females
Rods do not mediate color vision.
questions.x: The genes for M and L cone opsins lie on the X chromosome, so red–green color deficiency is X-linked recessive. Males are hemizygous, with one X, so a single defective allele is expressed; females usually carry a normal second copy. The S-cone opsin gene is autosomal and its defects cause rarer blue–yellow problems, not red–green ones.

questions.q: Why is it difficult to see colors at night under very dim light?
o: Cones become more sensitive than rods in dim light
Cones are less sensitive and stop responding in dim light.
The pupil constricts and blocks color wavelengths
The pupil dilates in the dark, and it does not filter wavelengths.
The lens absorbs all visible light at night
The lens transmits visible light regardless of time of day.
Only rods are active, and they have a single photopigment
Correct: scotopic vision relies on rods, which cannot compare wavelengths.
questions.x: In very dim (scotopic) light, cones lack the sensitivity to respond and vision depends on rods. All rods use the same photopigment, rhodopsin, so the brain cannot compare responses across receptor types to extract wavelength. The result is grayscale night vision. Cones are less, not more, sensitive than rods.

questions.q: A person walks from sunlight into a dark theater; after about 25 minutes, vision is much better. What mainly accounts for the slow later phase of this improvement?
o: Regeneration of rhodopsin in rods
Correct: rods recover slowly as bleached rhodopsin is regenerated.
Rapid recovery of cone photopigments
Cones recover within minutes, accounting for the early phase only.
Increased glutamate release by ganglion cells
Ganglion cells release glutamate centrally but this does not explain dark adaptation.
Thickening of the lens
Lens shape relates to focus, not light sensitivity.
questions.note: Dark adaptation curve: cone plateau (~7 min), then rod break.
questions.x: Dark adaptation follows two phases. Cones recover quickly and plateau within about 7 to 10 minutes, then rods, which regenerate rhodopsin more slowly, take over and keep improving sensitivity for 20 to 30 minutes. The late, large gain in sensitivity is therefore due to rod rhodopsin regeneration, not cone recovery.

questions.q: A person who sees near objects clearly but distant objects as blurry most likely has:
o: Hyperopia, with images focused behind the retina
Hyperopia blurs near objects more than distant ones.
Presbyopia from a stiff lens
Presbyopia impairs near focus with age.
Myopia, with images focused in front of the retina
Correct: nearsightedness from a long eyeball or overly strong refraction.
Damage to the optic chiasm
A chiasm lesion causes field loss, not blur.
questions.x: In myopia, the eye is too long or refracts too strongly, so light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina, while near objects still focus properly. In hyperopia, focus falls behind the retina and near vision suffers more. Presbyopia is the age-related loss of near focus, so it would produce the opposite complaint.

questions.q: Which lens corrects myopia, and why?
o: A converging lens, which moves the focal point forward
Converging lenses correct hyperopia, where focus falls behind the retina.
A diverging lens, which increases the eye's overall power
Diverging lenses decrease, not increase, total refractive power.
A cylindrical lens, which fixes all refractive errors
Cylindrical lenses correct astigmatism specifically.
A diverging lens, which moves the focal point back onto the retina
Correct: myopic eyes over-converge light, so a concave lens spreads it out.
questions.x: A myopic eye has too much converging power for its length, so images of distant objects focus in front of the retina. A diverging (concave) lens spreads incoming rays slightly, reducing total power and pushing the focal point back onto the retina. Converging lenses add power and are used for hyperopia and presbyopia.

questions.q: Shining a light in a patient's left eye constricts the right pupil but not the left. Light in the right eye constricts the right pupil only. Where is the lesion most likely?
o: Left optic nerve (afferent limb)
Then light in the left eye would fail to constrict either pupil.
Left oculomotor nerve (efferent limb)
Correct: both eyes sense light, but the left pupil cannot constrict, implicating the left CN III output.
Right optic nerve
Then light in the right eye would fail to constrict either pupil.
Right oculomotor nerve
Then the right pupil would fail to constrict, but it constricts normally.
questions.note: Afferent = CN II (sensing); efferent = CN III (constricting).
questions.x: The pupillary light reflex has an afferent limb (optic nerve, CN II) and an efferent limb (oculomotor nerve, CN III), and each eye's input drives both pupils. Since light in either eye constricts the right pupil, both optic nerves work. The left pupil never constricts, so its own efferent pathway, the left CN III, is damaged. An afferent lesion would instead block both pupils when that eye is lit.

questions.q: Pupillary constriction in bright light is mediated by:
o: Parasympathetic fibers to the iris sphincter muscle
Correct: parasympathetic signals via CN III contract the circular sphincter.
Sympathetic fibers to the iris sphincter
Sympathetic fibers act on the dilator muscle to widen the pupil.
Contraction of the ciliary muscle alone
The ciliary muscle adjusts the lens, not pupil diameter.
Somatic motor neurons in the facial nerve
Pupil control is autonomic, not somatic, and does not use CN VII.
questions.x: Pupil size is set by two smooth muscles under autonomic control. Parasympathetic fibers traveling with CN III contract the circular sphincter pupillae, constricting the pupil in bright light or for near vision. Sympathetic fibers contract the radial dilator pupillae and widen the pupil. Associating sympathetic input with the sphincter is the classic trap.

questions.q: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells containing melanopsin project mainly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus. Their main function is to:
o: Detect fine edges for form vision
Form vision depends on cones, bipolar cells and parvocellular pathways.
Distinguish red from green
Color depends on cone opponency, not melanopsin.
Entrain circadian rhythms to the light–dark cycle
Correct: these cells signal ambient light levels to the body clock.
Detect rapid motion in the periphery
Motion relies on magnocellular pathways.
questions.x: Some retinal ganglion cells contain melanopsin and respond to light directly. They signal overall light levels rather than images and project mainly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, the master circadian clock. This lets daylight entrain sleep–wake rhythms, even in some people who are blind for form vision.

questions.q: Researchers record from a retinal ganglion cell with an ON-center, OFF-surround receptive field. Which stimulus produces the highest firing rate?
o: A small spot of light filling only the center
Correct: center excitation without surround inhibition maximizes firing.
Uniform light covering both center and surround
Surround inhibition cancels much of the center response.
A ring of light on the surround only
Light in the surround inhibits an ON-center cell.
Complete darkness over the whole field
Darkness gives only baseline firing.
questions.note: Center–surround cells signal contrast, not overall brightness.
questions.x: An ON-center, OFF-surround ganglion cell is excited by light in its center and inhibited by light in its surround. A spot filling only the center gives maximal excitation with no inhibition. Uniform light stimulates both regions, so the surround cancels much of the center response. This shows ganglion cells signal local contrast rather than absolute brightness.

questions.q: The pigmented layer behind the retina that absorbs stray light and nourishes photoreceptors is the:
o: Sclera
The sclera is the tough white outer coat.
Iris
The iris controls the pupil and is in front of the lens.
Vitreous humor
The vitreous is a clear gel that transmits light.
Choroid and retinal pigment epithelium
Correct: these absorb scattered light and support photoreceptors.
questions.x: The retinal pigment epithelium, backed by the vascular choroid, lies behind the photoreceptors. Its melanin absorbs light that passes through the retina, reducing scatter, and it recycles retinal for photopigment regeneration and supports photoreceptors metabolically. The sclera is the outer white coat, and the vitreous is clear gel that transmits rather than absorbs light.

questions.q: Glaucoma damages the optic nerve and is commonly associated with:
o: Clouding of the lens
That describes cataracts.
Elevated intraocular pressure from impaired aqueous humor drainage
Correct: poor outflow through the canal of Schlemm raises pressure.
Loss of cones in the fovea
Central cone loss characterizes macular degeneration.
Excess rhodopsin production
Rhodopsin levels are not the cause of glaucoma.
questions.x: Aqueous humor is produced by the ciliary body and drains through the trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm. If drainage is impaired, intraocular pressure rises and compresses the optic nerve head, killing ganglion cell axons and causing gradual peripheral field loss. Clouding of the lens is a cataract, a different disorder.

questions.q: Which structure transmits sound vibrations from the eardrum to the oval window?
o: The cochlea
The cochlea receives vibrations at the oval window.
The ossicles: malleus, incus and stapes
Correct: the ossicle chain links the tympanic membrane to the oval window.
The Eustachian tube
The Eustachian tube equalizes middle ear pressure.
The semicircular canals
The semicircular canals detect head rotation.
questions.x: Sound enters the ear canal and vibrates the tympanic membrane. The three ossicles, malleus, incus and stapes, carry this vibration across the air-filled middle ear, and the stapes footplate pushes on the oval window of the cochlea. The Eustachian tube equalizes pressure but does not transmit sound vibrations.

questions.q: The middle ear amplifies pressure delivered to the oval window mainly because:
o: The cochlear fluid compresses easily
Fluid is nearly incompressible; that is why amplification is needed.
The Eustachian tube adds air pressure
The Eustachian tube equalizes pressure; it does not amplify sound.
Hair cells release extra glutamate
Hair cells are in the inner ear and act after mechanical transmission.
The tympanic membrane is much larger in area than the oval window
Correct: concentrating force on a smaller area raises pressure, with some ossicle lever gain.
questions.note: Pressure = force/area: big drum, small window.
questions.x: Sound must pass from air into cochlear fluid, which resists motion much more than air, so most energy would reflect without amplification. Since pressure equals force divided by area, collecting force over the large tympanic membrane and delivering it to the small oval window raises pressure many-fold; ossicle leverage adds a smaller gain. Fluid incompressibility is the reason amplification is needed, not its mechanism.

questions.q: Hair cells in the cochlea transduce sound when their stereocilia bend, opening channels that let in:
o: K⁺ from the endolymph, depolarizing the cell
Correct: endolymph is high in K⁺, so K⁺ influx depolarizes hair cells.
Na⁺ from the perilymph, hyperpolarizing the cell
Na⁺ influx would depolarize, and perilymph does not bathe the stereocilia.
Cl⁻ from the endolymph, depolarizing the cell
Cl⁻ influx typically hyperpolarizes, and K⁺ is the transduction ion.
Ca²⁺ only, causing hair cell contraction
Ca²⁺ entry helps neurotransmitter release but the main depolarizing current is K⁺.
questions.note: Unusual: K⁺ flows IN because endolymph is K⁺-rich.
questions.x: The stereocilia of cochlear hair cells sit in endolymph, which has an unusually high K⁺ concentration and positive potential. When stereocilia bend toward the tallest one, tip links open mechanically gated channels, and K⁺ flows in down its electrochemical gradient, depolarizing the cell. Elsewhere in the body K⁺ typically flows out, which makes this inward K⁺ current the key distinction.

questions.q: The receptor cells for hearing are located in the:
o: Utricle and saccule
Those otolith organs detect linear acceleration.
Tympanic membrane
The eardrum vibrates but contains no receptors for hearing.
Organ of Corti on the basilar membrane
Correct: inner and outer hair cells sit in the organ of Corti.
Auditory cortex
The cortex processes, not transduces, sound.
questions.x: Auditory transduction occurs in the organ of Corti, which rests on the basilar membrane in the cochlea. Its inner hair cells provide most afferent signals, and outer hair cells amplify motion. The tympanic membrane only vibrates, and the utricle and saccule contain hair cells that detect linear acceleration rather than sound.

questions.q: High-frequency sounds maximally vibrate which part of the basilar membrane?
o: The apex, where it is wide and flexible
The apex responds best to low frequencies.
The entire membrane equally
Place theory holds that frequencies map to specific locations.
The middle of the membrane only
High frequencies peak at the base, not the middle.
The base, near the oval window, where it is narrow and stiff
Correct: the stiff, narrow base resonates with high frequencies.
questions.note: Tonotopy: base = high, apex = low.
questions.x: The basilar membrane is narrow and stiff at the base near the oval window and wide and floppy at the apex. Stiff regions resonate with high frequencies, so high pitches peak at the base and low pitches travel to the apex. This tonotopic map is the basis of place theory. A uniform response across the membrane would make pitch coding by place impossible.

questions.q: A worker with years of exposure to loud machinery shows hearing loss mainly at high frequencies. Which explanation is best?
o: The ossicles have fused together
Ossicle fusion causes conductive loss across many frequencies.
The apical hair cells have been destroyed
Apical damage would affect low frequencies.
Hair cells near the cochlear base have been damaged
Correct: base hair cells code high frequencies and are vulnerable to noise.
The auditory nerve can no longer fire action potentials
Complete nerve failure would cause deafness at all frequencies.
questions.x: Because of tonotopy, hair cells at the cochlear base code high frequencies, and they bear the brunt of intense noise, making them most vulnerable to damage. Lost hair cells do not regenerate in mammals, so noise-induced hearing loss is permanent sensorineural loss, often starting near 4 kHz. Apical damage would affect low frequencies instead.

questions.q: Frequency theory (temporal coding) best explains the perception of:
o: Very high-pitched sounds above 10 kHz
Neurons cannot fire that fast; place coding dominates there.
Low-pitched sounds, as nerve firing rate matches the sound frequency
Correct: below a few hundred Hz, fibers can phase-lock to the waveform.
Loudness only
Loudness is coded mainly by number and rate of active fibers, not frequency theory.
Sound localization in the vertical plane
Vertical localization relies on the outer ear's filtering.
questions.x: Frequency theory proposes that pitch is coded by auditory nerve firing rate matching the sound's frequency. Because neurons have refractory periods, this works only for low frequencies, up to a few hundred hertz. Very high frequencies exceed any neuron's maximum firing rate and are coded by place on the basilar membrane, so frequency theory cannot explain them.

questions.q: The volley principle helps explain pitch perception for frequencies of roughly 1000–4000 Hz by proposing that:
o: Groups of neurons fire in staggered turns, so their combined output tracks the frequency
Correct: no single neuron fires that fast, but alternating groups together can.
Each neuron fires at 4000 Hz
Refractory periods prevent such rapid firing.
Only the cochlear apex vibrates at these frequencies
That contradicts place coding, where mid frequencies peak mid-membrane.
The ossicles vibrate at a fixed rate
Ossicle motion follows the incoming sound.
questions.x: No single neuron can fire 1000 to 4000 times per second because of its refractory period. The volley principle proposes that groups of fibers take turns firing on different cycles, so their combined output still marks each cycle of the wave. Higher frequencies rely mainly on place coding, so volleying bridges the gap between frequency and place theories.

questions.q: A patient has hearing loss in one ear. Placing a vibrating tuning fork on the forehead, she hears it louder in the affected ear. What type of hearing loss is most likely?
o: Sensorineural loss in the affected ear
Sensorineural loss makes sound louder in the healthy ear.
Damage to primary auditory cortex
Unilateral cortical damage rarely causes one-ear loss due to bilateral pathways.
Conductive loss in the affected ear
Correct: blocked air conduction reduces masking noise, so bone-conducted sound seems louder there.
Normal hearing in both ears
Normal hearing yields equal loudness in both ears.
questions.note: Weber test: lateralizes to the conductive-loss ear, away from the sensorineural-loss ear.
questions.x: In the Weber test, a tuning fork on the midline is heard through bone conduction. In conductive loss, the blocked ear receives less ambient noise that would normally mask the tone, so it sounds louder there. In sensorineural loss, the damaged cochlea or nerve responds poorly, so the tone lateralizes to the healthy ear instead.

questions.q: Cochlear implants bypass damaged hair cells by stimulating the auditory nerve directly. For an implant to convey different pitches, the electrodes should be arranged:
o: Along the length of the cochlea, with base electrodes for high frequencies
Correct: exploiting tonotopy lets location of stimulation signal pitch.
Together at the apex, varying only stimulus voltage
Voltage changes loudness; one location cannot code many pitches by place.
On the tympanic membrane
The eardrum is upstream of the damage and transduces nothing.
In the semicircular canals
Those detect rotation, not sound.
questions.x: The cochlea is tonotopically organized: high frequencies are coded at the base and low frequencies at the apex. Cochlear implants place an electrode array along the cochlea and stimulate different positions for different frequency bands, so the location of stimulation conveys pitch. Changing voltage at one site would change loudness, not pitch.

questions.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays auditory information to cortex?
o: Lateral geniculate nucleus
The LGN is visual.
Ventral posteromedial nucleus
The VPM relays face sensation and taste.
Pulvinar
The pulvinar is involved mainly in visual attention.
Medial geniculate nucleus
Correct: the MGN relays auditory signals to primary auditory cortex.
questions.x: The medial geniculate nucleus is the thalamic relay for hearing, sending auditory signals to primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. Its neighbor, the lateral geniculate nucleus, relays vision. The VPM relays face sensation and taste, and the VPL relays body sensation. Remember 'medial = music, lateral = light.'

questions.q: Primary auditory cortex is located in the:
o: Occipital lobe
The occipital lobe is visual.
Superior temporal lobe
Correct: A1 lies in Heschl's gyrus of the superior temporal lobe.
Postcentral gyrus
That is primary somatosensory cortex.
Prefrontal cortex
Prefrontal cortex handles executive functions.
questions.x: Primary auditory cortex (A1) sits in Heschl's gyrus on the superior temporal lobe, buried partly in the lateral sulcus. It is tonotopically organized like the cochlea. Nearby Wernicke's area helps with language comprehension. The postcentral gyrus is primary somatosensory cortex and the occipital lobe is visual.

questions.q: A sound source is directly to a listener's right. Which cue lets the brain localize a low-frequency (200 Hz) tone in this position?
o: Interaural intensity difference
Low frequencies diffract around the head, producing little intensity difference.
Interaural time difference
Correct: long low-frequency wavelengths bend around the head, so arrival-time differences are the key cue.
Spectral filtering by the pinna
Pinna cues mainly resolve elevation and front–back position and depend on high frequencies.
The tone's place of vibration on the basilar membrane
Place coding signals the tone's pitch, not where the source is.
questions.note: Low frequencies: timing; high frequencies: level (head shadow).
questions.x: The brain localizes sounds by comparing the two ears. Low-frequency sounds have wavelengths longer than the head, so they bend around it and reach both ears at similar intensity; the useful cue is the small difference in arrival time. High frequencies are shadowed by the head and create intensity differences instead. This duplex theory makes interaural intensity the wrong cue for a 200 Hz tone.

questions.q: The superior olive in the brainstem is important for hearing because it:
o: Transduces vibrations into receptor potentials
Hair cells do transduction.
Equalizes air pressure in the middle ear
That is the Eustachian tube's role.
Relays sound directly to the occipital lobe
Auditory signals go to the temporal lobe via the MGN.
Compares input from both ears to localize sound
Correct: it is the first site of binaural convergence.
questions.x: The superior olivary complex in the brainstem is the first place where signals from both ears converge. The medial superior olive compares arrival times (interaural time differences) and the lateral superior olive compares intensities (interaural level differences), allowing horizontal localization. Transduction happens earlier in hair cells, and auditory signals reach temporal, not occipital, cortex.

questions.q: The perceived loudness of a sound corresponds most closely to which physical property?
o: Amplitude of the sound wave
Correct: larger amplitude means greater pressure changes and louder sound.
Frequency of the sound wave
Frequency corresponds to pitch.
Speed of sound in air
Speed is set by the medium and does not differ between loud and soft sounds.
Complexity of the waveform
Complexity corresponds to timbre.
questions.x: Each perceptual attribute of sound maps mainly to a physical property: loudness to amplitude (pressure variation, measured in decibels), pitch to frequency, and timbre to waveform complexity. The speed of sound depends on the medium, not the sound's intensity. Frequency is the most common distractor because it also affects perceived loudness somewhat.

questions.q: Contraction of the tensor tympani and stapedius muscles in response to a very loud sound serves to:
o: Amplify the sound for better detection
The reflex attenuates rather than amplifies.
Open the Eustachian tube to drain fluid
Those muscles act on the ossicles and eardrum, not the tube.
Dampen ossicle movement and protect the inner ear
Correct: the acoustic reflex reduces sound transmission to the cochlea.
Bend the stereocilia toward the tallest one
The muscles do not act directly on hair cells.
questions.x: The acoustic (stapedius) reflex tightens the stapedius and tensor tympani in response to loud sounds. This stiffens the ossicular chain and reduces transmission of low-frequency sound energy to the cochlea, partly protecting hair cells. The reflex has a delay, so it cannot fully protect against sudden blasts, and it never amplifies sound.

questions.q: In an experiment, guinea pig outer hair cells are selectively destroyed while inner hair cells are spared. Auditory nerve recordings show reduced sensitivity and broader frequency tuning. What does this suggest?
o: Outer hair cells send most afferent signals to the brain
Inner hair cells provide most afferent nerve input.
Inner hair cells are not needed for hearing
Inner hair cells remain the main transducers sending signals to the brain.
Tuning depends entirely on the ossicles
Loss of outer hair cells alone changed tuning, so the cochlea contributes.
Outer hair cells act as cochlear amplifiers that sharpen tuning
Correct: outer hair cell electromotility boosts and sharpens basilar membrane motion.
questions.x: Inner hair cells send most afferent signals to the brain, while outer hair cells change length with membrane voltage (electromotility via prestin). This motion amplifies basilar membrane vibration at each place, increasing sensitivity and sharpening frequency tuning. Losing outer hair cells leaves transmission intact but makes hearing less sensitive and tuning broader, as observed.

questions.q: Which fluid fills the scala media and bathes the tops of the hair cells?
o: Perilymph, which is rich in K⁺
Perilymph resembles extracellular fluid and is Na⁺-rich.
Cerebrospinal fluid
CSF surrounds the brain and spinal cord, not the scala media.
Endolymph, which is rich in K⁺
Correct: endolymph has a high K⁺ concentration that drives transduction.
Aqueous humor
Aqueous humor is in the eye.
questions.x: The scala media (cochlear duct) contains endolymph, which is rich in K⁺ and low in Na⁺, with a positive endocochlear potential. Stereocilia project into it, so opening transduction channels lets K⁺ flow inward. Perilymph in the scala vestibuli and tympani resembles extracellular fluid and is Na⁺-rich, which is the trap in the first choice.

questions.q: Sound waves cause the tympanic membrane to vibrate. The structure that relieves pressure in the cochlea as the stapes pushes in is the:
o: Oval window
The oval window receives the stapes, not relieves pressure.
Round window
Correct: the round window bulges out as the oval window is pushed in.
Pinna
The pinna is the external ear flap.
Helicotrema
The helicotrema connects the scalae at the apex but does not relieve pressure to the middle ear.
questions.x: Cochlear fluid is nearly incompressible, so when the stapes pushes the oval window inward, the pressure wave travels through the cochlea and must be relieved elsewhere. The round window membrane bulges outward into the middle ear, allowing fluid movement and basilar membrane vibration. Without it, the stapes could barely move the fluid.

questions.q: A child repeatedly suffers middle ear infections that leave fluid behind the eardrum. Which type of hearing loss is expected?
o: Conductive
Correct: fluid hinders vibration of the eardrum and ossicles.
Sensorineural
Sensorineural loss involves the cochlea or auditory nerve.
Central
Central loss involves brain pathways.
Tonotopic
Tonotopic is an organizing principle, not a type of hearing loss.
questions.x: Conductive hearing loss arises from problems getting sound to the cochlea, such as wax, eardrum damage, ossicle problems or middle ear fluid. Fluid from otitis media damps vibration of the eardrum and ossicles. Sensorineural loss instead involves damage to hair cells or the auditory nerve, which a middle ear infection does not typically cause.

questions.q: Two tones differ in frequency but have the same amplitude. A listener reports the 3000 Hz tone as louder than the 100 Hz tone. What best explains this?
o: Loudness depends only on frequency
Amplitude remains the main determinant of loudness.
The 100 Hz tone was below the human hearing range
Humans hear down to about 20 Hz.
Human hearing sensitivity varies with frequency, peaking around 2–5 kHz
Correct: perceived loudness depends on frequency; mid frequencies sound louder at equal amplitude.
Higher frequencies always have larger amplitudes
The stem states the amplitudes are equal.
questions.x: Loudness depends mainly on amplitude, but the ear is not equally sensitive across frequencies. Equal-loudness contours show peak sensitivity around 2 to 5 kHz, partly due to ear canal resonance. A 3000 Hz tone therefore sounds louder than a 100 Hz tone of the same amplitude. The 100 Hz tone is still audible, since human hearing extends down to about 20 Hz.

questions.q: Which structures of the inner ear detect rotational (angular) acceleration of the head?
o: Semicircular canals
Correct: endolymph lagging in the canals bends hair cells in the cupula.
Utricle and saccule
These otolith organs detect linear acceleration and head tilt.
Cochlea
The cochlea detects sound.
Ossicles
The ossicles conduct sound in the middle ear.
questions.x: The three semicircular canals, oriented at right angles, detect rotational acceleration. When the head turns, endolymph lags behind because of inertia, bending the gelatinous cupula and the hair cells within it. The utricle and saccule instead use otolith crystals to detect linear acceleration and head tilt, which is the main confusion to avoid.

questions.q: Otoliths (otoconia) are calcium carbonate crystals that help the utricle and saccule detect:
o: Rotation of the head
Rotation is detected by the semicircular canals.
Sound frequency
Frequency is analyzed along the basilar membrane.
Blood pressure changes
Baroreceptors, not the inner ear, detect blood pressure.
Linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity
Correct: crystal inertia and weight shear the hair bundles.
questions.x: In the utricle and saccule, hair cells are covered by a gel layer topped with dense calcium carbonate otoconia. When the head tilts or accelerates linearly, the heavy crystals lag or are pulled by gravity, shearing the hair bundles. Because they respond to gravity and linear acceleration, otolith organs signal head position, while rotation is the semicircular canals' job.

questions.q: An elevator suddenly accelerates upward. Which vestibular organ is most directly stimulated?
o: Horizontal semicircular canal
This canal detects rotation in the horizontal plane.
Saccule
Correct: the saccule's vertically oriented macula senses vertical linear acceleration.
Cochlea
The cochlea does not sense acceleration.
Utricle only, because it senses vertical motion
The utricle mainly senses horizontal linear acceleration.
questions.note: Saccule ~ vertical (sack goes up and down); utricle ~ horizontal.
questions.x: Both otolith organs sense linear acceleration, but their maculae are oriented differently. The saccule's macula is mainly vertical, so it responds best to up-and-down acceleration such as an elevator starting; the utricle's macula is mainly horizontal and responds to forward, backward and sideways movement. Semicircular canals respond to rotation, not straight-line motion.

questions.q: After spinning in a chair for 30 seconds and stopping suddenly, a person feels as if spinning in the opposite direction. Why?
o: Otoliths detach and float freely in the canals
That describes benign positional vertigo, not post-rotation illusion.
Endolymph keeps moving after the head stops, deflecting the cupula the opposite way
Correct: fluid inertia bends hair cells as if rotation reversed.
The cochlea misinterprets the stop as a loud sound
The cochlea detects sound, not rotation.
The visual cortex adapts to the spinning image
The sensation persists with eyes closed, so it is vestibular.
questions.x: During sustained spinning, endolymph catches up with the canal and the cupula returns upright, so the sense of rotation fades. When the head stops abruptly, endolymph keeps moving by inertia and bends the cupula in the opposite direction, signaling rotation the other way. Because the illusion persists with the eyes closed, it is vestibular, not visual.

questions.q: Motion sickness is thought to arise mainly from:
o: Overstimulation of the cochlea by engine noise
Motion sickness occurs even in silence.
Low blood glucose during travel
Glucose is not the primary cause.
Damage to olfactory receptors
Olfaction is not central to motion sickness.
Conflict between vestibular and visual signals about motion
Correct: mismatched sensory inputs about self-motion are the leading explanation.
questions.x: The leading explanation, sensory conflict theory, holds that motion sickness arises when vestibular, visual and proprioceptive signals disagree about self-motion. Reading in a moving car is a classic case: the inner ear senses motion while the eyes report a stationary page. Noise and low blood glucose do not explain why the conflict between senses matters.

questions.q: A patient with vestibular damage can stand steadily with eyes open but sways and nearly falls when she closes her eyes. What does this reveal?
o: Vision was compensating for lost vestibular balance information
Correct: removing visual input exposes the vestibular deficit.
Her visual cortex is the source of the damage
She is stable with eyes open, so vision works.
Her muscles are too weak to support standing
Muscle weakness would impair standing with eyes open too.
Proprioception is completely absent
Her known lesion is vestibular, and she stands steadily with eyes open, so proprioception is not absent.
questions.note: Balance integrates vestibular, visual and proprioceptive input.
questions.x: Balance integrates vestibular, visual and proprioceptive input, and any two can partly compensate for a third. A patient with vestibular damage can stay upright when vision fills in, but closing the eyes removes that support and exposes the deficit, which is a positive Romberg sign. Muscle weakness is ruled out because it would also impair standing with the eyes open.

questions.q: Kinesthesia, the sense of limb position and movement, relies mostly on receptors such as:
o: Rods and cones
These are photoreceptors.
Taste receptor cells
These detect chemicals in the mouth.
Muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs
Correct: these proprioceptors signal muscle length and tension.
Olfactory sensory neurons
These detect odorants.
questions.x: Kinesthesia and proprioception tell us where our limbs are and how they move without looking. Muscle spindles signal muscle length and its rate of change, Golgi tendon organs signal tension, and joint receptors add further detail. These inputs travel in the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway and to the cerebellum, not through visual or chemical senses.

questions.q: Golgi tendon organs differ from muscle spindles in that Golgi tendon organs primarily signal:
o: Muscle length and stretch
That is the muscle spindle's role.
