Joint temperature
Thermoreceptors detect temperature.
Skin vibration
Vibration is sensed by Pacinian corpuscles.
Muscle tension
Correct: they sit in tendons and respond to force.
questions.x: Muscle spindles lie in parallel with muscle fibers and detect stretch, or length, driving the stretch reflex. Golgi tendon organs lie in series in the tendon, so they detect the force or tension the muscle generates and can inhibit contraction when tension is high. Mixing these two roles up is the most common error.

questions.q: Which receptor is most specialized to detect deep pressure and high-frequency vibration?
o: Meissner corpuscle
Meissner corpuscles sense light touch and low-frequency flutter.
Free nerve ending
Free nerve endings mainly detect pain and temperature.
Pacinian corpuscle
Correct: its layered capsule responds to vibration and rapid pressure changes.
Muscle spindle
Muscle spindles detect stretch.
questions.x: Pacinian corpuscles are large, onion-like encapsulated receptors deep in the skin. Their layered capsule filters out sustained pressure, so they adapt rapidly and respond best to high-frequency vibration and rapid pressure changes. Meissner corpuscles also adapt rapidly but are superficial and sense light touch and low-frequency flutter.

questions.q: Fingertips have much better two-point discrimination than the back. This is mainly because fingertips have:
o: More rapidly adapting nociceptors
Nociceptor type does not set two-point discrimination.
Higher receptor density and smaller receptive fields
Correct: dense, small fields allow fine spatial resolution.
Thicker skin
Thicker skin would not improve spatial resolution.
Fewer cortical neurons devoted to them
Fingertips have more, not fewer, cortical representation.
questions.x: Two-point discrimination depends on how many receptors cover an area and how small their receptive fields are. Fingertips have dense, small-field receptors, so two nearby points activate separate receptors; on the back, large fields mean both points fall in one field and feel like one. Fingertips also have a larger cortical representation, not a smaller one.

questions.q: Primary somatosensory cortex is located in the:
o: Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
Correct: S1 lies just behind the central sulcus.
Precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe
That is primary motor cortex.
Superior temporal gyrus
That holds auditory cortex.
Calcarine sulcus
That holds primary visual cortex.
questions.x: Primary somatosensory cortex (S1) is in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe, immediately behind the central sulcus. It receives touch, proprioception, pain and temperature signals via the thalamus and is organized as a body map. Primary motor cortex sits directly in front of it in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe, the most tempting distractor.

questions.q: In the somatosensory homunculus, the hands and lips occupy disproportionately large regions because:
o: They are the largest body surfaces
The back and legs are larger but have small cortical areas.
They contain the most pain receptors
Representation relates to overall receptor density and acuity, not pain alone.
They have high receptor density and need fine sensory resolution
Correct: cortical area reflects innervation density, not body size.
Their signals bypass the thalamus
Somatosensory signals relay through the thalamus.
questions.x: The somatosensory homunculus maps body regions in proportion to receptor density and the need for fine discrimination, not physical size. Lips, tongue and fingertips are densely innervated with small receptive fields, so they get large cortical territories. The back and legs are large but sparsely innervated, so they occupy little cortex.

questions.q: A patient has a lesion on the right side of the spinal cord. Fine touch and vibration are lost on the right below the lesion, while pain and temperature are lost on the left. What explains this pattern?
o: Fine touch ascends ipsilaterally in the dorsal columns; pain fibers cross near entry
Correct: the dorsal columns cross in the medulla, while spinothalamic fibers cross within a few segments.
Both pathways cross in the medulla
Then both losses would occur on the same side.
Pain fibers ascend ipsilaterally and touch fibers cross at entry
This reverses the actual crossing points.
The lesion affected only the motor cortex
A cortical lesion would not produce this split spinal pattern.
questions.note: Dorsal column (DCML): crosses in medulla; spinothalamic: crosses in cord.
questions.x: Fine touch, vibration and proprioception travel up the dorsal columns on the same side and cross only in the medulla, so a cord lesion causes ipsilateral loss. Pain and temperature fibers synapse in the dorsal horn and cross within a segment or two, ascending in the contralateral spinothalamic tract, so the loss is contralateral. This split is the Brown-Séquard pattern.

questions.q: Which fibers carry sharp, well-localized 'first pain' quickly?
o: Unmyelinated C fibers
C fibers carry slow, dull, burning 'second pain'.
Heavily myelinated Aβ fibers
Aβ fibers carry touch and vibration.
Motor neurons
Motor neurons carry efferent commands.
Thinly myelinated Aδ fibers
Correct: Aδ fibers conduct faster than C fibers and signal sharp pain.
questions.note: Aδ = sharp and fast; C = slow and burning.
questions.x: Nociceptive fibers come in two types. Thinly myelinated Aδ fibers conduct relatively fast and carry sharp, well-localized 'first pain.' Unmyelinated C fibers conduct slowly and carry dull, aching or burning 'second pain' that follows. Heavily myelinated Aβ fibers are even faster but carry touch and vibration, not pain.

questions.q: According to gate control theory, why does rubbing a bumped elbow reduce pain?
o: Rubbing destroys nociceptors
Rubbing does not damage receptors.
Touch fibers activate spinal interneurons that inhibit pain transmission
Correct: Aβ input 'closes the gate' in the dorsal horn.
Rubbing releases histamine, which blocks pain
Histamine promotes inflammation and itch, not analgesia.
Pain fibers adapt instantly to rubbing
Nociceptors adapt little; the effect is spinal gating.
questions.x: Gate control theory proposes that dorsal horn interneurons act as a gate for pain signals. Rubbing activates large Aβ touch fibers, which excite inhibitory interneurons that reduce transmission from nociceptive fibers to ascending neurons, closing the gate. Pain relief comes from spinal modulation, not from nociceptors adapting or being destroyed.

questions.q: Capsaicin from chili peppers produces a burning sensation by activating:
o: Sweet taste receptors
Capsaicin is not sensed as sweet.
TRPV1 receptors on nociceptors that also respond to heat
Correct: capsaicin opens the same channel activated by painful heat.
Cold receptors containing TRPM8
TRPM8 responds to cold and menthol.
Olfactory receptors only
The burn is a somatosensory, not olfactory, sensation.
questions.x: Capsaicin binds TRPV1, a cation channel on nociceptors that normally opens at painful heat above about 43 °C. Opening it depolarizes the neuron, so the brain interprets the signal as burning heat even though no temperature change occurs. This is why spiciness is a somatosensory sensation, not a taste, and why TRPM8, the cold and menthol channel, is the wrong answer.

questions.q: Menthol feels cool on the skin even at room temperature because it:
o: Lowers skin temperature by several degrees
Menthol's cooling feeling is mainly receptor activation, not real cooling.
Blocks all thermoreceptors
Blocking receptors would reduce, not create, a cold sensation.
Stimulates Pacinian corpuscles
Pacinian corpuscles sense vibration.
Activates TRPM8 cold-sensing channels
Correct: menthol opens the same channel that cold opens.
questions.x: TRPM8 is a cation channel on sensory neurons that opens in response to cool temperatures. Menthol binds and opens the same channel, depolarizing the neurons, so the brain reports cold even though skin temperature has barely changed. This parallels capsaicin activating the heat-sensing TRPV1 channel. Blocking thermoreceptors would remove sensation, not create coolness.

questions.q: Patients with congenital insensitivity to pain often have repeated injuries and shorter lifespans. This best supports which conclusion?
o: Pain serves a protective function by signaling tissue damage
Correct: without pain, people fail to avoid or notice injuries.
Pain receptors also mediate fine touch
These patients typically have normal touch.
Pain is purely a learned emotional response
An inborn absence argues for a biological basis.
Pain sensitivity has no genetic component
A congenital, inherited condition implies a genetic component.
questions.x: Congenital insensitivity to pain, caused by mutations such as loss of function in the Nav1.7 sodium channel, shows what pain is for. Affected people cannot detect injuries like burns, fractures or joint damage, so they suffer repeated harm. This indicates pain is a protective warning signal with a biological, genetic basis rather than a purely learned response.

questions.q: After a leg amputation, a patient feels pain in the missing foot. Which explanation is best supported by research on phantom limb pain?
o: Nociceptors in the missing foot are still active
The foot and its receptors are gone.
The patient is consciously imagining the pain
Phantom pain is a real neural phenomenon, not simple imagination.
Cortical maps reorganize and remaining neurons still generate limb sensations
Correct: somatosensory reorganization and residual pathway activity produce phantom sensations.
Pain fibers regrow into the missing limb
There is no limb for nerves to regrow into.
questions.x: After amputation, neurons that once represented the limb remain and receive new input, as neighboring cortical regions such as the face invade the hand area. Activity in these reorganized circuits, along with signals from cut nerve endings and spinal changes, is interpreted as coming from the missing limb. The pain is real neural activity, not imagination or activity in receptors that no longer exist.

questions.q: Referred pain, such as heart attack pain felt in the left arm, occurs because:
o: The heart contains Pacinian corpuscles
Pacinian corpuscles do not explain referred pain.
Blood flow to the arm stops during a heart attack
Arm blood flow is usually maintained.
The vagus nerve innervates the arm
The vagus does not supply arm skin.
Visceral and skin afferents converge on the same spinal neurons
Correct: the brain misattributes visceral input to the skin region sharing that spinal level.
questions.x: Visceral afferents from organs such as the heart enter the spinal cord at the same levels (about T1 to T4) as skin afferents from the chest and inner arm and converge on the same dorsal horn neurons. Because the brain rarely receives heart signals but often receives skin signals through those neurons, it attributes the pain to the skin region. This convergence explains referred pain patterns.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the five basic taste qualities?
o: Umami
Umami (glutamate) is a basic taste.
Bitter
Bitter is a basic taste.
Spicy
Correct: spiciness is a pain/heat sensation via TRPV1, not a taste.
Sour
Sour is a basic taste.
questions.x: The five basic tastes are sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami, each detected by taste receptor cells. Spiciness from chili peppers is not a taste but a pain and heat sensation, produced when capsaicin activates TRPV1 on trigeminal nociceptors in the mouth. Umami, the savory taste of glutamate, is a real basic taste despite being less familiar.

questions.q: Sweet, bitter and umami tastes are transduced by:
o: Ion channels that admit Na⁺ directly
Direct Na⁺ entry underlies salty taste.
G protein-coupled receptors
Correct: T1R and T2R families are GPCRs.
Mechanically gated channels
Taste is chemical, not mechanical.
Rhodopsin
Rhodopsin is a visual pigment.
questions.note: Salty and sour use channels; sweet, bitter, umami use GPCRs.
questions.x: Taste transduction uses two mechanisms. Sweet (T1R2/T1R3), umami (T1R1/T1R3) and bitter (T2Rs) bind GPCRs that activate second-messenger cascades. Salty taste relies on Na⁺ entering through ion channels such as ENaC, and sour on H⁺ acting through proton channels. The trap is assuming all tastes use direct ion entry.

questions.q: Sour taste is triggered mainly by:
o: H⁺ ions from acids
Correct: protons enter or act on channels in sour-sensing cells.
Na⁺ ions from salts
Na⁺ triggers salty taste.
Glutamate
Glutamate triggers umami taste.
Sugars
Sugars trigger sweet taste.
questions.x: Sour taste detects acidity. H⁺ ions from acids enter sour-sensing taste cells through proton channels (such as OTOP1) and also acidify the cell, blocking K⁺ channels, which depolarizes the cell. Salty taste is triggered by Na⁺, and sweet and umami by molecules binding GPCRs, so acidity specifically signals sourness.

questions.q: Taste information from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels in which cranial nerve?
o: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
CN IX carries taste from the posterior third.
Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
CN V carries general touch and pain from the tongue, not taste.
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Correct: the chorda tympani branch of CN VII carries anterior tongue taste.
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
CN XII is motor to tongue muscles.
questions.x: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels in the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). The posterior third uses the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), and the throat and epiglottis use the vagus (CN X). The trigeminal nerve carries general touch, temperature and pain from the anterior tongue, which makes it a tempting but incorrect choice.

questions.q: Research shows that all taste qualities can be detected across all regions of the tongue. What does this indicate about the classic 'tongue map'?
o: It is inaccurate, because taste receptor cells for each quality are widely distributed
Correct: each taste bud region contains cells for multiple qualities.
It is accurate for sweet but not for bitter
No quality is confined to one region.
Taste receptors exist only on the tip of the tongue
Taste buds are spread across the tongue, palate and throat.
Taste is determined entirely by smell
Smell contributes to flavor, but taste receptors detect the basic qualities.
questions.x: The classic tongue map, assigning sweet to the tip and bitter to the back, came from a misreading of early research. Taste buds containing receptor cells for all five qualities are spread across the tongue, soft palate and throat. Regional sensitivity differences are slight, so no taste quality is confined to one region.

questions.q: A person with a severe cold says food tastes bland. This mainly reflects:
o: Destruction of taste buds by the virus
Taste buds usually remain functional; basic tastes persist.
Inability to detect salty and sour
Basic tastes are generally preserved.
Damage to the gustatory cortex
A cold does not damage cortex.
Loss of retronasal smell, which contributes heavily to flavor
Correct: blocked olfaction removes much of what we perceive as flavor.
questions.x: Flavor combines taste from the tongue with smell, especially retronasal olfaction, where odor molecules from food in the mouth travel up the back of the throat to the nasal cavity. A cold blocks this airflow, so the basic tastes remain but most of the distinctive flavor disappears. The taste buds themselves are usually intact.

questions.q: Olfactory receptor neurons are located in the:
o: Olfactory bulb
The bulb receives receptor axons but is not where odorants are detected.
Olfactory epithelium in the upper nasal cavity
Correct: the epithelium contains receptor neurons with cilia in the mucus.
Tongue
The tongue houses taste receptors.
Vomeronasal organ only
The vomeronasal organ is specialized for pheromones and is vestigial in humans.
questions.x: Olfactory receptor neurons sit in the olfactory epithelium at the roof of the nasal cavity. Their cilia extend into the mucus, where odorants bind GPCRs, and their axons pass through the cribriform plate to synapse in the olfactory bulb. The bulb processes signals but contains no receptor neurons, which is the most tempting confusion.

questions.q: Olfactory receptor neurons that express the same odorant receptor send their axons to:
o: Random locations throughout the bulb
Projections are highly organized, not random.
The same one or two glomeruli in the olfactory bulb
Correct: convergence onto specific glomeruli creates an odor map.
The thalamus directly
Olfactory neurons synapse in the bulb first.
The primary visual cortex
Olfaction does not project to visual cortex.
questions.x: Each olfactory receptor neuron expresses one odorant receptor type. Neurons with the same receptor are scattered across the epithelium but their axons converge onto one or a few glomeruli in the olfactory bulb. This creates a spatial map in which each glomerulus represents one receptor type, letting odors be coded by patterns of glomerular activity.

questions.q: Humans have about 400 types of odorant receptors yet can distinguish thousands of odors. What is the best explanation?
o: Each receptor type responds to only one odor
Then only ~400 odors could be distinguished.
The olfactory bulb creates new receptors for each new smell
Receptor types are genetically fixed.
Odor identity is coded by sniff strength
Sniff strength affects intensity, not identity.
Each odor activates a unique combination of receptor types
Correct: combinatorial coding allows far more odors than receptor types.
questions.note: Combinatorial coding: patterns, not single labeled receptors.
questions.x: Most odorants bind several receptor types, and each receptor binds several odorants. The identity of an odor is therefore coded by the pattern or combination of receptor types activated, not by a single dedicated receptor. With about 400 receptor types, the number of possible combinations far exceeds the number of receptors, allowing discrimination of vast numbers of odors.

questions.q: Smells are known to trigger vivid emotional memories. This is best explained by olfactory connections to the:
o: Amygdala and hippocampus
Correct: olfactory pathways project directly to limbic structures.
Primary motor cortex
Motor cortex is not part of emotional memory circuits.
Cerebellum
The cerebellum coordinates movement.
Medial geniculate nucleus
The MGN is an auditory relay.
questions.x: Olfactory bulb output projects directly to the amygdala and to entorhinal cortex leading into the hippocampus, without first passing through the thalamus. These limbic structures are central to emotion and memory, which helps explain why odors evoke vivid emotional memories, the so-called Proust effect. Other senses reach these structures only after more processing.

questions.q: Olfactory receptor neurons are unusual among neurons because they:
o: Lack axons
They have axons forming the olfactory nerve.
Use rhodopsin to detect odors
They use odorant GPCRs, not rhodopsin.
Are replaced throughout life by stem cells
Correct: basal cells regenerate these neurons every few weeks to months.
Synapse directly onto the spinal cord
They synapse in the olfactory bulb.
questions.x: Most neurons are not replaced, but olfactory receptor neurons are directly exposed to the environment and are continually damaged. Basal stem cells in the olfactory epithelium divide and differentiate to replace them throughout life, and the new neurons send axons to the correct glomeruli. These neurons do have axons, which form the olfactory nerve (CN I).

questions.q: Pheromones are best defined as:
o: Hormones that act only within the body that releases them
Those are hormones, which act internally.
Odors used by predators to locate prey
Those are kairomones that benefit another species.
Neurotransmitters released at synapses
Neurotransmitters act across synapses inside one organism.
Chemicals released by an animal that affect the behavior or physiology of others of the same species
Correct: pheromones are intraspecies chemical signals.
questions.x: Pheromones are chemicals released by one individual that change the behavior or physiology of another member of the same species, for example in mating, territory marking or alarm. Hormones act within the body that makes them, and kairomones benefit a different species. The defining features of a pheromone are external release and same-species action.

questions.q: In many mammals, pheromones are detected primarily by the:
o: Cochlea
The cochlea detects sound.
Semicircular canals
These detect rotation.
Vomeronasal organ
Correct: this accessory olfactory organ projects to the accessory olfactory bulb.
Retina
The retina detects light.
questions.x: In many mammals, pheromones are detected mainly by the vomeronasal organ, an accessory olfactory structure in the nasal septum. Its receptor neurons project to the accessory olfactory bulb and then to the amygdala and hypothalamus, which influence reproductive and social behavior. In humans the organ is vestigial, but in rodents it is crucial for social behavior.

questions.q: Mice with a knocked-out gene essential for vomeronasal organ signaling fail to distinguish males from females and court both sexes. This supports which conclusion?
o: The main olfactory epithelium is needed for all mouse behavior
The study only targeted the vomeronasal system.
Vomeronasal pheromone detection helps mice identify the sex of other mice
Correct: losing VNO signaling disrupts sex discrimination.
Vision is the main cue mice use to identify sex
The deficit came from altering chemosensation, not vision.
Pheromones have no role in mammals
The results show the opposite.
questions.x: Knocking out a gene required for vomeronasal signaling removed pheromone detection while leaving other senses intact. The mice could no longer tell males from females and courted both, showing that vomeronasal pheromone cues help mice identify sex. Since only the vomeronasal pathway was altered, the result says nothing about vision being the main cue.

questions.q: In a study, subjects rate a constant odor's intensity every 30 seconds. Ratings drop steadily over 5 minutes, but a novel odor introduced at minute 5 is rated as strong. What best explains the results?
o: Odor-specific adaptation reduced response to the first odor
Correct: the drop is specific; a different odor is still detected strongly.
General loss of olfactory function over time
A general loss would also weaken the novel odor.
The constant odor's concentration dropped
The stem says the odor was constant.
Subjects habituated to all smells equally
The strong novel-odor rating rules out general habituation.
questions.x: Olfactory adaptation is stimulus specific: continuous exposure reduces responses to that odor, while other odors are still detected normally. Because the new odor was rated strong after 5 minutes, overall olfactory function and attention were intact, ruling out a general loss. The decline reflects reduced response to the unchanging first odor, which is why people stop noticing their own home's smell.

questions.q: When an image is stabilized on the retina so that it moves with every eye movement, it soon fades from view. What does this demonstrate?
o: The blind spot expands during fixation
The fading occurs across the whole image, not at the optic disc.
Cones are replaced by rods during prolonged viewing
Photoreceptors do not change type.
Visual receptors adapt to unchanging stimulation, so small eye movements keep images visible
Correct: tiny involuntary eye movements constantly refresh retinal input.
Stabilized images exceed the eye's difference threshold
Fading reflects adaptation, not a threshold being exceeded.
questions.note: Change drives sensory systems; constant input fades.
questions.x: Even during fixation, the eyes make tiny involuntary movements (microsaccades and drift) that keep shifting the image across receptors. If an image is stabilized so it stays on exactly the same receptors, they adapt to the constant input and the image fades. This shows sensory systems mainly signal change, and eye movements keep stationary scenes visible.

questions.q: Researchers find that bitter-sensing taste cells respond to many structurally unrelated toxins, and that each bitter cell expresses many T2R receptor types. Which functional interpretation fits best?
o: Bitter taste is tuned to broadly detect and reject potential poisons rather than discriminate among them
Correct: many receptors per cell feed one aversive 'bitter' signal.
Bitter taste allows precise identification of each specific toxin
Pooling many receptors in one cell limits discrimination between bitter compounds.
Bitter taste is transduced by Na⁺ channels like salty taste
T2Rs are GPCRs, not Na⁺ channels.
Bitter cells evolved to attract animals to nutrient-rich foods
Bitterness signals possible toxins and drives avoidance.
questions.x: Each bitter taste cell expresses many T2R receptors, and all feed into one 'bitter' signal. This broad tuning lets animals detect thousands of structurally different, potentially toxic compounds and avoid them, but it means bitter substances are hard to tell apart. Precise identification of each toxin would require separate cells with separate signals, which is not what was found.

questions.q: Participants shadow a story played to the right ear. Midway, the story jumps to the left ear, and many briefly start shadowing the left ear. Which model does this best support?
o: Broadbent's early-selection filter model
A strict early filter would block meaning in the unattended ear, so the story could not pull attention.
Treisman's attenuation model
Correct: unattended input is turned down, not blocked, so meaningful content can still break through.
Baddeley's working memory model
That model describes short-term storage components, not how an unattended channel is filtered.
Feature integration theory
That theory explains visual search for feature conjunctions, not dichotic listening.
questions.note: Attenuation = volume knob; Broadbent = on/off switch based on physical features.
questions.x: Treisman proposed that unattended channels are attenuated (turned down) rather than fully blocked, so meaningful or highly relevant content can still reach awareness. Following the story's meaning into the other ear shows semantic processing of the unattended channel. Broadbent's strict early filter selects only on physical features, so it predicts that meaning in the unattended ear should never capture attention.

questions.q: According to Broadbent's filter model, on what basis does the selective filter decide which sensory input is passed on for further processing?
o: The meaning of the input
Selection by meaning is a late-selection idea, not Broadbent's early filter.
The emotional relevance of the input
Emotional relevance requires semantic analysis, which Broadbent placed after the filter.
Whether the input has been rehearsed
Rehearsal is a memory process, not a criterion of the attentional filter.
Physical features such as pitch or location
Correct: Broadbent proposed early selection based on physical characteristics before meaning is analyzed.
questions.x: Broadbent's filter model is an early-selection model: sensory input is held briefly, then a filter passes one channel based on physical characteristics like pitch, loudness or ear of arrival. Meaning is analyzed only after the filter, so selection cannot depend on semantics. Choosing meaning or emotional relevance describes late-selection or attenuation ideas instead.

questions.q: While counting passes between players in a video, many viewers fail to notice a person in a bear costume walking across the court. What does this demonstrate?
o: Inattentional blindness
Correct: an unexpected, fully visible object is missed because attention is focused on another task.
Change blindness
Change blindness is failing to notice a change between scenes, not a new object in an attended scene.
Habituation
Habituation is a decreased response to a repeated stimulus, not missing a single novel event.
Sensory adaptation
Adaptation reduces receptor responsiveness to constant stimulation; it does not explain this miss.
questions.x: Inattentional blindness is failing to perceive a clearly visible, unexpected object because attention is absorbed by another task. Perception depends on attention, not just on light hitting the retina. Change blindness is the tempting alternative, but it refers to missing a difference between two views of a scene, not missing a new object within one continuously viewed scene.

questions.q: A researcher asks pedestrians for directions; during the chat, workers carrying a door pass between them and the researcher is swapped for a different person. Most pedestrians keep talking without noticing. Which phenomenon is this?
o: Inattentional blindness
That is missing an unexpected object in view, not failing to detect a change across a brief interruption.
Selective priming
Priming refers to prior exposure speeding later processing, not missing a change.
Change blindness
Correct: people often fail to detect changes in a scene, especially across an interruption.
Prosopagnosia
Prosopagnosia is a neurological inability to recognize faces, not a common failure in healthy people.
questions.x: Change blindness is the failure to notice that something in a scene has changed, especially when the change coincides with a brief interruption such as a blink, a cut or an object passing by. People store far less visual detail than they assume. Inattentional blindness is the trap: it concerns missing an unexpected object present in view, not failing to compare a before and after.

questions.q: Which pair of simultaneous tasks would most likely show the least performance cost from divided attention?
o: Solving math problems while writing an essay
Both tasks are effortful and draw on controlled processing, so interference is high.
Walking on a familiar route while holding a casual chat
Correct: a well-practiced, automatic task demands little attention, so it pairs well with another task.
Learning to drive while texting a friend
A novel, controlled task plus another controlled task produces large interference.
Listening to two different lectures at once
Two tasks in the same modality, both needing comprehension, compete heavily.
questions.note: Automatic processes need little attention; controlled ones compete.
questions.x: Divided attention costs depend on how much controlled processing each task needs and whether the tasks compete for the same resources. Highly practiced, automatic tasks like walking a familiar route need little attention, so they combine easily with conversation. Two effortful or same-modality tasks, like two lectures or learning to drive while texting, compete for limited capacity and interfere heavily.

questions.q: Naming the ink color of the word "BLUE" printed in red ink is slower than naming the ink color of a row of X's. Why?
o: Color perception is slower than word perception
Ink color is perceived quickly; the delay comes from response conflict.
The rods cannot detect red light
Rods do not mediate color vision at all; cones do, and the red ink is seen.
Word reading requires divided attention between eyes
Reading does not split attention between the eyes.
Reading is automatic and interferes with naming the color
Correct: the Stroop effect shows automatic word reading conflicting with the controlled color-naming task.
questions.x: The Stroop effect shows that reading is so overlearned it runs automatically, even when the task is only to name ink color. When the word names a different color, the automatic reading response conflicts with the controlled color-naming response, slowing reaction time. The delay comes from response conflict, not from slow color perception, since naming the color of X's is fast.

questions.q: In a visual search study, finding a red T among green Ts takes the same time for 4 or 32 items, but finding a red T among red Ls and green Ts gets slower as items increase. What best explains this?
o: Single features are detected in parallel; conjunctions require serial attention
Correct: feature integration theory predicts pop-out for one feature and serial search for feature combinations.
Color is processed after shape in the visual system
Color and shape are both extracted early and in parallel.
Larger displays cause retinal fatigue
Fatigue would slow both searches equally, not only the conjunction search.
Red items are harder to see among green items
The fast, flat search time shows the red target is easy to find among green ones.
questions.note: Flat slope = parallel pop-out; rising slope = serial search.
questions.x: Feature integration theory holds that basic features like color are registered in parallel across the visual field, so a target defined by one unique feature pops out regardless of display size. A target defined by a conjunction of features requires focused attention to bind features at each location, so search time rises with item number. Fatigue would not selectively slow only the conjunction search.

questions.q: In the classic information-processing (multi-store) model, in what order does information flow?
o: Short-term memory → sensory memory → long-term memory
Sensory memory comes first, before short-term memory.
Long-term memory → sensory memory → short-term memory
Incoming information cannot enter long-term memory first.
Sensory memory → short-term memory → long-term memory
Correct: input is briefly held in sensory memory, attended items enter STM, and encoded items reach LTM.
Sensory memory → long-term memory → short-term memory
Information must pass through STM to be encoded into LTM.
questions.x: The Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model has information enter sensory memory, where it lasts under a few seconds. Attended information moves into short-term memory, and rehearsal or elaborative encoding transfers it to long-term memory. Long-term memory cannot receive raw input directly; it is reached through STM, although LTM contents can later be retrieved back into working memory.

questions.q: An 8-month-old watches a toy get covered by a blanket and immediately pulls the blanket away to find it. Which cognitive milestone has the infant reached?
o: Conservation
Conservation develops in the concrete operational stage, years later.
Object permanence
Correct: understanding that hidden objects still exist emerges in the sensorimotor stage.
Theory of mind
Theory of mind, understanding others' beliefs, emerges around age 4.
Reversibility
Reversibility is a concrete operational skill, not an infant milestone.
questions.x: Object permanence, the understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight, develops during Piaget's sensorimotor stage and is evident when infants search for hidden objects, often around 8 months. Conservation and reversibility are concrete operational achievements around ages 7 to 11, and theory of mind emerges around age 4, so none fit an infant searching under a blanket.

questions.q: A 4-year-old shown a model of three mountains says a doll on the opposite side sees exactly the same view she does. What does this illustrate?
o: Lack of object permanence
She knows the doll and mountains exist; the error is about perspective.
Formal operational thought
Formal operations involve abstract reasoning and would allow perspective taking.
Animism
Animism is attributing life to objects, not assuming others share one's viewpoint.
Egocentrism in the preoperational stage
Correct: preoperational children struggle to take another's visual perspective.
questions.x: Piaget's three-mountain task tests egocentrism, the preoperational child's difficulty taking another person's perspective. The child assumes the doll sees what she sees. This is not a failure of object permanence, which was mastered in infancy, and not animism, which is attributing life or feelings to objects rather than assuming everyone shares one's viewpoint.

questions.q: A 5-year-old insists a wide row of 5 coins has more coins than a short row of 5 coins because it is longer. Which preoperational limitation explains this best?
o: Centration, focusing on one feature of a problem
Correct: the child attends only to row length and ignores number.
Egocentrism, inability to take another's view
Egocentrism concerns perspective taking, not attending to one dimension of an object.
Lack of object permanence
The child knows the coins exist; object permanence is mastered in infancy.
Hypothetical-deductive reasoning
That is a formal operational skill the child has not yet developed.
questions.note: Centration underlies failure of conservation.
questions.x: Centration is focusing on one salient dimension of a situation while ignoring others, and it is a key reason preoperational children fail conservation tasks. Here the child attends only to row length and ignores that the number of coins is unchanged. Egocentrism is tempting because it is also preoperational, but it concerns perspective taking, not attending to one feature of an object.

questions.q: A 9-year-old easily solves arithmetic with blocks but struggles with a counterfactual question like "If people could breathe underwater, where might cities be built?" Which stage fits best?
o: Sensorimotor
Sensorimotor infants cannot do arithmetic with blocks.
Preoperational
Preoperational children lack logical operations even with concrete objects.
Concrete operational
Correct: logical thinking about concrete objects is present, but abstract hypotheticals are still difficult.
Formal operational
Formal operational thinkers handle abstract and hypothetical problems well.
questions.x: In the concrete operational stage (about 7 to 11 years), children reason logically about real, tangible objects and master conservation and reversibility, but abstract or counterfactual problems remain hard. Formal operational thinking, beginning in adolescence, adds hypothetical-deductive reasoning. Preoperational children would struggle even with the concrete arithmetic, so the split pattern points to concrete operations.

questions.q: A teenager tests which factor controls a pendulum's swing period by changing one variable at a time while holding the others constant. Which Piagetian stage does this reflect?
o: Concrete operational
Concrete thinkers rarely isolate variables systematically in hypothetical tests.
Formal operational
Correct: systematic hypothesis testing and abstract reasoning define formal operations.
Preoperational
Preoperational children cannot perform logical operations at all.
Postconventional
Postconventional is a Kohlberg moral reasoning level, not a Piagetian cognitive stage.
questions.x: Piaget's pendulum problem is a classic test of formal operational thought: forming hypotheses and systematically testing variables one at a time while holding others constant. Concrete operational children tend to change several variables at once and reason less systematically about abstract possibilities. Postconventional is a tempting term but belongs to Kohlberg's theory of moral development.

questions.q: A toddler who knows the word "dog" sees a goat for the first time and calls it "doggy." Which process is this?
o: Accommodation
Accommodation would involve changing the schema or creating a new one.
Overregularization
Overregularization applies grammar rules too broadly, as in "goed."
Centration
Centration is focusing on one feature in a reasoning task, not labeling a new animal.
Assimilation
Correct: the child fits the new animal into an existing schema.
questions.note: Assimilate = fit into old schema; accommodate = change the schema.
questions.x: Assimilation means interpreting new experiences using an existing schema, so a toddler with a dog schema labels a goat as a dog. Accommodation is the complementary process of modifying a schema or creating a new one when new information does not fit. Overregularization is a language error of applying grammatical rules too broadly, not misclassifying an animal.

questions.q: After being told that the goat is not a dog, the toddler forms a separate category for goats. Which Piagetian process is this?
o: Accommodation
Correct: the child modifies the existing schema system to handle new information.
Assimilation
Assimilation would keep calling the goat a dog.
Habituation
Habituation is reduced responding to a repeated stimulus.
Conservation
Conservation concerns quantity remaining constant despite shape changes.
questions.x: Accommodation is changing existing schemas or creating new ones when experience does not fit. By forming a separate goat category, the child restructures knowledge rather than forcing the goat into the dog schema, which would be assimilation. Piaget saw development as balancing these two processes, called equilibration.

questions.q: A child cannot solve a puzzle alone but succeeds when a parent offers hints. According to Vygotsky, this task lies within the child's:
o: schema
A schema is a mental framework, not the gap between independent and assisted performance.
concrete operational stage
That is a Piagetian stage, not Vygotsky's concept.
zone of proximal development
Correct: tasks a child can do with guidance but not alone fall in the ZPD.
critical period
A critical period is a time window for development, not a range of assisted tasks.
questions.x: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is the range between what a learner can do independently and what they can do with guidance from a more skilled person. Support within this zone, called scaffolding, drives cognitive growth. Schemas and concrete operations are Piagetian concepts, and a critical period refers to a developmental time window, not a band of assisted performance.

questions.q: Compared with young adults, healthy adults in their 70s typically show which pattern?
o: Lower crystallized and higher fluid intelligence
This reverses the typical aging pattern.
Stable crystallized and lower fluid intelligence
Correct: accumulated knowledge holds up, while novel reasoning and speed decline.
Higher fluid and higher crystallized intelligence
Fluid intelligence generally declines with age.
Lower crystallized and lower fluid intelligence equally
Crystallized knowledge is relatively preserved in healthy aging.
questions.x: Crystallized intelligence, accumulated knowledge and vocabulary, stays stable or grows into late adulthood. Fluid intelligence, the ability to reason about novel problems and process quickly, peaks in early adulthood and then declines. So older adults typically show preserved crystallized but reduced fluid abilities, not an equal decline in both.

questions.q: In healthy aging, which type of memory is generally the most preserved?
o: Episodic memory for recent events
Episodic memory typically shows noticeable age-related decline.
Prospective memory for future tasks
Remembering to do things later often declines, especially without cues.
Working memory for manipulating information
Working memory capacity declines with age.
Semantic memory such as vocabulary
Correct: general knowledge and vocabulary remain stable or grow into late adulthood.
questions.x: Healthy aging affects memory systems unequally. Semantic memory, such as vocabulary and general knowledge, is well preserved and may grow, as is procedural memory. Episodic memory for recent events, working memory and prospective memory without cues typically decline. Working memory is a tempting choice but depends on processing speed and executive control, which drop with age.

questions.q: An older adult develops gradually worsening memory for new information over several years, and imaging shows hippocampal atrophy. Which neurotransmitter loss is most associated with this condition?
o: Acetylcholine
Correct: Alzheimer disease involves loss of cholinergic neurons, which is why cholinesterase inhibitors are used.
Dopamine
Dopamine loss in the substantia nigra is linked to Parkinson disease.
Serotonin
Serotonin is most linked to mood disorders, not this memory pattern.
Glycine
Glycine is an inhibitory transmitter of the spinal cord, not tied to Alzheimer disease.
questions.x: Gradual memory decline with hippocampal atrophy suggests Alzheimer disease, which involves loss of cholinergic neurons, especially from the nucleus basalis of Meynert, along with amyloid plaques and tau tangles. This is why acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are used to treat symptoms. Dopamine loss is the hallmark of Parkinson disease, which mainly causes motor symptoms.

questions.q: An 80-year-old hospitalized with an infection becomes confused over one day, with attention that fluctuates hour to hour. What best distinguishes this from dementia?
o: Memory loss is present
Memory problems can occur in both delirium and dementia.
The patient is elderly
Age is a risk factor for both conditions.
Acute onset with fluctuating attention
Correct: delirium starts suddenly with waxing and waning attention; dementia is gradual.
The confusion is permanent
Delirium is usually reversible once the cause is treated.
questions.note: Delirium = acute and fluctuating; dementia = insidious and progressive.
questions.x: Delirium is an acute, often reversible disturbance of attention and awareness that develops over hours to days and fluctuates, frequently triggered by infection, drugs or metabolic problems. Dementia develops gradually over months to years with relatively stable attention early on. Memory loss and older age occur in both, so they cannot separate the two conditions.

questions.q: Which problem-solving strategy guarantees a correct solution if followed, though it may be slow?
o: Heuristic
Heuristics are shortcuts that are fast but can fail.
Algorithm
Correct: an algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that always reaches the solution.
Insight
Insight is a sudden realization and offers no guarantee.
Trial and error
Random attempts may never hit the solution in a reasonable time.
questions.x: An algorithm is a systematic, step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution if one exists, though it may be slow, such as trying every possible combination. Heuristics are mental shortcuts that are faster but can lead to errors. Trial and error is tempting but involves unsystematic attempts with no guarantee of success in reasonable time.

questions.q: To plan a cross-country move, a student lists the gap between her current state and the goal, then picks steps that shrink the largest gap first. Which strategy is this?
o: Trial and error
She is not trying random options; each step is chosen to shrink a gap.
Functional fixedness
That is a barrier to problem solving, not a strategy.
Algorithm
She is not following a fixed procedure guaranteed to reach the goal.
Means-end analysis
Correct: means-end analysis breaks a problem into subgoals that reduce the difference from the goal.
questions.x: Means-end analysis compares the current state with the goal state and chooses actions that reduce the difference, often by creating subgoals. It is a heuristic, so it does not guarantee a solution like an algorithm would. Functional fixedness is an obstacle to problem solving rather than a strategy, and trial and error lacks the deliberate gap-reduction shown here.

questions.q: After seeing extensive news coverage of shark attacks, a person estimates sharks kill more people each year than car crashes. Which heuristic is at work?
o: Availability heuristic
Correct: vivid, easily recalled examples inflate judged frequency.
Representativeness heuristic
Representativeness judges by similarity to a prototype, not by ease of recall.
Anchoring heuristic
Anchoring involves an initial number biasing an estimate.
Confirmation bias
Confirmation bias is seeking evidence that supports an existing belief.
questions.x: The availability heuristic judges how frequent or likely an event is by how easily examples come to mind. Heavy, vivid media coverage makes shark attacks easy to recall, inflating their estimated frequency far above common but less memorable causes like car crashes. Representativeness is the tempting alternative, but it judges by similarity to a prototype, not ease of recall.

questions.q: Told that a group is 90 engineers and 10 poets, participants read about a quiet man who loves verse and judge him likely a poet. Which error is this?
o: Availability heuristic
The judgment is not based on how easily examples come to mind.
Belief perseverance
Belief perseverance is clinging to beliefs after they are discredited.
Base-rate neglect via the representativeness heuristic
Correct: judging by resemblance to a stereotype ignores that engineers vastly outnumber poets.
Framing effect
Framing is about how options are worded, such as gains versus losses.
questions.x: The representativeness heuristic judges probability by how well something matches a prototype. Because the description fits a stereotyped poet, people label him a poet and ignore the base rate that engineers outnumber poets 9 to 1, an error called base-rate neglect. Availability is tempting, but the judgment depends on resemblance, not on how easily examples are recalled.

questions.q: Half of participants are first asked whether a city's population is above 5 million; the rest, above 200,000. The first group gives much higher estimates. Which heuristic explains this?
o: Availability
Neither group recalls examples; the difference is caused by the number given.
Anchoring and adjustment
Correct: the initial value serves as an anchor and adjustments away from it are insufficient.
Representativeness
No comparison to a prototype is involved.
Hindsight bias
Hindsight bias is seeing outcomes as predictable after the fact.
questions.x: Anchoring and adjustment occurs when an initial value, even an arbitrary one, serves as a reference point and people adjust insufficiently away from it. The 5 million question anchors estimates high, while the 200,000 question anchors them low. Availability is not involved because the difference is produced by the number provided, not by recalling examples.

questions.q: A person needs to tighten a screw but has no screwdriver, and does not think of using a coin in her pocket. Which obstacle is this?
o: Mental set
Mental set is reusing a previously successful strategy, not failing to see a new use for an object.
Confirmation bias
Confirmation bias concerns evaluating evidence, not object use.
Overconfidence
Overconfidence is overestimating one's accuracy.
Functional fixedness
Correct: she sees the coin only in its usual role and misses its alternative use.
questions.x: Functional fixedness is the tendency to see objects only in their usual function, which blocks creative solutions such as using a coin as a screwdriver. It is a specific obstacle about object uses. Mental set is related but distinct: it is persisting with a strategy that worked before, rather than failing to see a new use for an object.

questions.q: After solving five puzzles with a three-step method, participants keep using it on a sixth puzzle that a one-step method would solve. This illustrates:
o: mental set
Correct: a previously successful approach persists even when a simpler one exists.
functional fixedness
Functional fixedness is about object uses, not reusing a solution strategy.
insight
Insight would be a sudden discovery of the simpler method.
the availability heuristic
No frequency estimate based on recall is involved.
questions.x: A mental set is a tendency to approach problems in a way that worked previously, even when a simpler or better method is available, as in Luchins' water jar studies. Repeated success with the three-step method creates the set. Functional fixedness is the tempting choice, but it concerns seeing objects only in their typical role, not rigidly reusing a procedure.

questions.q: After struggling with a riddle, a student takes a break and suddenly realizes the answer while showering. This sudden solution is best described as:
o: an algorithm
An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure, not a sudden realization.
trial and error
No sequence of attempts led to the answer.
insight
Correct: insight is a sudden understanding, often after an incubation period.
a mental set
A mental set is a rigid habit that hinders problem solving.
questions.x: Insight is the sudden realization of a solution, often after an incubation period when a person stops working on the problem consciously. The break may let fixations fade so a new representation of the problem emerges. An algorithm or trial and error involves step-by-step or repeated attempts, not an abrupt aha moment.

questions.q: A voter who supports a candidate reads only articles praising the candidate and dismisses critical reports as biased. Which bias is this?
o: Hindsight bias
Hindsight bias is believing one predicted an outcome after it happens.
Confirmation bias
Correct: seeking and favoring evidence that supports an existing belief.
Overconfidence
Overconfidence is overestimating the accuracy of one's judgments.
Anchoring
Anchoring involves reliance on an initial value.
questions.x: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek, interpret and remember information that supports existing beliefs while dismissing contradictory evidence. Reading only favorable articles and calling critics biased is a textbook example. Overconfidence is tempting, but it refers to overestimating the accuracy of one's own judgments, not to selectively choosing which evidence to consider.

questions.q: Participants receive fake feedback that they are excellent at a task. Even after being told the feedback was random, they still rate themselves as above average. What does this show?
o: Confirmation bias
Confirmation bias is selective search for evidence; here the belief survives after its basis is removed.
Hindsight bias
Nothing about predicting outcomes after the fact is measured.
Self-serving bias
Self-serving bias explains attributions for success and failure, not survival of discredited beliefs.
Belief perseverance
Correct: beliefs persist even after the evidence that created them is discredited.
questions.x: Belief perseverance is maintaining a belief even after the evidence that created it has been discredited. People generate their own explanations for the original belief, which survive when the evidence is withdrawn. Confirmation bias is the tempting answer, but it describes selectively seeking supportive evidence, whereas here the belief persists after its only basis was removed.

questions.q: On a trivia test, participants say they are 90% sure of their answers, but they are correct only 65% of the time. This reflects:
o: overconfidence
Correct: confidence in judgments exceeds actual accuracy.
belief perseverance
That would involve keeping a belief after it is discredited.
the framing effect
No change in option wording is involved.
functional fixedness
That concerns object use in problem solving.
questions.note: Calibration: confidence should match accuracy.
questions.x: Overconfidence is a calibration error in which subjective confidence exceeds actual accuracy, here 90% confidence versus 65% correct. Well-calibrated judges would be right about as often as their confidence predicts. Belief perseverance is tempting, but it involves keeping a belief after the evidence for it has been discredited, which is not tested here.

questions.q: Patients more often choose surgery described as having a "90% survival rate" than one with a "10% mortality rate." Which effect is this?
o: Anchoring
No initial number is used as a starting point for an estimate.
Availability
Recall of examples is not involved.
Framing
Correct: identical information presented as gains versus losses changes choices.
Belief perseverance
No discredited belief is involved.
questions.x: The framing effect occurs when logically equivalent information leads to different choices depending on whether it is presented as a gain or a loss. A 90% survival rate and a 10% mortality rate are identical, yet the positive survival frame is preferred. Anchoring is tempting because numbers appear, but no initial value is being used as a starting point for an estimate.

questions.q: A student observes that each of 20 swans she has seen is white and concludes all swans are white. What kind of reasoning is this?
o: Deductive reasoning
Deduction moves from general premises to a guaranteed specific conclusion.
Inductive reasoning
Correct: generalizing from specific observations to a broad conclusion is induction.
Algorithmic reasoning
An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure, not a generalization.
Divergent thinking
Divergent thinking generates many possible solutions to an open problem.
questions.note: Induction can be wrong even with true observations.
questions.x: Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a general conclusion; it can be strong but never guarantees truth, as the discovery of black swans shows. Deductive reasoning moves from general premises to a specific conclusion that must be true if the premises are true. Generalizing from 20 swans to all swans is therefore induction, not deduction.

questions.q: Spearman found that people who do well on one mental test tend to do well on others. He attributed this to:
o: multiple intelligences
Gardner's theory proposes separate, independent intelligences.
practical intelligence
Practical intelligence is part of Sternberg's triarchic theory.
emotional intelligence
Emotional intelligence concerns perceiving and managing emotions.
a general intelligence factor, g
Correct: Spearman proposed a single g factor underlying performance across tests.
questions.x: Spearman observed positive correlations among scores on diverse mental tests and proposed a general intelligence factor, g, that underlies performance on all of them, plus specific factors for each test. Gardner's multiple intelligences is the opposing view that abilities are relatively independent. Practical and emotional intelligence come from later theories by Sternberg and others.

questions.q: A theorist argues a gifted dancer and a gifted mathematician show different kinds of intelligence, each relatively independent. This matches:
o: Gardner's multiple intelligences
Correct: Gardner proposed separate intelligences, including bodily-kinesthetic and logical-mathematical.
Spearman's g
Spearman stressed one general factor shared across abilities.
Cattell's fluid and crystallized model
That divides intelligence into two broad types, not domain-specific talents like dance.
The Flynn effect
The Flynn effect is the rise in IQ scores over generations.
questions.x: Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences proposes several relatively independent intelligences, including bodily-kinesthetic, logical-mathematical, linguistic, musical and interpersonal. Excellence in dance and math reflects different intelligences in this view. Spearman's g is the opposite idea, a single general ability, and Cattell's fluid and crystallized split does not map onto domain talents like dance.

questions.q: In Sternberg's triarchic theory, a mechanic with modest test scores who excels at fixing any engine in real-world conditions shows high:
o: analytical intelligence
Analytical intelligence is measured by traditional academic problem solving.
creative intelligence
Creative intelligence is about novel ideas and adapting to new situations.
practical intelligence
Correct: practical intelligence is street smarts for handling everyday tasks.
crystallized intelligence
Crystallized intelligence is Cattell's term for accumulated knowledge.
questions.x: Sternberg's triarchic theory divides intelligence into analytical (academic problem solving measured by tests), creative (handling novel situations and generating ideas) and practical (adapting to everyday real-world demands). A mechanic who excels with real engines despite modest test scores shows practical intelligence. Analytical intelligence is what traditional test scores measure, so it is not his strength.

questions.q: Identical twins raised apart show IQ correlations near 0.75, while unrelated children raised together show about 0.3. What is the best conclusion?
o: IQ is fully determined by genes
A correlation well below 1.0 in identical twins shows that nongenetic factors also matter.
Both genes and shared environment contribute to IQ
Correct: high MZ-apart similarity shows genetic influence; unrelated siblings' similarity shows environmental influence.
Shared environment has no influence on IQ
Unrelated children reared together are still somewhat similar, implying environmental effects.
Heritability tells us how much of one person's IQ comes from genes
Heritability describes variation in a population, not an individual.
questions.x: Identical twins share all genes, so high similarity even when raised apart points to genetic influence. Unrelated children share no genes beyond chance, so similarity when raised together points to shared environmental influence. Neither correlation is 1.0 or 0, so both genes and environment contribute. Heritability describes variation within a population and cannot be applied to one person.

questions.q: Average IQ test scores rose substantially across the 20th century in many countries, requiring tests to be renormed. This finding is called:
o: regression to the mean
Regression to the mean is extreme scores moving toward average on retest.
the Pygmalion effect
That is expectations improving performance, not a population trend.
stereotype threat
Stereotype threat lowers performance under fear of confirming a stereotype.
the Flynn effect
Correct: generational gains in IQ scores are too fast to be genetic and suggest environmental causes.
questions.x: The Flynn effect is the substantial rise in average IQ scores across generations, roughly 3 points per decade in many 20th-century countries, which forces tests to be renormed. The change is too rapid to be genetic and is attributed to environmental factors like nutrition, schooling and test familiarity. Regression to the mean concerns individual extreme scores moving toward average on retest.

questions.q: On an IQ test with mean 100 and standard deviation 15, a score of 130 falls at roughly which percentile?
o: 98th
Correct: 130 is 2 SD above the mean, and about 97.5% of scores fall below it.
84th
84th percentile corresponds to 1 SD above the mean, a score of 115.
95th
95% lie within ±2 SD; 130 alone is above about 97.5% of scores.
That corresponds to about 3 SD above the mean, a score of 145.
questions.note: 68-95-99.7 rule: +2 SD ≈ 97.5th percentile.
questions.x: IQ scores are normally distributed with mean 100 and SD 15, so 130 is 2 SD above the mean. By the 68-95-99.7 rule, 95% of scores lie within ±2 SD, leaving 2.5% above +2 SD, so 130 is near the 97.5th, or about 98th, percentile. The tempting 95th percentile confuses the two-tailed 95% range with a one-sided cutoff.

questions.q: Solving a type of logic puzzle you have never seen before relies most on:
o: crystallized intelligence
Crystallized intelligence relies on stored knowledge, not novel reasoning.
semantic memory
Semantic memory provides facts, but new puzzles need flexible reasoning.
fluid intelligence
Correct: fluid intelligence is the ability to reason and solve novel problems.
procedural memory
Procedural memory supports practiced skills, not unfamiliar puzzles.
questions.x: Fluid intelligence is the capacity to reason, recognize patterns and solve unfamiliar problems independent of prior knowledge, which is exactly what a new type of logic puzzle demands. Crystallized intelligence draws on accumulated knowledge and experience, so it helps with familiar problems and vocabulary. Procedural and semantic memory support practiced skills and stored facts, not novel reasoning.

questions.q: A study finds students told a test measures "intelligence" score lower than identical students told it is a "puzzle task," but only for groups stereotyped as weaker in that domain. Which explanation fits best?
o: The Flynn effect
The Flynn effect describes long-term IQ gains, not a framing-dependent drop.
Regression to the mean
No group was selected for extreme scores, so regression to the mean cannot explain the difference.
Low test validity
The same test was given to both groups; only the description changed.
Stereotype threat
Correct: fear of confirming a negative stereotype impairs performance when the stereotype is made relevant.
questions.x: Stereotype threat is the anxiety of possibly confirming a negative stereotype about one's group, which consumes working memory and lowers performance. Calling the test a measure of intelligence makes the stereotype relevant, while calling it a puzzle task removes the threat, and only stereotyped groups are affected. Low validity cannot explain this, because the test itself was identical across conditions.

questions.q: A test is said to be reliable but not valid. What does this mean?
o: It measures the intended construct but gives inconsistent scores
That describes validity without reliability, which is not possible in a strict sense.
It gives consistent scores but does not measure what it claims to
Correct: reliability is consistency; validity is measuring the intended construct.
It predicts future performance but cannot be repeated
Prediction is a form of validity, and repeatability is reliability.
It has been standardized on a large sample
Standardization concerns norms, not reliability or validity.
questions.note: A test can be reliable without being valid, but not truly valid without being reliable.
questions.x: Reliability is consistency: the same person gets similar scores across time, items or raters. Validity is accuracy: the test measures the construct it claims to measure. A reliable but invalid test, like a scale that always reads 5 kg too heavy, gives consistent but wrong results. Reliability is necessary for validity, but it is not sufficient.

questions.q: An EEG recorded from a student actively solving a math problem would show mostly which waves?
o: Alpha waves
Alpha appears during relaxed wakefulness, often with eyes closed.
Delta waves
Delta waves mark deep slow-wave sleep.
Beta waves
Correct: beta waves are high-frequency, low-amplitude waves of alert, active thinking.
Theta waves
Theta waves dominate light N1 sleep and drowsiness.
questions.x: EEG frequency rises and amplitude falls with arousal. Beta waves (high frequency, low amplitude, desynchronized) dominate alert, active thinking such as solving a math problem. Alpha waves are the tempting choice because the person is awake, but alpha marks relaxed wakefulness, typically with eyes closed, not focused mental effort.

questions.q: A person lying calmly with eyes closed but fully awake would show which EEG pattern?
o: Alpha waves
Correct: alpha waves reflect relaxed, wakeful rest.
Sleep spindles
Spindles are bursts characteristic of stage N2 sleep.
Delta waves
Delta waves appear in N3 deep sleep.
K-complexes
K-complexes are large single waves seen in N2 sleep.
questions.x: Alpha waves, about 8 to 13 Hz, appear when a person is awake but relaxed, especially with eyes closed; opening the eyes or concentrating replaces them with beta. Sleep spindles and K-complexes mark N2 sleep, and delta waves mark N3, so none of those fit someone who is fully awake. The key distinction is relaxed wakefulness versus actual sleep.

questions.q: A participant drifting off to sleep reports a sudden falling sensation and jerks awake; EEG shows theta waves. Which stage is this?
o: REM
REM involves muscle atonia and vivid dreams, not drowsy theta with jerks.
N3
N3 is deep sleep dominated by delta waves.
N2
N2 shows spindles and K-complexes on top of theta activity.
N1
Correct: N1 is light transitional sleep with theta waves and hypnic jerks.
questions.x: N1 is the brief transition from wakefulness to sleep, when alpha gives way to theta waves and hypnic jerks with a falling sensation are common. N2 also has theta background but is identified by sleep spindles and K-complexes, which are not described here. REM has wake-like EEG and muscle atonia, so sudden body jerks while drifting off point to N1.

questions.q: Sleep spindles and K-complexes on an EEG identify which sleep stage?
o: N1
N1 has theta waves without spindles or K-complexes.
N2
Correct: spindles and K-complexes are hallmarks of N2 sleep.
N3
N3 is defined by high-amplitude delta waves.
REM
REM shows low-voltage, mixed-frequency, wake-like activity.
questions.x: Stage N2 is identified by two EEG features: sleep spindles (brief bursts of 12 to 14 Hz activity) and K-complexes (large single biphasic waves), which are thought to suppress arousal and support memory consolidation. N1 shows theta without these features, and N3 is defined by high-amplitude delta waves. N2 makes up the largest share of adult sleep.

questions.q: A sleeper who is very hard to awaken, shows high-amplitude low-frequency EEG waves, and has a peak in growth hormone release is most likely in:
o: N1
N1 is the lightest stage and easiest to wake from.
REM
REM is not characterized by delta waves or the GH peak.
N3
Correct: slow-wave sleep has delta waves, high arousal threshold, and peak growth hormone release.
N2
N2 is lighter, with spindles and K-complexes rather than mostly delta waves.
questions.x: N3, or slow-wave sleep, is dominated by high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves and has the highest arousal threshold, so sleepers are hard to wake and groggy if roused. Growth hormone secretion peaks during early-night slow-wave sleep. REM is tempting because it is also deep in a sense, but its EEG is fast and wake-like, not delta.

questions.q: How does the composition of sleep cycles change over a typical night?
o: Slow-wave sleep dominates early cycles; REM periods lengthen later
Correct: N3 is concentrated early in the night, and REM grows longer toward morning.
REM dominates early cycles; slow-wave sleep dominates later
This reverses the actual pattern.
Each cycle has the same stage proportions all night
Stage proportions shift markedly across the night.
Cycles shorten from 90 minutes to about 30 minutes by morning
Cycles stay roughly 90 minutes throughout the night.
questions.x: Sleep cycles last about 90 minutes all night, but their makeup shifts. Early cycles contain most of the night's N3 slow-wave sleep, while later cycles contain little N3 and progressively longer REM periods, so most REM occurs toward morning. Reversing this pattern is the common error; dreaming-rich REM dominates the end of the night.

questions.q: Participants are awakened whenever they enter REM for three nights. On the fourth night, sleeping undisturbed, what is most likely observed?
o: Less REM than usual
Deprivation produces a compensatory increase, not a decrease.
No REM sleep at all
REM still occurs and in fact increases.
More N1 sleep in place of REM
The compensation is in REM itself, not light sleep.
More REM than usual, entered sooner
Correct: REM rebound follows REM deprivation.
questions.x: REM rebound is the compensatory increase in REM sleep after REM deprivation: on recovery nights, people enter REM sooner and spend more total time in it. This suggests REM is homeostatically regulated, meaning the brain tracks and repays a REM deficit. The deficit is not made up by lighter N1 sleep; the compensation occurs in REM itself.

questions.q: Compared with young adults, older adults typically show which sleep change?
o: More time in slow-wave sleep
Slow-wave sleep declines with age, not increases.
Less slow-wave sleep and more nighttime awakenings
Correct: aging brings reduced N3 sleep and more fragmented sleep.
Total loss of REM sleep
REM decreases modestly but does not disappear.
Longer sleep cycles of about 3 hours
Cycle length stays roughly 90 minutes.
questions.x: With age, slow-wave N3 sleep declines markedly, sleep becomes more fragmented with more nighttime awakenings, and sleep timing often shifts earlier. REM decreases only modestly and never disappears, and cycles remain about 90 minutes. Thus the hallmark change is lighter, more broken sleep rather than more deep sleep or longer cycles.

questions.q: Which brain structure serves as the master circadian clock?
o: Pineal gland
The pineal secretes melatonin under the clock's control, but it is not the master clock.
Thalamus
The thalamus relays sensory signals and is not the circadian pacemaker.
Amygdala
The amygdala processes emotion, especially fear.
Suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus
Correct: the SCN receives retinal light input and sets daily rhythms.
questions.x: The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus is the master circadian pacemaker. It receives light information directly from the retina via the retinohypothalamic tract and synchronizes daily rhythms throughout the body. The pineal gland is the tempting distractor: it secretes melatonin, but on a schedule set by signals from the SCN, so it is an output, not the clock.

questions.q: Melatonin secretion from the pineal gland is highest under which condition?
o: At night in darkness
Correct: darkness increases melatonin release, promoting sleep.
In bright midday light
Light suppresses melatonin secretion.
Right after waking in the morning
Morning light shuts down melatonin release.
During intense exercise
Exercise is not the main signal for melatonin secretion.
questions.x: The pineal gland releases melatonin mainly at night; darkness removes the SCN-driven inhibition of its release, while light reaching the retina suppresses it. Rising melatonin in the evening signals biological night and promotes sleep. That is why bright morning light shuts melatonin down and why screens at night can delay sleep.

questions.q: Researchers lesion the suprachiasmatic nucleus in hamsters. Total daily sleep time is unchanged, but sleep and activity become scattered randomly across 24 hours. What does this suggest?
o: The SCN generates the need for sleep
Total sleep was unchanged, so the SCN is not the source of sleep need.
The SCN is required for REM sleep
The lesion changed timing, not a specific sleep stage.
The SCN controls the timing of sleep rather than its amount
Correct: timing was lost while total sleep was preserved, separating circadian timing from sleep drive.
Sleep is controlled entirely by the pineal gland
The data show only that the SCN times sleep, not that the pineal controls it.
questions.note: Two-process model: circadian timing (SCN) vs homeostatic sleep pressure (adenosine).
questions.x: Sleep regulation has two separable processes: a circadian process (SCN) that times when sleep occurs, and a homeostatic process (sleep pressure, linked to adenosine) that tracks how much sleep is needed. Losing the SCN scrambled sleep timing but left total sleep unchanged, showing the SCN times sleep rather than generating the need for it. The data say nothing specific about REM.

questions.q: Volunteers living in a cave with no clocks or daylight still keep a sleep-wake cycle, but it gradually drifts later each day. What does this show?
o: Circadian rhythms require sunlight to exist
Rhythms persisted without light, so light is not required for them to exist.
The internal clock runs slightly longer than 24 hours and is normally reset by light
Correct: a free-running rhythm of about 24.2 h drifts without light cues to entrain it.
Sleep is controlled only by homeostatic pressure
Homeostatic pressure alone would not produce a regular near-24 h cycle.
Melatonin is no longer produced in darkness
Darkness increases melatonin; it does not stop it.
questions.note: Zeitgeber: an external cue such as light that entrains the clock.
questions.x: Without external time cues, the human circadian clock free-runs with a period slightly longer than 24 hours, about 24.2 hours, so the sleep-wake cycle drifts later each day. Normally zeitgebers, especially morning light, reset the clock daily. The persistence of a rhythm in constant darkness shows the clock is internal, so light is needed to entrain it, not to create it.

questions.q: Most travelers find adjusting after flying east harder than after flying west across the same number of time zones. Why?
o: Eastward travel requires advancing the clock, while the natural rhythm tends to run long
Correct: an intrinsic period over 24 h makes delaying easier than advancing.
Eastward flights are longer than westward flights
Flight duration does not explain the circadian difference.
Melatonin is not produced after eastward flights
Melatonin is still produced; its timing is just misaligned.
Westward travel shortens the circadian period permanently
Travel shifts the phase; it does not permanently change the period.
questions.x: Because the intrinsic circadian period is a bit longer than 24 hours, the clock naturally drifts later, so delaying it is easier than advancing it. Flying west lengthens the day and requires a delay, while flying east shortens the day and requires a phase advance, which is harder. Flight duration and melatonin absence do not explain the asymmetry.

questions.q: Cortisol levels in a person with a normal day-night schedule are typically highest when?
o: Late evening before bed
Cortisol is near its lowest in the late evening.
Around midnight
Cortisol is low in the first part of the night.
Mid-afternoon
Cortisol declines across the day from its morning peak.
Shortly after waking in the morning
Correct: cortisol peaks in the early morning, helping promote alertness.
questions.x: Cortisol follows a circadian rhythm: it rises during the late night, peaks shortly after waking (the cortisol awakening response) and declines through the day to its lowest point around late evening and the first part of sleep. The morning peak mobilizes energy and supports alertness. Cortisol is a stress hormone, but its baseline rhythm is set by the circadian clock, not by evening fatigue.

questions.q: Which theory proposes that dreams arise when the cortex tries to make sense of random neural signals from the brainstem during REM?
o: Psychoanalytic theory
Freud saw dreams as disguised wish fulfillment, not interpretation of random signals.
Activation-synthesis theory
Correct: random pontine activity is synthesized by the cortex into a dream story.
Information-processing theory
That theory says dreams help sort and consolidate the day's memories.
Neurocognitive theory
That theory links dreams to waking cognitive development and concerns.
questions.x: Activation-synthesis theory (Hobson and McCarley) proposes that during REM the pons sends random bursts of activity to the cortex, which synthesizes them into a dream narrative. Dream content is thus a byproduct of the brain making sense of noise. Information-processing theory is the tempting alternative, but it holds that dreams help sort and consolidate the day's experiences.

questions.q: A Freudian therapist says a dream of losing one's teeth reflects hidden fears of aging. The hidden meaning is called the dream's:
o: manifest content
Manifest content is the literal storyline, such as losing teeth.
activation-synthesis
That is a biological theory of dreaming, not Freudian terminology.
latent content
Correct: latent content is the underlying, disguised meaning.
lucid content
Lucid dreaming is awareness that one is dreaming.
questions.x: Freud distinguished manifest content, the literal storyline a dreamer remembers, from latent content, the hidden, unconscious meaning disguised by dream work. Losing teeth is the manifest content, while fear of aging is the proposed latent content. Activation-synthesis is a biological theory that rejects hidden meaning entirely.
