questions.q: Students who sleep after learning a maze recall it better than those kept awake, and their dreams often include maze elements. Which dream theory does this support?
o: Information-processing (memory consolidation) theory
Correct: sleep and dreams help process and consolidate newly learned information.
Activation-synthesis theory
That theory sees dream content as random, not tied to learning.
Psychoanalytic theory
Freud focused on hidden wishes, not memory consolidation.
Restoration theory
Restoration theory explains sleep as bodily repair, not memory processing.
questions.x: Information-processing or memory-consolidation theories propose that sleep, and dreams, help process and store newly learned information. Better recall after sleep plus dreams that replay learned material supports this view. Activation-synthesis treats dream content as random brainstem noise, so it would not predict dreams tied to new learning or improved memory.

questions.q: A patient falls asleep suddenly at work, collapses with muscle weakness when laughing, and enters REM within minutes of falling asleep. Which is the most likely cause?
o: Obstructive sleep apnea
Apnea causes sleepiness from disrupted breathing, not cataplexy or sleep-onset REM.
Insomnia
Insomnia is difficulty falling or staying asleep.
Night terrors
Night terrors are N3 parasomnias with panic-like arousals.
Narcolepsy from loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons
Correct: narcolepsy features sudden sleep attacks, cataplexy, and early REM onset.
questions.x: Narcolepsy is a dyssomnia caused by loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the hypothalamus, which normally stabilize wakefulness. Its hallmarks are sudden sleep attacks, cataplexy (muscle weakness triggered by strong emotion like laughter) and entering REM within minutes of sleep onset. Sleep apnea also causes daytime sleepiness, but not cataplexy or sleep-onset REM.

questions.q: An obese man snores loudly, has repeated breathing pauses at night, and is very sleepy during the day. Which disorder is most likely?
o: Narcolepsy
Narcolepsy is not caused by breathing interruptions during sleep.
Obstructive sleep apnea
Correct: airway collapse during sleep causes pauses, snoring, and daytime sleepiness.
Somnambulism
Sleepwalking does not involve breathing pauses.
REM sleep behavior disorder
RBD involves acting out dreams, not breathing pauses.
questions.x: Obstructive sleep apnea occurs when the upper airway collapses during sleep, causing loud snoring, breathing pauses and repeated brief arousals that fragment sleep and produce daytime sleepiness. Obesity is a major risk factor. Narcolepsy also causes daytime sleepiness, but it stems from orexin loss, not from breathing interruptions during sleep.

questions.q: A 7-year-old sits up screaming an hour after falling asleep, cannot be comforted, and remembers nothing in the morning. In which stage does this usually occur?
o: REM
Nightmares occur in REM and are typically remembered.
N1
N1 is too light for this type of parasomnia.
N3
Correct: night terrors arise from slow-wave sleep, early in the night, with amnesia afterward.
N2
Night terrors are associated with slow-wave rather than N2 sleep.
questions.note: Night terror = N3, no memory; nightmare = REM, remembered.
questions.x: Night terrors are parasomnias arising from N3 slow-wave sleep, usually in the first third of the night and common in children. The child appears terrified and hard to console but has little or no memory afterward. Nightmares are the tempting alternative, but they occur in REM, often later in the night, and are typically remembered.

questions.q: A 68-year-old punches and kicks during sleep, acting out vivid dreams of being attacked. Which mechanism is most likely impaired?
o: Melatonin release from the pineal gland
Melatonin problems shift sleep timing; they do not cause dream enactment.
The muscle atonia that normally accompanies REM
Correct: in REM sleep behavior disorder, loss of atonia lets people act out dreams.
Slow-wave sleep generation
Dream enactment arises in REM, not N3.
Airway muscle tone during N2
Airway collapse causes apnea, not dream enactment.
questions.note: RBD can be an early sign of Parkinson disease.
questions.x: Normally, REM sleep includes muscle atonia, a brainstem-driven paralysis of skeletal muscles that prevents us from acting out dreams. In REM sleep behavior disorder this atonia fails, so people punch or kick during vivid dreams. It is often linked to later Parkinson disease or other synucleinopathies. Sleepwalking is different because it arises from N3, not REM.

questions.q: Sleepwalking most often occurs during which stage of sleep?
o: N3
Correct: somnambulism arises from slow-wave sleep, typically early in the night.
REM
REM involves muscle atonia, which prevents walking.
N1
N1 is a brief transition stage not usually linked to sleepwalking.
Relaxed wakefulness
Sleepwalking happens during sleep, not wakefulness.
questions.x: Sleepwalking (somnambulism) is a parasomnia that arises from N3 slow-wave sleep, usually in the first part of the night, and people rarely remember it. It cannot occur in REM because REM muscle atonia prevents complex movement. Assuming sleepwalking happens during dreaming is the common misconception.

questions.q: Which pair correctly classifies two sleep disorders?
o: Insomnia is a parasomnia; sleepwalking is a dyssomnia
This reverses the categories.
Narcolepsy is a parasomnia; night terrors are a dyssomnia
Narcolepsy is a dyssomnia and night terrors are a parasomnia.
Sleep apnea and sleepwalking are both parasomnias
Sleep apnea affects the amount and quality of sleep, making it a dyssomnia.
Insomnia is a dyssomnia; sleepwalking is a parasomnia
Correct: dyssomnias disturb sleep amount or timing; parasomnias are abnormal behaviors during sleep.
questions.x: Sleep disorders are classically divided into dyssomnias, which disturb the amount, quality or timing of sleep (insomnia, narcolepsy, sleep apnea), and parasomnias, which are abnormal behaviors or events during sleep (sleepwalking, night terrors, REM sleep behavior disorder). Insomnia is therefore a dyssomnia and sleepwalking a parasomnia. Apnea alters sleep quality, so it is a dyssomnia.

questions.q: Under hypnosis, which change is most consistently observed?
o: EEG patterns similar to N3 sleep
Hypnotized people show waking EEG patterns, not slow-wave sleep.
Ability to perform feats beyond normal strength
Hypnosis does not grant abilities beyond what motivated, unhypnotized people can do.
Increased suggestibility
Correct: hypnosis is a state of focused attention and heightened responsiveness to suggestion.
Perfectly accurate recall of past events
Hypnosis increases confidence and errors in recall, not accuracy.
questions.x: Hypnosis is best described as a state of focused attention with heightened suggestibility. Hypnotized people show waking EEG patterns, not sleep waves, and gain no abilities beyond what motivated people can do. Hypnosis is often believed to improve memory, but it actually increases confidence and suggestibility, which raises the risk of false memories.

questions.q: A hypnotized participant says she feels no pain with her hand in ice water, yet when asked to signal with a finger if "some part" feels pain, she signals. This supports which view of hypnosis?
o: Social-cognitive role-playing theory
That theory emphasizes playing an expected role; the hidden observer finding is the classic support for the alternative view.
Dissociation theory
Correct: a hidden observer suggests consciousness splits into separate streams under hypnosis.
Activation-synthesis theory
That is a theory of dreaming.
Opponent-process theory
That theory concerns emotion and color vision, not hypnosis.
questions.x: Hilgard's hidden observer studies supported dissociation theory, which holds that hypnosis splits consciousness so one stream can register pain while another reports none. The finger signal revealed this hidden awareness. Social-cognitive theory instead explains hypnosis as people acting out the role of a hypnotized subject, and the hidden observer finding was originally offered against that view.

questions.q: Police hypnotize a witness to help her recall a crime. What is the most likely effect?
o: Higher confidence with more false details
Correct: hypnosis raises confidence and suggestibility, increasing memory errors.
Accurate recovery of forgotten details
Hypnosis does not reliably improve accuracy.
No change in recall or confidence
Confidence and errors typically increase.
Complete loss of the memory
Hypnosis does not erase memories.
questions.x: Hypnosis increases suggestibility and confidence without improving accuracy, so hypnotized witnesses tend to report more details, including false ones, and believe them more strongly. Leading questions can easily implant information, which is why hypnotically refreshed testimony is often restricted in court. The belief that hypnosis unlocks accurate hidden memories is the key misconception.

questions.q: Experienced meditators are compared with novices during practice. Which finding is most consistent with research on meditation?
o: Beta waves increase and heart rate rises
Meditation lowers arousal rather than increasing it.
Delta waves dominate as in deep sleep
Meditators remain awake; delta waves are characteristic of slow-wave sleep.
Sympathetic activity increases
Meditation tends to shift balance toward parasympathetic activity.
Alpha and theta activity increase while heart rate falls
Correct: meditation is linked to relaxed alertness with more alpha and theta and lower arousal.
questions.x: Meditation is an altered state of relaxed alertness. Studies of practitioners report increased alpha and theta EEG activity along with lower heart rate, breathing rate and sympathetic arousal, shifting balance toward parasympathetic activity. Delta waves are tempting because meditation is calm, but delta marks deep slow-wave sleep, and meditators remain awake.

questions.q: Alcohol produces sedation and reduced anxiety mainly by:
o: blocking dopamine reuptake
That is the main mechanism of cocaine.
enhancing GABA-A receptor activity
Correct: alcohol increases inhibitory GABA signaling and also inhibits glutamate receptors.
activating opioid receptors directly
Opioid drugs bind opioid receptors directly; alcohol acts mainly on GABA.
antagonizing adenosine receptors
That is caffeine's mechanism, which increases arousal.
questions.x: Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant that acts mainly as a positive modulator of GABA-A receptors, increasing chloride influx and neuronal inhibition, while also inhibiting NMDA glutamate receptors. Together these reduce neural excitability, causing sedation and reduced anxiety. Blocking dopamine reuptake is cocaine's mechanism, and alcohol's rewarding effects on dopamine are indirect.

questions.q: A person who drinks heavily every day abruptly stops and develops tremors, agitation, and a seizure. What best explains this?
o: Alcohol withdrawal causes excess GABA activity
Withdrawal reduces inhibition; excess GABA would sedate.
The seizure is a direct toxic effect of alcohol in the blood
Symptoms appeared after stopping, when blood alcohol was falling.
The brain adapted to chronic inhibition, leaving it overexcited without alcohol
Correct: compensatory changes produce rebound hyperexcitability opposite to alcohol's depressant effect.
Thiamine deficiency suddenly destroyed the hippocampus
Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, not acute withdrawal seizures.
questions.note: Withdrawal symptoms are roughly the opposite of the drug's effects.
questions.x: With chronic alcohol use, the brain compensates for constant extra inhibition by reducing GABA-A responsiveness and increasing glutamate (NMDA) signaling. When alcohol is suddenly removed, these adaptations leave the brain hyperexcitable, producing tremors, agitation and seizures. Withdrawal effects are generally opposite to a drug's acute effects, which is why excess GABA cannot be the cause.

questions.q: Cocaine increases synaptic dopamine mainly by which mechanism?
o: Blocking dopamine reuptake transporters
Correct: cocaine blocks reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin.
Stimulating dopamine synthesis enzymes
Cocaine does not mainly act by increasing synthesis.
Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase
That raises acetylcholine, not dopamine.
Binding GABA-A receptors
That is the action of depressants such as alcohol and benzodiazepines.
questions.x: Cocaine blocks the transporters that remove dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin from the synapse, so these neurotransmitters stay in the cleft longer and keep stimulating receptors. Increased dopamine in the nucleus accumbens drives its reward. It does not mainly boost synthesis, and blocking acetylcholinesterase would raise acetylcholine, not dopamine.

questions.q: Amphetamine differs from cocaine mainly because amphetamine:
o: acts as a depressant at high doses
Amphetamine is a stimulant at all doses.
blocks opioid receptors
Amphetamine does not act at opioid receptors; blocking them is the action of antagonists such as naloxone.
has no effect on dopamine
Amphetamine strongly raises dopamine.
also drives release of monoamines from the neuron
Correct: amphetamine causes release of dopamine and norepinephrine, not just blocked reuptake.
questions.x: Cocaine mainly blocks monoamine reuptake. Amphetamine enters the presynaptic neuron, disrupts vesicular storage and reverses the transporters, actively driving dopamine and norepinephrine out into the synapse in addition to reducing reuptake. Both are stimulants that raise dopamine, so the difference lies in the release mechanism, not in whether dopamine is affected.

questions.q: A patient found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and very slow breathing is given naloxone and quickly recovers. Which drug class was most likely involved?
o: Stimulants
Stimulants cause dilated pupils and fast breathing.
Opioids
Correct: opioids cause miosis and respiratory depression, which naloxone reverses.
Hallucinogens
Hallucinogens rarely cause respiratory depression and are not reversed by naloxone.
Cannabinoids
Cannabis does not cause this picture, and naloxone does not reverse it.
questions.x: Opioid overdose classically produces the triad of unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils (miosis) and respiratory depression, the main cause of death. Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist that displaces the drug and rapidly reverses these effects. Stimulants are the opposite case, causing dilated pupils and fast breathing, and naloxone does not reverse other drug classes.

questions.q: LSD produces visual distortions mainly by acting at which receptor?
o: Dopamine D2 receptor
Antipsychotics block D2; LSD's main effects come from serotonin receptors.
NMDA glutamate receptor
NMDA blockade is the mechanism of PCP and ketamine.
Serotonin 5-HT2A receptor
Correct: classic hallucinogens act as agonists at 5-HT2A receptors.
Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
That is nicotine's target.
questions.x: Classic hallucinogens such as LSD, psilocybin and mescaline produce perceptual distortions mainly as agonists at serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, especially in the cortex. Dissociative drugs like PCP and ketamine act differently, by blocking NMDA glutamate receptors. Dopamine D2 is tempting because psychosis involves dopamine, but it is not LSD's primary target.

questions.q: A study finds that people who used marijuana an hour earlier recall fewer words from a list just learned. This most likely reflects THC acting on:
o: cannabinoid receptors, impairing short-term memory
Correct: THC binds CB1 receptors, including in the hippocampus, and impairs short-term memory.
opioid receptors, causing respiratory depression
THC does not act mainly on opioid receptors.
adenosine receptors, increasing alertness
That is caffeine's mechanism.
GABA-A receptors, inducing deep sleep
THC's memory effects are tied to cannabinoid receptors.
questions.x: THC, the main psychoactive compound in marijuana, binds CB1 cannabinoid receptors, which are dense in the hippocampus, cerebellum and basal ganglia. Activation of hippocampal CB1 receptors disrupts the encoding of new memories, explaining poorer recall of a recently learned list. THC does not act mainly through opioid, adenosine or GABA receptors.

questions.q: A festival-goer who took MDMA develops a dangerously high body temperature. MDMA's main mechanism is:
o: blocking adenosine receptors
That is caffeine.
triggering massive serotonin release
Correct: MDMA releases serotonin (and dopamine), producing euphoria and risk of hyperthermia.
activating mu opioid receptors
That is the action of opioids.
enhancing GABA-A receptors
That is the action of depressants.
questions.x: MDMA (ecstasy) reverses the serotonin transporter, causing massive serotonin release along with dopamine and norepinephrine release. This produces euphoria and emotional closeness but also impairs temperature regulation, which with dancing in hot crowds can cause dangerous hyperthermia. Repeated use may deplete serotonin. It does not act on adenosine, opioid or GABA receptors.

questions.q: Caffeine increases alertness mainly by:
o: stimulating melatonin release
Melatonin promotes sleep, not alertness.
blocking dopamine reuptake
That is cocaine's mechanism.
activating GABA receptors
GABA activation would sedate.
blocking adenosine receptors
Correct: adenosine builds up with wakefulness and promotes sleep; caffeine blocks its receptors.
questions.x: Adenosine accumulates in the brain during wakefulness and acts on its receptors to promote sleepiness, contributing to homeostatic sleep pressure. Caffeine is an adenosine receptor antagonist, so it blocks this sleep signal and increases alertness. Blocking dopamine reuptake is cocaine's mechanism, and activating GABA receptors would sedate rather than arouse.

questions.q: Nicotine produces its stimulant and rewarding effects primarily by binding to:
o: nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Correct: nicotine activates nAChRs, which indirectly increases dopamine release.
muscarinic acetylcholine receptors
Nicotine is named for, and acts at, nicotinic receptors.
serotonin 5-HT2A receptors
Those are targets of hallucinogens.
cannabinoid CB1 receptors
Those are targets of THC.
questions.x: Nicotine is an agonist at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, ligand-gated ion channels found in the brain, autonomic ganglia and neuromuscular junction. In the ventral tegmental area, nicotinic activation increases dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens, which drives reinforcement. Muscarinic receptors are a separate, G protein-coupled acetylcholine receptor class that nicotine does not target.

questions.q: Which pathway is most central to the reinforcing effects shared by many addictive drugs?
o: Nigrostriatal dopamine from substantia nigra to striatum
That pathway mainly controls movement.
Serotonin projections from raphe nuclei to cortex
Raphe serotonin is important in mood, but not the core reward pathway.
Mesolimbic dopamine from ventral tegmental area to nucleus accumbens
Correct: most addictive drugs increase dopamine in the nucleus accumbens.
Cholinergic projections from basal forebrain to hippocampus
Those support memory and attention.
questions.x: The mesolimbic pathway carries dopamine from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens and is the core reward pathway; most addictive drugs raise dopamine there, directly or indirectly. The nigrostriatal pathway is the tempting distractor because it also uses dopamine, but it runs from the substantia nigra to the striatum and mainly controls movement, as Parkinson disease shows.

questions.q: A chronic opioid user needs higher doses to get the same effect. Which change in the nervous system best explains this?
o: Increased opioid receptor number
More receptors would increase sensitivity, not reduce it.
Lower blood-brain barrier permeability to the drug
Tolerance mainly reflects neural adaptation, not a barrier change.
Sensitization of the reward pathway
Sensitization increases response to a drug, the opposite of tolerance.
Downregulation and desensitization of opioid receptors
Correct: tolerance arises as receptors decrease in number or responsiveness.
questions.x: Tolerance is a reduced response to a drug after repeated use, so larger doses are needed for the same effect. For opioids, neurons adapt by downregulating receptor number and desensitizing receptor signaling. Sensitization is the opposite process, in which repeated exposure increases a response, and adding receptors would make the drug more potent, not less.

questions.q: A person tolerant to alcohol also needs higher doses of barbiturates to be sedated. Why?
o: Both drugs block dopamine reuptake
Neither drug works mainly by blocking dopamine reuptake.
Both drugs enhance GABA-A signaling, so adaptation to one affects the other
Correct: cross-tolerance occurs between drugs acting on the same system.
Alcohol destroys barbiturates in the bloodstream
There is no such chemical interaction.
Barbiturates are a type of opioid
Barbiturates are sedative-hypnotics acting at GABA-A receptors.
questions.x: Cross-tolerance occurs when tolerance to one drug reduces the effect of another that acts on the same neural system. Alcohol and barbiturates both enhance GABA-A receptor function, so adaptations from chronic drinking also blunt barbiturate sedation. This shared mechanism also makes combining these drugs dangerous, since their depressant effects add together.

questions.q: Which list correctly pairs each drug with its class?
o: Heroin: stimulant; caffeine: depressant
Heroin is an opioid and caffeine is a stimulant.
Alcohol: stimulant; LSD: opioid
Alcohol is a depressant and LSD is a hallucinogen.
Benzodiazepines: depressant; methamphetamine: stimulant
Correct: benzodiazepines enhance GABA, while methamphetamine increases monoamine release.
Nicotine: hallucinogen; morphine: depressant of GABA
Nicotine is a stimulant and morphine is an opioid.
questions.x: Psychoactive drugs are grouped by effect: depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates) lower CNS activity, often via GABA; stimulants (caffeine, nicotine, cocaine, amphetamines) raise arousal; opioids (heroin, morphine) act on opioid receptors; and hallucinogens (LSD) alter perception. Only the benzodiazepine-depressant and methamphetamine-stimulant pairing classifies both drugs correctly.

questions.q: Which component of the brainstem is most responsible for maintaining wakefulness and arousal?
o: Reticular activating system
Correct: the RAS projects to the thalamus and cortex to maintain alertness; damage can cause coma.
Cerebellum
The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.
Medulla's respiratory center
That center controls breathing, not arousal.
Superior colliculus
The superior colliculus directs visual orienting.
questions.x: The reticular activating system is a network of brainstem nuclei that projects through the thalamus and hypothalamus to the cortex to maintain wakefulness and alertness and to filter incoming stimuli. Damage to it can cause coma. The medulla's respiratory center is tempting because it is also brainstem, but it controls breathing rather than arousal.

questions.q: In a study, volunteers kept awake 24 hours show slower reaction times that are worst around 4 a.m., then partly improve by 10 a.m. despite even longer wakefulness. What best explains the improvement?
o: Adenosine is fully cleared during wakefulness
Adenosine keeps accumulating with continued wakefulness.
REM rebound occurs while awake
REM rebound happens during recovery sleep, not wakefulness.
Melatonin levels peak in the morning
Melatonin is suppressed in the morning.
Circadian alerting signals rise in the morning, offsetting sleep pressure
Correct: the circadian rhythm boosts alertness in daytime even as homeostatic sleep pressure grows.
questions.x: Alertness reflects two interacting processes: homeostatic sleep pressure, which keeps rising with time awake, and a circadian alerting signal from the SCN, which is lowest in the early morning hours and rises during the day. Around 4 a.m. high pressure combines with the circadian trough, so performance is worst; by mid-morning the rising circadian signal partly offsets accumulated pressure.

questions.q: Participants judge words as either "Does it rhyme with 'cat'?" or "Is it a type of animal?" On a surprise recall test, the animal-question words are recalled far better. What explains this?
o: Rhyme judgments use the visuospatial sketchpad
Rhyme judgments are phonological, and the finding concerns depth, not a storage component.
The rhyme words were more vulnerable to proactive interference
Interference was not manipulated; only the type of processing differed.
Semantic processing produces deeper encoding
Correct: levels-of-processing theory holds that meaning-based encoding yields stronger memories.
Maintenance rehearsal was used for the animal words
No rehearsal was required; the judgment type changed how deeply words were processed.
questions.x: Levels-of-processing theory holds that memory strength depends on how deeply information is processed at encoding. Judging meaning (is it an animal?) is deep, semantic processing, while judging sound (does it rhyme?) is shallower phonological processing, so semantically processed words are better remembered. No rehearsal or interference differed; only the type of judgment changed.

questions.q: Students remember trait words better when asked "Does this word describe you?" than "Does this word describe the mayor?" This is the:
o: self-reference effect
Correct: relating information to oneself produces especially deep, elaborate encoding.
spacing effect
The spacing effect concerns distributing study sessions over time.
primacy effect
Primacy is better recall for early list items.
misinformation effect
That is memory distortion from misleading post-event information.
questions.x: The self-reference effect is better memory for information related to oneself. Asking whether a trait describes you engages rich, elaborate encoding tied to the extensive, well-organized knowledge you have about yourself, which creates many retrieval cues. Judging the mayor involves meaning too, but with less personal elaboration, so recall is weaker.

questions.q: Without trying, you can recall roughly how many times you ate pizza last month. This is an example of:
o: effortful processing
Effortful processing requires attention and rehearsal.
maintenance rehearsal
Rehearsal is a deliberate repetition strategy.
chunking
Chunking groups items into larger units.
automatic processing
Correct: frequency, time, and location information are often encoded without effort.
questions.x: Automatic processing encodes some information, such as frequency, time and location, with little conscious effort or attention. That is why you can estimate how often you ate pizza without having tried to track it. Effortful processing, such as rehearsal and chunking, requires deliberate attention and is needed for things like new vocabulary or formulas.

questions.q: Two groups study vocabulary for 3 hours total: one in a single session, the other in six 30-minute sessions over two weeks. A month later, the second group remembers more. This shows:
o: the serial position effect
Serial position concerns recall by list position.
the spacing effect
Correct: distributed practice yields better long-term retention than massed practice.
state-dependent memory
No internal state differed between learning and testing.
retroactive interference
Interference would predict worse, not better, recall for one group.
questions.x: The spacing effect, or distributed practice, means that studying in several sessions spread over time produces better long-term retention than the same total time crammed into one session (massed practice). Spacing allows forgetting and effortful re-retrieval between sessions, strengthening memory traces. Total study time was equal, so the difference comes from distribution alone.

questions.q: Remembering the digits 1-9-4-5-2-0-0-1 as "1945" and "2001" is an example of:
o: elaborative rehearsal
Elaborative rehearsal links information to meaning; here digits are grouped into units.
priming
Priming is unconscious facilitation from prior exposure.
chunking
Correct: grouping items into meaningful units increases what short-term memory can hold.
the method of loci
The method of loci uses imagined locations.
questions.x: Chunking groups individual items into larger, meaningful units, which effectively expands short-term memory capacity of about 7 ± 2 items. Eight separate digits become two familiar years, easily held as two chunks. Elaborative rehearsal is tempting because meaning is used, but it refers to linking information to existing knowledge for long-term storage rather than regrouping items.

questions.q: A 3×4 grid of letters is flashed for 50 ms. When a tone right after the flash cues one row to report, participants recall most letters in that row, but the advantage vanishes if the tone is delayed 1 second. What does this show?
o: Iconic memory holds much of the image but fades within about a second
Correct: the partial report advantage shows high capacity, and its loss with delay shows rapid decay.
Short-term memory holds only one row at a time
Any cued row is well reported, so most of the display was briefly available.
Echoic memory decays faster than iconic memory
Echoic memory lasts longer, a few seconds; this experiment tests visual memory.
The tone interferes with long-term memory
The effect concerns sensory memory lasting under a second, not long-term storage.
questions.note: Partial report > whole report means sensory memory holds more than we can report.
questions.x: Sperling's partial-report technique showed that iconic (visual sensory) memory briefly holds nearly the whole display, since any cued row could be reported well. Because the cue came after the display, the advantage means most letters were available at that moment. When the cue was delayed about a second, the advantage disappeared, showing iconic memory decays within roughly a second.

questions.q: Participants who repeat "the, the, the" aloud while memorizing a list of words recall fewer words, but their memory for the positions of dots on a screen is unaffected. Which conclusion fits Baddeley's model?
o: The central executive has been fully disabled
A disabled executive would impair both tasks.
Long-term memory consolidation is blocked
The tasks test immediate working memory, not consolidation.
The phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad are separate components
Correct: articulatory suppression loads the phonological loop but spares visuospatial storage.
Verbal and spatial information share one storage buffer
If they shared a buffer, both tasks would suffer.
questions.x: In Baddeley's working memory model, the phonological loop holds verbal information, the visuospatial sketchpad holds visual and spatial information, and a central executive directs attention. Repeating a word aloud (articulatory suppression) occupies the phonological loop, impairing verbal recall but sparing spatial memory. That selective impairment shows the two stores are separate.

questions.q: Repeating a phone number over and over keeps it in mind but does little for long-term retention. Which strategy would most improve long-term storage?
o: Elaborative rehearsal linking the number to meaningful facts
Correct: connecting information to existing knowledge creates durable long-term memories.
More maintenance rehearsal
Rote repetition keeps items in STM but encodes them shallowly.
Studying it only in one long session
Massed practice is less effective than spaced study.
Reducing attention to the number
Less attention would weaken encoding.
questions.x: Maintenance rehearsal, simple repetition, keeps information active in short-term memory but encodes it shallowly. Elaborative rehearsal connects new information to existing knowledge, such as linking digits to meaningful dates, creating richer encoding and more retrieval cues for long-term storage. More repetition alone is the tempting but weak strategy.

questions.q: Remembering how to ride a bicycle after years without practice reflects which memory type?
o: Episodic memory
Episodic memory stores specific personal experiences.
Semantic memory
Semantic memory stores facts and concepts.
Sensory memory
Sensory memory lasts only seconds.
Procedural memory
Correct: procedural memory is implicit memory for motor skills.
questions.x: Procedural memory is implicit memory for skills and habits, such as riding a bike, expressed through performance rather than conscious recall. It depends heavily on the basal ganglia and cerebellum and is very resistant to forgetting. Episodic and semantic memory are explicit (declarative) systems for events and facts, which you consciously retrieve.

questions.q: Recalling the details of your tenth birthday party is an example of which memory?
o: Semantic memory
Semantic memory is general knowledge, not a personal event.
Episodic memory
Correct: episodic memory stores personally experienced events in time and place.
Procedural memory
Procedural memory stores skills.
Implicit memory
This recall is conscious and declarative.
questions.x: Episodic memory is explicit memory for personally experienced events tied to a specific time and place, such as your tenth birthday party. Semantic memory stores general facts and knowledge without reference to when they were learned, such as knowing the date of your birthday. Both are declarative, so conscious recall of the party is not implicit memory.

questions.q: Participants exposed to the word "ELEPHANT" in an unrelated task are later more likely to complete "EL_____" with that word, even though they don't recall seeing it. This shows:
o: implicit memory through priming
Correct: prior exposure influences later responses without conscious recollection.
episodic memory for the first task
They cannot consciously recall the word, so the effect is not explicit episodic memory.
retroactive interference
Nothing new blocked an old memory; prior exposure helped performance.
the misinformation effect
No misleading information distorted a memory.
questions.x: Priming is a form of implicit memory in which prior exposure to a stimulus influences later processing without conscious awareness of the earlier exposure. Participants complete the word stem with ELEPHANT more often even though they cannot recall having seen it. Episodic memory would require conscious recollection of the original task, which they lack.

questions.q: People verify "A robin is a bird" faster than "A robin is an animal." Which model explains this best?
o: The serial position effect
That concerns position in a list.
The levels-of-processing model
That concerns encoding depth, not speed of verifying stored facts.
A hierarchical semantic network in which retrieval travels between linked nodes
Correct: "animal" is farther from "robin" in the network, so verification takes longer.
Baddeley's working memory model
That model describes short-term components, not organization of semantic knowledge.
questions.x: Collins and Quillian's hierarchical semantic network stores concepts as linked nodes, with properties at the most general applicable level. Verifying that a robin is a bird requires moving one link, while verifying that it is an animal requires moving two, so it takes longer. Levels of processing concerns encoding depth, not how long stored facts take to retrieve.

questions.q: In a lexical decision task, people decide faster that "nurse" is a word if it follows "doctor" than if it follows "table." Which concept explains this?
o: Proactive interference
Interference would slow, not speed, the response.
Spreading activation
Correct: activating one concept partially activates linked concepts in the semantic network.
Chunking
Chunking groups items for storage, not speeded recognition.
Decay
Decay is loss of memory over time.
questions.x: Spreading activation describes how activating one concept in a semantic network partially activates related concepts. Reading doctor pre-activates nurse, so recognizing nurse as a word is faster, an example of semantic priming. Unrelated words like table provide no head start. Proactive interference is tempting but would slow responses, not speed them.

questions.q: Which type of retrieval is usually easiest?
o: Free recall
Free recall gives no cues and is the hardest.
Cued recall
Cued recall provides hints but is still harder than recognition.
Serial recall
Recalling items in order adds difficulty.
Recognition
Correct: identifying a previously seen item among options needs the fewest retrieval cues.
questions.x: Recognition is usually the easiest form of retrieval because the target item itself is presented and serves as a strong retrieval cue; you only need to judge familiarity. Cued recall provides partial hints, and free recall provides none, making it hardest. This is why multiple-choice questions feel easier than fill-in-the-blank or essay questions.

questions.q: Ebbinghaus learned a list, forgot it completely, then relearned it in 40% fewer trials than the first time. What does this show?
o: The list was fully erased from memory
Faster relearning shows some trace remained.
Memory traces remain even when recall fails
Correct: savings in relearning reveal stored information that recall could not access.
Interference strengthened the original memory
Interference weakens memory; it does not help.
Recognition is harder than recall
Relearning is a separate retention measure; recognition is generally easier than recall.
questions.x: Ebbinghaus measured retention with the savings method: how much less effort is needed to relearn material compared with learning it originally. Relearning faster after apparently total forgetting shows that a memory trace persisted even though it could not be recalled. Relearning is therefore the most sensitive retention measure, more sensitive than both recognition and recall.

questions.q: According to Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, how is information lost over time?
o: Slowly at first, then rapidly
This reverses the curve's shape.
At a constant rate
Forgetting is not linear.
Rapidly at first, then leveling off
Correct: most forgetting happens soon after learning, and the remainder declines slowly.
Not at all for meaningless information
Nonsense syllables were forgotten quickly in his studies.
questions.x: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve shows that retention drops steeply soon after learning, then levels off, so what remains after a few days declines only slowly. The curve is not linear or delayed. This rapid early loss is why reviewing material shortly after learning and spacing later reviews is so effective.

questions.q: Divers learn word lists underwater or on land and are tested in the same or the other setting. Recall is best when learning and testing settings match. Which principle does this support?
o: Encoding specificity (context-dependent memory)
Correct: matching external context at retrieval provides effective cues.
State-dependent memory
State dependence concerns internal states, such as mood or drugs, not physical settings.
The spacing effect
Study was not distributed over time differently.
Levels of processing
Depth of processing was not manipulated.
questions.x: Encoding specificity holds that memory is best when the context at retrieval matches the context at encoding, because contextual features are stored with the memory and serve as cues. The diver study shows context-dependent memory for external physical environments. State-dependent memory is the tempting alternative, but it concerns internal states such as mood or drug effects.

questions.q: Students who study after drinking coffee recall more on a test if they also drink coffee before the test. This best illustrates:
o: context-dependent memory
Context dependence refers to external environments, not internal states.
the self-reference effect
No self-relevance was manipulated.
proactive interference
Interference involves competing memories, not matching states.
state-dependent memory
Correct: matching internal physiological state at study and test aids retrieval.
questions.x: State-dependent memory is improved recall when one's internal physiological or psychological state at testing matches the state during learning, such as being caffeinated both times. The internal state acts as a retrieval cue. Context-dependent memory is the tempting alternative, but it refers to external surroundings like the room or setting.

questions.q: A depressed patient easily recalls past failures but struggles to recall happy events. This is:
o: state-dependent memory based on drug use
No drug is involved here.
mood-congruent memory
Correct: current mood biases retrieval toward memories with matching emotional tone.
retrograde amnesia
Amnesia would affect memories regardless of emotional content.
the misinformation effect
No misleading information was introduced.
questions.x: Mood-congruent memory is the tendency to recall memories whose emotional tone matches one's current mood, so a depressed person more readily retrieves sad or failure-related events. This can reinforce depressive thinking. It differs from state-dependent memory, which is about matching the state at encoding and retrieval, not about the emotional content of what is recalled.

questions.q: You know an actor's name, can recall it starts with "M," but cannot produce it. This is an example of:
o: the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon, a retrieval failure
Correct: the memory is stored, and partial information is available, but full retrieval fails.
an encoding failure
Knowing the first letter shows the name was encoded.
decay
Decay implies the trace is lost; partial access shows it is stored.
anterograde amnesia
That is an inability to form new memories.
questions.x: The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon is a temporary retrieval failure: the memory is stored, and partial information such as the first letter or number of syllables is accessible, but the full item cannot be produced. Because partial access shows the information was encoded and retained, neither encoding failure nor decay explains it.

questions.q: After learning Spanish, a student starting French keeps producing Spanish words instead of the new French ones. This is:
o: retroactive interference
Retroactive interference is new learning disrupting old memories.
source amnesia
Source amnesia is forgetting where information came from.
proactive interference
Correct: older learning disrupts recall of newer information.
decay theory
Decay is fading from disuse, not competition between memories.
questions.note: Proactive = old blocks new; retroactive = new blocks old.
questions.x: Proactive interference occurs when previously learned information disrupts learning or recall of newer information, so old Spanish words intrude on new French ones. Retroactive interference is the reverse, when new learning disrupts recall of older material. Remember: proactive acts forward in time, from old to new, while retroactive acts backward, from new to old.

questions.q: Groups learn a word list, then either sleep or stay awake for 8 hours before testing. The sleep group recalls more. Why does this argue against pure decay theory?
o: Sleep increases how fast memory traces decay
Faster decay would predict worse recall after sleep.
Both groups were exposed to the same interference
The awake group experienced more interfering activity.
Decay predicts that the sleep group should recall more
Decay depends only on time, which was equal across groups.
Equal time passed, so differences point to interference or consolidation
Correct: decay depends only on elapsed time; the difference suggests waking interference and sleep consolidation.
questions.x: Pure decay theory says forgetting depends only on time passing. Since both groups waited the same 8 hours, decay alone predicts equal recall. The sleep group's advantage instead points to interference from waking experiences, which the sleep group was spared, and to sleep-dependent consolidation that strengthens new memories.

questions.q: Witnesses watch a video of a car crash. Those later asked how fast the cars were going when they "crashed into" each other report higher speeds than those asked about cars that "bumped." This shows:
o: proactive interference
No earlier learning disrupted the memory.
the misinformation effect
Correct: wording of later questions alters reconstructed memories.
context-dependent memory
Context of learning and testing was the same for both groups.
the self-reference effect
No self-relevance was involved.
questions.x: The misinformation effect, shown by Loftus and Palmer, is the distortion of memory by misleading information encountered after an event. The verb crashed implies a violent collision, so witnesses reconstruct the memory with higher speeds, and some later even report seeing broken glass that was not there. This shows memory is reconstructive rather than a fixed recording.

questions.q: A man vividly remembers hearing a story from a friend, when he actually read it in a magazine. This error is called:
o: source monitoring error
Correct: the content is remembered, but its origin is misattributed.
retroactive interference
Interference involves competing memories blocking recall.
decay
The memory itself is intact; its source is wrong.
encoding failure
The content was encoded; only its source was confused.
questions.x: A source monitoring error, also called source misattribution, occurs when the content of a memory is retained but its origin is misremembered, such as believing a friend told you something you actually read. Source memory is especially fragile. Decay and encoding failure do not fit, because the content itself is intact and only its source is wrong.

questions.q: Participants study "bed, rest, tired, dream, pillow, snore" and later many confidently recall "sleep," which was never shown. What does this show?
o: Short-term memory has limited capacity
Capacity limits cannot explain recalling an unpresented word.
Iconic memory decays quickly
The words were not briefly flashed, and decay would not add a word.
Memory is reconstructive and influenced by semantic associations
Correct: activated related concepts can produce confident false memories.
The list was encoded too shallowly
Shallow encoding would reduce recall of studied words, not create a new one.
questions.x: In the Deese-Roediger-McDermott paradigm, studying words strongly associated with an unpresented lure such as sleep leads many people to confidently recall the lure. Spreading activation in the semantic network activates the lure, and reconstructive retrieval treats it as studied. Shallow encoding or capacity limits would reduce recall of studied words, not add a new one.

questions.q: Participants read a story from an unfamiliar culture and, when retelling it later, change odd details to fit their own cultural expectations. This shows that memory retrieval is influenced by:
o: sensory memory
Sensory memory lasts seconds and does not reshape stories.
schemas
Correct: existing knowledge frameworks guide how memories are reconstructed.
procedural memory
Procedural memory is for skills, not story content.
the spacing effect
Study timing was not manipulated.
questions.x: Bartlett's War of the Ghosts studies showed that people reconstruct memories using schemas, organized frameworks of prior knowledge and expectations. Unfamiliar details were distorted, shortened or replaced to fit the reteller's cultural schemas. Memory retrieval is therefore an active reconstruction rather than a faithful replay, which also helps explain everyday memory errors.

questions.q: After surgery removing both medial temporal lobes, a patient cannot remember new people or events but improves daily at a mirror-drawing task he insists he has never done. What does this show?
o: The hippocampus stores all long-term memories permanently
His new skill learning occurred without the hippocampus, so it cannot be the store for all long-term memory.
Procedural memory depends on the hippocampus
His skill learning improved despite hippocampal loss.
He has retrograde amnesia only
He cannot form new explicit memories, which is anterograde amnesia.
Explicit and implicit memory rely on different brain systems
Correct: declarative memory needs the hippocampus, but procedural learning uses other structures.
questions.x: Patient H.M. lost both medial temporal lobes, including the hippocampi, and developed severe anterograde amnesia for new facts and events. Yet he improved at mirror drawing without remembering practicing, showing that implicit procedural learning depends on other structures such as the basal ganglia and cerebellum. Thus explicit and implicit memory rely on different brain systems.

questions.q: After a head injury, a woman cannot recall events from the year before the accident but remembers her childhood well and forms new memories normally. She has:
o: retrograde amnesia
Correct: loss of memories formed before the injury, often sparing older memories.
anterograde amnesia
She can form new memories, so anterograde function is intact.
source amnesia
Source amnesia involves forgetting where information came from.
Korsakoff syndrome
Korsakoff syndrome involves anterograde amnesia with confabulation from thiamine deficiency.
questions.note: Recent memories are lost first in retrograde amnesia; older ones are spared.
questions.x: Retrograde amnesia is loss of memories formed before an injury, typically with a temporal gradient: recent memories are lost and older ones such as childhood are spared, because older memories are more consolidated. Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories after the injury, which she does not have since new learning is normal.

questions.q: At hippocampal synapses, strong high-frequency stimulation produces long-lasting increases in response strength. Which event is required to start this long-term potentiation?
o: GABA binding that hyperpolarizes the postsynaptic cell
Hyperpolarization would prevent, not trigger, LTP.
Blocking all postsynaptic sodium channels
Without depolarization, the Mg²⁺ block on NMDA receptors could not be relieved.
Depolarization removing Mg²⁺ from NMDA receptors, allowing Ca²⁺ influx
Correct: Ca²⁺ entry through NMDA receptors triggers signaling that strengthens the synapse.
A decrease in AMPA receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
AMPA receptors are added, not removed, in LTP.
questions.x: LTP requires coincident presynaptic glutamate release and postsynaptic depolarization. Glutamate binds AMPA receptors, depolarizing the cell enough to expel the Mg²⁺ ion that blocks the NMDA receptor channel. Ca²⁺ then enters through NMDA receptors and activates kinases that insert more AMPA receptors, strengthening the synapse. Hyperpolarization or fewer AMPA receptors would oppose LTP.

questions.q: People often have unusually vivid memories of where they were when they heard shocking news. Which structure most enhances encoding of such emotional memories?
o: Cerebellum
The cerebellum supports motor learning and coordination.
Amygdala
Correct: the amygdala modulates hippocampal encoding of emotionally arousing events.
Occipital lobe
The occipital lobe processes vision, not emotional enhancement.
Basal ganglia
The basal ganglia support habits and procedural learning.
questions.note: Flashbulb memories feel vivid but are not always accurate.
questions.x: The amygdala responds to emotional arousal and, partly via stress hormones such as norepinephrine, enhances the hippocampus's consolidation of emotional memories. This explains flashbulb memories, which feel vivid and are held with high confidence, though their accuracy often degrades over time like other memories. The basal ganglia support habits rather than emotional enhancement.

questions.q: A man with long-term heavy alcohol use cannot form new memories and fills in gaps with made-up stories he believes are true. What is the most likely underlying cause?
o: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency
Correct: Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine deficiency and features anterograde amnesia and confabulation.
Loss of orexin neurons
Orexin loss causes narcolepsy.
Destruction of the suprachiasmatic nucleus
SCN damage disrupts circadian rhythms, not memory formation.
Dopamine loss in the substantia nigra
That is the cause of Parkinson disease.
questions.x: Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most often from chronic alcohol use with poor nutrition. It damages structures such as the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus, causing severe anterograde amnesia and confabulation, sincerely believed invented stories that fill memory gaps. It often follows acute Wernicke encephalopathy.

questions.q: In typical language development, about when do most children speak their first recognizable words?
o: About 2 months
At 2 months infants coo but do not speak words.
About 6 months
Around 6 months infants begin babbling.
About 12 months
Correct: first words usually appear around the first birthday.
About 36 months
By 3 years children are speaking in sentences.
questions.x: Language develops in a predictable sequence: cooing at about 2 months, babbling at about 6 months, first words around 12 months, two-word telegraphic speech around 18 to 24 months, and simple sentences by about 3 years. Babbling is the tempting distractor because it sounds speech-like, but it consists of syllables without meaning.

questions.q: A 3-year-old says "I goed to the park and saw two mouses." What does this error suggest?
o: The child is imitating adult speech exactly
Adults do not say "goed," so this is not pure imitation.
The child is applying grammatical rules too broadly
Correct: overregularization shows the child has learned rules for past tense and plurals.
The child has a language disorder
Overregularization is a normal stage of development.
The child is in the telegraphic speech stage
Telegraphic speech omits function words, as in "go park."
questions.x: Overregularization occurs when children apply a grammatical rule, such as adding -ed for past tense or -s for plurals, to irregular words, producing goed or mouses. Because adults do not say these forms, the errors show children are extracting rules rather than simply imitating. It is a normal developmental stage and often follows earlier correct use of irregular forms.

questions.q: A 2-year-old says "Daddy go car" to mean that Daddy is going to the car. This kind of speech is called:
o: babbling
Babbling consists of repeated syllables without meaning.
overregularization
Overregularization is overextending grammar rules.
holophrastic speech
Holophrastic speech uses one word to express a whole idea.
telegraphic speech
Correct: telegraphic speech uses key content words and omits function words.
questions.x: Telegraphic speech, typically around 18 to 24 months, uses mainly content words such as nouns and verbs in the right order while omitting function words, articles and inflections, like a telegram. Daddy go car fits this pattern. Holophrastic speech is the earlier one-word stage, where a single word like car conveys a whole idea.

questions.q: Chomsky argued that children learn language too quickly and uniformly to be explained by imitation alone. His theory proposes:
o: an innate language acquisition device
Correct: the nativist view holds that humans have an inborn capacity for universal grammar.
operant conditioning of speech sounds
That is Skinner's learning theory, which Chomsky opposed.
that language determines thought
That is linguistic determinism, the strong Sapir-Whorf view.
that social interaction alone builds language
That is the interactionist view.
questions.x: Chomsky's nativist theory proposes an innate language acquisition device containing universal grammar, which explains why children everywhere acquire complex grammar rapidly and in similar stages despite limited input. Skinner's behaviorist theory explains language through reinforcement and imitation, which Chomsky argued could not account for novel sentences children produce.

questions.q: A parent smiles and praises a baby each time she says "mama," and her use of the word increases. This supports which theory of language acquisition?
o: Nativist theory
Nativists emphasize innate mechanisms rather than reinforcement.
Linguistic relativity
Linguistic relativity concerns language shaping thought.
Learning (behaviorist) theory
Correct: Skinner proposed language is shaped through reinforcement.
Critical period hypothesis
That concerns a time window for learning language.
questions.x: The learning, or behaviorist, theory of language acquisition, associated with Skinner, proposes that language is shaped through operant conditioning: utterances that are reinforced, such as with praise, increase in frequency. Increased use of mama after praise fits this view. Nativist theory emphasizes innate mechanisms rather than reinforcement history.

questions.q: A child isolated from language until age 13 later learns many words but never masters grammar. Which hypothesis does this case best support?
o: Linguistic relativity
This case concerns acquiring language, not language shaping thought.
Activation-synthesis
That is a theory of dreaming.
Behaviorist theory
She received reinforcement later but still failed to master grammar, which reinforcement alone would not predict.
A critical period for language acquisition
Correct: grammar may be hard to acquire if exposure is missing early in life.
questions.x: The critical period hypothesis proposes that language, especially grammar, is most readily acquired during a window in early life, and that missing exposure during this window makes full mastery very difficult. A child isolated until 13 who later learns vocabulary but not grammar supports this. Behaviorism would predict that later reinforcement should eventually produce grammatical speech.

questions.q: Six-month-old English-learning infants can tell apart two Hindi speech sounds, but by 12 months most cannot, while Hindi-learning infants still can. What does this show?
o: Perception narrows to the phonemes of the native language
Correct: infants start sensitive to many phoneme contrasts and lose those not used in their language.
English infants develop hearing loss
They can still hear; only discrimination of non-native contrasts declines.
Hindi sounds are learned through reinforcement
No reinforcement was manipulated.
Language determines color perception
The study concerns speech sounds, not color.
questions.x: Infants are born able to distinguish phoneme contrasts from many languages, but during the first year their perception narrows to the contrasts used in their native language. By about 10 to 12 months, sensitivity to non-native contrasts declines while native ones are kept. This reflects perceptual tuning to linguistic experience, not hearing loss.

questions.q: How many morphemes are in the word "unhappiness"?
o: "Unhappiness" can be split into meaningful parts.
This misses one of the meaningful units.
Correct: un- (not) + happy + -ness (state of) are three morphemes.
Syllables are not the same as morphemes; there are only three units of meaning.
questions.note: Morpheme = smallest unit of meaning; phoneme = smallest unit of sound.
questions.x: A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning in a language. Unhappiness contains three: the prefix un- (not), the root happy, and the suffix -ness (state of being). A common mistake is counting syllables instead of meaningful units, which gives the four-syllable un-hap-pi-ness rather than three morphemes.

questions.q: Asked "Can you pass the salt?" a child answers "Yes" without moving. The child is missing which aspect of language?
o: Phonology
The child heard and pronounced the words correctly.
Syntax
The sentence's structure was understood.
Semantics
The literal meaning was understood.
Pragmatics
Correct: pragmatics is understanding language use in social context, such as indirect requests.
questions.x: Pragmatics is the use of language in social context, including understanding indirect requests, tone and conversational rules. Can you pass the salt? is literally a yes-or-no question but is socially a request. The child's literal answer shows intact phonology, syntax and semantics but missing pragmatic understanding of the speaker's intent.

questions.q: Speakers of a language with separate words for light and dark blue discriminate those shades slightly faster than speakers of a language with one word for both. This supports:
o: strong linguistic determinism
The strong view says thought is impossible without the words; both groups could still tell the shades apart.
weak linguistic relativity
Correct: language subtly influences perception and thought without fully determining it.
the nativist theory of language
Nativism concerns acquisition, not effects of vocabulary on perception.
the critical period hypothesis
No timing of language exposure was examined.
questions.x: The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis comes in two forms. Strong linguistic determinism claims language determines thought, so concepts without words cannot be perceived; weak linguistic relativity claims language merely influences thought and perception. A small speed advantage, with both groups still able to distinguish the shades, supports the weak version rather than the strong one.

questions.q: After a stroke, a patient understands speech but produces slow, effortful speech with few function words. Which area is most likely damaged?
o: Broca's area in the frontal lobe
Correct: Broca's aphasia is nonfluent with relatively intact comprehension.
Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe
Wernicke's aphasia produces fluent speech with poor comprehension.
The arcuate fasciculus
Damage there mainly impairs repetition.
The occipital lobe
The occipital lobe processes vision.
questions.x: Broca's area, in the left inferior frontal lobe, supports speech production. Damage causes Broca's (expressive, nonfluent) aphasia: slow, effortful, telegraphic speech with few function words, but relatively preserved comprehension, and patients are often aware and frustrated. Wernicke's aphasia is the opposite pattern, fluent speech with poor comprehension.

questions.q: A patient speaks fluently in long sentences that make little sense and seems unaware of errors and unable to follow commands. Which area is most likely damaged?
o: Broca's area
Broca's damage produces nonfluent speech with good comprehension.
Primary motor cortex
Motor cortex damage causes weakness, not meaningless fluent speech.
Wernicke's area
Correct: Wernicke's aphasia features fluent but meaningless speech and poor comprehension.
Cerebellum
Cerebellar damage may slur speech but does not cause loss of meaning.
questions.x: Wernicke's area, in the left posterior superior temporal lobe, supports language comprehension. Damage causes Wernicke's (receptive, fluent) aphasia: speech has normal rhythm but is filled with wrong or invented words and makes little sense, comprehension is poor, and patients are often unaware of their errors. Broca's damage instead produces nonfluent speech with good comprehension.

questions.q: A patient speaks fluently and understands well but cannot repeat a sentence spoken to her. Which structure is most likely damaged?
o: Broca's area
Broca's damage would make speech nonfluent.
Wernicke's area
Wernicke's damage would impair comprehension.
Corpus callosum
Callosal damage disconnects the hemispheres but does not typically cause this pattern.
Arcuate fasciculus
Correct: conduction aphasia results from damage to fibers linking Wernicke's and Broca's areas.
questions.x: Conduction aphasia classically results from damage to the arcuate fasciculus, the fiber bundle connecting Wernicke's area to Broca's area. Because both language areas still work, speech is fluent and comprehension is good, but the patient cannot repeat what was heard. Broca's or Wernicke's damage would impair fluency or comprehension instead.

questions.q: A split-brain patient briefly sees a picture of a key in the left visual field. She cannot name it but can pick out a key by touch with her left hand. Why?
o: The left hemisphere sees the left visual field
The left visual field projects to the right hemisphere.
The right hemisphere saw the key but language is mostly in the left hemisphere
Correct: the right hemisphere can guide the left hand but cannot pass information to left-sided language areas.
The patient has lost her semantic memory for keys
She recognizes the key by touch, so knowledge is intact.
The optic chiasm was cut in surgery
Split-brain surgery cuts the corpus callosum, not the optic chiasm.
questions.x: Each visual field projects to the opposite hemisphere, so an image in the left visual field reaches the right hemisphere. In most people speech is controlled by the left hemisphere, and with the corpus callosum cut the right hemisphere cannot share what it saw. It can still direct the left hand, which it controls, to find the key by touch, showing the knowledge is intact.

questions.q: Which set lists the three components of emotion as usually described in psychology?
o: Sensory, perceptual, motor
These describe stages of processing a stimulus, not the parts of an emotional experience.
Conscious, preconscious, unconscious
These are Freud's levels of awareness, not components of emotion.
Physiological, cognitive, behavioral
Correct: emotion involves bodily arousal, a subjective appraisal or feeling, and an outward expression.
Primary, secondary, tertiary
These terms describe appraisal stages or reinforcers, not emotion components.
questions.x: Psychologists usually describe emotion as a three-part experience: physiological arousal (heart rate, sweating), a cognitive component (the subjective feeling and appraisal), and a behavioral component (facial expressions, actions). Freud's conscious/preconscious/unconscious are levels of awareness and have nothing to do with how an emotion is built.

questions.q: A student hears footsteps behind her at night, notices her pounding heart, thinks 'I might be in danger,' and walks faster. The thought 'I might be in danger' represents which component of emotion?
o: Cognitive
Correct: the subjective interpretation of the situation is the cognitive component.
Physiological
The pounding heart is the physiological component, not the thought.
Behavioral
Walking faster is the behavioral component.
Motivational
Motivation is a related concept but is not one of the three classic emotion components.
questions.x: Breaking an emotional episode into parts: the pounding heart is physiological, walking faster is behavioral, and the thought interpreting the situation as dangerous is cognitive. Motivation is closely tied to emotion but is not one of the three classic components, so it is the tempting outsider here.

questions.q: Smiling, frowning, and clenching the fists during an emotional episode are examples of which emotion component?
o: Cognitive
The cognitive component is the internal appraisal or feeling, not visible actions.
Physiological
Physiological changes include heart rate and sweating, which are internal bodily responses.
Perceptual
Perception concerns interpreting sensory input, not emotional expression.
Behavioral
Correct: observable expressions and actions make up the behavioral component.
questions.x: The behavioral component of emotion is what others can observe: facial expressions, posture, gestures and actions. It is easy to confuse with the physiological component, but that one refers to internal autonomic changes such as heart rate, blood pressure and sweating, not visible muscle actions.

questions.q: Which observation is the best example of the physiological component of emotion?
o: Rating a film clip as 'very sad' on a questionnaire
A self-report reflects the cognitive, subjective component.
Increased skin conductance while viewing frightening images
Correct: sweating measured as skin conductance is an autonomic, physiological change.
Turning away from a disgusting smell
Turning away is a behavioral response.
Recalling a happy memory when asked to
Memory retrieval is a cognitive process, not a bodily change.
questions.x: The physiological component is the bodily, mostly autonomic side of emotion. Skin conductance rises when sympathetic activity makes the sweat glands active, so it is a classic physiological index of arousal. A questionnaire rating is a self-report of feeling (cognitive), and turning away is an overt action (behavioral).

questions.q: Which emotion is NOT among the six basic emotions Paul Ekman proposed as universally recognized from facial expressions?
o: Disgust
Disgust is one of Ekman's six universal emotions.
Jealousy
Correct: jealousy is a complex, socially shaped emotion without a universal facial signature.
Surprise
Surprise is one of Ekman's six universal emotions.
Fear
Fear is one of Ekman's six universal emotions.
questions.note: Ekman's six: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust (contempt sometimes added).
questions.x: Ekman's cross-cultural studies found six basic emotions with recognizable facial expressions everywhere: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust (contempt was later proposed as a seventh). Complex social emotions such as jealousy, guilt and pride depend more on cultural context and lack a universal facial signature.

questions.q: Members of an isolated community with no media exposure correctly match photographs of Western faces to stories about fear and anger. This finding most directly supports which idea?
o: Emotions are learned through observational modeling
No exposure means they could not have learned these specific Western expressions by modeling.
Display rules are identical across cultures
Display rules govern when emotions are shown and do vary by culture.
Physiological arousal precedes emotional labeling
The study tests recognition of expressions, not the timing of arousal and labeling.
Some emotional expressions are biologically universal
Correct: recognition without cultural contact suggests innate, shared expressions.
questions.x: If people with no exposure to Western media still match Western faces to emotional stories, the expressions cannot have been learned from that culture, which points to biologically universal expressions. Display rules, by contrast, are learned cultural norms about when to show emotion and they differ across cultures.

questions.q: In one culture, people suppress open displays of grief at funerals in public but weep freely in private. This pattern is best explained by:
o: cultural display rules
Correct: display rules are learned norms about when and where it is acceptable to show emotions.
the facial feedback hypothesis
Facial feedback concerns expressions influencing felt emotion, not social norms about display.
the absence of universal emotions
Weeping in private shows the emotion itself is present; only its display is regulated.
the Cannon-Bard theory
Cannon-Bard explains the timing of arousal and feeling, not cultural norms.
questions.x: Display rules are culturally learned norms about when, where and how strongly emotions may be shown. Weeping freely in private shows the grief itself is fully present; only its public display is regulated. The facial feedback hypothesis is about expressions shaping feelings, not about social norms controlling expressions.

questions.q: Darwin argued that emotional expressions are similar across humans and other animals because they:
o: are learned in early childhood from caregivers
Darwin emphasized inheritance and evolution, not learning.
are produced solely by cognitive appraisal
Appraisal-based theories came later and do not explain cross-species similarity.
evolved as adaptive signals that aided survival
Correct: Darwin viewed expressions as evolved, communicative behaviors.
arise from conditioned associations with rewards
That is a behaviorist account, not Darwin's evolutionary one.
questions.x: In The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, Darwin argued that expressions are inherited, evolved signals that helped survival, for example by communicating threat or submission. This evolutionary view predicts similarity across species and cultures, whereas learning or conditioning accounts would predict expressions that vary with experience.

questions.q: Participants who hold a pen between their teeth (forcing a smile) rate cartoons as funnier than those who hold it with their lips (preventing a smile). Which idea does this support?
o: Schachter-Singer two-factor theory
The study manipulated facial muscles, not arousal plus a cognitive label.
Cannon-Bard theory
Cannon-Bard says bodily changes do not cause emotion, which this result contradicts.
Yerkes-Dodson law
Yerkes-Dodson relates arousal to performance, not facial muscles to mood.
Facial feedback hypothesis
Correct: facial muscle activity feeds back to influence the emotion experienced.
questions.x: The facial feedback hypothesis says that facial muscle activity feeds back to the brain and shapes the emotion felt. The pen task changed only facial muscles, not arousal or labels, so it targets this idea rather than two-factor theory. Note that large replication attempts of this exact task have produced mixed results.

questions.q: A researcher finds that the facial feedback effect shrinks to near zero when participants are filmed during the task. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
o: Facial expressions are not universal across cultures
Universality is about recognition across cultures, not about this lab manipulation.
Emotion is entirely determined by cognitive labels
One moderator does not show that cognition is the only cause of emotion.
Self-awareness may disrupt the influence of facial muscles on feelings
Correct: a moderating variable (being observed) reduces the effect without proving it never exists.
Physiological arousal and emotion occur simultaneously
The study did not measure the timing of arousal and emotion.
questions.x: A moderator is a variable that changes the strength of an effect. If the facial feedback effect disappears when people know they are filmed, being observed (heightened self-awareness) is likely interfering with how facial muscles influence feeling. One moderator does not show the effect is fake or that emotions are purely cognitive.

questions.q: According to the James-Lange theory, a person feels afraid because:
o: the thalamus sends signals to cortex and body at the same time
That is the Cannon-Bard theory.
they notice their body's physiological response to the threat
Correct: James-Lange says the felt emotion is the perception of bodily arousal.
they cognitively label unexplained arousal as fear
That is the Schachter-Singer two-factor theory.
they appraise the situation before any arousal occurs
That is Lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory.
questions.x: James-Lange theory reverses common sense: a stimulus triggers bodily arousal, and perceiving that arousal is the emotion (we feel afraid because we tremble). Simultaneous thalamic signaling is Cannon-Bard, labeling unexplained arousal is Schachter-Singer, and appraisal before arousal is Lazarus.

questions.q: Which theory states that physiological arousal and the conscious experience of emotion occur simultaneously and independently?
o: Cannon-Bard
Correct: Cannon-Bard says the thalamus triggers arousal and feeling at the same time.
James-Lange
James-Lange says arousal comes first and causes the feeling.
Schachter-Singer
Schachter-Singer requires arousal plus a cognitive label to produce emotion.
Lazarus appraisal
Lazarus says appraisal comes first, then arousal and emotion.
questions.x: Cannon-Bard theory proposes that the thalamus sends signals at the same time to the cortex (producing the feeling) and to the body (producing arousal), so neither causes the other. James-Lange is the tempting alternative but makes arousal come first and cause the feeling.

questions.q: Suppose patients with high spinal cord injuries, who receive less bodily feedback, reported that their emotions felt less intense. Which theory would this finding best support?
o: James-Lange
Correct: if feelings depend on bodily feedback, reducing that feedback should weaken them.
Cannon-Bard
Cannon-Bard predicts emotions would be unaffected because feelings do not depend on bodily feedback.
Lazarus appraisal
Appraisal theory emphasizes thought, not the intensity of bodily feedback.
Opponent-process
Opponent-process theory concerns emotional rebound over time, not bodily feedback.
questions.note: Reduced bodily feedback → weaker emotion would support James-Lange.
questions.x: James-Lange holds that emotion is the perception of bodily changes, so less bodily feedback should mean weaker emotions. Cannon-Bard predicts no change, since feeling and arousal are independent outputs of the thalamus. Real data are mixed: Hohmann reported weaker emotions after spinal injury, but later studies often did not, so treat this as a prediction test.

questions.q: Walter Cannon criticized the James-Lange theory partly because:
o: emotions can be recognized across many cultures
Universality was not part of Cannon's critique.
very different emotions produce similar patterns of visceral arousal
Correct: if fear and anger look alike in the body, arousal alone cannot tell us which we feel.
cognitive labels are unnecessary for emotion
Cannon did not argue this; the point is about arousal patterns.
the hypothalamus plays no role in emotion
Cannon actually emphasized subcortical structures in emotion.
questions.x: One of Cannon's key objections was that visceral arousal is too similar across emotions: fear, anger and even excitement all raise heart rate and breathing. If the body looks the same, perceiving the body cannot tell us which emotion we feel, which undercuts James-Lange. Cannon's other main objection concerned timing.

questions.q: Cannon also argued that visceral changes are too slow to be the source of emotion. Which finding would best support this objection?
o: Injecting epinephrine produces arousal without a specific emotion
This supports a different Cannon point, that arousal is nonspecific, not the timing argument.
Facial expressions are recognized across cultures
This addresses universality, not timing of arousal versus feeling.
People report feeling fear before autonomic changes such as sweating begin
Correct: if feelings come first, bodily changes cannot be their cause.
Emotions vary with cognitive appraisal of the stressor
This supports appraisal theories, not the specific timing objection.
questions.x: Cannon argued that autonomic changes take seconds to develop, yet feelings arise almost immediately, so bodily changes cannot be the source of emotion. Evidence that fear is reported before sweating or heart-rate changes begin would support this timing argument. The epinephrine finding supports his separate point that arousal is nonspecific.

questions.q: The Schachter-Singer theory proposes that emotion results from:
o: physiological arousal alone
Arousal alone is the James-Lange view.
a cognitive appraisal that precedes any arousal
Appraisal first, then arousal, is Lazarus's view.
simultaneous thalamic signals to cortex and body
That describes Cannon-Bard.
physiological arousal plus a cognitive label for that arousal
Correct: the two factors are arousal and the interpretation of its cause.
