questions.x: Schachter-Singer two-factor theory says emotion requires both physiological arousal and a cognitive label explaining that arousal; the same arousal can become anger or euphoria depending on context. Arousal alone is James-Lange, and appraisal before arousal is Lazarus.

questions.q: In a study, aroused participants told 'the injection may cause a racing heart' showed little emotional reaction to an angry confederate, while uninformed participants became angry. Why did the informed group react less?
o: They experienced no physiological arousal at all
Both groups received the arousing injection; the difference was in interpretation.
They attributed their arousal to the injection rather than the situation
Correct: an available nonemotional explanation removes the need for an emotional label.
Their thalamus blocked the cortical experience of emotion
This is not how Cannon-Bard or the study explains the difference.
They used problem-focused coping to remove the confederate
Participants did not change the situation; their attribution differed.
questions.note: Two-factor theory: explained arousal does not get an emotional label.
questions.x: In two-factor theory, arousal becomes an emotion only when we label it with an emotional cause. Informed participants already had a nonemotional explanation (the injection), so they did not attribute their racing heart to the angry confederate. Both groups were aroused, which rules out the idea that the informed group felt no arousal.

questions.q: Men interviewed by an attractive researcher on a swaying suspension bridge more often called her later than men interviewed on a stable bridge. This result is usually explained by:
o: misattribution of arousal from fear to attraction
Correct: arousal from the bridge was labeled as romantic interest, consistent with two-factor theory.
the mere exposure effect
Exposure time was similar in both conditions, so familiarity cannot explain the difference.
the facial feedback hypothesis
Facial muscles were not manipulated in this design.
habituation to the fearful stimulus
Habituation would reduce arousal, not create attraction.
questions.x: In the classic bridge study, fear-related arousal from the swaying bridge was misattributed to attraction to the interviewer, a prediction of two-factor theory: unexplained arousal gets labeled using cues in the situation. Mere exposure cannot explain it because contact with the interviewer was similar on both bridges.

questions.q: According to Lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory of emotion, which event occurs first?
o: Physiological arousal
Arousal first is the James-Lange view.
Labeling of unexplained arousal
Labeling arousal is the key step in Schachter-Singer, after arousal occurs.
Facial expression of the emotion
Expression preceding emotion is the facial feedback idea.
Interpretation of the stimulus as harmful or beneficial
Correct: Lazarus held that appraisal comes before arousal and emotion.
questions.x: Lazarus held that cognitive appraisal comes first: we judge whether a stimulus is harmful, threatening or beneficial, and that judgment produces both arousal and the emotion. Schachter-Singer is the tempting confusion, but there labeling happens after arousal and serves to explain it.

questions.q: Two hikers see the same snake. One thinks 'harmless garter snake' and feels calm; the other thinks 'venomous!' and feels terror. Which theory best explains the different emotions?
o: James-Lange theory
James-Lange focuses on bodily responses, not on interpretations that differ before arousal.
Cannon-Bard theory
Cannon-Bard does not explain why identical stimuli yield different emotions.
Lazarus cognitive appraisal theory
Correct: the same stimulus produced different emotions because of different appraisals.
Facial feedback hypothesis
No facial manipulation explains the difference here.
questions.x: The stimulus is identical, yet the emotions differ completely, so the difference must come from how each person interprets the snake. That is the core of Lazarus's appraisal theory. James-Lange cannot explain it well, because it starts from bodily responses, which here would themselves depend on the prior appraisal.

questions.q: A researcher wants to distinguish Schachter-Singer from Lazarus. Which result would favor Lazarus?
o: Unexplained arousal is labeled according to a confederate's mood
This is the classic support for Schachter-Singer.
Emotions feel weaker after spinal cord injury
This supports James-Lange.
Emotional reports change with appraisal even when arousal is held constant and explained
Correct: emotion tracking appraisal without needing unexplained arousal supports Lazarus.
Arousal and feeling begin at the same moment
This supports Cannon-Bard.
questions.x: Schachter-Singer predicts emotion depends on labeling unexplained arousal, while Lazarus predicts emotion follows appraisal of the situation, with arousal as a consequence. Showing that emotions change with appraisal even when arousal is fixed and already explained removes the role of labeling and favors Lazarus. The confederate-mood result is the classic Schachter-Singer support.

questions.q: A person says, 'I trembled, so I realized I must be terrified.' This statement best matches which theory?
o: Cannon-Bard
Cannon-Bard would have the trembling and terror occur together, not one causing the other.
Lazarus appraisal
Lazarus would place the appraisal of danger before the trembling.
Opponent-process
This theory concerns emotional after-reactions, not inference from bodily cues.
James-Lange
Correct: the emotion is inferred from the perceived bodily response.
questions.x: James-Lange says we infer emotion from our bodily state: I tremble, therefore I am afraid. In Cannon-Bard, trembling and terror would arise together with neither causing the other, and in Lazarus the appraisal of danger would come first and produce the trembling.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts the Schachter-Singer and James-Lange theories?
o: Only Schachter-Singer requires a cognitive label for arousal
Correct: James-Lange says perception of arousal is the emotion; Schachter-Singer adds labeling.
Only James-Lange holds that arousal occurs before emotion
Both theories place arousal before the felt emotion.
Only Schachter-Singer says arousal is unimportant
Arousal is one of the two required factors in Schachter-Singer.
Only James-Lange involves the thalamus as a relay
Thalamic relay is the hallmark of Cannon-Bard.
questions.x: Both James-Lange and Schachter-Singer place arousal before the felt emotion. The difference is that James-Lange treats the perception of arousal itself as the emotion, while Schachter-Singer adds a second step, a cognitive label for why one is aroused. The thalamic relay belongs to Cannon-Bard, not either of these.

questions.q: In which theory of emotion does the thalamus play the central role in sending signals simultaneously to the cortex and the autonomic nervous system?
o: Schachter-Singer
Schachter-Singer is about arousal and labeling, not a thalamic relay.
Cannon-Bard
Correct: this is why it is sometimes called the thalamic theory.
James-Lange
James-Lange emphasizes peripheral bodily feedback.
Lazarus appraisal
Lazarus emphasizes cortical appraisal, not thalamic relay.
questions.x: Cannon-Bard is sometimes called the thalamic theory: a stimulus reaches the thalamus, which sends signals at the same time to the cortex (conscious feeling) and to the autonomic nervous system and body (arousal). James-Lange instead emphasizes feedback from peripheral bodily changes.

questions.q: Research shows fear and anger produce somewhat different patterns of heart rate and skin temperature. This finding partly weakens which criticism?
o: Lazarus's claim that appraisal precedes emotion
The finding is about arousal patterns, not the order of appraisal.
Ekman's claim that facial expressions are universal
The finding concerns autonomic patterns, not facial expressions.
Darwin's claim that expressions are adaptive
Arousal patterns do not bear on whether expressions are adaptive.
Cannon's claim that arousal patterns are too similar to distinguish emotions
Correct: distinct patterns suggest bodily states could contribute to which emotion is felt.
questions.x: Cannon argued that visceral arousal is too uniform to distinguish emotions, which seemed to sink James-Lange. Later work found partly distinct autonomic patterns, for example anger tending to warm the hands more than fear, which weakens Cannon's criticism and leaves room for bodily states to contribute to emotion.

questions.q: Which brain structure is most closely associated with detecting threats and generating fear responses?
o: Hippocampus
The hippocampus mainly supports forming new explicit memories.
Amygdala
Correct: the amygdala evaluates threat and drives fear and fear conditioning.
Cerebellum
The cerebellum coordinates movement and motor learning.
Broca's area
Broca's area supports speech production.
questions.x: The amygdala, deep in the temporal lobe, evaluates emotional significance, especially threat, and drives fear responses and fear conditioning through outputs to the hypothalamus and brainstem. The hippocampus is next door and is involved in emotional memory, but its main role is forming new explicit memories.

questions.q: A patient with bilateral amygdala damage would most likely show which deficit?
o: Inability to form new declarative memories
That is the classic result of hippocampal damage.
Loss of coordinated, smooth movement
That follows cerebellar damage.
Difficulty recognizing fear in others' facial expressions
Correct: amygdala damage impairs fear recognition and fear learning.
Inability to produce fluent speech
That follows damage to Broca's area.
questions.x: Patients with bilateral amygdala damage, such as the well-studied patient S.M., have trouble recognizing fear in faces and show little fear themselves, while memory and movement remain largely intact. Inability to form new declarative memories is the hallmark of hippocampal damage, a neighboring structure that is easy to confuse.

questions.q: A patient with hippocampal damage undergoes fear conditioning (tone paired with a loud noise). She shows a skin-conductance response to the tone but cannot say the tone was paired with the noise. A patient with amygdala damage shows the opposite. What does this double dissociation suggest?
o: The amygdala supports conditioned emotional responses and the hippocampus supports explicit memory of the pairing
Correct: each structure supports a different aspect of the fear memory.
Both structures are required for any form of fear learning
Each patient retained one form of learning, so neither structure is required for both.
The hippocampus generates autonomic fear responses
The hippocampal patient kept autonomic responses, so the hippocampus is not needed for them.
Fear conditioning depends only on the cerebellum
The deficits map onto amygdala and hippocampus damage, not the cerebellum.
questions.x: A double dissociation shows two functions depend on different structures. The hippocampal patient kept the conditioned autonomic response but lost explicit knowledge of the pairing; the amygdala patient knew the pairing but lacked the conditioned response. So the amygdala supports implicit emotional learning and the hippocampus supports declarative memory.

questions.q: Monkeys with bilateral temporal lobe lesions that include the amygdala become unusually tame, explore objects with their mouths, and show reduced fear. This pattern is called:
o: Klüver-Bucy syndrome
Correct: tameness, hyperorality, and reduced fear follow bilateral anterior temporal damage.
Korsakoff syndrome
Korsakoff syndrome is a thiamine-deficiency memory disorder.
Wernicke aphasia
Wernicke aphasia is a language comprehension disorder.
Learned helplessness
Learned helplessness is passivity after uncontrollable stress, not a lesion syndrome.
questions.x: Klüver-Bucy syndrome follows bilateral damage to the anterior temporal lobes, including the amygdala. Animals become tame and fearless, explore objects orally (hyperorality) and may show hypersexuality and visual agnosia. The loss of fear fits the amygdala's role in threat evaluation. Korsakoff syndrome is a thiamine-deficiency memory disorder.

questions.q: Phineas Gage survived an iron rod passing through his frontal lobe and became impulsive and socially inappropriate. His case highlights the role of the prefrontal cortex in:
o: producing basic fear responses
Basic fear generation relies on the amygdala, which was largely spared.
forming new long-term memories
Memory formation relies mainly on the hippocampus.
regulating emotion and planning behavior
Correct: prefrontal damage impaired impulse control and social judgment.
controlling heart rate and breathing
Vital functions are controlled by the brainstem.
questions.x: Phineas Gage's prefrontal damage left his intellect and memory relatively intact but made him impulsive, profane and poor at planning. The case is a classic illustration that the prefrontal cortex regulates emotion and guides social behavior and long-term planning. Basic fear and vital functions depend on subcortical structures he kept.

questions.q: Patients with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex score normally on IQ tests but make repeatedly poor financial and social decisions. This suggests the region:
o: stores semantic knowledge about money
Normal IQ suggests knowledge is intact; integration of emotion is the problem.
integrates emotional signals into decision-making
Correct: without emotional input, choices become poorly guided despite intact intellect.
is the main site of fear conditioning
Fear conditioning depends mainly on the amygdala.
controls sympathetic outflow to the heart
Autonomic control centers lie in the hypothalamus and brainstem.
questions.x: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex links emotional signals (such as gut feelings about risk) to choices. Damage leaves IQ and factual knowledge intact but impairs real-world decisions, which is the basis of the somatic marker hypothesis. Normal IQ rules out a loss of stored knowledge as the explanation.

questions.q: Which limbic structure links the nervous and endocrine systems and helps produce autonomic responses during emotion?
o: Hippocampus
The hippocampus is mainly involved in memory.
Cingulate gyrus
The cingulate is involved in attention and emotional conflict, not endocrine control.
Olfactory bulb
The olfactory bulb processes smell.
Hypothalamus
Correct: the hypothalamus controls the ANS and the pituitary gland.
questions.x: The hypothalamus is the bridge between the nervous and endocrine systems: it controls the autonomic nervous system and, through releasing hormones such as CRH, the pituitary gland. That makes it central to the bodily arousal of emotion and to the stress response. The hippocampus is a limbic structure too, but it mainly supports memory.

questions.q: In early experiments, cats whose cortex was removed but whose hypothalamus was intact showed sudden, poorly directed hissing and clawing. This 'sham rage' suggests that:
o: the cortex alone produces emotional behavior
Rage appeared without the cortex, so the cortex is not required to produce it.
the hippocampus produces aggression
The hippocampus was not the structure isolated in these studies.
the hypothalamus can generate emotional behavior while the cortex helps direct and inhibit it
Correct: the rage pattern persisted without cortex but lacked direction and restraint.
emotion requires cognitive labeling
Sham rage occurred without the cortical structures needed for labeling.
questions.x: Removing the cortex while leaving the hypothalamus intact produced intense but undirected rage, so the hypothalamus can generate the emotional behavior pattern on its own. The poor direction and lack of restraint show the cortex normally aims and inhibits that behavior. This contradicts the idea that the cortex alone produces emotion.

questions.q: fMRI shows that when participants reappraise a disturbing image as staged, prefrontal activity increases and amygdala activity decreases. This best supports which statement?
o: The prefrontal cortex can down-regulate amygdala responses
Correct: reappraisal engaged prefrontal regions as amygdala activity fell.
The amygdala causes reappraisal to occur
Amygdala activity fell, so it is unlikely to be driving the reappraisal.
Reappraisal has no effect on emotional processing
The amygdala change shows emotional processing was affected.
fMRI proves the prefrontal cortex causes all emotions
Correlational imaging cannot prove a structure causes all emotion.
questions.note: Imaging is correlational unless a variable is manipulated.
questions.x: Cognitive reappraisal is a regulation strategy in which a situation is reinterpreted to change its emotional impact. Rising prefrontal activity together with falling amygdala activity fits the idea that the prefrontal cortex can down-regulate the amygdala. Imaging is correlational, though, so it cannot prove the prefrontal cortex causes all emotion.

questions.q: Emotional events are often remembered more vividly than neutral ones. This enhancement is most closely tied to interaction between the amygdala and the:
o: cerebellum
The cerebellum is involved in motor learning, not emotional memory enhancement.
occipital lobe
The occipital lobe processes vision.
medulla
The medulla controls vital autonomic functions.
hippocampus
Correct: amygdala activity strengthens hippocampal memory consolidation for emotional events.
questions.x: Emotional arousal activates the amygdala, which in turn enhances consolidation in the nearby hippocampus, so emotional events are often remembered more vividly. This is why stress hormones and norepinephrine boost memory for emotional events. The cerebellum supports motor learning, not emotional enhancement of episodic memory.

questions.q: Rats given a β-blocker right after a frightening training session later show weaker memory for it than controls given saline. What is the best conclusion?
o: β-blockers erase all previously stored memories
Only the newly trained memory was tested, and older memories were not.
Adrenergic signaling after an event helps strengthen emotional memories
Correct: blocking norepinephrine's β-receptors weakened consolidation.
The hippocampus is not involved in memory
The study does not test the hippocampus directly.
Cortisol has no effect on memory
Cortisol was not manipulated in this study.
questions.x: After an emotional event, norepinephrine acting on β-adrenergic receptors (especially in the amygdala) strengthens memory consolidation. Blocking those receptors right after training weakened the memory, so adrenergic signaling helps consolidate emotional memories. The study tested only the new memory, so it says nothing about erasing older ones.

questions.q: LeDoux described a fast 'low road' for fear. Which pathway does it describe?
o: Sensory cortex to hippocampus to prefrontal cortex
That route is slower and is not the low road.
Thalamus directly to amygdala, bypassing the sensory cortex
Correct: this quick, crude route allows rapid fear responses before conscious analysis.
Amygdala to cerebellum to spinal cord
This is not the described fear pathway.
Retina directly to the hypothalamus only
This retinal pathway mainly regulates circadian rhythm.
questions.x: LeDoux described two fear routes. The low road goes from the thalamus directly to the amygdala, giving a fast but crude response (jumping at a stick that looks like a snake). The high road passes through sensory cortex for slower, detailed analysis, which can then confirm or cancel the fear response.

questions.q: Which division of the autonomic nervous system produces the 'fight-or-flight' response?
o: Parasympathetic
The parasympathetic division supports 'rest and digest' functions.
Somatic
The somatic system controls voluntary skeletal muscle and is not autonomic.
Enteric
The enteric system governs the gut and does not drive fight-or-flight.
Sympathetic
Correct: the sympathetic division mobilizes the body for action.
questions.x: The autonomic nervous system has sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions. The sympathetic division produces fight-or-flight: faster heart rate, dilated pupils and bronchioles, and energy mobilization. The parasympathetic division does the opposite (rest and digest), and the somatic system controls voluntary skeletal muscle, not autonomic responses.

questions.q: Which change would you expect during strong sympathetic activation?
o: Pupil dilation
Correct: sympathetic activity dilates the pupils to let in more light.
Increased saliva production for digestion
Increased digestive secretion is parasympathetic.
Slowed heart rate
Slowed heart rate is a parasympathetic effect.
Constriction of the bronchioles
Sympathetic activity dilates the bronchioles.
questions.x: Sympathetic activation prepares the body for action: pupils dilate, heart rate rises, bronchioles widen and digestion slows. Increased salivation for digestion, slowed heart rate and bronchial constriction are all parasympathetic effects. A useful rule is that anything aiding digestion or slowing the heart belongs to rest and digest.

questions.q: After a near-miss car accident, a driver's heart rate gradually returns to normal. Which system is mainly responsible for this recovery?
o: Sympathetic nervous system
The sympathetic system raised the heart rate in the first place.
Somatic nervous system
The somatic system controls skeletal muscle, not the heart.
Parasympathetic nervous system
Correct: parasympathetic output, largely via the vagus nerve, slows the heart.
Adrenal medulla
The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine, which raises the heart rate.
questions.x: Once the threat passes, parasympathetic output, carried mainly by the vagus nerve, slows the heart back to resting rate. The sympathetic system raised the heart rate in the first place, and the adrenal medulla releases epinephrine, which keeps it elevated. The somatic system controls skeletal muscle, not the heart.

questions.q: During a fight-or-flight response, the adrenal medulla releases mainly:
o: cortisol
Cortisol comes from the adrenal cortex.
aldosterone
Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex and regulates sodium.
acetylcholine
Acetylcholine is a neurotransmitter, not the main adrenal medulla hormone.
epinephrine
Correct: the adrenal medulla releases mostly epinephrine with some norepinephrine.
questions.x: The adrenal medulla is essentially a modified sympathetic ganglion. When stimulated by sympathetic preganglionic fibers it releases mostly epinephrine plus some norepinephrine into the blood. Cortisol and aldosterone come from the adrenal cortex, a separate tissue controlled by hormones rather than direct nerve input.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is released by preganglionic neurons in both divisions of the autonomic nervous system?
o: Norepinephrine
Norepinephrine is released by most sympathetic postganglionic neurons.
Dopamine
Dopamine is not the standard autonomic preganglionic transmitter.
Acetylcholine
Correct: all autonomic preganglionic neurons are cholinergic.
Epinephrine
Epinephrine is a hormone released by the adrenal medulla.
questions.x: All autonomic preganglionic neurons, sympathetic and parasympathetic, release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors in the ganglia. The divisions differ at the target organ: parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine, while most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine, which is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: Polygraph tests try to detect lying by measuring heart rate, breathing, and skin conductance. Their main weakness is that:
o: autonomic responses cannot be measured reliably
These measures are recorded reliably; the issue is what they mean.
anxiety from many causes produces the same autonomic arousal as deception
Correct: arousal is not specific to lying, so innocent but anxious people may 'fail.'
lying reduces sympathetic activity
The test assumes lying raises arousal, but arousal is not unique to lying.
the parasympathetic system blocks all arousal during questioning
Arousal is clearly present during questioning.
questions.x: Polygraphs record heart rate, breathing and skin conductance accurately, but these signals reflect general arousal, not lying specifically. Fear, embarrassment or anxiety about being tested can produce the same pattern, so innocent people may fail and calm liars may pass. This is the same nonspecific-arousal problem Cannon raised about emotion.

questions.q: According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, performance on a complex task is best at:
o: a relatively low to moderate level of arousal
Correct: hard tasks peak at lower arousal than easy tasks.
the highest possible level of arousal
Very high arousal impairs complex performance.
zero arousal
Too little arousal leads to poor focus and motivation.
any arousal level, since arousal does not affect performance
Yerkes-Dodson shows a clear inverted-U relationship.
questions.note: Inverted U: easier tasks tolerate higher arousal.
questions.x: The Yerkes-Dodson law describes an inverted-U relation between arousal and performance: too little arousal brings poor focus, and too much brings anxiety and errors. The optimum depends on the task, and complex or unfamiliar tasks peak at relatively lower arousal than simple ones. Maximal arousal hurts complex performance.

questions.q: A researcher plots exam scores against students' measured arousal and finds an inverted-U curve. If students take an easier exam instead, where would the peak most likely shift?
o: To a higher level of arousal
Correct: simple tasks are performed best at higher arousal than complex ones.
To a lower level of arousal
Lower optimal arousal applies to harder tasks, not easier ones.
The curve would become a straight downward line
Yerkes-Dodson predicts an inverted U for both task types.
The peak would stay at exactly the same arousal level
Task difficulty shifts the optimum.
questions.x: Yerkes-Dodson predicts an inverted U for both easy and hard tasks, but the peak shifts with difficulty. Simple, well-practiced tasks are performed best at higher arousal, while complex tasks are disrupted sooner. Switching to an easier exam should therefore move the optimum toward higher arousal, not lower.

questions.q: A person's heart pounds in an exciting roller coaster ride and also when being chased by a dog. That the same arousal accompanies very different emotions is used to support which theory?
o: James-Lange
James-Lange would require distinct bodily patterns for distinct emotions.
Schachter-Singer
Correct: if arousal is similar, a cognitive label is needed to tell emotions apart.
Facial feedback hypothesis
This example is about arousal, not facial muscles.
General adaptation syndrome
GAS describes stress response stages, not how emotions are labeled.
questions.x: If excitement and fear produce the same racing heart, arousal alone cannot specify the emotion; something else, the cognitive label based on context, must distinguish them. That is the heart of Schachter-Singer. The same observation is a problem for James-Lange, which needs different bodily patterns for different emotions.

questions.q: Which statement about the autonomic nervous system is correct?
o: It controls voluntary movement of skeletal muscle
That is the role of the somatic nervous system.
It is part of the central nervous system
The ANS is part of the peripheral nervous system.
It controls involuntary functions such as heart rate and digestion
Correct: the ANS regulates internal organs largely without conscious control.
It is active only during stress
The ANS works continuously, including at rest.
questions.x: The autonomic nervous system is part of the peripheral nervous system and regulates involuntary functions such as heart rate, digestion, sweating and pupil size. It works constantly, not only under stress, and its parasympathetic branch dominates at rest. Voluntary control of skeletal muscle belongs to the somatic nervous system.

questions.q: A drug that blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors is given to a volunteer at rest. Which effect is most likely?
o: Pupil constriction
Pupil constriction is parasympathetic and would be blocked.
Increased salivation
Salivation is parasympathetic and would decrease.
Increased gut motility
Gut motility is parasympathetic and would decrease.
Increased heart rate
Correct: blocking parasympathetic input to the heart removes its slowing influence.
questions.x: Muscarinic receptors mediate parasympathetic effects on target organs. At rest, vagal tone slows the heart, so blocking muscarinic receptors (as atropine does) removes that brake and heart rate rises. The same blockade reduces salivation, gut motility and pupil constriction, since those are parasympathetic actions.

questions.q: In Lazarus's model of stress, primary appraisal involves:
o: judging whether one has the resources to cope
That is secondary appraisal.
judging whether a situation is irrelevant, benign, or threatening
Correct: primary appraisal asks 'Is this a threat to me?'
reacting automatically with sympathetic arousal
Appraisal is a cognitive evaluation, not an automatic bodily reaction.
recalling past stressful events in detail
Appraisal evaluates the present situation, not memory retrieval.
questions.x: Lazarus split stress appraisal into two steps. Primary appraisal asks whether an event is irrelevant, benign-positive or stressful (a threat, harm or challenge). Secondary appraisal then asks whether I have the resources to cope with it. Swapping these two definitions is the most common trap.

questions.q: A student facing a hard exam asks herself, 'Do I have enough time and notes to prepare?' This is an example of:
o: secondary appraisal
Correct: evaluating coping resources is secondary appraisal.
primary appraisal
Primary appraisal decides whether the exam is threatening at all.
emotion-focused coping
She is evaluating resources, not yet regulating her feelings.
the exhaustion stage
Exhaustion is the last stage of the general adaptation syndrome.
questions.x: The student already sees the exam as demanding; she is now asking whether her time and notes are enough to meet it. Evaluating coping resources is secondary appraisal. Primary appraisal would be the earlier judgment of whether the exam is a threat at all, and emotion-focused coping would be an attempt to manage her feelings.

questions.q: Two employees learn their company will reorganize. One sees it as a chance to advance; the other fears losing his job. Their different stress levels mainly reflect differences in:
o: the type of stressor
The stressor is identical for both employees.
the adrenal medulla's capacity
There is no evidence of a physiological difference here.
display rules
Display rules govern emotional expression, not appraisal.
cognitive appraisal
Correct: the same event is interpreted as a challenge by one and a threat by the other.
questions.x: Both employees face the identical stressor, so the difference in stress has to come from interpretation. One appraises the reorganization as a challenge (a chance to gain), the other as a threat (possible loss). This is the core claim of Lazarus's approach: stress depends on appraisal, not just on the event.

questions.q: Appraising a stressor as a 'challenge' rather than a 'threat' is generally associated with:
o: more anxiety and worse performance
Those outcomes are more typical of threat appraisals.
complete absence of physiological arousal
Challenge appraisals still involve arousal, just a more adaptive pattern.
better performance and less harmful physiological effects
Correct: challenge appraisals link to adaptive coping and healthier responses.
skipping secondary appraisal
Judging resources as adequate is part of what makes something a challenge.
questions.x: Challenge and threat appraisals both involve arousal, but they differ in pattern. Challenge, where resources are judged adequate for the demand, links to efficient cardiovascular responding and better performance; threat, where demands seem to exceed resources, links to more anxiety and a less healthy physiological profile.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a catastrophic stressor?
o: Getting married
Marriage is a significant life change.
Sitting in daily traffic
Traffic is a daily hassle.
A hurricane destroying an entire town
Correct: catastrophes are sudden, large-scale events affecting many people.
Ongoing noise from a nearby highway
Persistent background noise is an ambient (environmental) stressor.
questions.x: Stressors are often grouped as catastrophes (sudden, large-scale events affecting many people, such as disasters or war), significant life changes (marriage, divorce, moving), daily hassles (traffic, lost keys) and ambient stressors (noise, crowding, pollution). A hurricane wiping out a town fits the catastrophe category.

questions.q: Losing your keys, waiting in long lines, and arguing over chores are examples of:
o: catastrophes
Catastrophes are large-scale disasters.
significant life changes
Life changes are major events such as divorce or moving.
approach-approach conflicts
These are not choices between two desirable options.
daily hassles
Correct: small, frequent irritations are daily hassles.
questions.x: Daily hassles are small, frequent irritations of everyday life, such as lost keys, lines and minor arguments. Although each is minor, they accumulate. Significant life changes are major events like divorce or moving, and approach-approach conflicts are choices between two desirable goals.

questions.q: Some research finds that the number of daily hassles predicts health problems better than the number of major life events. The best explanation is that:
o: frequent minor stressors add up to chronic activation of the stress response
Correct: repeated small stressors can produce lasting physiological wear.
major life events cause no stress
Major events do cause stress; the finding is about comparative predictive power.
daily hassles are always appraised as positive
Hassles are, by definition, annoying.
hassles trigger the exhaustion stage immediately
Exhaustion comes only after prolonged stress, not immediately.
questions.x: Major life events are rare, but daily hassles happen constantly, so they keep activating the sympathetic and HPA stress systems. That repeated activation adds up to chronic physiological wear, which may explain why hassles predict health problems well. The finding is about predictive power and does not mean major events cause no stress.

questions.q: The Social Readjustment Rating Scale counts both positive events (such as marriage) and negative events (such as being fired) because:
o: positive events reduce the effect of negative ones
Positive events add life change units; they do not subtract.
any event requiring major adjustment can be stressful
Correct: stress comes from the demand to readjust, regardless of whether the event is welcome.
only positive events cause physical illness
Both kinds contribute to the total score.
negative events are not considered stressors
Negative events are central items on the scale.
questions.x: Holmes and Rahe's Social Readjustment Rating Scale assigns life change units to events according to how much readjustment they demand. Welcome events like marriage or a new job still force change, so they add to the total just as losses do. Positive events never subtract from the score.

questions.q: A study finds that people with high Social Readjustment Rating Scale scores report more illness in the following year. Which conclusion is justified?
o: Life changes directly cause illness
Without random assignment, causation cannot be concluded.
Illness causes people to experience more life changes
Illness was measured after the scores, and the design cannot prove this direction either.
Positive life events protect against illness
The scale adds positive events to the total; it does not show they protect.
High life-change scores are associated with later illness
Correct: the design is correlational, so it shows an association only.
questions.x: The study measured life-change scores and later illness without manipulating anything, so it is correlational. It can show that high scores predict later illness, but third variables such as income, health habits or existing conditions could explain both. Only random assignment to a condition could justify a causal claim.

questions.q: Constant crowding and air pollution in a city are examples of which type of stressor?
o: Catastrophe
Catastrophes are sudden disasters, not ongoing conditions.
Environmental (ambient) stressor
Correct: ongoing background conditions in the surroundings are environmental stressors.
Significant life change
Life changes are discrete personal events.
Approach-avoidance conflict
Conflicts involve choices between goals, not environmental conditions.
questions.x: Environmental, or ambient, stressors are chronic background conditions such as noise, crowding, pollution and extreme temperatures. They differ from catastrophes, which are sudden and large-scale, and from life changes, which are discrete personal events. The ongoing, low-level quality is the key feature.

questions.q: A student must choose between two excellent summer research programs and can attend only one. This is a(n):
o: avoidance-avoidance conflict
That involves choosing between two unpleasant options.
approach-avoidance conflict
That involves one goal with both good and bad features.
approach-approach conflict
Correct: both options are attractive, and choosing one gives up the other.
double approach-avoidance conflict
That involves two options each with good and bad features.
questions.x: In an approach-approach conflict, a person must choose between two attractive options, and picking one means losing the other. These are usually the least stressful conflicts. Avoidance-avoidance involves two unpleasant options, and approach-avoidance involves a single goal with both good and bad features.

questions.q: A patient must choose between painful physical therapy and losing mobility in his knee. This is best described as:
o: an avoidance-avoidance conflict
Correct: both choices are undesirable.
an approach-approach conflict
Neither option is attractive here.
an approach-avoidance conflict
That involves one goal with both appealing and unappealing features.
a daily hassle
This is a significant decision, not a minor irritation.
questions.x: Both options are undesirable: painful therapy or losing knee mobility. Choosing between two negatives is an avoidance-avoidance conflict, often described as choosing the lesser of two evils. It is not approach-avoidance, because there are two separate options, each of which he would prefer to avoid.

questions.q: A person wants a high-paying job but dreads the long commute it requires. As the start date approaches, her anxiety grows. This is an example of:
o: an approach-avoidance conflict
Correct: one goal has both appealing and unappealing features.
an approach-approach conflict
There is only one option, and it has a clear downside.
an avoidance-avoidance conflict
The job itself is desired, so this is not a choice between two negatives.
a catastrophic stressor
A personal job decision is not a large-scale disaster.
questions.note: Trap: one option with pros and cons = approach-avoidance.
questions.x: An approach-avoidance conflict involves one goal that is both attractive and unattractive, here the high salary and the dreaded commute. Avoidance tendencies often grow faster than approach tendencies as the goal gets closer, which is why her anxiety rises as the start date nears.

questions.q: Which hormone is the main end product of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis during stress?
o: Insulin
Insulin comes from the pancreas and is not part of the HPA axis.
Oxytocin
Oxytocin is released by the posterior pituitary and is not the HPA end product.
Cortisol
Correct: the adrenal cortex releases cortisol in response to ACTH.
Melatonin
Melatonin is released by the pineal gland.
questions.x: In the HPA axis, the hypothalamus releases CRH, the anterior pituitary releases ACTH, and the adrenal cortex releases cortisol, the main end product and the classic stress hormone. Oxytocin is a tempting distractor because it is involved in stress-related affiliation, but it comes from the posterior pituitary and is not the HPA end product.

questions.q: What is the correct order of signaling in the HPA axis?
o: ACTH from hypothalamus → CRH from pituitary → cortisol from adrenal medulla
The order of CRH and ACTH is reversed, and cortisol comes from the cortex.
CRH from hypothalamus → ACTH from anterior pituitary → cortisol from adrenal cortex
Correct: each step stimulates the next.
CRH from hypothalamus → ACTH from posterior pituitary → epinephrine from adrenal cortex
ACTH comes from the anterior pituitary; the cortex releases cortisol.
Cortisol from hypothalamus → ACTH from pituitary → CRH from adrenal gland
The chain begins with CRH, not cortisol.
questions.x: The HPA cascade runs hypothalamus → anterior pituitary → adrenal cortex: CRH stimulates ACTH release, and ACTH stimulates cortisol release. Two traps are common: ACTH comes from the anterior, not posterior, pituitary, and cortisol comes from the adrenal cortex, while the medulla releases epinephrine.

questions.q: Which effect of cortisol helps provide energy during prolonged stress?
o: Increasing insulin release to store glucose
Cortisol opposes insulin and raises blood glucose.
Increasing protein synthesis in muscle
Cortisol promotes protein breakdown to provide gluconeogenic substrates.
Strengthening inflammatory responses
Cortisol suppresses inflammation.
Increasing blood glucose through gluconeogenesis
Correct: cortisol raises glucose to fuel the body.
questions.x: Cortisol is a glucocorticoid: it raises blood glucose by promoting gluconeogenesis in the liver and breaking down muscle protein to supply amino acids. This keeps fuel available during prolonged stress. It also opposes insulin and suppresses inflammation, which is why chronic cortisol can impair immunity.

questions.q: Medical students show lower immune cell activity during exam weeks than during vacation. This is best explained by:
o: parasympathetic overactivity during exams
Stress shifts balance toward sympathetic and HPA activity.
reduced cortisol levels during exams
Stress raises cortisol, not lowers it.
stress hormones such as cortisol suppressing immune function
Correct: prolonged cortisol release dampens immune responses.
the alarm stage strengthening immunity permanently
Chronic stress weakens immunity rather than strengthening it.
questions.x: Stress activates the HPA axis, and cortisol suppresses many immune functions, such as lymphocyte activity and inflammation. Exam periods are a natural stressor, so reduced immune cell activity then fits higher stress hormones. Stress raises cortisol rather than lowering it, and it shifts balance toward sympathetic, not parasympathetic, activity.

questions.q: Volunteers who reported chronic stress were more likely to develop a cold after viral exposure. Why can this study NOT show that stress causes illness?
o: Stress was measured rather than randomly assigned, so other variables may explain the link
Correct: without manipulation, confounds such as sleep or health habits remain possible.
All participants received the same virus
Equal exposure is a strength of the design, not the reason it is correlational.
Illness was the dependent variable
Having an outcome measure is normal and does not block causal claims.
Colds are not affected by the immune system
Resistance to colds clearly depends on immune function.
questions.x: Causation requires manipulating the independent variable. Here stress was only measured, so people with high stress may also differ in sleep, smoking, diet or other factors that affect immunity. Giving everyone the same virus controls exposure, which is a strength, but it does not make the stress variable experimental.

questions.q: Chronically elevated cortisol is associated with damage to which brain structure, which may help explain memory problems in people under long-term stress?
o: Cerebellum
The cerebellum is not the main structure linked to stress-related memory problems.
Primary visual cortex
The visual cortex processes visual input, not memory consolidation.
Pons
The pons relays signals and regulates sleep and breathing.
Hippocampus
Correct: the hippocampus has many glucocorticoid receptors and can shrink under chronic stress.
questions.x: The hippocampus has a high density of glucocorticoid receptors. Prolonged high cortisol can damage hippocampal neurons and reduce neurogenesis and volume, which may contribute to memory problems with chronic stress. The cerebellum, pons and visual cortex are not the main sites linking stress hormones to memory.

questions.q: Which component of the Type A behavior pattern is most strongly linked to coronary heart disease?
o: Ambition
Ambition alone has not been strongly tied to heart disease.
Hostility
Correct: research points to hostility and anger as the most harmful Type A features.
Sense of time urgency
Time urgency is part of Type A but is less predictive than hostility.
Introversion
Introversion is not a Type A trait.
questions.x: Early research linked the whole Type A pattern (competitiveness, time urgency, hostility) to coronary heart disease. Later studies found that hostility, especially cynical hostility and anger, carries most of the risk, while ambition and time urgency predict little. Introversion is a personality dimension, not a Type A trait.

questions.q: Prolonged stress can contribute to high blood pressure mainly because:
o: parasympathetic activity raises blood pressure
Parasympathetic activity tends to lower heart rate.
repeated sympathetic activation constricts blood vessels and raises heart rate
Correct: chronic sympathetic and hormonal activation strains the cardiovascular system.
cortisol lowers blood glucose
Cortisol raises blood glucose.
stress reduces epinephrine release
Stress increases epinephrine release.
questions.x: Stress activates the sympathetic nervous system and releases epinephrine and norepinephrine, which constrict blood vessels and raise heart rate, increasing blood pressure. Repeated activation strains the cardiovascular system over time. Parasympathetic activity works the other way, and stress raises rather than reduces epinephrine.

questions.q: During which stage of the general adaptation syndrome does the body maintain elevated cortisol and seem to cope, while still using up resources?
o: Alarm
Alarm is the initial burst of sympathetic activation.
Exhaustion
In exhaustion, resources are depleted and coping fails.
Recovery
Recovery is not one of Selye's three stages.
Resistance
Correct: the body adapts to a continuing stressor at the cost of its reserves.
questions.x: Selye's general adaptation syndrome has three stages: alarm (initial sympathetic burst), resistance (sustained adaptation with elevated cortisol) and exhaustion (resources depleted, illness more likely). In resistance the body seems to cope, but it is using up reserves. Recovery is not one of the three stages.

questions.q: A soldier under months of constant combat stress becomes ill, fatigued, and unable to cope. Selye would place him in which stage?
o: Exhaustion
Correct: long-term stress depletes resources and raises vulnerability to illness.
Alarm
Alarm occurs at the start of the stress response.
Resistance
In resistance, the body is still coping.
Appraisal
Appraisal belongs to Lazarus's model, not Selye's stages.
questions.x: After months of unrelenting stress, the body's ability to keep resisting runs out: fatigue, illness and inability to cope signal Selye's exhaustion stage. In resistance the person would still be coping, if at a cost. Appraisal comes from Lazarus's cognitive model and is not a stage of the GAS.

questions.q: A driver suddenly sees a deer in the road and feels a jolt of adrenaline. Which stage of the general adaptation syndrome is she in?
o: Resistance
Resistance follows only if the stressor continues.
Exhaustion
Exhaustion requires prolonged stress.
Alarm
Correct: the alarm stage is the immediate sympathetic reaction to a stressor.
Secondary appraisal
Secondary appraisal is a cognitive step in Lazarus's model, not a GAS stage.
questions.x: The alarm stage is the immediate response to a stressor: a sympathetic surge with adrenaline release that mobilizes the body. Resistance follows only if the stressor continues, and exhaustion requires prolonged stress. Secondary appraisal is a cognitive step in Lazarus's model, not part of Selye's physiological sequence.

questions.q: Selye's model has been criticized mainly because it:
o: fails to include any physiological measures
Selye's model is built on physiological changes.
claims stress always improves health
Selye linked prolonged stress to illness.
applies only to positive events
GAS was proposed for stressors in general.
describes a uniform bodily response and largely ignores cognitive appraisal
Correct: later work showed that how a stressor is interpreted shapes the response.
questions.x: Selye described a general, largely uniform physiological response to any stressor. Later researchers, especially Lazarus, showed that psychological factors such as appraisal, predictability and control strongly shape the response, so the same event can produce very different reactions. Selye's model is physiological, so it does not lack physiological measures.

questions.q: Rats exposed to unpredictable shocks develop more stomach ulcers than rats given the same shocks preceded by a warning tone. What does this suggest?
o: Shock intensity is the only factor that matters
Intensity was held constant, yet outcomes differed.
Warning tones increase stress hormone release
The warned rats did better, not worse.
Predictability reduces the harmful effects of a stressor
Correct: the shock amount was equal; only predictability differed.
Ulcers are caused only by bacteria, not stress
The groups differed only in predictability, which changed ulcer rates.
questions.x: Both groups received identical shocks, so the extra ulcers in the unwarned rats must come from unpredictability. A warning signal also tells the animal when it is safe, allowing it to relax between shocks. This shows psychological features of a stressor, not just its physical intensity, determine its harm.

questions.q: In a 'yoked' design, one rat can turn a wheel to stop shocks, while a second rat receives exactly the same shocks but has no control. The second rat develops more stress-related illness. The key variable shown to matter is:
o: the total amount of shock received
Shock amount was identical in the yoked pair.
perceived control over the stressor
Correct: both rats got identical shocks; only control differed.
physical exercise from turning the wheel
Exercise could be a confound, but the design is built to test control.
genetic differences between rats
Random assignment to roles makes genetics an unlikely explanation.
questions.x: The yoked design equalizes the physical stressor: both rats receive exactly the same shocks, and only one can control them. Since the helpless rat becomes sicker, control itself reduces the harm of stress. Wheel-turning exercise is a possible confound, but it cannot be the key variable the design was built to isolate.

questions.q: Dogs exposed to inescapable shocks later failed to escape shocks even when escape was easy. This phenomenon is called:
o: learned helplessness
Correct: experience with uncontrollable stress led to passive giving up.
habituation
Habituation is a reduced response to a repeated harmless stimulus.
negative reinforcement
Negative reinforcement would increase escape behavior, not reduce it.
extinction
Extinction is the loss of a learned response when reinforcement stops.
questions.x: Seligman found that dogs given inescapable shocks later failed to escape even when escape was easy: they had learned that their actions do not matter. This learned helplessness is the opposite of what negative reinforcement would produce, since successful escape would normally strengthen escape behavior.

questions.q: Learned helplessness has been proposed as a model for which psychological disorder?
o: Major depressive disorder
Correct: passivity and hopelessness after uncontrollable events resemble depression.
Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia involves psychosis, not mainly learned passivity.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder
OCD involves obsessions and compulsions, not giving up.
Specific phobia
Phobias involve intense fear of a particular object or situation.
questions.x: Learned helplessness produces passivity, low motivation and giving up after uncontrollable events, which resembles major depression. Seligman's later attributional version linked depression to explaining bad events as internal, stable and global. Schizophrenia, OCD and phobias have different core features.

questions.q: A student stressed about a lab report makes a detailed schedule and starts writing. This is an example of:
o: emotion-focused coping
Emotion-focused coping manages feelings rather than the problem.
problem-focused coping
Correct: she is acting directly on the source of the stress.
denial
She is facing the problem, not refusing to acknowledge it.
learned helplessness
She is taking action, the opposite of helplessness.
questions.x: Problem-focused coping acts directly on the source of stress, for example by planning, studying or seeking information. Making a schedule and starting the report attacks the problem itself. Emotion-focused coping would instead manage the feelings, for example through venting, relaxation or distraction.

questions.q: After a breakup, a man spends time with friends and writes in a journal to feel better. This best illustrates:
o: problem-focused coping
Problem-focused coping would aim to change the situation itself.
primary appraisal
Primary appraisal is judging whether the event is threatening.
emotion-focused coping
Correct: he is managing his feelings because the event cannot be undone.
the alarm reaction
The alarm reaction is an immediate physiological response.
questions.x: Emotion-focused coping aims to reduce distress rather than change the stressor. A breakup cannot be undone, so seeking friends and journaling to feel better is emotion-focused. Problem-focused coping would mean trying to change the situation itself, which is often not possible after a loss.

questions.q: Problem-focused coping tends to be most effective when a stressor is:
o: uncontrollable
When nothing can be changed, emotion-focused coping is usually more useful.
already resolved
A resolved stressor needs little coping at all.
catastrophic and widespread
Large disasters are usually beyond an individual's control.
controllable
Correct: acting on a problem helps when the situation can actually be changed.
questions.x: Coping works best when matched to the stressor. If a situation can be changed, problem-focused coping removes or reduces the stressor. If it cannot (a loss, a disaster, a terminal diagnosis), problem-solving efforts fail, and emotion-focused strategies are usually more helpful.

questions.q: A patient awaiting biopsy results insists 'there is nothing wrong' and refuses to discuss the test. This response is best described as:
o: problem-focused coping
She is not taking any action on the problem.
denial, a defensive emotion-focused strategy
Correct: refusing to acknowledge a threat reduces distress without changing the situation.
secondary appraisal
She is not evaluating her coping resources.
sublimation
Sublimation redirects impulses into acceptable activities.
questions.x: Denial is a defense mechanism in which a person refuses to acknowledge a threatening reality. It reduces distress in the short term, so it counts as emotion-focused coping, but it does nothing to change the situation and can delay needed action. Sublimation, by contrast, redirects unacceptable impulses into socially valued activities.

questions.q: Which stress-management technique trains people to control physiological processes such as muscle tension by showing them real-time measurements?
o: Biofeedback
Correct: monitoring signals like muscle activity helps people learn to regulate them.
Systematic desensitization
This pairs relaxation with feared stimuli to treat phobias.
Flooding
Flooding exposes a person to an intense feared stimulus all at once.
Free association
Free association is a psychoanalytic technique.
questions.x: Biofeedback uses instruments to show real-time readings of processes such as muscle tension, heart rate or skin temperature, so people can learn to control them voluntarily and relax. Systematic desensitization and flooding are exposure therapies for anxiety, and free association is a psychoanalytic technique.

questions.q: Regular aerobic exercise is recommended for stress management mainly because it:
o: permanently stops cortisol production
Cortisol is still produced, as the body requires it.
raises resting sympathetic activity
Fitness usually lowers resting heart rate and sympathetic tone.
eliminates all daily hassles
Exercise changes the response to stressors, not the stressors themselves.
reduces stress hormone reactivity and improves mood
Correct: exercise lowers physiological stress responses and releases endorphins.
questions.x: Regular aerobic exercise lowers resting heart rate, dampens physiological reactivity to stressors and improves mood, partly through endorphins. It changes the body's response to stress, not the stressors themselves. Cortisol is never permanently shut off, since the body needs it for normal metabolism.

questions.q: Mindfulness meditation and deep breathing reduce stress primarily by:
o: increasing sympathetic activity
Sympathetic activation is the stress response these methods reduce.
raising cortisol to fight stress
These practices tend to lower cortisol.
increasing parasympathetic activity
Correct: slow breathing and relaxation shift the body toward 'rest and digest.'
blocking all cognitive appraisal
Mindfulness changes how thoughts are noticed, not whether appraisal occurs.
questions.x: Slow breathing, meditation and relaxation techniques shift autonomic balance toward the parasympathetic, rest-and-digest division, lowering heart rate, blood pressure and often cortisol. They counter the sympathetic stress response rather than increase it. Mindfulness changes how one relates to thoughts but does not abolish appraisal.

questions.q: Studies show that patients with strong social support recover faster from surgery. Which explanation is most consistent with stress research?
o: Social support increases cortisol release
Support is associated with lower, not higher, stress hormones.
Social support prevents all stressors from occurring
Support helps people cope; it does not remove stressors.
Social support buffers the physiological effects of stress
Correct: supportive relationships reduce stress reactivity and promote healthier behavior.
Social support works only through problem-focused coping
Support helps through emotional as well as practical means.
questions.x: Social support acts as a stress buffer: people with supportive relationships show smaller cardiovascular and cortisol responses to stressors and often have healthier habits, which can speed recovery. Support works through both emotional comfort and practical help, so it is not limited to problem-focused coping.

questions.q: Researchers randomly assign stressed employees to either an 8-week meditation course or a waitlist. Afterward, the meditation group has lower cortisol. Why can the researchers make a causal claim here?
o: Cortisol is an objective measure
An objective measure alone does not establish causation.
The sample consisted only of stressed employees
A specific sample affects generalizability, not causal inference.
The study lasted eight weeks
Duration alone does not support causal claims.
Random assignment makes the groups equivalent except for the intervention
Correct: randomization controls for preexisting differences.
questions.x: Random assignment spreads preexisting differences such as motivation, health and baseline stress evenly across groups, so the only systematic difference is the intervention. A later difference in cortisol can then be attributed to meditation. An objective measure or a long duration improves a study but does not by itself allow causal claims.

questions.q: The 'tend-and-befriend' response describes a stress reaction in which people, especially women:
o: protect offspring and seek social support
Correct: this pattern is linked to oxytocin and affiliation under threat.
withdraw from others and fight
This resembles fight-or-flight, not tend-and-befriend.
show no physiological arousal
Physiological arousal still occurs in tend-and-befriend.
rely on denial as their main coping strategy
Tend-and-befriend involves caretaking and affiliation, not denial.
questions.x: Shelley Taylor proposed tend-and-befriend as a stress response, more common in women, in which people protect offspring and seek social support rather than fight or flee. It is linked to oxytocin and endogenous opioids that promote affiliation. Arousal still occurs; it is channeled toward caretaking and connection.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common maladaptive behavioral response to chronic stress?
o: Increased physical exercise
Exercise is an adaptive response.
Increased alcohol use
Correct: substance use is a common but harmful way of coping with stress.
Seeking social support
Seeking support is generally adaptive.
Planning to solve the problem
Planning is adaptive problem-focused coping.
questions.x: Maladaptive coping reduces distress briefly but creates new problems. Increased alcohol use is a common example, because it numbs stress while harming health and judgment. Exercise, seeking social support and planning are adaptive strategies that reduce stress without such costs.

questions.q: People with an internal locus of control generally experience less stress because they:
o: believe luck determines what happens to them
That is an external locus of control.
avoid appraising events at all
They still appraise events; they feel more able to act.
have lower baseline sympathetic tone from birth
Locus of control is a learned belief, not a fixed biological baseline.
believe their actions can influence outcomes
Correct: a sense of control encourages active coping and lowers perceived threat.
questions.x: Locus of control describes whether people see outcomes as driven by their own actions (internal) or by luck and others (external). Internals believe they can influence events, so stressors seem more manageable and they cope more actively. Believing luck runs one's life is an external locus, the opposite.

questions.q: Psychologists describe 'hardiness' as a set of traits that buffer stress. Which trio defines it?
o: Competition, urgency, and hostility
These are Type A features, some linked to heart disease.
Commitment, control, and challenge
Correct: hardy people stay involved, feel in control, and see change as a challenge.
Denial, projection, and repression
These are defense mechanisms, not hardiness traits.
Alarm, resistance, and exhaustion
These are Selye's GAS stages.
questions.x: Kobasa described hardiness as three Cs: commitment (involvement in life), control (belief that one can influence events) and challenge (seeing change as an opportunity). Hardy people tend to stay healthier under stress. Competition, urgency and hostility are Type A features, with hostility the one linked to heart disease.

questions.q: A nurse after years of long shifts feels emotionally drained, detached from patients, and ineffective. This syndrome is called:
o: learned helplessness
Learned helplessness is passivity after uncontrollable events, not job-specific exhaustion.
the alarm reaction
The alarm reaction is acute, not years-long.
burnout
Correct: burnout is exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced effectiveness from chronic work stress.
approach-avoidance conflict
A conflict involves a decision, not ongoing exhaustion.
questions.x: Burnout results from chronic work-related stress and has three features: emotional exhaustion, depersonalization or cynicism toward the people served, and reduced sense of accomplishment. Learned helplessness is passivity after uncontrollable events in general, not this specific occupational syndrome.

questions.q: A therapist teaches a client to replace the thought 'I'll fail this interview and ruin my life' with 'This interview is one opportunity among many.' This technique targets stress by changing:
o: the appraisal of the stressor
Correct: cognitive restructuring changes how threatening a stressor seems.
the stressor itself
The interview is still happening; only its interpretation changes.
parasympathetic output directly
Effects on arousal follow from the changed thought, not from direct control.
the client's locus of control to external
Making locus of control external would likely increase stress.
questions.x: Cognitive restructuring targets irrational or catastrophic thoughts and replaces them with more realistic ones. The interview itself is unchanged; what changes is how threatening it appears, which is the appraisal. Lower arousal may follow, but only as a result of the new interpretation, not through direct control of the parasympathetic system.

questions.q: According to the opponent-process theory of emotion, a person who first feels intense fear while skydiving will later most likely feel:
o: strong relief or elation as the fear fades
Correct: an opposing emotional process follows the first one.
even more intense fear that lasts for days
The opposing process produces the opposite emotion, not more fear.
no emotion at all
The theory predicts an opposite after-reaction, not emotional numbness.
anger directed at the instructor
The theory predicts the opposite of the first emotion, not an unrelated one.
questions.x: Solomon's opponent-process theory proposes that a strong emotional reaction triggers an opposing process that follows and outlasts it. Intense fear during the jump is therefore followed by relief or elation as the fear fades. The theory predicts the opposite emotion, not more of the same emotion or an unrelated one like anger.

questions.q: With repeated skydives, first-time terror lessens while post-jump elation grows. Opponent-process theory explains this by proposing that:
o: the initial emotion strengthens with each repetition
The theory predicts the felt initial reaction diminishes.
cognitive labels of arousal become more accurate
That is closer to two-factor theory, not opponent-process.
the opposing process strengthens with repetition while the net initial reaction weakens
Correct: the growing opposing process offsets more of the initial reaction.
the sympathetic system stops responding entirely
Arousal still occurs; its emotional balance shifts.
questions.x: In opponent-process theory, the opposing process grows stronger with repetition while the initial process stays about the same, so the net initial reaction weakens and the after-reaction strengthens. Experienced skydivers feel less terror and more elation. The same logic is used to explain drug tolerance and withdrawal.

questions.q: During a stressful public speech, a speaker's mouth feels dry. Which explanation is correct?
o: Parasympathetic activation reduces saliva
Parasympathetic activity increases salivation.
Sympathetic activation reduces watery saliva secretion
Correct: sympathetic activity shifts resources away from digestion.
Cortisol directly blocks the salivary glands
Dry mouth reflects fast autonomic control, not cortisol action.
The somatic system shuts down the salivary glands
Salivary glands are controlled by the autonomic system.
questions.x: Salivation is driven mainly by parasympathetic input, which produces large amounts of watery saliva. Under stress, sympathetic activation shifts resources away from digestion and parasympathetic secretion falls, leaving a small amount of thicker saliva and a dry mouth. This is fast autonomic control, not a direct cortisol effect.

questions.q: Which statement best defines stress in psychology?
o: Any situation that causes physical injury
Stress need not involve injury; many stressors are psychological.
The automatic release of cortisol in all situations
Cortisol release is part of the response, not the definition.
A negative emotion that occurs only in dangerous situations
Positive events and non-dangerous demands can also be stressful.
The process of appraising and responding to events seen as threatening or challenging
Correct: stress involves both the evaluation of demands and the response to them.
questions.x: Psychologists define stress as the process of perceiving events as threatening or challenging (appraisal) and responding to them physically, emotionally and behaviorally. Stressors need not be dangerous or negative, since positive changes and everyday demands also count. Cortisol release is one part of the response, not the definition.

questions.q: Two groups give a stressful speech. Group A is told beforehand that arousal improves performance; Group B gets no instructions. Group A shows better cardiovascular efficiency and performance. Which concept best explains the result?
o: Group A experienced no arousal at all
Arousal was reinterpreted, not removed.
The general adaptation syndrome skipped the alarm stage
GAS stages are not skipped by instructions.
Reappraising arousal as helpful shifts a threat response toward a challenge response
Correct: changing the interpretation of arousal changed both bodily and behavioral outcomes.
Group B used problem-focused coping
No coping strategy was manipulated for Group B.
questions.x: Group A was taught to reinterpret their arousal as useful, which shifted a threat response toward a challenge response. Challenge is linked to more efficient cardiovascular responding and better performance. The arousal was still present but was reappraised, so the result is not explained by an absence of arousal.

questions.q: Which input directly triggers the release of epinephrine from the adrenal medulla?
o: Sympathetic preganglionic fibers
Correct: the adrenal medulla acts like a sympathetic ganglion and is stimulated by preganglionic fibers.
Parasympathetic fibers of the vagus nerve
The vagus nerve supplies parasympathetic input, not adrenal stimulation.
ACTH from the anterior pituitary
ACTH acts on the adrenal cortex to release cortisol.
Somatic motor neurons
Somatic neurons control skeletal muscle.
questions.note: Medulla: fast, neural (epinephrine). Cortex: slow, hormonal (cortisol).
questions.x: The adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion: sympathetic preganglionic fibers release acetylcholine onto its chromaffin cells, which secrete epinephrine and some norepinephrine. This neural control makes the medulla fast. ACTH is the trap, because it controls the adrenal cortex and cortisol, not the medulla.

questions.q: Cortisol released during stress eventually inhibits further CRH and ACTH release. This is an example of:
o: positive feedback
Positive feedback would amplify further CRH and ACTH release.
the alarm reaction
The alarm reaction is the initial stress response, not a regulatory loop.
sympathetic activation
HPA feedback is hormonal, not a sympathetic neural effect.
negative feedback
Correct: the end product suppresses earlier steps, limiting the response.
questions.x: In negative feedback, a pathway's end product inhibits earlier steps. Cortisol acts on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary to reduce CRH and ACTH release, which keeps the stress response from running unchecked. Positive feedback would amplify the signal instead. Chronic stress can blunt this feedback.

questions.q: Which emotion pairing reflects a positive emotion and a negative emotion, respectively?
o: Anger and contentment
Anger is negative and contentment is positive, the reverse order.
Joy and fear
Correct: joy is pleasant and fear is unpleasant.
Sadness and disgust
Both are negative emotions.
Happiness and pride
Both are positive emotions.
questions.x: Emotions are often classified by valence, whether they feel pleasant (positive) or unpleasant (negative). Joy is positive and fear is negative, matching the requested order. Anger and contentment include one of each but in the reverse order, which is the main trap here.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is most closely linked to the brain's reward pathway and the reinforcing effects of addictive drugs?
o: Dopamine
Correct: mesolimbic dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens underlies reward and reinforcement.
Acetylcholine
Acetylcholine is tied to muscle activation, attention and memory, not primarily reward.
Glycine
Glycine is an inhibitory transmitter mostly in the spinal cord and brainstem.
GABA
GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter; it is not the core reward signal.
questions.note: Mesolimbic pathway: VTA → nucleus accumbens.
questions.x: Dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area project to the nucleus accumbens (the mesolimbic pathway), and nearly all addictive drugs raise dopamine there, which tags behaviors as worth repeating. GABA is tempting because many drugs act on it, but GABA is inhibitory and is not the reward signal itself.

questions.q: A patient taking a drug that blocks dopamine D₂ receptors develops tremor and rigidity. Which brain pathway is most likely affected?
o: Nigrostriatal pathway
Correct: dopamine from the substantia nigra to the striatum supports smooth movement; blocking it mimics Parkinsonism.
Tuberoinfundibular pathway
Blocking this pathway raises prolactin; it does not cause tremor.
Mesocortical pathway
This pathway affects cognition and motivation in the prefrontal cortex, not movement.
Mesolimbic pathway
Blocking mesolimbic D₂ reduces positive psychotic symptoms, not motor control.
questions.note: Antipsychotic motor side effects come from the nigrostriatal pathway.
questions.x: D₂ blockade acts on every dopamine pathway, so the side effect tells you which pathway was hit. Tremor and rigidity are motor signs, and motor control depends on the nigrostriatal pathway from substantia nigra to striatum, the same circuit lost in Parkinson disease. Mesolimbic blockade is the intended antipsychotic effect, not the cause of movement problems.

questions.q: Benzodiazepines reduce anxiety mainly by enhancing the effect of which neurotransmitter?
o: Norepinephrine
Enhancing norepinephrine raises arousal and could worsen anxiety.
GABA
Correct: benzodiazepines increase GABA-A receptor Cl⁻ channel opening, boosting inhibition.
Dopamine
Benzodiazepines do not act mainly through dopamine receptors.
Glutamate
Glutamate is excitatory; enhancing it would increase, not reduce, arousal.
questions.x: Benzodiazepines bind a site on the GABA-A receptor and make its Cl⁻ channel open more often when GABA binds, hyperpolarizing neurons and calming activity. They do not act on their own, they amplify GABA. Glutamate is the trap: it is the main excitatory transmitter, so boosting it would increase arousal rather than reduce anxiety.

questions.q: SSRIs, a first-line treatment for major depressive disorder, work by increasing synaptic levels of which neurotransmitter?
o: Acetylcholine
Acetylcholine deficits are linked to Alzheimer disease, not the SSRI mechanism.
Histamine
Histamine affects wakefulness; SSRIs do not target it.
Serotonin
Correct: SSRIs block serotonin reuptake, so serotonin stays in the synapse longer.
Glutamate
SSRIs do not target glutamate reuptake.
questions.x: SSRIs block the serotonin transporter, so serotonin stays in the synapse longer; the monoamine hypothesis linked depression to low serotonin, though the real picture is more complex. Acetylcholine is the tempting distractor because it is tied to another disorder (Alzheimer disease), but SSRIs do not change cholinergic signaling.

questions.q: Damage to the hippocampus would most likely impair which ability?
o: Producing fluent speech
Speech production depends on Broca's area in the frontal lobe.
Learning a new motor skill
Procedural learning relies on the basal ganglia and cerebellum.
Recalling memories from early childhood
Remote memories stored in cortex are largely spared after hippocampal damage.
Forming new explicit long-term memories
Correct: the hippocampus consolidates new declarative memories.
questions.note: Hippocampal damage → anterograde amnesia.
questions.x: The hippocampus is needed to consolidate new explicit (declarative) memories into long-term storage, so damage causes anterograde amnesia, as in patient H.M. Older memories already consolidated into cortex are largely spared, and procedural skills depend on the basal ganglia and cerebellum, so H.M. could still learn new motor tasks.

questions.q: Which brain structure is most central to fear conditioning and detecting threats?
o: Amygdala
Correct: the amygdala assigns emotional significance, especially fear, to stimuli.
Occipital lobe
The occipital lobe processes vision.
Thalamus
The thalamus relays sensory input but does not store fear associations.
Cerebellum
The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.
questions.x: The amygdala links stimuli to emotional value, especially threat, and is required for learning fear associations in classical fear conditioning. The thalamus is tempting because it relays sensory signals to the amygdala, but it does not store the fear association itself.

questions.q: A man becomes impulsive and socially inappropriate after a rod injures the front of his brain. Which region was most likely damaged?
o: Parietal lobe
Parietal damage affects spatial attention and somatosensation.
Medulla oblongata
Medulla damage disrupts breathing and heart rate, often fatally.
Prefrontal cortex
Correct: the prefrontal cortex supports planning, impulse control and social judgment.
Temporal lobe
Temporal damage mainly affects hearing, language comprehension or memory.
questions.x: This describes Phineas Gage, whose prefrontal damage left his intellect largely intact but destroyed impulse control and social judgment. The prefrontal cortex is the executive center for planning and inhibiting inappropriate behavior. Temporal damage would mainly disrupt memory, hearing or language comprehension rather than social conduct.

questions.q: The hypothalamus influences motivated behavior mainly by regulating which of the following?
o: Fine voluntary movements of the hands
Fine movement is controlled by motor cortex and cerebellum.
Hunger, thirst, body temperature and sex drive
Correct: the hypothalamus maintains homeostasis and controls the pituitary.
Language comprehension
Comprehension depends on Wernicke's area.
Visual object recognition
Object recognition relies on the ventral visual stream in the temporal lobe.
questions.note: Hypothalamus: the four F's (feeding, fighting, fleeing, mating).
questions.x: The hypothalamus is the homeostatic control center: it monitors body state, drives hunger, thirst, temperature regulation and sexual behavior, and controls the pituitary gland. It does not handle higher cognitive functions like language or object recognition, which belong to cortical areas.

questions.q: In rats, destroying the lateral hypothalamus typically produces which result?
o: Loss of temperature regulation only
The classic lateral lesion finding is reduced feeding.
Overeating and obesity
