That follows ventromedial hypothalamus lesions, the satiety center.
Loss of interest in eating
Correct: the lateral hypothalamus acts as a hunger center; lesions cause aphagia.
Constant thirst
Lateral lesions reduce, not increase, consummatory drive.
questions.note: Lateral = 'lack of hunger' if lesioned; ventromedial = overeating.
questions.x: Lesion studies identified the lateral hypothalamus as a feeding center and the ventromedial hypothalamus as a satiety center. Destroying the lateral area removes the drive to eat (aphagia), whereas destroying the ventromedial area removes the stop signal, producing overeating and obesity, the tempting reversed answer.

questions.q: In split-brain patients, an image of a key is flashed only to the left visual field. What is the most likely result?
o: They see nothing because the corpus callosum is cut
The image still reaches the right hemisphere's visual cortex.
They cannot name it but can pick out a key with the left hand
Correct: left field goes to the right hemisphere, which lacks speech but controls the left hand.
They can name it and pick it out with the right hand
The right hand is controlled by the left hemisphere, which did not see it.
They can name it but cannot pick it out with either hand
Naming needs the left hemisphere, which never received the image.
questions.note: Left visual field → right hemisphere → left hand.
questions.x: Each visual field projects to the opposite hemisphere, so a left-field image reaches only the right hemisphere when the corpus callosum is cut. Speech is usually in the left hemisphere, so the patient cannot name the object, yet the right hemisphere controls the left hand and can select the key by touch.

questions.q: In most right-handed people, which hemisphere is dominant for language?
o: Both hemispheres equally
Language is strongly lateralized, not evenly shared.
Right hemisphere
The right hemisphere is more involved in spatial and prosodic processing.
Neither; language is in the cerebellum
The cerebellum is not the language center.
Left hemisphere
Correct: language is left-lateralized in about 95% of right-handers.
questions.x: Language is strongly lateralized: in about 95% of right-handers, and most left-handers too, Broca's and Wernicke's areas are in the left hemisphere. The right hemisphere contributes prosody and context but is not dominant for language production or grammar.

questions.q: A stroke patient speaks fluently but produces meaningless sentences and cannot understand speech. Where is the damage most likely?
o: The right occipital lobe
Occipital damage causes visual deficits, not aphasia.
The arcuate fasciculus
Conduction aphasia mainly impairs repetition; comprehension is intact.
Broca's area in the left frontal lobe
Broca aphasia causes halting, effortful speech with intact comprehension.
Wernicke's area in the left temporal lobe
Correct: Wernicke aphasia is fluent but meaningless with poor comprehension.
questions.x: Wernicke's area in the left temporal lobe supports language comprehension, so damage yields fluent but meaningless speech and poor understanding. Broca's area damage produces the opposite pattern: effortful, broken speech with fairly intact comprehension. Conduction aphasia from arcuate fasciculus damage mainly impairs repetition.

questions.q: Which statement about the right hemisphere is best supported by lateralization research?
o: It is the primary site of grammar and speech production
Grammar and speech production are left-lateralized.
It is inactive unless the left hemisphere is damaged
Both hemispheres are always active; they differ in specialization.
It controls the right side of the body
Motor control is contralateral; the right hemisphere controls the left side.
It is relatively specialized for spatial processing and recognizing facial emotion
Correct: the right hemisphere excels at visuospatial tasks and emotional cues.
questions.x: The hemispheres are specialized rather than one being active and the other idle: the left typically handles language and sequential analysis, while the right excels at visuospatial processing, face recognition and reading emotional cues. Motor control is contralateral, so the right hemisphere controls the left side of the body.

questions.q: Elevated cortisol during prolonged stress is released from which gland?
o: Thyroid gland
The thyroid releases T₃ and T₄.
Adrenal cortex
Correct: the HPA axis ends with cortisol release from the adrenal cortex.
Adrenal medulla
The medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine, not cortisol.
Anterior pituitary
The anterior pituitary releases ACTH, which stimulates cortisol release.
questions.note: HPA axis: CRH → ACTH → cortisol.
questions.x: In the HPA axis the hypothalamus releases CRH, the anterior pituitary releases ACTH, and ACTH makes the adrenal cortex secrete cortisol, the slow, sustained stress hormone. The adrenal medulla is the tempting trap: it releases epinephrine and norepinephrine for the fast fight-or-flight response, not cortisol.

questions.q: Oxytocin, a hormone linked to social bonding, labor contractions and milk ejection, is released into the blood from which structure?
o: Anterior pituitary
The anterior pituitary releases tropic hormones such as ACTH and LH, not oxytocin.
Pineal gland
The pineal gland releases melatonin.
Posterior pituitary
Correct: oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.
Adrenal medulla
The adrenal medulla releases catecholamines.
questions.x: Oxytocin and ADH are made by hypothalamic neurons and carried down their axons to be released from the posterior pituitary, which is neural tissue. The anterior pituitary is glandular and secretes its own hormones such as ACTH, LH and prolactin under hypothalamic releasing hormones, so it does not release oxytocin.

questions.q: Studies find that higher testosterone is associated with more dominance behavior, and winning a competition raises testosterone further. What do these findings best illustrate?
o: Behavior has no effect on hormone levels
Winning raising testosterone shows behavior does affect hormones.
Testosterone is the sole cause of aggression
The data show a two-way, correlational link, not a sole cause.
Hormones and behavior influence each other bidirectionally
Correct: testosterone affects behavior, and behavior outcomes change testosterone.
Testosterone only matters in males
Testosterone affects behavior in all sexes.
questions.x: Hormones and behavior influence each other in both directions: testosterone can promote dominance-seeking, and the outcome of a contest feeds back to raise or lower testosterone. Calling testosterone the sole cause overreaches, because correlational data plus feedback effects cannot support a one-way, single-cause claim.

questions.q: Melatonin, which promotes sleepiness as light fades, is secreted by which gland?
o: Pituitary gland
The pituitary does not secrete melatonin.
Pineal gland
Correct: the pineal gland secretes melatonin in darkness.
Adrenal gland
Adrenal hormones include cortisol and epinephrine.
Thyroid gland
The thyroid regulates metabolism.
questions.x: The pineal gland secretes melatonin when darkness is signaled by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, helping time the sleep-wake cycle; bright light suppresses its release. The pituitary is a common mix-up because it is the best-known gland, but it does not make melatonin.

questions.q: Which finding would most strongly suggest that a trait is highly heritable?
o: The trait is common in the general population
Prevalence says nothing about heritability.
Adopted children resemble their adoptive parents
That points to environmental, not genetic, influence.
Monozygotic twins are far more concordant than dizygotic twins
Correct: greater MZ than DZ similarity points to genetic influence.
Siblings raised together are similar on the trait
Shared environment could explain sibling similarity.
questions.x: MZ twins share nearly all their genes and DZ twins about half, while both pairs share a family environment. So when MZ twins are much more concordant than DZ twins, the extra similarity points to genes. Sibling similarity alone is ambiguous because siblings share both genes and environment.

questions.q: A study reports a heritability of 0.6 for a personality trait in a population. Which interpretation is correct?
o: 60% of each person's trait level comes from genes
Heritability does not apply to individuals.
About 60% of the trait's variation in that population is attributable to genetic differences
Correct: heritability describes the source of variance across a population.
Children have a 60% chance of inheriting the trait
Heritability is not a transmission probability.
The trait cannot be changed by the environment
Highly heritable traits can still be strongly shaped by environment.
questions.note: Trap: heritability is a population statistic, never individual.
questions.x: Heritability is the proportion of trait variation in a specific population, at a specific time, that is linked to genetic differences among its members. It says nothing about how much of one person's trait comes from genes, and it can change if the environment changes. High heritability also does not mean a trait is unchangeable.

questions.q: In an adoption study, adopted children's IQ correlates more strongly with their biological mothers than with their adoptive mothers. This mainly supports what?
o: That IQ is entirely fixed at birth
Genetic influence does not mean environment has no effect.
No role for genes in IQ
The result points toward, not away from, genetic influence.
A shared-environment contribution to IQ
Shared environment would predict resemblance to adoptive parents.
A genetic contribution to IQ
Correct: resemblance to biological parents who did not raise them reflects shared genes.
questions.x: Adoption studies separate genes from rearing environment: biological parents give genes but not the home, and adoptive parents give the home but not the genes. Stronger resemblance to biological mothers therefore points to a genetic contribution. It does not mean IQ is fixed, since environment still contributes.

questions.q: Why do twin studies comparing MZ and DZ twins raised together possibly overestimate heritability?
o: MZ twins come from two separate eggs
MZ twins come from a single fertilized egg.
MZ twins may be treated more alike than DZ twins
Correct: if MZ twins share more similar environments, extra similarity is wrongly credited to genes.
Twins never share an environment
Twins raised together share family environment.
DZ twins share 100% of their genes
DZ twins share about 50% of segregating genes, like ordinary siblings.
questions.note: Equal environments assumption.
questions.x: The classic twin method assumes MZ and DZ twins share environments to the same degree (the equal environments assumption). If MZ twins are dressed alike, treated alike and spend more time together, some of their extra similarity is environmental, yet the method attributes it to genes, inflating heritability estimates.

questions.q: A child carries a gene variant linked to aggression but only shows aggression if also maltreated. This illustrates what?
o: Pure genetic determinism
The gene alone did not produce aggression.
Gene–environment interaction
Correct: the gene's effect depends on the environment.
Incomplete dominance
Incomplete dominance is a Mendelian inheritance pattern, not an environment effect.
Pure environmental determinism
Maltreatment's effect depended on the genotype.
questions.x: Gene-environment interaction means the effect of a gene depends on the environment, or the effect of an environment depends on genotype. Here the variant raises aggression only with maltreatment. That rules out genetic determinism, and it differs from incomplete dominance, which describes how two alleles combine, not an environmental effect.

questions.q: Children with a genetic tendency toward sociability seek out more social situations, which further builds their social skills. This is an example of what?
o: Evocative gene–environment correlation
Evocative correlation is when a child's traits elicit responses from others.
Epigenetic silencing
Epigenetics concerns chemical changes in gene expression, not niche-picking.
Passive gene–environment correlation
Passive correlation is when parents provide both genes and environment.
Active gene–environment correlation
Correct: people select environments that fit their genetic tendencies.
questions.x: Gene-environment correlation describes how genes shape the environments people experience. Active correlation is niche-picking: as people gain independence, they seek settings that fit their inherited tendencies. Evocative correlation is the tempting alternative, but it describes others reacting to a person's traits, not the person choosing settings.

questions.q: Rat pups that receive more licking and grooming from mothers show lasting changes in methylation of stress-hormone receptor genes. This is an example of what?
o: Epigenetic effects of the environment
Correct: experience altered gene expression without changing DNA sequence.
Natural selection within one generation
Selection acts on populations over generations.
A change in DNA base sequence
Methylation changes expression, not the nucleotide sequence.
A purely genetic trait
The trait depended on maternal behavior, an environmental factor.
questions.x: Epigenetic changes, such as DNA methylation and histone modification, alter how much a gene is expressed without changing its base sequence, and experience can cause them. Meaney's work showed maternal care changed methylation of glucocorticoid receptor genes in pups, altering their adult stress responses. A change in base sequence would be a mutation, which did not occur.

questions.q: The nature vs nurture debate asks about the relative contributions of what?
o: Heredity and environment to development
Correct: nature is genetic inheritance; nurture is experience and environment.
The left and right hemispheres
That is lateralization, not nature vs nurture.
Classical and operant conditioning
These are both forms of learning, i.e., nurture.
Conscious and unconscious processes
That contrast is central to psychoanalysis, not nature vs nurture.
questions.x: Nature refers to inherited genetic influences and nurture to environment and experience. Modern research treats development as the product of both acting together, through heritability, gene-environment interaction and epigenetics, rather than either one alone. Classical and operant conditioning are both nurture, so they cannot be the two sides of the debate.

questions.q: Which part of the nervous system becomes most active during the fight-or-flight response?
o: Parasympathetic nervous system
The parasympathetic system supports rest and digest.
Enteric nervous system
The enteric system governs digestion locally.
Sympathetic nervous system
Correct: sympathetic activation raises heart rate and mobilizes energy.
Somatic nervous system
The somatic system controls voluntary skeletal muscle.
questions.x: The sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system drives fight-or-flight: it raises heart rate and blood pressure, dilates pupils and bronchi, and releases glucose, partly via adrenal epinephrine. The parasympathetic division does the opposite (rest and digest). The somatic system controls voluntary muscles, not automatic arousal.

questions.q: A drug blocks acetylcholinesterase in the brain. Which condition is it most likely designed to treat?
o: Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia is treated mainly with dopamine antagonists.
Bipolar I disorder
Bipolar disorder is treated mainly with mood stabilizers such as lithium.
Alzheimer disease
Correct: cholinesterase inhibitors raise acetylcholine to offset loss of cholinergic neurons.
Generalized anxiety disorder
Anxiety is treated with SSRIs or GABA enhancers.
questions.x: Acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine, so blocking it raises acetylcholine in synapses. Alzheimer disease involves loss of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain, so cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil modestly improve symptoms. Schizophrenia is the tempting distractor, but its drug treatment targets dopamine receptors.

questions.q: A patient has involuntary jerky movements, mood changes and cognitive decline, and genetic testing shows an expanded CAG repeat. Which disorder is most likely?
o: Parkinson disease
Parkinson causes resting tremor and slowed movement, not CAG repeats.
Multiple sclerosis
MS is an autoimmune demyelinating disease, not a repeat expansion.
Alzheimer disease
Alzheimer presents mainly with memory loss, not chorea.
Huntington disease
Correct: an autosomal dominant CAG repeat causes chorea and basal ganglia degeneration.
questions.x: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant trinucleotide (CAG) repeat expansion that causes degeneration of the striatum, producing chorea, psychiatric changes and dementia. Parkinson disease is also a basal ganglia disorder, but it causes slowed movement and resting tremor from loss of dopamine neurons, not jerky movements from a repeat expansion.

questions.q: Parkinson disease results mainly from loss of dopamine-producing neurons in which structure?
o: Hippocampus
Hippocampal loss is prominent in Alzheimer disease.
Locus coeruleus
The locus coeruleus is the main norepinephrine nucleus.
Substantia nigra
Correct: degeneration of nigral dopamine neurons depletes the striatum.
Raphe nuclei
The raphe nuclei produce serotonin.
questions.x: Parkinson disease results from degeneration of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, which reduces dopamine in the striatum and causes slowed movement, rigidity and resting tremor. Treatments like L-dopa replace dopamine. The locus coeruleus and raphe nuclei make norepinephrine and serotonin, not the dopamine lost in Parkinson disease.

questions.q: Which pair of brain changes is characteristic of Alzheimer disease?
o: Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra
Lewy bodies are characteristic of Parkinson disease.
Demyelinated plaques in white matter
That describes multiple sclerosis.
β-amyloid plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles
Correct: these are the hallmark pathologies of Alzheimer disease.
Enlarged ventricles from CSF blockage
That describes hydrocephalus.
questions.x: Alzheimer disease shows two hallmark lesions: extracellular β-amyloid plaques and intracellular tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau, along with cortical and hippocampal atrophy. Lewy bodies are the tempting distractor because they are also neurodegenerative inclusions, but they characterize Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia.

questions.q: Researchers find that people with more education show the same amount of Alzheimer brain pathology at autopsy but fewer symptoms in life. Which concept best explains this?
o: Neurogenesis reversing plaques
Neurogenesis does not clear amyloid plaques.
Retrograde amnesia
Retrograde amnesia is loss of past memories, not resilience.
Cognitive reserve
Correct: richer neural networks let the brain tolerate damage before symptoms appear.
Diagnostic overshadowing
That term refers to misattributing symptoms to an existing diagnosis.
questions.x: Cognitive reserve is the idea that education, mental activity and richer neural networks let the brain compensate for damage, so symptoms appear later despite equal pathology. Neurogenesis is a tempting idea, but adding new neurons does not remove amyloid plaques; reserve works through compensation, not by reversing pathology.

questions.q: According to Freud, which part of personality operates on the pleasure principle?
o: Preconscious
The preconscious is a level of awareness, not a personality structure.
Id
Correct: the id seeks immediate gratification of instinctual drives.
Superego
The superego represents internalized moral standards.
Ego
The ego follows the reality principle, mediating between id and world.
questions.x: Freud's id is the unconscious, inborn reservoir of drives that demands immediate gratification (the pleasure principle). The ego develops to satisfy those demands realistically (the reality principle), and the superego adds internalized moral standards. The preconscious is a level of awareness, not one of the three structures.

questions.q: A student wants to cheat on an exam but feels intense guilt just thinking about it. In Freudian terms, the guilt comes from which structure?
o: Libido
Libido is psychic energy of the life instincts.
Ego
The ego weighs realistic consequences rather than producing moral guilt.
Id
The id drives the desire to cheat, not the guilt.
Superego
Correct: the superego punishes moral violations with guilt.
questions.x: The superego is the internalized conscience formed from parental and social standards; when a person even considers violating them, it generates guilt. The ego is tempting, but it weighs practical consequences, such as getting caught, rather than producing moral guilt.

questions.q: A man who harbors strong attraction to a coworker accuses the coworker of flirting with him. Which defense mechanism is this?
o: Projection
Correct: he attributes his own unacceptable feelings to someone else.
Sublimation
Sublimation channels impulses into socially valued activities.
Rationalization
Rationalization is giving a logical-sounding excuse for behavior.
Reaction formation
Reaction formation would mean acting hostile toward the coworker.
questions.x: Projection is attributing one's own unacceptable impulses or feelings to someone else, which lets the person avoid admitting them. Reaction formation is the likely confusion, but it would mean acting in a way opposite to the feeling, such as being cold or hostile to the coworker, rather than claiming the coworker is the one attracted.

questions.q: A person with aggressive urges becomes a successful competitive boxer. Freud would call this what?
o: Regression
Regression is reverting to childish behavior.
Repression
Repression pushes impulses out of awareness rather than channeling them.
Denial
Denial is refusing to accept reality.
Sublimation
Correct: unacceptable impulses are redirected into a socially acceptable outlet.
questions.note: Sublimation is considered the most mature defense.
questions.x: Sublimation channels an unacceptable impulse into a socially valued activity, so the energy is expressed rather than blocked, which is why it is considered a mature defense. Repression is the tempting alternative, but repression keeps the urge out of awareness instead of redirecting it into a productive outlet.

questions.q: A woman who deeply resents her mother-in-law is lavishly and conspicuously sweet to her. Which defense mechanism is this?
o: Reaction formation
Correct: she expresses the opposite of her unacceptable feeling.
Intellectualization
Intellectualization means focusing on abstract analysis to avoid emotion.
Projection
Projection would mean believing the mother-in-law resents her.
Displacement
Displacement redirects feelings toward a safer target.
questions.x: Reaction formation turns an unacceptable feeling into its exaggerated opposite, so hidden resentment shows up as excessive, showy kindness. The over-the-top quality is the clue. Displacement would redirect the resentment toward a safer target, such as snapping at her spouse, instead of reversing it.

questions.q: In Erikson's psychosocial theory, the central conflict of adolescence is which?
o: Industry vs inferiority
This is the conflict of school age.
Trust vs mistrust
This is the conflict of infancy.
Intimacy vs isolation
This is the conflict of young adulthood.
Identity vs role confusion
Correct: adolescents work to form a coherent sense of self.
questions.x: Erikson proposed eight psychosocial stages, each centered on a conflict. Adolescence is identity vs role confusion, where teens explore roles and values to build a coherent self. Intimacy vs isolation is the next stage, in young adulthood, and builds on a secure identity.

questions.q: Which neo-Freudian proposed a collective unconscious containing universal archetypes?
o: Erik Erikson
Erikson proposed psychosocial stages across the lifespan.
Carl Jung
Correct: Jung described archetypes such as the persona and shadow.
Alfred Adler
Adler emphasized inferiority feelings and striving for superiority.
Karen Horney
Horney emphasized basic anxiety and social influences in childhood.
questions.x: Jung proposed that, beyond the personal unconscious, all humans share a collective unconscious of inherited archetypes such as the persona, shadow, anima and animus. Adler and Horney also broke from Freud but stressed social factors, inferiority and basic anxiety, not universal inherited images.

questions.q: Alfred Adler would explain a short man's intense drive to become a powerful CEO mainly in terms of what?
o: Conditioned reinforcement history
That is a behaviorist explanation.
Compensation for feelings of inferiority
Correct: Adler said striving for superiority compensates for felt inferiority.
An unresolved Oedipal conflict
That is Freud's explanation, which Adler rejected.
Collective unconscious archetypes
Archetypes are Jung's concept.
questions.x: Adler argued that people are driven by feelings of inferiority, often starting in childhood, and strive for superiority to compensate. An unresolved Oedipal conflict is Freud's sexual explanation, which Adler rejected in favor of social and compensatory motives.

questions.q: Which approach to personality emphasizes free will, personal growth and the drive toward self-actualization?
o: Humanistic
Correct: Rogers and Maslow focused on growth and fulfilling potential.
Psychoanalytic
Psychoanalysis emphasizes unconscious conflict and early experience.
Biological
The biological approach emphasizes genes, brain and physiology.
Behaviorist
Behaviorism explains personality as learned responses to reinforcement.
questions.x: Humanistic theorists like Maslow and Rogers saw people as basically good and oriented toward growth, emphasizing free will, subjective experience and self-actualization. This contrasts with psychoanalytic views, which stress unconscious conflict, and behaviorism, which explains personality as learned responses rather than chosen growth.

questions.q: According to Carl Rogers, anxiety and maladjustment arise mainly when what occurs?
o: The id overpowers the superego
That is a Freudian explanation.
There is a mismatch between the real self and the ideal self
Correct: Rogers called this incongruence.
A person scores high on neuroticism
That describes a trait, not Rogers' mechanism.
Behavior goes unreinforced
That is a behaviorist account.
questions.x: Rogers said each person has a self-concept (real self) and an ideal self; when they clash, the resulting incongruence produces anxiety. Conditions of worth, where love depends on meeting standards, widen this gap. The id-superego conflict is Freud's explanation, not Rogers'.

questions.q: A therapist accepts and values a client completely regardless of what the client says or does. Which humanistic concept is this?
o: Unconditional positive regard
Correct: Rogers held that acceptance without conditions fosters growth.
Systematic desensitization
This is a behavioral exposure technique.
Free association
Free association is a psychoanalytic technique.
Conditions of worth
Conditions of worth mean love is given only for meeting standards.
questions.x: Unconditional positive regard is complete acceptance of a person regardless of behavior, which Rogers saw as essential for healthy growth and central to client-centered therapy. Conditions of worth is the opposite idea: acceptance given only when certain standards are met, which Rogers thought produced incongruence.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the Big Five personality traits?
o: Conscientiousness
Correct: the Big Five are openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism.
Locus of control
Locus of control is Rotter's concept, not a Big Five trait.
Psychoticism
Psychoticism is from Eysenck's three-factor model, not the Big Five.
Self-efficacy
Self-efficacy is a social cognitive concept, not a Big Five trait.
questions.note: Big Five: OCEAN.
questions.x: The Big Five (OCEAN) are openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism, broad dimensions found across many cultures. Psychoticism is tempting because it is a real trait dimension, but it belongs to Eysenck's three-factor model, not the Big Five.

questions.q: A person who is anxious, moody and easily upset would score high on which Big Five dimension?
o: Agreeableness
Agreeableness reflects warmth and cooperativeness.
Openness
Openness reflects curiosity and imagination.
Conscientiousness
Conscientiousness reflects organization and self-discipline.
Neuroticism
Correct: neuroticism reflects emotional instability and negative affect.
questions.x: Neuroticism is the tendency to experience negative emotions such as anxiety, moodiness and irritability; its low end is emotional stability. Agreeableness can sound related because it involves how people get along, but it measures warmth and cooperativeness, not emotional instability.

questions.q: Gordon Allport described a single trait that dominates and shapes nearly all of a person's behavior. What did he call it?
o: A cardinal trait
Correct: cardinal traits are rare, all-pervasive dispositions.
A central trait
Central traits are the 5 to 10 major characteristics most people have.
A source trait
Source traits are Cattell's underlying factors.
A secondary trait
Secondary traits appear only in certain situations.
questions.x: Allport described three levels of traits: rare cardinal traits that dominate nearly all behavior, central traits that describe most of a person's personality, and secondary traits seen only in certain situations. Source traits belong to Cattell's factor-analytic model, not Allport's.

questions.q: A critic argues that trait theories are limited because people's behavior varies widely across situations. This criticism was most associated with whom?
o: Walter Mischel
Correct: Mischel's person–situation debate challenged cross-situational consistency of traits.
Raymond Cattell
Cattell developed the 16-factor trait model.
Hans Eysenck
Eysenck defended trait dimensions with a biological basis.
Abraham Maslow
Maslow was a humanistic theorist.
questions.x: Walter Mischel argued in the 1960s that traits predict behavior across situations only weakly, starting the person-situation debate. The modern resolution is interactionist: traits predict behavior averaged over many situations, and people show stable if-then patterns. Eysenck and Cattell were trait theorists who defended traits, not critics of them.

questions.q: Hans Eysenck's model of personality included which three dimensions?
o: Cardinal, central and secondary
These are Allport's trait levels.
Id, ego and superego
These are Freud's personality structures.
Extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism
Correct: Eysenck's PEN model has these three biologically based dimensions.
Openness, agreeableness and conscientiousness
These are three of the Big Five, not Eysenck's model.
questions.x: Eysenck used factor analysis to propose three broad, biologically based dimensions: psychoticism, extraversion and neuroticism (PEN). The Big Five is the tempting confusion because it shares extraversion and neuroticism, but it replaces psychoticism with openness, agreeableness and conscientiousness.

questions.q: Eysenck proposed that introverts avoid loud parties because of what biological difference?
o: A smaller amygdala
Eysenck's theory centered on the reticular arousal system, not amygdala size.
Excess dopamine in the striatum
Eysenck did not attribute introversion to striatal dopamine excess.
Higher baseline cortical arousal
Correct: introverts are already highly aroused, so they avoid extra stimulation.
Lower baseline cortical arousal
Low baseline arousal was Eysenck's explanation for extraverts' stimulation seeking.
questions.x: Eysenck tied extraversion to the reticular activating system: introverts have higher baseline cortical arousal, so extra stimulation pushes them past their comfort level and they avoid it. Extraverts have low baseline arousal and seek stimulation to reach an optimal level, which is why the reversed choice is wrong.

questions.q: Albert Bandura's idea that behavior, personal factors and environment all influence one another is called what?
o: Operant conditioning
Operant conditioning focuses on consequences alone.
Psychic determinism
This is Freud's view that unconscious causes underlie all behavior.
Biological determinism
That view holds that genes alone fix behavior.
Reciprocal determinism
Correct: this three-way interaction is central to social cognitive theory.
questions.x: Bandura's reciprocal determinism says behavior, personal factors (beliefs, expectations, self-efficacy) and the environment all shape one another; people both respond to and change their surroundings. Operant conditioning is the tempting choice, but it is one-directional, with consequences shaping behavior.

questions.q: A student believes she can master organic chemistry if she studies hard, so she persists after a bad quiz. Which concept best describes her belief?
o: Learned helplessness
Learned helplessness involves giving up after uncontrollable failure.
High self-esteem
Self-esteem is overall self-worth, not task-specific competence.
High self-efficacy
Correct: self-efficacy is belief in one's ability to succeed at a specific task.
External locus of control
An external locus attributes outcomes to luck or others.
questions.x: Self-efficacy is the belief that one can succeed at a specific task, and high self-efficacy predicts effort and persistence after setbacks. Self-esteem is tempting but differs: it is an overall judgment of self-worth, and a person can have high self-esteem but low self-efficacy for organic chemistry.

questions.q: A behaviorist would most likely explain a child's outgoing personality as the result of what?
o: Resolution of early psychosexual stages
That is a psychoanalytic explanation.
An inborn temperament
That is a biological explanation.
Strivings toward self-actualization
That is a humanistic explanation.
A history of reinforcement for social behavior
Correct: behaviorists view personality as learned patterns of behavior.
questions.x: Behaviorists such as Skinner explain personality as patterns of learned behavior shaped by reinforcement and punishment; a child praised for socializing becomes more outgoing. An inborn temperament is a biological explanation, which behaviorists set aside in favor of observable environmental contingencies.

questions.q: Which personality perspective is most criticized for relying on concepts that are difficult to test scientifically?
o: Biological
Biological approaches use genetic and physiological measures.
Behaviorist
Behaviorism focuses on observable, measurable behavior.
Trait
Trait models are measured with validated questionnaires.
Psychoanalytic
Correct: unconscious drives and defenses are hard to falsify.
questions.x: Freud's central constructs (unconscious drives, defense mechanisms, psychosexual conflicts) are hard to measure or falsify, because almost any outcome can be explained after the fact. Behaviorism is the opposite case: it was built around observable, measurable behavior precisely to be testable.

questions.q: Researchers find that infants who show strong distress to novel stimuli tend to become shy, inhibited adolescents. This supports which view of personality?
o: Personality cannot be measured before adulthood
The study measured traits successfully in infancy.
Personality reflects only unconscious conflict
Observable infant reactivity is a biological, not psychoanalytic, measure.
Personality is formed entirely by adolescent peer groups
Continuity from infancy argues against purely adolescent origins.
Temperament provides a biological basis for later personality
Correct: early, stable temperament suggests biological roots of personality.
questions.x: Temperament is an early, biologically based style of reacting, such as Kagan's behaviorally inhibited infants who react strongly to novelty. Its continuity into shy adolescence suggests personality has biological roots. The infant measurements were behavioral and physiological, not evidence of unconscious conflict.

questions.q: A researcher gives participants a projective test in which they describe stories about ambiguous pictures. Which personality approach is she most likely using?
o: Social cognitive
Social cognitive researchers measure beliefs like self-efficacy and expectancies.
Psychoanalytic
Correct: projective tests like the TAT aim to reveal unconscious motives.
Trait
Trait researchers use self-report inventories like the NEO-PI.
Behaviorist
Behaviorists observe behavior and its consequences directly.
questions.x: Projective tests like the Thematic Apperception Test and Rorschach present ambiguous stimuli on the idea that people project unconscious motives into their responses, which comes from the psychoanalytic tradition. Trait researchers instead use structured self-report inventories with fixed items, such as the NEO-PI.

questions.q: Which statement shows an external locus of control?
o: I failed because I did not study enough.
Attributing outcomes to one's own effort is an internal locus.
I failed because the questions were unfair.
Correct: blaming outside forces reflects an external locus.
I will pass next time if I change my strategy.
Believing one's actions control outcomes is internal.
My hard work led to my good grade.
Crediting one's own work is internal.
questions.x: Locus of control (Rotter) is whether people attribute outcomes to their own actions (internal) or to outside forces such as luck, others or task difficulty (external). Blaming unfair questions is external. Saying a new strategy will help is internal, because it assumes one's actions control the result.

questions.q: The biomedical approach to psychological disorders focuses mainly on what?
o: Physical causes such as genetics and brain chemistry
Correct: it treats disorders like diseases with biological causes.
Biological, psychological and social factors together
That is the biopsychosocial approach.
Unconscious childhood conflicts
That is the psychoanalytic approach.
Cultural norms that label behavior as abnormal
That is a sociocultural view.
questions.x: The biomedical approach treats psychological disorders like physical diseases with biological causes, such as genes, neurotransmitters and brain abnormalities, and favors treatments like medication. The biopsychosocial approach is the tempting answer, but it adds psychological and social factors to biology rather than focusing on biology alone.

questions.q: A clinician treating depression considers the patient's serotonin function, negative thought patterns and recent job loss. Which approach is this?
o: Biopsychosocial
Correct: it integrates biological, psychological and social factors.
Behaviorist
Behaviorism would focus on reinforcement contingencies.
Psychodynamic
A psychodynamic approach would focus on unconscious conflict.
Biomedical
A biomedical approach would focus only on brain chemistry.
questions.x: The biopsychosocial model explains disorders as arising from biological (serotonin), psychological (negative thinking) and social (job loss) factors together. A biomedical approach would focus only on the serotonin piece, so considering all three domains is the clue.

questions.q: The diathesis–stress model proposes that psychological disorders develop when what happens?
o: Childhood conflicts are repressed
That is a psychoanalytic explanation.
A predisposition interacts with environmental stressors
Correct: vulnerability plus stress triggers the disorder.
Stress alone exceeds a fixed threshold in anyone
The model requires an underlying vulnerability.
Genes alone determine onset
The model requires stress to trigger the vulnerability.
questions.x: The diathesis-stress model says a predisposition (diathesis), whether genetic, biological or psychological, makes someone vulnerable, but a disorder emerges only when enough stress acts on it. The more vulnerable the person, the less stress it takes. That rules out explanations based on genes alone or stress alone.

questions.q: The DSM-5 classifies psychological disorders mainly on the basis of what?
o: Their presumed unconscious causes
The DSM avoids theory-based causes.
Response to medication
Treatment response is not used to define disorders.
Brain imaging findings
Imaging is not a DSM diagnostic criterion for most disorders.
Observable symptoms and their duration
Correct: DSM diagnoses use descriptive symptom criteria, largely atheoretical about cause.
questions.x: The DSM-5 is mostly descriptive and atheoretical: diagnoses are based on specific symptoms, their duration and the distress or impairment they cause, not on presumed causes. That lets clinicians from different theoretical backgrounds agree on a diagnosis. Brain imaging is not a diagnostic criterion for most disorders.

questions.q: Which is a positive symptom of schizophrenia?
o: Flat affect
Flat affect is a negative symptom (loss of normal function).
Auditory hallucinations
Correct: positive symptoms add experiences that are normally absent.
Alogia
Alogia, poverty of speech, is a negative symptom.
Avolition
Avolition, lack of motivation, is a negative symptom.
questions.note: Positive = added; negative = taken away.
questions.x: Positive symptoms of schizophrenia add experiences not normally present: hallucinations, delusions and disorganized speech or behavior. Negative symptoms are losses of normal function, such as flat affect, alogia, avolition and anhedonia. Positive does not mean good; it means added.

questions.q: A patient with schizophrenia rarely speaks, shows little facial expression and has no interest in activities. These are best described as what?
o: Catatonic excitement
Catatonic excitement involves purposeless excessive movement.
Negative symptoms
Correct: alogia, flat affect and avolition reflect diminished normal functions.
Manic symptoms
Mania involves elevated mood and energy.
Positive symptoms
Positive symptoms include hallucinations and delusions.
questions.x: Rare speech (alogia), reduced facial expression (flat affect) and lack of motivation (avolition) are negative symptoms, losses of normal function. They usually respond less well to classic D₂-blocking antipsychotics than positive symptoms do. Catatonia is tempting, but catatonic excitement involves excessive, purposeless movement, not mere withdrawal.

questions.q: A man believes that the television news anchor is sending him secret personal messages. What is this?
o: A delusion of reference
Correct: he believes neutral events are specifically directed at him.
A delusion of grandeur
Grandiose delusions involve beliefs of special power or fame.
Thought broadcasting
Thought broadcasting is believing others can hear one's thoughts.
A hallucination
A hallucination is a false perception, not a false belief.
questions.x: A delusion is a fixed false belief, and a delusion of reference is the belief that neutral events, such as TV broadcasts, contain messages specifically meant for oneself. A hallucination is a false perception, such as hearing a voice nobody spoke, which is why that choice is wrong here.

questions.q: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia is supported by which observation?
o: Drugs that block D₂ receptors reduce positive symptoms
Correct: antipsychotic efficacy tracks D₂ blockade.
SSRIs cure hallucinations
SSRIs are not effective antipsychotics.
L-dopa reduces delusions
L-dopa raises dopamine and can worsen or cause psychosis.
Schizophrenia is caused by low glutamate in the cerebellum
This does not relate to the dopamine hypothesis.
questions.x: The dopamine hypothesis holds that excess dopamine activity, especially in mesolimbic pathways, drives positive symptoms. Its key support is that antipsychotic potency tracks D₂ blockade, and dopamine-raising drugs such as amphetamine or L-dopa can trigger psychosis. L-dopa reducing delusions would contradict the hypothesis.

questions.q: Which brain finding is most consistently reported in people with schizophrenia?
o: Increased gray matter in the temporal lobes
Gray matter tends to be reduced, not increased.
Enlarged ventricles
Correct: ventricular enlargement reflects reduced surrounding brain tissue.
Absence of the corpus callosum
This is not a typical finding in schizophrenia.
Enlarged frontal lobes
Schizophrenia is linked to reduced frontal activity (hypofrontality).
questions.x: The most replicated structural finding in schizophrenia is enlarged lateral and third ventricles, reflecting loss of surrounding brain tissue, along with reduced cortical gray matter and lower frontal activity (hypofrontality). Choices claiming increased gray matter or enlarged frontal lobes get the direction backward.

questions.q: Schizophrenia concordance is about 45% in identical twins and 15% in fraternal twins. What can best be concluded?
o: Schizophrenia is entirely genetic
If entirely genetic, MZ concordance would be near 100%.
Genes play no role in schizophrenia
MZ concordance three times DZ shows genetic influence.
Genes contribute substantially, but environment also matters
Correct: higher MZ concordance shows genetic influence; MZ concordance below 100% shows non-genetic factors.
Shared family environment is the main cause
Both twin types share family environment, yet differ in concordance.
questions.x: MZ concordance (45%) is three times DZ concordance (15%), which shows genes matter. But because MZ twins are nearly genetically identical, concordance well below 100% shows that non-genetic factors also play a large role. This fits a diathesis-stress view rather than a purely genetic or purely environmental cause.

questions.q: Brief psychotic disorder differs from schizophrenia mainly in what way?
o: It occurs only in older adults
It can occur at any adult age.
It always involves a manic episode
Mania is a feature of bipolar disorder.
Symptoms last less than one month
Correct: brief psychotic disorder lasts 1 day to 1 month; schizophrenia requires 6 months.
It involves no hallucinations or delusions
It includes psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations.
questions.x: Psychotic disorders in the DSM are separated largely by duration: brief psychotic disorder lasts at least 1 day but less than 1 month, schizophreniform disorder 1 to 6 months, and schizophrenia at least 6 months including prodromal and residual phases. All three involve delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech.

questions.q: To diagnose major depressive disorder, symptoms must last at least how long?
o: Two weeks
Correct: a major depressive episode requires at least 2 weeks of symptoms.
Two years
Two years is the criterion for persistent depressive disorder in adults.
Two days
Two days is far too short for the DSM criterion.
Six months
Six months is the duration criterion for schizophrenia and GAD.
questions.x: A major depressive episode requires at least five symptoms, including depressed mood or anhedonia, nearly every day for at least 2 weeks. Two years is the tempting distractor because it is a real criterion, but it applies to persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia), the chronic, usually milder form.

questions.q: A woman has felt mildly depressed most days for three years but has never met full criteria for a major depressive episode. Which diagnosis best fits?
o: Bipolar II disorder
Bipolar II requires hypomania and a major depressive episode.
Cyclothymic disorder
Cyclothymia requires both hypomanic and depressive symptoms.
Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia)
Correct: chronic depressed mood for at least 2 years defines dysthymia.
Major depressive disorder
She never met full criteria for a major episode.
questions.x: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) is depressed mood most days for at least 2 years in adults, often milder than a major episode. Because she never met full criteria for a major episode, MDD does not fit. Cyclothymia also lasts 2 years but requires hypomanic symptoms as well, which she lacks.

questions.q: What is anhedonia?
o: Loss of pleasure in previously enjoyed activities
Correct: anhedonia is a core symptom of major depression.
Excessive worry about many events
That describes generalized anxiety disorder.
Inability to recall personal information
That describes dissociative amnesia.
An inflated sense of self-importance
That is grandiosity, seen in mania.
questions.x: Anhedonia is the loss of interest or pleasure in previously rewarding activities, and it is one of the two core symptoms of major depression along with depressed mood. It is also a negative symptom of schizophrenia. Excessive worry is the tempting mix-up, but that is the hallmark of generalized anxiety disorder, not depression.

questions.q: Depression symptoms that regularly appear in winter and lift in spring are classified as what?
o: Bipolar I disorder
Bipolar I requires a manic episode.
Cyclothymic disorder
Cyclothymia involves alternating hypomanic and depressive symptoms.
Major depressive disorder with seasonal pattern
Correct: seasonal affective disorder is a specifier of MDD, often treated with bright light.
Adjustment disorder
Adjustment disorder follows a specific identifiable stressor.
questions.x: When depressive episodes reliably begin in fall or winter and remit in spring, the DSM-5 adds the specifier 'with seasonal pattern', commonly called seasonal affective disorder. It is not its own disorder, and it is often treated with bright light therapy. Adjustment disorder requires a specific identifiable stressor rather than a seasonal cycle.

questions.q: Bipolar I disorder is distinguished from bipolar II disorder by the presence of what?
o: Psychotic symptoms lasting 6 months
That points toward schizophrenia.
At least one major depressive episode
Major depression is required for bipolar II, not bipolar I.
Hypomania only
Hypomania without full mania defines bipolar II or cyclothymia.
At least one full manic episode
Correct: bipolar I requires mania; bipolar II has hypomania plus major depression.
questions.note: Bipolar I: mania needed; depression optional.
questions.x: Bipolar I requires at least one full manic episode; depressive episodes are common but not required. Bipolar II requires at least one hypomanic episode and at least one major depressive episode, with no full mania ever. So a major depressive episode is required for bipolar II, not bipolar I.

questions.q: During a week-long episode, a man sleeps 2 hours a night, talks rapidly, and spends his savings on a scheme to buy an island. These symptoms best describe what?
o: A manic episode
Correct: decreased need for sleep, pressured speech and grandiose risky behavior for ≥1 week.
A panic attack
Panic attacks are brief bursts of intense fear.
Generalized anxiety
GAD involves worry, not elevated mood and grandiosity.
A hypomanic episode
Hypomania is milder and does not cause severe impairment.
questions.x: A manic episode involves elevated or irritable mood and increased energy for at least 1 week, or any duration if hospitalized, with symptoms such as reduced need for sleep, pressured speech and grandiose, risky behavior causing marked impairment. Hypomania has similar symptoms but lasts at least 4 days without severe impairment, so losing one's savings points to mania.

questions.q: Which medication is classically used as a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder?
o: Methylphenidate
Methylphenidate is a stimulant for ADHD.
Lithium
Correct: lithium reduces manic episodes and suicide risk.
Fluoxetine alone
An SSRI alone can trigger mania in bipolar patients.
Diazepam
Diazepam is a benzodiazepine for anxiety.
questions.x: Lithium is the classic mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder: it reduces manic and depressive episodes and lowers suicide risk, but it has a narrow therapeutic window that requires blood monitoring. An antidepressant like fluoxetine given alone is avoided because it can trigger a switch into mania.

questions.q: Seligman found that dogs exposed to inescapable shocks later failed to escape avoidable shocks. This model is most often used to explain which disorder?
o: Specific phobia
Phobias are explained mainly by fear conditioning.
Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia is not modeled by learned helplessness.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder
OCD involves compulsions to reduce anxiety, not helplessness.
Major depressive disorder
Correct: learned helplessness models the passivity and hopelessness of depression.
questions.x: Learned helplessness is when repeated uncontrollable aversive events teach an organism that its actions do not matter, so it stops trying even when escape becomes possible. The passivity and hopelessness resemble depression, so the model is used to explain it. Phobias come from fear conditioning, not from helplessness.

questions.q: According to Beck's cognitive theory, depression is maintained by which pattern?
o: Overreinforcement of social behavior
Behavioral models cite reduced, not excess, reinforcement.
Unconscious anger turned outward
Psychoanalysts described anger turned inward, and this is not Beck's model.
Excess dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway
That relates to the dopamine hypothesis of psychosis.
Negative views of the self, the world and the future
Correct: Beck's cognitive triad drives depressive thinking.
questions.x: Beck's cognitive theory holds that depression is maintained by a cognitive triad of negative beliefs about the self, the world and the future, reinforced by distortions such as overgeneralization. Cognitive therapy targets these thoughts directly. The choice about anger turned outward misstates the psychoanalytic view, which described anger turned inward.

questions.q: A woman worries constantly about her health, finances and family for over six months and has trouble sleeping. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Social anxiety disorder
Social anxiety centers on fear of scrutiny by others.
Generalized anxiety disorder
Correct: excessive, hard-to-control worry about many domains for ≥6 months.
Specific phobia
A phobia involves fear of one particular object or situation.
Panic disorder
Panic disorder centers on recurrent unexpected panic attacks.
questions.x: Generalized anxiety disorder is excessive, hard-to-control worry about many areas of life on most days for at least 6 months, with symptoms such as restlessness, fatigue and poor sleep. Specific phobia and social anxiety are focused on one feared object or on judgment by others, while GAD is diffuse and spread across many areas.

questions.q: After several unexpected panic attacks, a man stays home because he fears being trapped in places where escape would be hard. What does this describe?
o: Agoraphobia
Correct: fear of situations where escape or help might be unavailable.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder
OCD involves obsessions and compulsions.
Social anxiety disorder
Social anxiety focuses on being judged, not on escape.
Claustrophobia
Claustrophobia is a specific phobia of enclosed spaces only.
questions.x: Agoraphobia is fear and avoidance of situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable, such as crowds, public transport or open spaces, and it often develops after panic attacks. It can become so broad the person rarely leaves home. Claustrophobia is narrower: a specific phobia limited to enclosed spaces.

questions.q: A child is bitten by a dog and afterward panics whenever she sees any dog. Learning theory explains the onset of this phobia mainly through what?
o: Operant extinction
Extinction weakens, not creates, a response.
Classical conditioning
Correct: the dog (neutral stimulus) was paired with the painful bite (US) and became a conditioned stimulus for fear.
Observational learning only
She was directly bitten, so direct conditioning applies.
Latent learning
Latent learning is learning without reinforcement that appears later.
questions.note: Avoidance then maintains the phobia via negative reinforcement.
questions.x: In classical conditioning, a neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus. Here the dog (neutral stimulus) was paired with the painful bite (unconditioned stimulus), so dogs now trigger conditioned fear. Observational learning is tempting, but she was bitten herself, so direct conditioning explains the onset.

questions.q: Why does avoiding a feared object tend to maintain a phobia over time?
o: Avoidance causes spontaneous recovery
Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished response after a pause.
Avoidance reduces anxiety, which negatively reinforces the avoidance
Correct: relief strengthens avoidance and prevents extinction of the fear.
Avoidance positively punishes the fear response
Avoidance removes an aversive state, which is negative reinforcement.
Avoidance speeds extinction of the fear
Extinction requires exposure without the feared outcome.
questions.x: Mowrer's two-factor theory says fear is acquired by classical conditioning and then maintained by operant conditioning: avoiding the feared object brings relief, and removing an aversive state is negative reinforcement, which strengthens avoidance. Avoidance also blocks exposure, so the fear never gets the chance to extinguish.

questions.q: A man repeatedly checks that his stove is off because he is plagued by thoughts of his house burning down. The checking is best described as what?
o: A compulsion
Correct: compulsions are repetitive acts performed to reduce obsession-driven anxiety.
A tic
Tics are sudden involuntary movements, not anxiety-driven rituals.
An obsession
The intrusive thought is the obsession; the checking is the compulsion.
A delusion
He recognizes the thought as excessive, unlike a fixed delusion.
questions.x: In OCD, obsessions are intrusive, unwanted thoughts that cause anxiety, and compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts done to reduce that anxiety. The fear of fire is the obsession and the stove checking is the compulsion. Calling the checking an obsession mixes up the thought with the act it drives.

questions.q: In the DSM-5, obsessive-compulsive disorder is grouped with which other condition rather than with the anxiety disorders?
o: Generalized anxiety disorder
DSM-5 moved OCD out of the anxiety disorders class.
Posttraumatic stress disorder
PTSD is in the trauma- and stressor-related class.
Body dysmorphic disorder
Correct: OCD, BDD, hoarding and trichotillomania form their own class.
Panic disorder
Panic disorder remains an anxiety disorder.
questions.x: DSM-5 moved OCD out of the anxiety disorders into a new class, obsessive-compulsive and related disorders, which also includes body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania and excoriation disorder. PTSD likewise left the anxiety disorders, but for a different class: trauma- and stressor-related disorders.

questions.q: A woman spends hours daily examining a tiny facial blemish that others barely notice, and avoids going out. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Anorexia nervosa
Anorexia involves restricting food due to fear of weight gain.
Body dysmorphic disorder
Correct: preoccupation with a perceived flaw that is minor or not observable.
Social anxiety disorder
Her fear stems from a perceived defect, which defines BDD.
Illness anxiety disorder
Illness anxiety is preoccupation with having a serious disease.
questions.x: Body dysmorphic disorder is preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance that is minor or not visible to others, with repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking. It belongs in the obsessive-compulsive class. Social anxiety is tempting because she avoids going out, but her avoidance stems from the perceived defect, not general fear of scrutiny.

questions.q: Which symptom cluster is characteristic of posttraumatic stress disorder?
o: Intrusive memories, avoidance, negative mood changes and hyperarousal
Correct: these four clusters, lasting over a month after trauma, define PTSD.
Recurrent unexpected panic attacks without a trigger
This describes panic disorder.
Persistent elevated mood and decreased need for sleep
These describe mania.
Hallucinations and disorganized speech
These describe psychosis.
questions.x: PTSD follows exposure to trauma and involves four symptom clusters lasting more than 1 month: intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance of reminders, negative changes in mood and thinking, and changes in arousal and reactivity such as hypervigilance. Panic disorder involves unexpected attacks not tied to a traumatic memory.

questions.q: A soldier develops nightmares, flashbacks and hypervigilance that begin after combat and last two weeks, then resolve. Which diagnosis fits best?
o: Adjustment disorder
Adjustment disorder lacks the full trauma symptom profile.
Posttraumatic stress disorder
PTSD requires symptoms lasting more than one month.
Generalized anxiety disorder
GAD is not tied to a trauma and needs 6 months.
Acute stress disorder
Correct: trauma symptoms lasting 3 days to 1 month indicate acute stress disorder.
questions.x: Acute stress disorder and PTSD share the same trauma-related symptoms but differ in timing: acute stress disorder covers 3 days to 1 month after the trauma, and PTSD requires symptoms lasting more than 1 month. Because these symptoms resolved after two weeks, PTSD cannot be diagnosed.

questions.q: A woman cannot recall any details of her identity and is found living under a new name in another city. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Alzheimer disease
Alzheimer causes progressive decline, not abrupt identity loss with travel.
Depersonalization/derealization disorder
This involves feeling detached, with memory intact.
Dissociative identity disorder
DID involves two or more distinct identities alternating control.
Dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue
Correct: loss of identity memory with unexpected travel is fugue.
questions.x: Dissociative amnesia is an inability to recall important personal information, usually after trauma or stress. When it includes purposeful travel or wandering with confusion about identity, DSM-5 adds the specifier 'with dissociative fugue'. DID is tempting, but it requires two or more distinct identities, not loss of one identity.

questions.q: A man repeatedly feels as if he is watching himself from outside his body, though he knows this is not real. Which disorder does this suggest?
o: Schizophrenia
In schizophrenia reality testing is typically impaired.
Conversion disorder
Conversion involves neurological symptoms without medical cause.
Depersonalization/derealization disorder
Correct: detachment from self with intact reality testing.
Dissociative identity disorder
DID involves separate identities, not just detachment.
questions.x: Depersonalization is feeling detached from one's own body or mind, as if watching oneself from outside; derealization is feeling that surroundings are unreal. Reality testing stays intact, as he knows it is not real. That rules out schizophrenia, where psychotic experiences are typically believed to be real.

questions.q: Which disorder involves two or more distinct personality states that alternate in controlling behavior?
o: Borderline personality disorder
BPD involves unstable relationships and identity, not separate identities.
Bipolar disorder
Bipolar disorder involves mood episodes.
Dissociative identity disorder
Correct: formerly called multiple personality disorder.
Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia means a split from reality, not multiple personalities.
questions.note: Trap: schizophrenia is not split personality.
questions.x: Dissociative identity disorder, formerly multiple personality disorder, involves two or more distinct identity states that take control of behavior, with memory gaps between them. Schizophrenia is the classic trap: its name means split from reality, and it does not involve multiple personalities.

questions.q: After a severe argument, a woman suddenly cannot move her right arm, but neurological tests are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Illness anxiety disorder
Illness anxiety involves worry about illness with few symptoms.
Factitious disorder
Factitious disorder involves deliberately faking symptoms.
Somatic symptom disorder
Somatic symptom disorder centers on excessive worry about symptoms, not an unexplained loss of motor function.
Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder)
Correct: neurological symptoms inconsistent with medical findings, often after stress.
questions.x: Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) involves real motor or sensory symptoms, such as paralysis or blindness, that do not fit known neurological disease, and it often follows stress. The symptoms are not intentionally faked, which separates it from factitious disorder and malingering.

questions.q: A man has few physical symptoms but is convinced he has a serious undiagnosed disease despite repeated normal tests. Which diagnosis fits best?
o: Conversion disorder
Conversion involves an actual neurological symptom.
Somatic symptom disorder
Somatic symptom disorder requires distressing physical symptoms.
Illness anxiety disorder
Correct: preoccupation with having an illness with absent or mild symptoms.
Malingering
Malingering is faking symptoms for external gain.
questions.x: Illness anxiety disorder is preoccupation with having or getting a serious illness when physical symptoms are absent or mild, and normal test results do not reassure. Somatic symptom disorder is the close confusion: it requires distressing physical symptoms, with the excessive concern focused on those symptoms.

questions.q: A patient has chronic pain and spends most of the day worrying about it, though she accepts the pain is real. Which DSM category does her primary diagnosis fall under?
o: Somatic symptom and related disorders
Correct: distressing somatic symptoms with excessive thoughts and behaviors about them.
Anxiety disorders
Her worry centers on bodily symptoms, which DSM classifies separately.
Dissociative disorders
Dissociative disorders involve disrupted memory or identity.
Neurocognitive disorders
Neurocognitive disorders involve cognitive decline.
questions.x: Somatic symptom disorder means one or more distressing physical symptoms, real or not, combined with excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviors about them, such as constant worry. The pain need not be medically unexplained. The anxiety disorders are the tempting category, but DSM-5 places worry about bodily symptoms in the somatic symptom and related disorders class.

questions.q: Personality disorders in the DSM-5 are grouped into how many clusters?
o: Two (positive and negative)
Positive and negative describe schizophrenia symptoms.
Four (one per Big Five factor)
The clusters are not based on the Big Five.
Five (one per DSM axis)
DSM-5 removed the multiaxial system and uses three clusters.
Three (A, B and C)
Correct: odd/eccentric (A), dramatic/erratic (B) and anxious/fearful (C).
questions.x: DSM-5 groups the ten personality disorders into three descriptive clusters: A is odd or eccentric (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal), B is dramatic or erratic (antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic), and C is anxious or fearful (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive). The old five-axis system was removed in DSM-5.

questions.q: Which personality disorder belongs to Cluster A (odd or eccentric)?
o: Avoidant personality disorder
Avoidant is in Cluster C.
Histrionic personality disorder
Histrionic is in Cluster B.
Schizotypal personality disorder
Correct: Cluster A includes paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal.
Borderline personality disorder
Borderline is in Cluster B.
questions.x: Cluster A is odd or eccentric: paranoid, schizoid and schizotypal personality disorders, which share social detachment and unusual thinking, and schizotypal is linked to the schizophrenia spectrum. Avoidant is tempting because it also involves social withdrawal, but it is driven by fear of rejection, which places it in Cluster C.

questions.q: A woman has intense, unstable relationships, fears abandonment, self-harms and swings rapidly between idealizing and devaluing others. Which diagnosis fits best?
o: Dependent personality disorder
Dependent involves submissiveness and need to be cared for, not splitting.
Borderline personality disorder
Correct: instability in relationships, self-image and affect, plus splitting.
Histrionic personality disorder
Histrionic centers on attention seeking and dramatic emotion.
Bipolar II disorder
Bipolar mood episodes last days to weeks, not shifting within hours with relationships.
questions.x: Borderline personality disorder is marked by instability in relationships, self-image and emotion, frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, self-harm and splitting (seeing others as all good or all bad). Bipolar II is tempting because of mood swings, but bipolar episodes last days or weeks, while borderline shifts happen within hours and are triggered by relationships.

questions.q: A man repeatedly lies, steals and shows no remorse for hurting others, and has done so since age 15. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Paranoid personality disorder
Paranoid centers on pervasive distrust of others.
Narcissistic personality disorder
Narcissism centers on grandiosity and need for admiration.
Antisocial personality disorder
Correct: disregard for others' rights, deceit and lack of remorse in an adult.
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
OCPD centers on perfectionism and control.
questions.note: ASPD requires age 18+ with conduct disorder evidence before 15.
questions.x: Antisocial personality disorder is a pervasive disregard for others' rights shown by lying, theft, aggression and lack of remorse. It can be diagnosed only at age 18 or older, with evidence of conduct disorder before age 15. Narcissistic PD also involves low empathy, but it centers on grandiosity and needing admiration rather than rule-breaking.

questions.q: A man avoids social contact because he desperately wants friends but fears rejection and criticism. Which diagnosis fits best?
o: Avoidant personality disorder
Correct: avoidant individuals want connection but fear rejection.
Paranoid personality disorder
Paranoid individuals avoid others from suspicion, not fear of rejection.
Antisocial personality disorder
Antisocial means disregard for others, not social avoidance.
Schizoid personality disorder
Schizoid individuals are indifferent to relationships rather than fearful.
questions.note: Avoidant wants friends; schizoid doesn't care.
questions.x: Both avoidant and schizoid individuals have few relationships, but for different reasons. Avoidant personality disorder involves wanting connection while feeling inadequate and fearing criticism or rejection. Schizoid personality disorder involves genuine indifference to relationships and limited emotional expression, so wanting friends points to avoidant.

questions.q: How does obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) typically differ from OCD?
o: OCPD involves intrusive unwanted thoughts the person resists
That describes OCD obsessions, which are ego-dystonic.
OCPD involves pervasive perfectionism seen as acceptable by the person, without true obsessions
Correct: OCPD traits are ego-syntonic; OCD obsessions are intrusive and unwanted.
OCPD is always more impairing than OCD
There is no rule that OCPD is more impairing.
OCPD is a psychotic disorder
OCPD involves no psychosis.
questions.x: OCD involves ego-dystonic obsessions: intrusive thoughts the person sees as unwanted and tries to resist, often with compulsions. OCPD is a pervasive personality style of perfectionism, orderliness and control that the person sees as correct (ego-syntonic), with no true obsessions or compulsions. The two can co-occur but are distinct.

questions.q: A man needs constant admiration, exaggerates his achievements and lacks empathy for colleagues. Which personality disorder does this suggest?
o: Dependent
Dependent involves submissiveness and clinging.
Histrionic
Histrionic involves attention seeking through dramatic or seductive behavior.
Narcissistic
Correct: grandiosity, need for admiration and low empathy define narcissistic PD.
Schizotypal
Schizotypal involves odd beliefs and eccentric behavior.
questions.x: Narcissistic personality disorder involves grandiosity, a need for admiration and a lack of empathy, often hiding fragile self-esteem. Histrionic PD also seeks attention, but through dramatic, emotional or seductive behavior rather than claims of superiority.

questions.q: A clinician notes that a patient's distress about his symptoms is low because he sees his rigid traits as simply 'the right way to be.' This feature is most typical of which group of disorders?
o: Anxiety disorders
Anxiety symptoms are typically distressing and unwanted.
Dissociative identity disorder
DID usually involves distress and memory gaps.
Personality disorders
Correct: personality disorder traits are often ego-syntonic, viewed as part of the self.
Major depressive disorder
Depression involves marked personal distress.
questions.x: Personality disorders are usually ego-syntonic: the traits feel like a natural part of who the person is, so the person may feel little distress and may blame others for conflicts. Most other disorders, such as anxiety and depression, are ego-dystonic, experienced as unwanted and distressing, which often prompts people to seek treatment.

questions.q: A 70-year-old has gradually worsening memory loss over years that now interferes with daily life. Which DSM-5 category does this fall under?
o: Delirium
Delirium has acute onset and fluctuating attention.
Somatic symptom disorder
This category involves distress over bodily symptoms.
Dissociative amnesia
Dissociative amnesia is linked to stress or trauma, not gradual decline.
Major neurocognitive disorder
Correct: dementia is now called major neurocognitive disorder.
questions.x: DSM-5 replaced the term dementia with major neurocognitive disorder: a significant, usually gradual decline in cognition, such as memory, that interferes with independence; Alzheimer disease is the most common cause. Delirium also affects cognition but has acute onset and fluctuating attention, unlike this slow, years-long course.

questions.q: A hospitalized older patient suddenly becomes confused, with attention that fluctuates hour to hour, after starting a new medication. How does this differ from dementia?
o: Delirium is a personality disorder
Delirium is a neurocognitive disorder.
Delirium always progresses to death within months
Delirium is often reversible once the cause is treated.
Delirium has acute onset and fluctuating attention and is often reversible
Correct: delirium is sudden and fluctuating; dementia is gradual and progressive.
Delirium involves only memory loss with intact attention
Impaired attention is the core feature of delirium.
questions.x: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that develops over hours to days, fluctuates during the day, and has an identifiable cause such as medication, infection or metabolic imbalance. It is often reversible once the cause is treated. Dementia, by contrast, develops gradually and progresses, with attention relatively spared early on.

questions.q: Which theory states that behavior is motivated by the need to reduce internal tension caused by unmet biological needs?
o: Drive-reduction theory
Correct: needs create drives, and behavior reduces the drive to restore homeostasis.
Incentive theory
Incentive theory says external rewards pull behavior.
Instinct theory
Instinct theory says behavior stems from innate, fixed patterns.
Arousal theory
Arousal theory says we seek an optimal arousal level.
questions.x: Drive-reduction theory (Hull) says a physiological need creates an aversive internal tension, the drive, that motivates behavior to reduce it and restore homeostasis. Incentive theory is the contrast: it explains behavior as being pulled by external rewards rather than pushed by internal needs.

questions.q: Which behavior is hardest for drive-reduction theory to explain?
o: Eating when hungry
Eating reduces the hunger drive.
Putting on a coat when cold
This restores temperature homeostasis.
Riding a roller coaster for the thrill
Correct: seeking stimulation increases arousal rather than reducing a drive.
Drinking water when thirsty
Thirst reduction is a classic drive-reduction example.
questions.x: Drive-reduction theory explains behaviors that relieve biological needs, such as eating, drinking or getting warm. Thrill-seeking does the reverse: it deliberately raises arousal and satisfies no physiological need. Arousal theory handles such cases by proposing that people seek an optimal level of stimulation.

questions.q: A person studies harder for a scholarship worth 10,000 dollars than for one worth 500 dollars. Which theory best explains this?
o: Drive-reduction theory
No biological need is being reduced.
Opponent-process theory
Opponent-process explains emotional rebounds, as in addiction.
Instinct theory
Studying for money is not an innate fixed pattern.
Incentive theory
Correct: larger external rewards pull more motivated behavior.
questions.x: Incentive theory holds that behavior is pulled by external rewards, and bigger or more valued incentives produce more effort. No internal biological need is reduced by winning a scholarship, which rules out drive reduction, and studying for money is not an innate fixed pattern, which rules out instinct theory.

questions.q: Instinct theory of motivation was criticized mainly because it did what?
o: Applied only to humans
Instinct theory was drawn heavily from animal behavior.
Focused only on cognitive processes
It focused on innate patterns, not cognition.
Named behaviors without truly explaining them
Correct: labeling a behavior an instinct is circular and not explanatory.
Ignored biology entirely
Instinct theory is fundamentally biological.
questions.x: Early instinct theorists listed hundreds of instincts, which made the theory circular: a behavior was explained by an instinct whose only evidence was the behavior itself. Naming is not explaining. Instinct theory did rely on biology and animal behavior, so choices claiming it ignored biology are wrong.

questions.q: According to the Yerkes–Dodson law, how does optimal arousal differ for a complex task compared with a simple task?
o: Complex tasks are best at zero arousal
Too little arousal also impairs performance.
Optimal arousal is lower for complex tasks
Correct: difficult tasks are best performed at lower arousal; simple tasks tolerate more.
Optimal arousal is higher for complex tasks
High arousal disrupts performance on difficult tasks.
Optimal arousal is the same for all tasks
The optimum shifts with task difficulty.
questions.x: The Yerkes-Dodson law describes an inverted-U: performance improves with arousal up to an optimum, then declines. For complex or unfamiliar tasks the peak occurs at lower arousal, because high arousal disrupts careful thinking; simple or well-practiced tasks peak at higher arousal. Zero arousal is never optimal.

questions.q: In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which needs must generally be met first?
o: Belongingness needs
Belonging comes after physiological and safety needs.
Self-actualization
Self-actualization is the top of the hierarchy.
Physiological needs such as food and water
Correct: physiological needs form the base of the pyramid.
Esteem needs
