Self-esteem is higher in collectivist cultures
The study measured self-descriptions, not self-esteem.
Self-concept is unaffected by culture
The cultural difference contradicts this.
questions.x: Markus and Kitayama distinguished independent self-construals, which define the self by personal traits and are common in individualist cultures, from interdependent self-construals, which define the self by relationships and roles and are common in collectivist cultures such as Japan.

questions.q: Children who watched an adult hit an inflatable doll later hit the doll themselves when left alone with it. This demonstrates:
o: Classical conditioning
No neutral stimulus was paired with an unconditioned stimulus.
Operant shaping
The children were not reinforced for successive approximations.
Observational learning
Correct: behavior was acquired by watching a model.
Habituation
Habituation is a decreased response to a repeated stimulus.
questions.x: Observational learning (Bandura's Bobo doll study) is acquiring behavior by watching a model, without direct reinforcement or pairing of stimuli. The children learned aggression simply by seeing it. Classical conditioning would require a neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus.

questions.q: Children who saw a model punished for aggression imitated less, but when later offered rewards to imitate, they reproduced the aggression as well as children who saw the model rewarded. This shows that:
o: Learning can occur without being performed
Correct: they had learned the behavior; consequences affected performance.
Punishing a model erases what observers learned
The rewarded test showed the learning was intact.
Imitation requires direct reinforcement of the observer
They learned without being reinforced themselves.
Modeling works only when the model is a peer
The model was an adult.
questions.note: Bandura: acquisition vs. performance.
questions.x: Bandura distinguished acquiring a behavior from performing it. Seeing a model punished suppressed imitation, but offering rewards revealed the children had learned the aggression just as well. Vicarious consequences change motivation to perform, not whether learning occurred.

questions.q: Neurons that fire both when an animal performs an action and when it watches another perform the same action are proposed to support imitation. These are:
o: Place cells
Place cells encode spatial location in the hippocampus.
Grid cells
Grid cells support spatial navigation in entorhinal cortex.
Nociceptors
Nociceptors are pain receptors.
Mirror neurons
Correct: mirror neurons respond to both doing and observing actions.
questions.x: Mirror neurons, first found in the premotor cortex of monkeys, fire both when an individual performs an action and when it watches another perform that action. They are proposed to support imitation, observational learning and empathy. Place and grid cells instead encode spatial location.

questions.q: In Mead's account of the self, 'role-taking' refers to:
o: Copying observed behavior without understanding it
That is imitation in the preparatory stage.
Imagining another's perspective to anticipate their response
Correct: taking the role of the other lets one see oneself as an object.
Performing the duties of one's occupation
That is role performance, not role-taking.
Conforming to group norms under pressure
That is conformity.
questions.x: For Mead, role-taking means mentally adopting another person's perspective to anticipate how they will respond. By viewing ourselves from others' standpoints we come to see ourselves as social objects, which is how the self develops. Mere imitation without understanding marks the earlier preparatory stage.

questions.q: According to social learning theory, a child is most likely to imitate a model who:
o: Is punished for the behavior
Vicarious punishment reduces imitation.
Seems very different from the child
Dissimilar models are imitated less.
Seems similar to the child and is rewarded
Correct: similarity and vicarious reinforcement increase imitation.
Performs a behavior beyond the child's ability
Imitation requires the capacity to reproduce the behavior.
questions.x: Social learning theory predicts more imitation when the model is similar, competent or high-status and when the model is rewarded (vicarious reinforcement). Seeing a model punished reduces imitation. A child also cannot imitate what they lack the ability to reproduce.

questions.q: A child watches a pianist closely and remembers each step but lacks the finger dexterity to play the piece. Which of Bandura's modeling processes is the obstacle?
o: Reproduction
Correct: the child cannot physically carry out the observed behavior.
Attention
The child watched closely.
Retention
The child remembers the steps.
Motivation
Nothing suggests a lack of desire to perform.
questions.x: Bandura identified four processes in modeling: attention, retention, reproduction and motivation. Reproduction requires the physical and cognitive ability to carry out what was observed. The child attended and remembered, so the barrier is the inability to execute the behavior.

questions.q: Bandura's view that behavior, personal factors and environment all influence one another is called:
o: Behavioral genetics
That field studies heritability of traits.
Operant conditioning
That holds behavior is shaped by consequences alone.
Social facilitation
That is improved performance on simple tasks in front of others.
Reciprocal determinism
Correct: the three factors interact in both directions.
questions.x: Reciprocal determinism is Bandura's idea that behavior, personal factors (such as beliefs and expectations) and the environment all influence one another in both directions. It contrasts with strict operant views that treat behavior as shaped by environmental consequences alone.

questions.q: Compared with people with an external locus of control, people with an internal locus of control tend to:
o: Attribute outcomes mainly to luck or fate
That describes externals.
Take more active steps, such as following health regimens, to shape outcomes
Correct: believing effort matters encourages proactive behavior.
Show more learned helplessness
Helplessness is linked to an external locus.
Report lower self-efficacy
An internal locus tends to accompany higher self-efficacy.
questions.x: People with an internal locus of control believe their actions shape outcomes, so they tend to take proactive steps like following medical advice or seeking information. Externals attribute outcomes to luck, fate or powerful others and are more prone to helplessness when effort seems useless.

questions.q: The concept of locus of control was introduced by:
o: Albert Bandura
Bandura introduced self-efficacy.
Carl Rogers
Rogers developed client-centered theory and the ideal self.
Julian Rotter
Correct: Rotter proposed internal vs. external locus of control.
Abraham Maslow
Maslow proposed the hierarchy of needs.
questions.x: Julian Rotter introduced locus of control in the 1950s and 1960s as part of his social learning theory, distinguishing internal from external expectancies about what controls outcomes. Bandura's related but distinct concept is self-efficacy, a belief about one's capability at specific tasks.

questions.q: Researchers measure locus of control, then give participants an unsolvable puzzle described as either skill-based or chance-based. Theory predicts which group will persist longest?
o: Internals in the skill condition
Correct: they believe effort determines success on skill tasks.
Externals in the skill condition
Externals expect outcomes to depend little on effort.
Internals in the chance condition
Effort cannot help on a chance task, even for internals.
Externals in the chance condition
Both their disposition and the framing discourage effort.
questions.x: Persistence depends on expecting effort to pay off. Internals believe outcomes reflect their effort, and a skill framing reinforces that belief, so they keep working longest on an unsolvable puzzle. When a task is framed as chance, effort seems pointless even to internals.

questions.q: Before an exam, a student stays out late so that if he does poorly he can blame fatigue rather than lack of ability. This strategy is best described as:
o: Self-verification
Self-verification is seeking feedback that confirms existing self-views, not creating excuses.
Learned helplessness
He is acting strategically, not passively giving up after uncontrollable failure.
Downward social comparison
He is not comparing himself with worse-off others.
Self-handicapping
Correct: creating an obstacle in advance lets failure be blamed on it, protecting self-esteem.
questions.note: Self-handicapping protects self-esteem at the cost of performance.
questions.x: Self-handicapping means creating an obstacle before a performance so that a failure can be blamed on that obstacle rather than on lack of ability. It protects self-esteem at the cost of actual performance. Self-verification is different: it means seeking feedback that confirms existing self-views.

questions.q: Attributing one's successes to ability but one's failures to bad luck mainly serves to:
o: Increase accuracy of self-knowledge
The bias distorts, rather than sharpens, self-knowledge.
Protect self-esteem
Correct: the self-serving bias keeps self-evaluations positive.
Raise self-discrepancy
It reduces, not raises, felt gaps between selves.
Strengthen an external locus of control overall
Successes are credited internally, so it is not a general external orientation.
questions.x: The self-serving bias attributes successes to internal causes like ability and failures to external causes like luck. This pattern protects and enhances self-esteem rather than improving accuracy. Because successes are still credited internally, it is not a general external locus of control.

questions.q: Women who were reminded of a negative gender stereotype about math before a test scored lower than women who were not reminded. This illustrates:
o: Fundamental attribution error
That concerns over-attributing others' behavior to disposition.
Self-serving bias
That concerns attributions for one's own outcomes.
Stereotype threat
Correct: fear of confirming a group stereotype impairs performance.
Just-world hypothesis
That is the belief people get what they deserve.
questions.x: Stereotype threat (Steele and Aronson) occurs when awareness of a negative stereotype about one's group creates anxiety that impairs performance in that domain. Reminding women of a math stereotype lowered their scores. It concerns one's own performance, unlike attribution errors about others.

questions.q: Teachers were told that randomly chosen students were about to 'bloom' intellectually, and those students later showed larger test gains. This best illustrates:
o: Self-fulfilling prophecy
Correct: others' expectations changed behavior and outcomes to match.
Stereotype threat
No negative group stereotype was activated in the students.
Halo effect
Gains appeared on objective tests, not just subjective ratings.
Regression to the mean
Random selection rules out choosing students with extreme scores.
questions.x: A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when an expectation leads people to act in ways that make it come true. In the Pygmalion study, teachers' raised expectations for randomly chosen students apparently changed how they treated them. Random selection rules out regression to the mean.

questions.q: Which is generally considered the primary agent of socialization in early childhood?
o: Mass media
Media matter but are secondary to caregivers in early childhood.
Family
Correct: family shapes the earliest language, norms and self-concept.
School
School becomes important later in childhood.
Peers
Peer influence grows mainly in later childhood and adolescence.
questions.x: Family is the primary agent of socialization in early childhood, teaching language, basic norms, values and an initial self-concept. Schools, peers and media become more influential as children grow older, but the earliest and most formative socialization happens at home.

questions.q: During adolescence, which agent of socialization typically grows most in its influence on tastes, norms and identity?
o: Family
Family influence persists but declines relative to peers.
Religion
Religious influence varies widely and does not typically surge.
Government
Government is a distant agent of socialization.
Peer group
Correct: adolescents increasingly look to peers for norms and identity.
questions.x: During adolescence peers become an increasingly important agent of socialization, shaping tastes, norms, behavior and identity as teens seek independence from parents. Family influence persists, especially on core values, but declines relative to peers in day-to-day matters.

questions.q: Military basic training that strips recruits of prior identities and instills new norms and values is an example of:
o: Anticipatory socialization
That is adopting norms before joining a group.
Primary socialization
That occurs in early childhood within the family.
Resocialization
Correct: old norms are replaced, often within a total institution.
Role exit
Role exit is disengaging from a central role, not acquiring new norms.
questions.x: Resocialization is the process of discarding old norms and behaviors and adopting new ones, often deliberately within total institutions such as military basic training, prisons or psychiatric hospitals. Anticipatory socialization differs because it adopts a group's norms before joining.

questions.q: Identity theory proposes that a person's many identities are arranged in a hierarchy of salience. The most salient identity is the one that:
o: Is most likely to be enacted across situations
Correct: higher salience means a higher chance of being invoked.
Was assigned at birth
Salience depends on commitment, not on being ascribed.
Is suppressed under stress
Salient identities tend to guide behavior, not vanish.
Is determined only by others' perceptions
Salience reflects one's own commitment to the identity.
questions.x: Identity theory (Stryker) says each person holds many identities ranked in a salience hierarchy. Salience is the likelihood an identity will be invoked across situations, and it rises with commitment to the relationships tied to that identity. Salient identities guide behavior rather than being suppressed.

questions.q: Social identity theory proposes that part of a person's self-concept comes from:
o: Unconscious childhood conflicts
That reflects Freud's psychodynamic view.
Membership in social groups
Correct: group memberships contribute to self-concept and self-esteem.
Observing one's own behavior
That is self-perception theory.
Inherited personality traits
Social identity theory focuses on groups, not genetics.
questions.x: Social identity theory (Tajfel and Turner) holds that part of the self-concept and self-esteem comes from belonging to social groups. Because group membership feeds self-esteem, people tend to favor their in-group. Inferring attitudes from one's own behavior is self-perception theory instead.

questions.q: Participants assigned to groups by a coin flip still give more rewards to members of their own group. This finding best supports the claim that:
o: Competition over scarce resources is needed for bias
No real conflict existed between the groups.
Prior friendships drive in-group favoritism
Participants were strangers assigned at random.
People default to equal allocation
They favored their own group.
Mere categorization is enough to produce in-group favoritism
Correct: the minimal group paradigm shows bias from trivial grouping.
questions.x: Tajfel's minimal group paradigm assigned people to groups on trivial or random grounds, with no history, interaction or competition, yet participants still favored their own group. This shows that mere categorization is enough to produce in-group bias, contrary to the idea that real conflict is required.

questions.q: A student notices that she volunteers every weekend and concludes, 'I must really care about my community.' This best illustrates:
o: Cognitive dissonance
She feels no discomfort from conflicting cognitions.
Looking-glass self
She infers from her own behavior, not others' judgments.
Self-perception theory
Correct: people infer their attitudes by observing their own behavior.
Self-verification
She is not seeking confirming feedback from others.
questions.x: Self-perception theory (Bem) proposes that when internal states are unclear, people infer their own attitudes by observing their behavior, as an outside observer would. Concluding 'I must care' from volunteering fits. Cognitive dissonance would require discomfort from inconsistent cognitions.

questions.q: People with negative self-views sometimes prefer friends who see them negatively over friends who see them positively. This is best explained by:
o: Self-verification
Correct: people seek feedback that confirms their existing self-concept.
Self-enhancement
Self-enhancement would favor positive feedback.
Self-handicapping
That creates excuses before performance.
Downward social comparison
That involves comparing with worse-off others.
questions.x: Self-verification theory (Swann) proposes that people seek feedback confirming their existing self-views because consistency feels predictable and controllable, even when the self-view is negative. Self-enhancement predicts the opposite, a preference for positive feedback regardless of self-view.

questions.q: Young children describe themselves in concrete terms such as 'I have a dog.' Adolescents more often describe themselves in terms of:
o: Physical features only
This is more typical of young children.
Abstract traits and values
Correct: formal operational thinking supports abstract self-descriptions.
Possessions and favorite activities only
That is the concrete style of early childhood.
No consistent characteristics
Adolescents form increasingly organized self-concepts.
questions.x: Self-descriptions grow more abstract with age. Young children describe themselves by concrete features, possessions and activities, while adolescents, aided by formal operational thought, describe themselves with abstract traits, values and beliefs that organize their self-concept.

questions.q: In the rouge test, toddlers who touch a red mark on their own nose when looking in a mirror are demonstrating:
o: Object permanence
That is knowing objects exist when unseen.
Theory of mind
That is understanding others' mental states, tested with false-belief tasks.
Conservation
That is a Piagetian concrete operational skill.
Visual self-recognition
Correct: recognizing the reflection as oneself, emerging around 18 to 24 months.
questions.x: In the rouge (mirror) test, a mark is placed on a child's face; touching their own face, not the mirror, shows they recognize the reflection as themselves. This visual self-recognition typically emerges around 18 to 24 months. Theory of mind is tested later with false-belief tasks.

questions.q: A 5-year-old talks aloud to herself while working through a puzzle. Vygotsky viewed this private speech as:
o: Egocentric speech with no function
That was Piaget's interpretation.
A sign of language delay
Private speech is normal at this age.
A self-regulation tool that later becomes inner speech
Correct: social speech is internalized to guide thought and action.
Mere imitation of parents with no cognitive role
Vygotsky saw it as cognitively important.
questions.x: Vygotsky saw private speech as a tool children use to guide and regulate their own thinking and actions. Speech starts as social exchange, becomes audible self-talk, and is gradually internalized as silent inner speech. Piaget instead treated it as egocentric speech with little function.

questions.q: In Vygotsky's theory, the person who guides a learner within the zone of proximal development is called the:
o: More knowledgeable other
Correct: a peer or adult with greater skill provides guidance.
Generalized other
That is Mead's concept of internalized societal expectations.
Significant other
That is Mead's term for specific important people.
Reference group
That is a group used as a standard for self-evaluation.
questions.x: In Vygotsky's theory the more knowledgeable other is anyone, adult or peer, with greater skill who guides a learner within the zone of proximal development. Generalized other and significant other are terms from Mead's theory of the social self, not from Vygotsky.

questions.q: Children in a culture that uses the abacus daily develop mental arithmetic strategies that mimic bead movements. Which theorist's view does this best support?
o: Freud
Freud focused on psychosexual drives.
Vygotsky
Correct: cultural tools shape the way thinking develops.
Kohlberg
Kohlberg focused on moral reasoning.
Erikson
Erikson focused on psychosocial crises.
questions.x: Vygotsky argued that cultural tools, from language to number systems to devices like the abacus, shape the way thinking develops. Children who internalize bead movements as mental arithmetic show a cultural tool becoming a cognitive strategy, a hallmark of sociocultural theory.

questions.q: In Freud's structural model, the part of the personality that internalizes parental and societal moral standards is the:
o: Id
The id seeks immediate gratification.
Ego
The ego mediates between the id and reality.
Preconscious
The preconscious is a level of awareness, not a structure.
Superego
Correct: the superego holds internalized morals and ideals.
questions.x: Freud's structural model has three parts: the id (instinctual drives, pleasure principle), the ego (realistic mediator, reality principle) and the superego (internalized moral standards and ideals from parents and society). The preconscious is a level of awareness, not one of these structures.

questions.q: According to Freud, the ego operates on the:
o: Pleasure principle
That governs the id.
Morality principle
That loosely describes the superego.
Reality principle
Correct: the ego seeks realistic ways to satisfy the id's drives.
Repetition compulsion
That is a later Freudian idea about repeating trauma.
questions.x: The ego operates on the reality principle: it seeks realistic, socially acceptable ways to satisfy the id's demands while respecting the superego. The id operates on the pleasure principle, seeking immediate gratification regardless of consequences. The ego can delay gratification; the id cannot.

questions.q: A key difference between Erikson's and Freud's developmental theories is that Erikson:
o: Emphasized social conflicts spanning the entire lifespan
Correct: Erikson extended development through old age and stressed social relationships.
Rejected stage models of development
Erikson proposed eight stages.
Focused only on childhood sexuality
That describes Freud more closely.
Denied that development involves conflicts
Each Erikson stage is defined by a conflict.
questions.x: Freud's five psychosexual stages end at puberty and focus on sexual drives. Erikson kept a stage model with a conflict at each stage, but stressed social relationships and extended development across the whole lifespan in eight stages, through old age.

questions.q: Successful resolution of Erikson's identity vs. role confusion stage yields which virtue?
o: Hope
Hope comes from trust vs. mistrust.
Fidelity
Correct: fidelity, the ability to stay loyal to commitments, follows identity resolution.
Wisdom
Wisdom comes from integrity vs. despair.
Competence
Competence comes from industry vs. inferiority.
questions.x: Each Erikson stage yields a virtue when resolved: hope (trust), will (autonomy), purpose (initiative), competence (industry), fidelity (identity), love (intimacy), care (generativity) and wisdom (integrity). Fidelity means staying loyal to chosen values and commitments.

questions.q: A citizen argues that an unjust law should be changed through democratic means because laws are agreements meant to serve the common good. Which Kohlberg stage fits best?
o: Law and order
Stage 4 treats laws as fixed duties to uphold.
Good interpersonal relationships
Stage 3 reasons from others' approval.
Social contract
Correct: stage 5 sees laws as changeable agreements for the public good.
Obedience and punishment
Stage 1 reasons from avoiding punishment.
questions.x: Kohlberg's stage 5, social contract, views laws as agreements that serve the common good and that can be changed by democratic means when they fail to. Stage 4 sees laws as fixed duties that maintain order. Stage 6 would appeal to universal principles that may justify disobedience.

questions.q: Kohlberg found that most adults reason at which level of moral development?
o: Preconventional
Most children, not adults, reason this way.
Postconventional
Relatively few adults reach this level consistently.
Preoperational
This is a Piaget stage, not a Kohlberg level.
Conventional
Correct: most adults reason from social norms and laws.
questions.x: Kohlberg found that most adolescents and adults reason at the conventional level, judging morality by social approval (stage 3) and law and order (stage 4). Only a minority consistently reach postconventional reasoning. Preoperational is a Piagetian cognitive stage, not a moral level.

questions.q: Researchers find that people in some collectivist societies rarely score at Kohlberg's postconventional stages, yet show sophisticated community-centered moral reasoning. This most directly challenges:
o: The universality of Kohlberg's scoring criteria
Correct: it suggests the stages reflect Western, individualist values.
The order of Erikson's stages
Erikson's theory is not about moral reasoning.
Vygotsky's zone of proximal development
The ZPD concerns guided learning.
Freud's latency stage
Latency concerns psychosexual development.
questions.x: Kohlberg claimed his stages were universal, but his highest stages reflect Western, individualist ideals of rights and justice. Findings that people in collectivist cultures reason in sophisticated community-centered ways yet rarely score as postconventional suggest cultural bias in the scoring.

questions.q: An immigrant teen keeps her heritage language and traditions while also adopting the host country's norms. Which acculturation strategy is this?
o: Assimilation
Assimilation abandons the heritage culture.
Integration
Correct: keeping both heritage and host cultures is integration.
Separation
Separation keeps heritage culture but rejects the host culture.
Marginalization
Marginalization rejects both cultures.
questions.x: Berry's acculturation model crosses two questions: is heritage culture maintained, and is the host culture adopted? Integration keeps both, assimilation adopts only the host, separation keeps only the heritage, and marginalization keeps neither. Keeping both cultures is integration.

questions.q: A family abandons its native language and customs in order to fully adopt the host country's culture. This acculturation strategy is:
o: Integration
Integration retains the heritage culture.
Separation
Separation retains the heritage culture and rejects the host.
Assimilation
Correct: the heritage culture is replaced by the host culture.
Multiculturalism
That describes a society valuing many cultures, not this family's choice.
questions.x: In Berry's model, assimilation means giving up the heritage culture and fully adopting the host culture. Integration and separation both keep the heritage culture, differing in whether the host culture is also adopted. Multiculturalism describes a society's policy, not an individual's strategy.

questions.q: In a study, adults watching the same crying infant described it as 'angry' when told it was a boy and 'scared' when told it was a girl. This best illustrates:
o: Biological sex differences in emotion
The infant was identical in both conditions.
Gender constancy in infants
Gender constancy develops in early childhood, not infancy.
The infant's temperament
Temperament was held constant across conditions.
Adults' gender expectations shaping how a child is perceived
Correct: gender socialization begins with others' expectations.
questions.x: In the 'Baby X' design, adults saw the same infant behavior but interpreted it differently depending on the gender label. Because the infant was identical, the difference must come from adults' gender expectations, showing gender socialization begins with how others perceive a child.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy says he will turn into a girl if he grows his hair long. He has not yet developed:
o: Gender constancy
Correct: understanding that gender is stable across appearance changes.
Object permanence
He knows objects persist; this concerns gender stability.
Sexual orientation
Orientation concerns attraction, not gender stability.
Gender expression
He clearly expresses gender; he misunderstands its permanence.
questions.x: Gender constancy is the understanding that one's gender stays the same despite changes in appearance or activities, usually achieved around ages 5 to 7. A 3-year-old who thinks long hair would turn him into a girl lacks it. Gender expression concerns outward presentation, which he already shows.

questions.q: A person who scores high on both stereotypically masculine and stereotypically feminine traits is described as:
o: Undifferentiated
Undifferentiated means low on both.
Androgynous
Correct: high levels of both sets of traits.
Gender-typed
Gender-typed means high only in traits matching one's gender.
Cross-typed
Cross-typed means high only in traits of the other gender.
questions.x: Bem classified people by two independent dimensions, masculine and feminine traits. High on both is androgynous, low on both is undifferentiated, and high only on the traits typical of one's own gender is gender-typed. Androgyny reflects flexibility rather than a lack of gendered traits.

questions.q: Among cardiac patients with similar disease severity, those with higher exercise self-efficacy attended more rehab sessions. What most limits causal conclusions?
o: Patients were randomly assigned
They were not, and random assignment would strengthen causal claims.
The study was double-blind
Blinding would not weaken causal inference.
Self-efficacy was measured, not manipulated
Correct: a correlational design cannot rule out confounds or reverse causation.
The sample was too homogeneous in severity
Matching on severity controls a confound; it does not limit causality.
questions.x: The study observed naturally occurring self-efficacy and attendance, so it is correlational. Without manipulating self-efficacy, a third variable such as motivation or social support could drive both, or attending rehab could raise efficacy. Matching on severity controls one confound but not all.

questions.q: According to Bandura, people with high self-efficacy for a task are most likely to:
o: Avoid the task when it becomes difficult
That describes low self-efficacy.
Attribute failure to a lack of ability
High-efficacy people attribute failure to effort or strategy.
Give up quickly after setbacks
Low efficacy predicts quitting.
Persist and treat hard tasks as challenges
Correct: strong efficacy beliefs sustain effort.
questions.x: Bandura found that high self-efficacy leads people to choose harder goals, persist longer and view difficulties as challenges to master. Low-efficacy people avoid hard tasks, give up quickly and attribute failure to low ability. Belief in capability sustains effort through setbacks.

questions.q: A coach tells a nervous swimmer, 'You've trained hard, and you're ready to win.' Which source of self-efficacy is the coach using?
o: Verbal persuasion
Correct: encouragement from others can raise efficacy beliefs.
Mastery experience
The swimmer's own success is not the source here.
Vicarious experience
No model is being observed.
Physiological states
The coach is not reinterpreting bodily arousal.
questions.x: Verbal persuasion is encouragement from others that one can succeed; it can boost self-efficacy, though it is weaker and more fragile than mastery experience. The coach's pep talk is persuasion. Mastery would require the swimmer drawing on her own past successes.

questions.q: A student interprets her racing heart before an exam as a sign she is unprepared, lowering her confidence. Which source of self-efficacy does this reflect?
o: Mastery experience
No past performance is being drawn on.
Emotional and physiological states
Correct: how one reads bodily arousal shifts efficacy beliefs.
Vicarious experience
She is not observing others.
Verbal persuasion
No one is persuading her.
questions.x: Bandura listed emotional and physiological states as a source of self-efficacy. People read arousal such as a racing heart as information about their capability, so interpreting it as unpreparedness lowers efficacy. Reinterpreting the same arousal as readiness can raise it instead.

questions.q: Researchers find that global self-esteem correlates only weakly with exam scores, whereas academic self-efficacy correlates more strongly. Which explanation fits best?
o: Self-esteem is unrelated to the self-concept
Self-esteem is the evaluative part of the self-concept.
Self-efficacy is the same construct as self-esteem
The different correlations suggest distinct constructs.
Task-specific beliefs predict task-specific outcomes better than global worth
Correct: efficacy is tied to the domain being measured.
High self-esteem causes poor exam performance
A weak positive correlation does not imply harm.
questions.x: Specific attitudes predict specific outcomes better than global ones. Academic self-efficacy is tied to the very domain being tested, while global self-esteem is a broad sense of worth that is only loosely linked to any single performance. Different correlations mean distinct constructs.

questions.q: A teen deliberately adopts styles and opinions opposite to those of a clique he dislikes. For him, that clique serves as a:
o: Primary group
A primary group involves close, enduring personal ties.
In-group
He does not identify as a member.
Secondary group
Secondary groups are large, impersonal and goal-oriented.
Negative reference group
Correct: a group whose norms one defines oneself against.
questions.x: A reference group can work in either direction. A positive reference group sets standards to emulate, while a negative reference group is one whose norms a person deliberately rejects to define who they are not. He neither belongs to nor emulates the clique, so it is a negative reference group.

questions.q: Adolescents' self-ratings of competence correlated more strongly with what they believed their parents thought of them than with parents' actual ratings. This best supports:
o: Cooley's looking-glass self
Correct: perceived, not actual, appraisals shape self-views.
Bandura's reciprocal determinism
The finding concerns imagined appraisals, not interacting factors.
Marcia's identity statuses
No exploration or commitment was measured.
Rotter's locus of control
No attributions of control were measured.
questions.x: Cooley's looking-glass self predicts self-views track imagined appraisals, what we think others think of us, rather than their actual opinions. The finding that teens' self-ratings matched perceived parental views more than parents' real ratings supports exactly this.

questions.q: In Mead's play stage, children take on the roles of specific important individuals in their lives, called:
o: Generalized others
The generalized other emerges in the game stage.
Significant others
Correct: specific people such as parents whose roles are adopted.
Reference groups
Reference groups are groups used for self-evaluation.
Out-groups
Out-groups are groups one does not identify with.
questions.x: In Mead's play stage, children take the role of significant others, specific important people such as parents or teachers, one at a time. Only in the later game stage do they internalize the generalized other, the organized expectations of the whole group or society.

questions.q: Piaget held that development must precede learning. Vygotsky instead held that:
o: Development must be complete before any learning
That is close to Piaget's view.
Development is fixed by genetics alone
Vygotsky emphasized social and cultural influences.
Learning through social interaction leads development
Correct: guided learning in the ZPD pulls development forward.
Only adolescents can learn from peers
Vygotsky applied his ideas across childhood.
questions.x: Piaget held that children must reach a developmental stage before they can learn related concepts. Vygotsky reversed this: learning through guided social interaction within the zone of proximal development pulls development forward, so instruction should aim slightly ahead of current ability.

questions.q: After exploring several career paths and weighing her values, a student firmly commits to a career in public health. Which identity status fits best?
o: Foreclosure
Foreclosure lacks exploration.
Moratorium
Moratorium lacks commitment.
Diffusion
Diffusion lacks both.
Identity achievement
Correct: commitment following active exploration.
questions.x: Identity achievement in Marcia's model is a firm commitment made after active exploration of alternatives. This student explored career paths and values, then committed. Foreclosure involves commitment too, but without exploration, usually adopting choices from parents or others.

questions.q: An adult who chews pens, smokes heavily and is overly dependent on others would, per Freud, be fixated at which stage?
o: Anal
Anal fixation shows as orderliness or messiness.
Oral
Correct: oral fixation shows as oral habits and dependency.
Phallic
Phallic fixation involves Oedipal themes.
Latency
Latency is not typically described as a fixation point.
questions.x: Freud linked the oral stage of infancy to pleasure from sucking and feeding. Fixation, from too much or too little gratification, was said to produce adult oral habits such as smoking, nail-biting or overeating and a dependent personality. Anal fixation instead shows as orderliness or messiness.

questions.q: In attribution theory, explaining a behavior by pointing to a person's traits, abilities or character is called what?
o: A situational attribution
Situational attributions point to external circumstances, not traits.
A stable-external attribution
External causes are situational, so this cannot describe a trait-based explanation.
A self-serving attribution
Self-serving bias is a pattern across outcomes, not the label for any trait explanation.
A dispositional attribution
Correct: dispositional (internal) attributions locate the cause inside the person.
questions.note: Dispositional = internal; situational = external.
questions.x: Attribution theory sorts explanations of behavior by where the cause is located. A dispositional (internal) attribution places it inside the person: traits, abilities, effort or character. A situational (external) attribution places it in circumstances. Self-serving bias is not a type of attribution but a pattern of choosing internal causes for success and external causes for failure.

questions.q: A student says her roommate failed an exam because the room was noisy and the test was scheduled during a fire drill. What kind of attribution is this?
o: Dispositional
A dispositional explanation would cite the roommate's ability or effort.
Fundamental attribution error
The FAE is overweighting traits; this explanation emphasizes the situation.
Situational
Correct: noise and scheduling are external circumstances.
Just-world reasoning
Just-world reasoning blames victims for deserving outcomes, which she does not do.
questions.x: Noise and a fire drill are features of the environment, so this is a situational (external) attribution. The fundamental attribution error is the opposite tendency: underweighting situations like these and overweighting traits when explaining someone else's behavior. Naming a bias requires a distortion; this explanation simply cites external causes.

questions.q: Kelley's covariation model predicts a situational attribution when a behavior shows which combination of consensus, distinctiveness and consistency?
o: Low consensus, low distinctiveness, high consistency
This pattern points to the person, a dispositional attribution.
High consensus, high distinctiveness, high consistency
Correct: everyone does it, only in this situation, reliably, so the situation is the cause.
High consensus, low distinctiveness, low consistency
Low consistency suggests a fluke or transient circumstance, not a clear situational cause.
Low consensus, high distinctiveness, low consistency
Low consistency undermines any stable attribution.
questions.note: Trap: low consensus + low distinctiveness + high consistency = dispositional.
questions.x: Kelley's covariation model uses three cues. High consensus (others act the same way), high distinctiveness (the person acts this way only toward this stimulus) and high consistency (it happens reliably) point to the situation or stimulus. Low consensus and low distinctiveness with high consistency point to the person. Low consistency suggests a passing circumstance rather than a stable cause.

questions.q: Mateo laughs loudly at every comedian, while few other audience members laugh at tonight's act, and he always laughs this way. By Kelley's model, observers will most likely attribute his laughter to what?
o: Something about the comedian
A stimulus attribution needs high consensus and high distinctiveness.
Something about Mateo
Correct: low consensus, low distinctiveness and high consistency yield a person attribution.
A temporary circumstance
Transient-circumstance attributions follow low consistency, but his laughter is consistent.
The audience's mood that night
Low consensus means the rest of the audience is not reacting the same way.
questions.x: Mateo laughs at every comedian (low distinctiveness), few others laugh at this act (low consensus), and he always does it (high consistency). That combination tells observers the behavior comes from Mateo himself. A stimulus attribution to the comedian would require that most people laugh at this act and that Mateo laughs at this act but not others.

questions.q: Observers watching a classmate trip on stairs conclude he is clumsy and ignore the wet floor. Which bias does this best illustrate?
o: Fundamental attribution error
Correct: the observer overweights traits and underweights the wet floor.
Self-serving bias
Self-serving bias concerns explanations of one's own successes and failures.
Halo effect
The halo effect spreads one positive trait to unrelated judgments.
False consensus effect
False consensus is overestimating how many people share one's views.
questions.x: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to overweight dispositional causes and underweight situational ones when explaining another person's behavior. Here a clear situational cause, the wet floor, is ignored in favor of a trait. Self-serving bias would be tempting only if the observer were explaining his own stumble; it concerns attributions about oneself.

questions.q: Researchers have participants read an essay they are told was assigned to the writer by a coin flip. Participants still rate the writer's true attitude as matching the essay. What does this most directly demonstrate?
o: Actor-observer bias
Actor-observer bias needs a comparison of self versus other explanations.
Cognitive dissonance
Dissonance concerns one's own inconsistent cognitions, not judging another's essay.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
No expectation is shown to change the writer's actual behavior.
Correspondence bias
Correct: people infer an attitude matching behavior even when the behavior was externally forced.
questions.note: Correspondence bias is another name for the fundamental attribution error.
questions.x: In this classic design, observers know the essay position was imposed, yet they still infer the writer holds that attitude. Inferring a disposition that corresponds to behavior despite obvious situational constraints is the correspondence bias, another name for the fundamental attribution error. Actor-observer bias would require comparing how people explain their own behavior versus others'.

questions.q: When Dana is late, she blames traffic; when her coworker is late, she decides he is irresponsible. Which concept best fits?
o: Self-handicapping
Self-handicapping is creating obstacles in advance to excuse possible failure.
Just-world hypothesis
She does not claim the coworker deserved a bad outcome.
Actor-observer bias
Correct: situational explanations for oneself, dispositional ones for others.
Ultimate attribution error
That bias applies the FAE to whole out-groups, not one coworker.
questions.x: Actor-observer bias is the asymmetry between explaining one's own behavior situationally and others' behavior dispositionally. Actors see the situation pressing on them, while observers see the person as the most salient cause. The ultimate attribution error is similar but applies trait blame to an entire out-group, not a single coworker.

questions.q: A soccer player credits a win to her skill but blames a loss on bad refereeing. Which bias is shown?
o: Fundamental attribution error
The FAE concerns explaining other people's behavior.
Optimism bias
Optimism bias is overestimating the chance of good future events.
Self-serving bias
Correct: internal attribution for success, external attribution for failure.
Confirmation bias
Confirmation bias is seeking evidence that supports existing beliefs.
questions.x: Self-serving bias means taking internal credit for successes and assigning failures to external causes. The player attributes the win to her skill (internal) and the loss to referees (external). The fundamental attribution error is tempting, but it describes how we explain other people's behavior, not our own outcomes.

questions.q: The self-serving bias is generally thought to serve which psychological function?
o: Reducing cognitive load during social judgments
Load reduction explains heuristics like stereotyping, not motivated self-attributions.
Protecting and enhancing self-esteem
Correct: taking credit for success and deflecting blame for failure preserves self-worth.
Increasing accuracy of self-assessment
The bias distorts self-assessment rather than improving it.
Strengthening in-group cohesion
That is closer to the group-serving bias, not the individual self-serving bias.
questions.x: The self-serving bias is usually explained as motivated reasoning that protects and enhances self-esteem: credit for success boosts self-worth and blaming circumstances for failure shields it. Because it distorts reality, it reduces rather than increases accuracy. Cognitive shortcuts that save effort, such as heuristics, are a different, cold-cognition explanation for bias.

questions.q: After hearing about a mugging, a listener insists the victim was careless to walk alone at night. Which belief most likely underlies this reaction?
o: The just-world hypothesis
Correct: believing people get what they deserve leads to blaming victims.
Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is a performance effect on the stereotyped person.
Ethnocentrism
Ethnocentrism judges other cultures by one's own standards.
Actor-observer bias
No self-versus-other comparison is involved.
questions.x: The just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve and deserve what they get. Seeing an innocent person suffer threatens that belief, so people restore it by finding fault with the victim, called victim blaming. Actor-observer bias does not fit because the listener is not comparing explanations of their own behavior with someone else's.

questions.q: Researchers find that participants who score high on belief in a just world rate an innocent victim of random violence as less likable after learning the perpetrator was never caught. Which explanation best fits?
o: Unresolved crimes trigger stereotype threat in observers
Stereotype threat affects members of stereotyped groups during performance.
Participants are showing the self-serving bias
The outcome is not about the participants' own success or failure.
The halo effect reverses when a crime is unsolved
The halo effect is trait spreading, unrelated to justice concerns.
Derogating the victim restores the belief that the world is fair
Correct: if justice cannot be restored, devaluing the victim makes the outcome seem deserved.
questions.note: Just-world beliefs are strongest when victims' suffering cannot be fixed.
questions.x: When an injustice cannot be corrected, for example because the perpetrator is never caught, people with strong just-world beliefs face a threat to the idea that the world is fair. Derogating the victim resolves it: if the victim is less worthy, the outcome seems less unjust. The self-serving bias does not apply because the participants' own successes or failures are not at stake.

questions.q: Compared with people from individualist cultures, people from collectivist cultures are on average more likely to do what when explaining others' behavior?
o: Rely exclusively on dispositional traits
No group relies only on traits; a stronger dispositional emphasis is typical of individualist cultures.
Show a stronger self-serving bias
Self-serving bias tends to be weaker, not stronger, in collectivist samples.
Ignore social roles and relationships
Collectivist thinking emphasizes roles and relationships.
Weigh situational and contextual factors
Correct: collectivist cultures emphasize context and roles, reducing the FAE.
questions.x: Collectivist cultures emphasize interdependence, roles and relationships, so people there more readily consider situational and contextual causes of others' behavior and show a weaker fundamental attribution error. Individualist cultures emphasize the autonomous self and lean toward dispositional explanations. No culture relies exclusively on traits, and self-serving bias also tends to be weaker in collectivist samples.

questions.q: A content analysis compared English-language American newspapers and Chinese-language newspapers covering the same murders. The American papers emphasized the killer's personality, while the Chinese-language papers emphasized circumstances and relationships. This finding best supports which claim?
o: The fundamental attribution error is biologically fixed
Cross-cultural variation argues against a fixed, invariant bias.
East Asian writers show a stronger actor-observer bias
Both sets of reports explained another person's behavior; no self-versus-other comparison was made.
The fundamental attribution error is shaped by culture
Correct: dispositional emphasis varied with cultural background, so the bias is not universal in strength.
American writers show stronger stereotype threat
Stereotype threat concerns performance, not newspaper explanations.
questions.x: If the fundamental attribution error were a fixed, universal feature of cognition, coverage of the same events should show similar dispositional emphasis everywhere. Instead, American reports stressed personality while Chinese-language reports stressed context, showing that culture shapes how strongly people favor trait explanations. Actor-observer bias is ruled out because no one compared explanations of their own behavior.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes prejudice from discrimination?
o: Prejudice is a behavior; discrimination is a belief
This reverses the two terms.
Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is a behavior
Correct: prejudice is a prejudgment or feeling, discrimination is unequal treatment.
Prejudice is always conscious; discrimination is always unconscious
Either can be implicit or explicit.
Prejudice targets individuals; discrimination targets only institutions
Both can apply to individuals and groups.
questions.note: Stereotype = cognitive, prejudice = affective, discrimination = behavioral.
questions.x: Social psychology separates the ABCs of intergroup attitudes: a stereotype is a cognitive belief, prejudice is an affective attitude or evaluation, and discrimination is behavior, meaning unequal treatment. Prejudice and discrimination can occur independently of each other. Both can be explicit or implicit, which is why the conscious-versus-unconscious split is wrong.

questions.q: The belief that all members of a group share a particular trait is best described as what?
o: A stereotype
Correct: a stereotype is an overgeneralized belief about a group's traits.
Prejudice
Prejudice is the evaluative or emotional attitude, not the belief itself.
Discrimination
Discrimination is behavior, not a belief.
Ethnocentrism
Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by one's own culture's standards.
questions.x: A stereotype is the cognitive component of intergroup attitudes: an overgeneralized belief that members of a group share certain traits. Prejudice is the evaluative or emotional reaction that often accompanies the belief, and discrimination is the resulting behavior. The tempting distractor, prejudice, describes the feeling, not the belief itself.

questions.q: A landlord privately dislikes a certain ethnic group but rents to its members on equal terms because of fair-housing laws. This landlord shows what?
o: Prejudice without discrimination
Correct: a negative attitude is present, but treatment is equal.
Discrimination without prejudice
There is a negative attitude, and no unequal treatment occurs.
Institutional discrimination
Institutional discrimination is embedded in policies; none disadvantages the group here.
Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is experienced by the stereotyped, not the holder of prejudice.
questions.x: Prejudice (an attitude) and discrimination (a behavior) do not always go together. This landlord holds a negative attitude but treats tenants equally because the law constrains behavior, which is prejudice without discrimination. The reverse case, discrimination without prejudice, occurs when unequal treatment comes from rules or pressure rather than personal dislike.

questions.q: A company that holds no negative views of any group requires applicants to have graduated from a few private schools that historically excluded certain minorities. The resulting hiring disparity best exemplifies what?
o: Individual prejudice
The stem specifies that decision makers hold no negative attitudes.
Stereotype threat
No one is underperforming due to a stereotype reminder.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
No expectation is shaping applicants' behavior here.
Institutional discrimination
Correct: a neutral-seeming policy produces unequal outcomes without individual prejudice.
questions.note: Discrimination can exist without prejudice when it is built into rules.
questions.x: Institutional discrimination occurs when policies, practices or structures produce unequal outcomes for groups, even when no individual decision maker holds prejudiced attitudes. Requiring degrees from schools that historically excluded minorities carries past exclusion forward. Individual prejudice is ruled out by the stem, which specifies that the company holds no negative views.

questions.q: Judging another culture's food customs as strange or inferior because they differ from one's own customs is called what?
o: Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism judges practices within their own cultural context.
Xenocentrism
Xenocentrism is preferring other cultures over one's own.
Ethnocentrism
Correct: using one's own culture as the standard to judge others.
Cultural diffusion
Diffusion is the spread of cultural traits between groups.
questions.x: Ethnocentrism is evaluating other cultures using one's own culture as the standard, often seeing differences as strange or inferior. Cultural relativism is the opposite stance of understanding practices within their own context. Xenocentrism is also a biased comparison, but in the reverse direction: it treats other cultures as superior to one's own.

questions.q: An anthropologist studying a ritual tries to understand its meaning to participants rather than judging it by her home culture's norms. This approach is called what?
o: Ethnocentrism
Ethnocentrism uses one's own culture as the yardstick.
Cultural relativism
Correct: understanding a practice in terms of its own cultural context.
Cultural assimilation
Assimilation is a group adopting the dominant culture.
Culture shock
Culture shock is disorientation in an unfamiliar culture, not a research stance.
questions.x: Cultural relativism is the practice of understanding beliefs and customs in terms of the culture in which they occur rather than by outside standards. It is the standard stance in anthropological fieldwork and is the opposite of ethnocentrism. Culture shock is tempting because it also involves encountering another culture, but it is a feeling of disorientation, not an analytic approach.

questions.q: Which effect describes a person underperforming after being reminded of a negative stereotype about a group they belong to?
o: Self-serving bias
Self-serving bias concerns explanations of outcomes, not performance itself.
Stereotype threat
Correct: worry about confirming a stereotype impairs performance.
Social facilitation
Social facilitation is improved performance on easy tasks in front of others.
Halo effect
The halo effect is a rater's judgment bias.
questions.x: Stereotype threat is the anxiety of possibly confirming a negative stereotype about one's group, which impairs performance on relevant tasks. It is triggered by situational cues that make the stereotype salient, such as identity reminders. Social facilitation is also about performance, but it concerns the presence of others, not stereotypes, and improves performance on easy tasks.

questions.q: In a stereotype threat study, the same difficult verbal test is described to one group as diagnostic of intelligence and to another as a nondiagnostic puzzle task. Stereotyped students score lower only in the diagnostic condition. What is the independent variable?
o: How the test is described
Correct: the researchers manipulated the framing of the test.
Students' test scores
Scores are the measured outcome, the dependent variable.
Students' group membership alone
Group membership is a participant variable, not the manipulated factor described.
Difficulty of the test items
Item difficulty was held constant across conditions.
questions.x: The independent variable is what the researcher deliberately manipulates; here, whether the test is framed as diagnostic of intelligence or as a nondiagnostic puzzle. Test scores are the dependent variable. Group membership cannot be randomly assigned, so it is a participant (quasi-independent) variable rather than the manipulated factor this question describes.

questions.q: Which result would most strongly support the claim that stereotype threat works partly by consuming working memory?
o: Threatened participants report liking the test less
Liking is not a measure of working memory.
Non-stereotyped participants score equally in both conditions
This shows the effect is group-specific, not how it works.
Threatened participants spend more time on the first question
Time spent does not directly measure working memory capacity.
Threatened participants show lower working memory span, which statistically accounts for their lower scores
Correct: a mediator that explains the effect supports the proposed mechanism.
questions.note: Mechanism questions need a mediator, not just the main effect.
questions.x: Testing a mechanism requires showing a mediator: the proposed process must change with the manipulation and must statistically account for the effect on the outcome. Lower working memory span that explains the score drop does exactly that. Showing that only stereotyped groups are affected, or that people dislike the test, confirms the effect exists but not how it operates.

questions.q: Which intervention has been shown to reduce stereotype threat effects on test performance?
o: Emphasizing group identity just before the test
Making identity salient typically worsens threat effects.
Telling students the test measures innate ability
Fixed-ability framing increases stereotype relevance.
Framing the test as not diagnostic of group differences
Correct: removing the relevance of the stereotype reduces the threat.
Increasing the presence of out-group evaluators
Being a numerical minority in front of evaluators tends to heighten threat.
questions.x: Stereotype threat depends on the stereotype being relevant to the task. Telling test takers that the test does not reveal group differences, or is not diagnostic of ability, removes that relevance and reduces the performance gap. Emphasizing group identity or presenting the test as a measure of innate ability does the opposite by making the stereotype more salient.

questions.q: A teacher believes a quiet student is gifted, gives her extra attention and harder challenges, and the student's performance rises. This best illustrates what?
o: Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat lowers performance through anxiety about a negative stereotype.
Fundamental attribution error
No trait-versus-situation error in explaining behavior is described.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
Correct: an expectation changed behavior, producing the expected outcome.
Just-world hypothesis
No claim about deserved outcomes is made.
questions.x: A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when an expectation, even an unfounded one, changes behavior in ways that make the expectation come true. The teacher's belief led to more attention and challenge, which raised the student's performance. Stereotype threat is the contrasting case: a negative stereotype lowers performance through the target's own anxiety.

questions.q: Researchers randomly label some students as 'expected bloomers' and tell their teachers. At year's end, labeled students show larger gains. Why is random assignment of the label essential to the conclusion?
o: It guarantees that teachers will not discover the deception
Randomization does not affect whether the deception is detected.
It ensures differences in gains are due to teacher expectations rather than preexisting student ability
Correct: randomization rules out the labels simply tracking real differences.
It makes the sample representative of all schools
Representativeness comes from random sampling, not random assignment.
It eliminates the need for a control group
The unlabeled students serve as the control group.
questions.note: Random assignment = internal validity; random sampling = external validity.
questions.x: Random assignment makes the labeled and unlabeled students equivalent on average in ability and motivation, so a later difference in gains can be attributed to the manipulated teacher expectation. This protects internal validity. Random sampling is the tempting confusion: it concerns whether the sample represents the population, which affects external validity, not causal inference.

questions.q: Favoring members of one's own group over members of other groups is called what?
o: In-group bias
Correct: preferential evaluation and treatment of one's own group.
Out-group homogeneity
That is perceiving out-group members as all alike.
Group polarization
Group polarization is discussion pushing views to extremes.
Deindividuation
Deindividuation is the loss of self-awareness in groups.
questions.x: In-group bias is the tendency to evaluate and treat members of one's own group more favorably than members of out-groups. It can appear even with arbitrary groupings. Out-group homogeneity is related but distinct: it concerns perceiving out-group members as more alike, not favoring one's own group.

questions.q: In minimal group studies, people are divided by a trivial criterion, such as preference for one painter. What do these studies typically show?
o: Participants show no bias without a history of conflict
Minimal groups show bias without any conflict or history.
Participants favor the out-group to appear fair
Allocations typically favor the in-group.
Bias appears only when groups compete for resources
Competition is not required in the minimal group paradigm.
Participants favor their own group even when groups are meaningless
Correct: mere categorization is enough to produce in-group favoritism.
questions.x: The minimal group paradigm assigns people to groups on trivial grounds, with no history, interaction or competition. Participants still allocate more rewards to their own group, showing that mere categorization is enough to produce in-group favoritism. This challenges the idea that bias requires competition over resources, which is the claim of realistic conflict theory.

questions.q: Social identity theory explains in-group favoritism mainly as a way of doing what?
o: Resolving conflict over scarce resources
That is realistic conflict theory.
Reducing cognitive dissonance about past behavior
Dissonance theory does not center on group membership.
Learning behaviors through observation
That is social learning theory.
Boosting self-esteem through positive group distinctiveness
Correct: people derive self-worth from groups they belong to.
questions.x: Social identity theory holds that part of self-concept comes from group memberships, so people are motivated to see their groups as positively distinct, and favoring the in-group boosts self-esteem. It explains why trivial groups still produce bias. Realistic conflict theory is the main alternative, attributing hostility to competition for scarce resources.

questions.q: A fan says the rival team's supporters 'are all the same,' but describes his own team's fans as diverse individuals. This illustrates what?
o: In-group heterogeneity bias
No such standard term; the recognized effect concerns out-group sameness.
Group polarization
Group polarization concerns attitude extremity after discussion.
Out-group homogeneity effect
Correct: out-group members are seen as more alike than in-group members.
Just-world hypothesis
No claim about deserved outcomes is made.
questions.x: The out-group homogeneity effect is the perception that out-group members are more similar to one another than in-group members, captured by the phrase 'they are all alike, we are diverse.' It arises partly because people know more varied individuals in their own group. Group polarization is unrelated; it describes discussion pushing a group's views toward extremes.

questions.q: Realistic conflict theory proposes that prejudice between groups arises mainly from what?
o: Trivial categorization alone
That is the minimal group finding explained by social identity theory.
Competition over limited resources
Correct: perceived scarcity sets groups against each other.
Frustration displaced onto convenient targets
That is scapegoating, explained by frustration-aggression ideas.
Repeated exposure to the out-group
Exposure tends to increase liking (mere exposure effect).
questions.x: Realistic conflict theory holds that intergroup prejudice grows out of competition for limited resources such as jobs, land or prizes. It predicts that hostility rises with competition and falls when groups share goals. Social identity theory, by contrast, explains bias through categorization and self-esteem even when nothing tangible is at stake.

questions.q: In a summer camp study, two groups of boys became hostile while competing for prizes. Hostility dropped most when they had to cooperate to fix the camp's broken water supply. Which concept explains the reduction?
o: Superordinate goals
Correct: shared goals requiring both groups' cooperation reduce intergroup conflict.
Mere contact
Simple contact during competition had not reduced hostility.
Deindividuation
Deindividuation increases, not reduces, antisocial group behavior.
Social loafing
Social loafing is reduced individual effort in groups.
questions.note: Contact helps most with equal status and shared goals.
questions.x: In the Robbers Cave study, competition created intergroup hostility, and simple contact such as shared meals did not reduce it. Hostility dropped when the groups faced superordinate goals, problems that neither group could solve alone and that required cooperation. Mere contact is the tempting answer, but contact helps only under conditions like shared goals and equal status.

questions.q: According to the contact hypothesis, which condition makes intergroup contact most likely to reduce prejudice?
o: Equal status and cooperative goals
Correct: equal-status cooperation with institutional support is key.
Brief, superficial encounters
Superficial contact has little effect on prejudice.
Competition for rewards
Competition tends to increase hostility.
One group holding authority over the other
Unequal status can reinforce stereotypes.
questions.x: The contact hypothesis states that intergroup contact reduces prejudice when certain conditions are met: equal status, common or cooperative goals, intergroup cooperation and support from authorities or norms. Without these conditions, contact can confirm stereotypes. Competition and unequal-status contact tend to sustain or worsen hostility.

questions.q: Assuming that an attractive person is also kind and intelligent is an example of what?
o: The primacy effect
Primacy concerns the order of information, not one trait spreading.
Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is a performance effect on the stereotyped person.
The false consensus effect
False consensus concerns overestimating agreement with oneself.
The halo effect
Correct: one positive trait colors judgments of unrelated traits.
questions.x: The halo effect is the tendency for one positive characteristic, often physical attractiveness, to create a favorable impression that spreads to unrelated traits like kindness or intelligence. The primacy effect is tempting because it also shapes impressions, but it concerns the order in which information arrives, not one trait coloring others.

questions.q: Mock jurors rate an attractive defendant as less likely to be guilty than an unattractive defendant with identical evidence. Which bias best explains this?
o: Just-world hypothesis
Just-world reasoning would blame victims, not favor attractive defendants.
Actor-observer bias
The jurors are not comparing their own behavior with the defendant's.
Halo effect
Correct: attractiveness spreads to judgments of character.
Self-serving bias
The jurors' own outcomes are not involved.
questions.x: Holding evidence constant isolates the effect of attractiveness. Jurors rating the attractive defendant as less likely to be guilty shows the halo effect, in which a positive trait spreads to judgments of character and honesty. The just-world hypothesis concerns believing people deserve their outcomes and would not predict favoring attractive defendants specifically.

questions.q: Participants read a description of a person listed as 'intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn, envious' or the same traits in reverse order. The first group rates the person more favorably. What does this show?
o: Recency effect in impression formation
Recency would favor the group that heard the positive traits last.
Primacy effect in impression formation
Correct: early information carries more weight in forming impressions.
Out-group homogeneity
No group comparison is involved.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
No expectation changes the target's behavior.
questions.x: The two lists contain identical traits in opposite order, so any difference in ratings reflects order. The group hearing positive traits first formed a more favorable impression, showing the primacy effect: early information sets an interpretive frame for later information. A recency effect would predict the opposite, favoring the group that heard positive traits last.

questions.q: In impression formation, central traits such as 'warm' versus 'cold' are notable because they do what?
o: Are ignored when other traits are listed
Central traits have outsized, not negligible, influence.
Strongly shape the interpretation of other traits
Correct: changing one central trait shifts the overall impression.
Only matter when presented last
Their influence does not depend on recency.
Affect only judgments of competence
Warmth strongly affects judgments of likability and sociability.
questions.x: Central traits, such as warm versus cold, carry disproportionate weight in impression formation and change how other traits are interpreted; 'intelligent' reads differently in a warm person than in a cold one. Peripheral traits, like polite versus blunt in the classic studies, shift impressions much less. Warmth mainly affects judgments of sociability and likability, not only competence.

questions.q: Students told a guest lecturer was 'rather cold' rated him less favorably and asked fewer questions than students told he was 'very warm,' though all saw the same lecture. What does the difference in questions suggest?
o: Impressions can influence behavior toward the target, not just ratings
Correct: expectations changed how students interacted with him.
The lecturer gave different lectures to each group
The stem states all students saw the same lecture.
Students showed the self-serving bias
Students were not explaining their own outcomes.
Warm and cold are peripheral traits
The large effect shows they act as central traits.
questions.x: Because everyone saw the same lecture, the only difference was the label. Students expecting a cold lecturer both rated him lower and asked fewer questions, showing that impressions shape actual behavior toward a person, not just private judgments. This behavioral effect is the first step of a self-fulfilling prophecy, since the target may respond to the reduced engagement.

questions.q: Social perception refers to which process?
o: Detecting physical stimuli through the senses
That is sensation.
Changing one's behavior to match a group
That is conformity.
Storing information in long-term memory
That is encoding and storage in memory.
Forming impressions and making inferences about other people
Correct: social perception is how we understand others.
questions.x: Social perception, or social cognition, is the process of forming impressions of others and making inferences about their traits, intentions and behavior. It includes attribution and impression formation. Sensation is the tempting confusion because 'perception' suggests the senses, but social perception concerns understanding people, not detecting stimuli.

questions.q: Which of the following is generally considered one of the three main components of social perception?
o: The bystander
Bystanders are part of the bystander effect, not a social perception component.
The reference group
Reference groups relate to social comparison and norms.
The perceiver
Correct: social perception involves the perceiver, the target and the situation.
The conditioned stimulus
Conditioned stimuli belong to classical conditioning.
questions.note: Perceiver, target, situation.
questions.x: Social perception is commonly described as having three components: the perceiver, whose experiences, motives and mood shape interpretation; the target, the person being perceived; and the situation, which supplies context. Reference groups are tempting because they are social, but they relate to social comparison and norms rather than the structure of perception.

questions.q: A manager sees an employee yawning and assumes he is lazy, never considering that he worked a night shift. What would most reduce this error?
o: Relying on first impressions
First impressions often drive the error rather than correct it.
Increasing cognitive load while judging
Load makes people rely more on dispositional shortcuts.
Considering situational explanations before judging
Correct: deliberate attention to context counters the fundamental attribution error.
Observing the employee for less time
Less information tends to increase reliance on trait inferences.
questions.x: The manager commits the fundamental attribution error by inferring a trait (laziness) while ignoring an obvious situational cause (a night shift). Deliberately generating situational explanations counteracts this, because correcting a trait inference requires effortful thought. Distraction, less information or reliance on first impressions all increase dependence on quick trait judgments.

questions.q: Participants judge a speaker's anxiety while silently memorizing a long number or not. Those memorizing rely more on the speaker's visible fidgeting and ignore a stressful topic. Which model best explains this?
o: A purely situational model of attribution
The results show more, not less, dispositional reliance.
A two-step model: automatic trait inference followed by effortful situational correction
Correct: cognitive load blocks the effortful correction step.
The just-world hypothesis
No fairness judgment about outcomes is made.
Social facilitation theory
Social facilitation concerns performance in front of others.
questions.note: Load makes the FAE worse: correction for situation takes effort.
questions.x: Two-step models of attribution propose that people automatically infer a trait from behavior and then, if they have the cognitive resources, effortfully correct for situational causes. Memorizing a number consumes those resources, so participants stop at the trait inference and ignore the stressful topic. The results show greater dispositional reliance, ruling out a purely situational account.

questions.q: Implicit personality theory refers to what?
o: Assumptions about which traits tend to go together in people
Correct: we hold intuitive beliefs that certain traits co-occur.
A formal psychological test of personality
It is an informal, everyday set of beliefs, not a test.
The idea that personality is entirely situational
That is closer to situationism in the person-situation debate.
Unconscious drives that shape personality
That describes psychodynamic theory.
questions.x: Implicit personality theory is the everyday, intuitive set of beliefs people hold about which traits go together, such as assuming a funny person is also outgoing. These beliefs let perceivers fill in unobserved traits from a few cues, which speeds impression formation but invites error. It is not a formal test; it is a lay theory that operates largely automatically.

questions.q: After learning a new coworker is 'artistic,' Jamal also assumes she is disorganized and sensitive, though he has no evidence. Which concept best explains his inferences?
o: Self-serving bias
He is not explaining his own outcomes.
Actor-observer bias
No comparison of his own behavior with hers is involved.
Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat would affect the coworker's performance, not his inferences.
Implicit personality theory
Correct: he infers traits he believes go together with 'artistic.'
questions.x: Jamal fills in traits he has not observed because he believes they cluster with 'artistic.' That is implicit personality theory: lay assumptions about which traits co-occur. Stereotype threat is tempting because it involves expectations, but it describes a stereotyped person's performance being impaired, not an observer's inferences.

questions.q: In the courtroom, a witness's last statement is the one jurors remember best and weigh most heavily. This reflects which effect?
o: Primacy effect
Primacy would favor the first statement.
Halo effect
The halo effect involves one trait coloring others, not order of information.
Mere exposure effect
Mere exposure is increased liking from repeated exposure.
Recency effect
Correct: the most recent information is weighted heavily.
