questions.x: The recency effect is the greater influence of the most recently presented information. It is strongest when judgment immediately follows the last information, as when jurors deliberate right after closing testimony. The primacy effect is the opposite, in which the first information dominates, and is the usual default in impression formation.

questions.q: Primacy usually dominates impression formation. Under which condition is a recency effect most likely instead?
o: All information is presented rapidly in one session
Rapid single presentation typically favors primacy.
The perceiver is distracted during the later information
Distraction during later information would reduce its impact.
A long delay separates the two sets of information and judgment follows the second set
Correct: delay weakens the first information, so the most recent dominates.
The first information is especially vivid
Vivid early information strengthens primacy.
questions.x: Primacy usually wins because early information shapes how later information is interpreted. When a long delay separates the first and second sets and the judgment is made right after the second, the earlier information has faded from memory, so the most recent information dominates. Distraction during the later information would weaken it, which favors primacy rather than recency.

questions.q: A woman's coworkers assume she is incompetent at everything after she makes one embarrassing mistake. This negative counterpart to the halo effect is called what?
o: Primacy effect
Primacy concerns order of information, not one trait spreading.
Horn effect
Correct: one negative trait spreads to unrelated judgments.
Spotlight effect
The spotlight effect is overestimating how much others notice you.
Just-world hypothesis
No claim about deserved outcomes is made.
questions.x: The horn effect, sometimes called the reverse halo, is the tendency for one negative trait or event to color judgments of unrelated qualities. A single mistake leads to an overall impression of incompetence. The primacy effect is tempting because one early event dominates here, but primacy concerns information order, whereas the horn effect is one trait spreading to others.

questions.q: In Weiner's model, attributing a failed exam to bad luck classifies the cause as what?
o: External, unstable and uncontrollable
Correct: luck is outside the person, varies and cannot be controlled.
Internal, stable and uncontrollable
That describes low ability.
Internal, unstable and controllable
That describes effort.
External, stable and uncontrollable
That describes task difficulty.
questions.x: Weiner classifies causes on three dimensions: locus (internal or external), stability (stable or unstable) and controllability. Luck is external, unstable and uncontrollable. Ability is internal, stable and uncontrollable; effort is internal, unstable and controllable; task difficulty is external, stable and uncontrollable. The stability dimension separates luck from task difficulty.

questions.q: According to Weiner's attribution model, a student who attributes failure to low ability rather than low effort is most likely to do what?
o: Expect future failure and feel less motivated
Correct: ability is stable and uncontrollable, so failure seems likely to repeat.
Study harder for the next exam
That follows an unstable, controllable attribution such as effort.
Blame the teacher for unfair grading
That is an external attribution, not low ability.
Expect future success because luck will change
That follows a luck attribution.
questions.note: Stability of the cause predicts expectations for the future.
questions.x: In Weiner's model, stability predicts expectations about the future. Low ability is internal, stable and uncontrollable, so the student expects failure to repeat and loses motivation, a pattern linked to learned helplessness. Attributing failure to low effort, which is unstable and controllable, instead predicts working harder next time.

questions.q: Observers feel more anger toward a person whose poverty they attribute to laziness than toward one whose poverty they attribute to a factory closing. This difference is best explained by perceived what?
o: Consensus of the behavior
Consensus concerns whether others behave the same way.
Primacy of the information
No order effect is described.
Distinctiveness of the behavior
Distinctiveness concerns whether the behavior is unique to one situation.
Controllability of the cause
Correct: controllable causes elicit blame and anger; uncontrollable ones elicit sympathy.
questions.x: Weiner's model links the controllability of a cause to emotions and helping. When a negative outcome is attributed to a controllable cause such as laziness, observers feel anger and withhold help; uncontrollable causes such as a factory closing elicit sympathy. Consensus and distinctiveness are Kelley's covariation cues, which concern how a person decides between internal and external causes.

questions.q: A sports fan explains his team's wins by their talent but their losses by poor officiating, and explains the rival's wins by luck. This extension of self-serving bias to groups is called what?
o: Out-group homogeneity
That concerns perceived sameness of the out-group.
Group polarization
That concerns attitudes becoming more extreme after discussion.
Group-serving bias
Correct: favorable attributions for the in-group, unfavorable for the out-group.
Groupthink
Groupthink is faulty group decision making driven by desire for harmony.
questions.x: Group-serving bias, sometimes called the ultimate attribution error, extends the self-serving bias to groups: in-group successes are credited to internal causes and failures to external ones, while out-group successes are dismissed as luck. Out-group homogeneity is tempting because it involves the rival group, but it concerns perceived similarity, not attributions for outcomes.

questions.q: When an out-group member performs a positive act, prejudiced observers often say it was luck or an exception. Which bias does this describe?
o: Self-serving bias
Self-serving bias concerns one's own outcomes, not out-group members'.
Ultimate attribution error
Correct: out-group positives are explained away situationally, negatives attributed to disposition.
False consensus effect
False consensus is overestimating agreement with one's views.
Recency effect
No order of information is involved.
questions.x: The ultimate attribution error applies attribution bias to whole groups. Negative acts by out-group members are attributed to disposition, while positive acts are explained away as luck, special circumstances or exceptions. This lets prejudiced beliefs survive disconfirming evidence. Self-serving bias is similar in structure but concerns explanations of one's own outcomes.

questions.q: Believing that most people share your political opinions more than they actually do is called what?
o: False uniqueness effect
False uniqueness is underestimating how common one's positive traits are.
False consensus effect
Correct: overestimating how common one's own views are.
Out-group homogeneity
That concerns perceiving out-group members as alike.
Confirmation bias
Confirmation bias is favoring evidence that fits existing beliefs.
questions.x: The false consensus effect is overestimating how many people share one's own opinions, preferences and behaviors. It arises partly because people associate with like-minded others and because their own view feels obviously correct. The false uniqueness effect is the contrasting bias of underestimating how common one's desirable traits or abilities are.

questions.q: A person who often lies assumes that most other people also lie frequently. This illustrates how self-perceptions shape perceptions of others through what?
o: Projection or false consensus
Correct: people assume others share their own traits and behaviors.
Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is a performance effect.
The just-world hypothesis
No claim about deserved outcomes is involved.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism concerns judging practices in context.
questions.x: People use themselves as a reference point when judging others, so their own traits and behaviors color their perceptions. Projection and the false consensus effect both describe assuming that others share one's characteristics, here frequent lying. The other choices do not involve self-based inference about others; stereotype threat is a performance effect on stereotyped individuals.

questions.q: Residents of a crime-ridden neighborhood become more suspicious of strangers in general. This best illustrates which idea in social perception?
o: The halo effect
The halo effect spreads one trait of a target to other traits.
Self-serving bias
No explanation of one's own outcomes is involved.
Out-group homogeneity
No in-group versus out-group sameness comparison is made.
Perceptions of the environment shape perceptions of others
Correct: a threatening setting biases how people interpret others.
questions.x: Social perception depends on the perceiver, the target and the situation or environment. A threatening environment primes vigilance, so residents interpret strangers' ambiguous behavior as more suspicious. The halo effect is tempting because it is a perception bias, but it involves one trait of a specific target spreading to that target's other traits, not a setting shaping judgments of everyone.

questions.q: Participants randomly assigned to watch either a frightening or a neutral film clip then rate the same set of ambiguous faces. Those who saw the frightening clip rate the faces as more hostile. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: The faces in the frightening condition were objectively more hostile
The same ambiguous faces were used in both conditions.
Frightening films cause permanent hostility
A single short session cannot show permanent effects.
The perceiver's emotional state can bias social perception
Correct: random assignment to clips links mood to face ratings.
Perceivers in the neutral condition showed stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is a performance effect, not a rating of faces.
questions.x: Because participants were randomly assigned and rated the same faces, the only systematic difference was the clip, which altered their emotional state. Mood therefore biased how they interpreted ambiguous social cues, showing that the perceiver's internal state shapes social perception. A single brief session cannot support claims about permanent effects.

questions.q: Perceiving a relationship between two variables, such as a minority group and a rare behavior, when none exists is called what?
o: Confirmation bias
Confirmation bias is seeking supporting evidence for existing beliefs.
Base-rate fallacy
The base-rate fallacy ignores prior probabilities in judgments.
Illusory correlation
Correct: distinctive pairings seem related even when they are not.
Belief perseverance
Belief perseverance is clinging to beliefs after they are discredited.
questions.x: An illusory correlation is perceiving a relationship between two variables that are unrelated or only weakly related. It is especially likely when two distinctive or rare things co-occur, such as a minority group and an uncommon behavior, because those pairings are memorable. Confirmation bias can maintain such beliefs, but it describes selective search for supporting evidence, not the perception of a link itself.

questions.q: Participants read statements about two groups. Group A is described in twice as many statements as Group B, and in both groups undesirable behaviors are a minority of statements in the same proportion. Participants rate Group B more negatively. What best explains this?
o: Group B actually showed more undesirable behaviors per member
The proportions were identical.
Pairing a minority group with infrequent behaviors creates an illusory correlation
Correct: two distinctive things co-occurring stand out and seem linked.
Participants showed out-group homogeneity for Group A
No in-group/out-group distinction was established.
Participants showed a recency effect
Information order was not manipulated.
questions.note: Distinctiveness-based illusory correlation helps explain how stereotypes form.
questions.x: This is the distinctiveness-based illusory correlation. Statements about the smaller group are rarer, and undesirable behaviors are rarer, so their co-occurrence is doubly distinctive and better remembered. Participants then overestimate how often Group B acted badly although the proportions were identical. Option A is ruled out by design, which held the proportion of undesirable behavior constant.

questions.q: A man who believes women are bad drivers notices every bad driver who is a woman but overlooks bad drivers who are men. This maintains his stereotype through what?
o: Confirmation bias
Correct: he attends to evidence that confirms and ignores evidence that disconfirms.
Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat would affect women's driving performance itself.
Self-serving bias
He is not explaining his own outcomes.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is a stance toward other cultures.
questions.x: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek, notice and remember information that supports existing beliefs while overlooking information that contradicts them. Here it maintains a stereotype by making confirming cases memorable and disconfirming cases invisible. Stereotype threat is tempting because a stereotype is involved, but it affects members of the stereotyped group, not the stereotype holder.

questions.q: When a prejudiced person meets a friendly, competent member of a disliked group, he labels her 'an exception' and keeps his stereotype. This process is called what?
o: Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is a performance effect on the stereotyped person.
Superordinate goal formation
Superordinate goals reduce conflict through cooperation.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
No expectation is changing the target's behavior.
Subtyping
Correct: disconfirming members are placed in a special subcategory so the stereotype survives.
questions.x: Subtyping places stereotype-disconfirming individuals into a separate subcategory, such as 'the exception,' so the overall stereotype remains intact. It is a major reason stereotypes resist change after contact with individual counterexamples. Changing stereotypes works better when disconfirming information is spread across many typical group members rather than concentrated in a few.

questions.q: Stereotypes are often explained as cognitive shortcuts. Which statement best reflects this view?
o: Stereotypes form only through deliberate reasoning
Stereotypes often operate automatically.
Stereotypes are always accurate summaries of groups
Shortcuts are often inaccurate overgeneralizations.
Stereotypes require strong negative emotion to form
The cognitive view emphasizes categorization, not emotion.
Stereotypes save mental effort by grouping people into categories
Correct: categorization simplifies a complex social world.
questions.x: The cognitive view holds that stereotypes arise from categorization, a natural way of simplifying a complex social world and conserving mental effort. The cost is overgeneralization, so stereotypes are often inaccurate and are applied automatically. This view emphasizes categorization rather than strong emotion, which is the focus of affective accounts of prejudice.

questions.q: Which finding best supports the role of emotion in prejudice?
o: Participants recall stereotype-consistent information better
That supports a cognitive (memory) account.
Participants overestimate group differences when tired
That supports a cognitive-resource account.
Inducing anger in participants increases negative judgments of an out-group
Correct: manipulating emotion changes prejudiced evaluations.
Participants assign rewards based on a coin-flip grouping
That supports social identity theory.
questions.x: Showing that emotion contributes to prejudice requires manipulating emotion and measuring prejudiced judgments. Inducing anger and observing more negative out-group evaluations does this experimentally. Better recall of stereotype-consistent information is tempting because it involves bias, but it supports a cognitive, memory-based account rather than an emotional one.

questions.q: After a factory layoff, unemployed workers blame a powerless immigrant group for their hardship. This best illustrates what?
o: Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism avoids judging other groups by one's own standards.
Scapegoating
Correct: frustration is displaced onto a convenient, less powerful target.
Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is a performance effect on the stereotyped.
Halo effect
The halo effect spreads positive impressions.
questions.x: Scapegoating, rooted in frustration-aggression theory, is displacing blame and hostility for one's frustrations onto a less powerful group that did not cause them. The real source of frustration, such as economic forces, is hard to attack, so a vulnerable target is chosen instead. Stereotypes may be involved, but stereotype threat describes a performance effect on the target group.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that dominant groups promote stereotypes of subordinate groups because those beliefs justify unequal access to wealth and status. Which processes does this argument emphasize as sources of prejudice?
o: Power, prestige and class
Correct: prejudice is seen as maintaining existing hierarchies.
Individual cognitive limitations
The argument focuses on group interests, not mental shortcuts.
Random variation in personality
The argument is structural, not about individual personality.
Biological threat detection
The argument is about social hierarchy, not evolved fear.
questions.x: Conflict and structural perspectives hold that prejudice serves dominant groups by justifying unequal access to resources: stereotypes rationalize hierarchies of power, prestige and class. This places the origin of prejudice in social structure and group interests. Cognitive limitations are a valid source of stereotyping, but they are an individual-level explanation that the argument does not emphasize.

questions.q: In sociology, stigma refers to what?
o: A trait that discredits a person and reduces them in others' eyes
Correct: stigma marks a person as socially undesirable.
A cultural norm with strong moral weight
That describes a more.
A positive attribute that raises social status
Stigma is negative, not positive.
A role conflict between two statuses
That is role conflict.
questions.x: Goffman described stigma as an attribute that deeply discredits a person, reducing them from a whole person to a tainted, discounted one in the eyes of others. Stigma can attach to physical traits, behaviors or group membership. Mores are strongly held moral norms, which may define what is stigmatized but are not themselves the mark of discredit.

questions.q: A man diagnosed with depression begins to believe he is weak and worthless because of his diagnosis, and stops seeking help. This illustrates what?
o: Public stigma
Public stigma is others' negative attitudes, not his own internalization.
Stereotype lift
Stereotype lift is improved performance from comparison with a stereotyped out-group.
Courtesy stigma
Courtesy stigma affects people associated with a stigmatized person.
Self-stigma
Correct: the person internalizes negative societal views about his condition.
questions.x: Self-stigma occurs when a person internalizes society's negative stereotypes about a condition and applies them to himself, lowering self-esteem and reducing help seeking. Public stigma is the tempting alternative, but it refers to the general public's negative attitudes, not the person's own internalization. Courtesy stigma affects those associated with the stigmatized person.

questions.q: Family members of a person with a stigmatized illness experience social rejection because of their association. This is called what?
o: Self-stigma
Self-stigma is internalized stigma by the affected person.
Ethnocentrism
Ethnocentrism concerns judging other cultures.
Courtesy stigma
Correct: stigma extended to those connected with the stigmatized person.
Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is a performance effect.
questions.x: Courtesy stigma, also called associative stigma, is stigma extended to people connected to a stigmatized individual, such as family members or caregivers. They face rejection because of their association rather than any trait of their own. Self-stigma is the tempting distractor, but it describes the affected person's internalization of negative views.

questions.q: A researcher finds that patients who strongly endorse negative beliefs about mental illness skip more therapy appointments. Which conclusion is justified by this finding alone?
o: Negative beliefs cause patients to skip appointments
Correlation alone cannot establish causation.
Endorsement of these beliefs is associated with missing appointments
Correct: a correlational finding supports only an association.
Skipping appointments causes negative beliefs
Reverse causation cannot be confirmed either.
Stigma has no effect on treatment
The data show an association, contradicting no relationship.
questions.x: This is a correlational finding: belief endorsement and missed appointments were measured, not manipulated. Correlation supports an association but not the direction of causation, since beliefs might cause missed sessions, missed sessions might reinforce beliefs, or a third variable such as symptom severity might drive both. Concluding that beliefs cause skipping is the tempting overreach.

questions.q: The Implicit Association Test measures bias by comparing what?
o: Self-reported attitudes on a questionnaire
Self-report measures explicit, not implicit, attitudes.
Reaction times when pairing concepts with evaluative categories
Correct: faster pairings indicate stronger automatic associations.
Heart rate during group discussions
The IAT is a sorting task based on response latency.
Number of out-group friends a person lists
Friendship counts are not part of the IAT.
questions.x: The Implicit Association Test measures automatic associations through reaction times. People sort concepts, such as faces from two groups, together with evaluative words; faster responses when a group shares a key with 'good' rather than 'bad' indicate a stronger association. Questionnaires measure explicit attitudes, which people can consciously control and may report differently.

questions.q: A person scores low on a self-report prejudice scale but shows strong automatic bias on a reaction-time test. What does this pattern best suggest?
o: Explicit and implicit attitudes can diverge
Correct: conscious self-reports and automatic associations are distinct.
The self-report scale measured implicit bias
Self-report scales measure explicit attitudes.
The person must be lying on the questionnaire
Implicit bias can exist without awareness, so lying is not required.
Reaction-time tests cannot detect bias
The test did detect a bias in this case.
questions.x: Explicit attitudes are consciously endorsed and measured by self-report, while implicit attitudes are automatic associations measured indirectly, such as by reaction times. The two can diverge, so a person can sincerely report low prejudice and still show automatic bias. Lying is the tempting explanation, but implicit associations can exist without awareness, so no deception is required.

questions.q: A person who sincerely endorses equality avoids an out-group member only in ambiguous situations where a nonracial excuse is available. This pattern is best described as what?
o: Overt discrimination
Overt discrimination is open and does not depend on available excuses.
Institutional discrimination
Institutional discrimination arises from policies, not individual avoidance.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is understanding practices in context.
Aversive racism
Correct: egalitarian self-image coexists with subtle bias that appears when it can be justified.
questions.x: Aversive racism describes people who sincerely hold egalitarian values yet harbor unacknowledged negative feelings. Their bias appears mainly when behavior can be attributed to a nonracial reason, which protects their egalitarian self-image. Overt discrimination is open and does not depend on such excuses, and institutional discrimination comes from policies rather than individual avoidance.

questions.q: Men talk by phone with a woman they believe, from a randomly assigned photo, is either attractive or unattractive. Women believed to be attractive come across as warmer to independent raters who hear only the women's side. What does this demonstrate?
o: The women's actual attractiveness caused warmth
Photos were assigned, not matched to the women's actual looks.
Stereotype threat in the women
The women did not know the stereotype was active.
Behavioral confirmation of the men's expectations
Correct: the men's behavior elicited the very warmth they expected.
Self-serving bias in the raters
Raters were not judging their own outcomes.
questions.note: Behavioral confirmation is the interpersonal mechanism of a self-fulfilling prophecy.
questions.x: Because the photos were randomly assigned, the women's actual looks did not differ between conditions. Men expecting an attractive partner behaved more warmly, and the women responded in kind, so their behavior confirmed the men's expectation. This behavioral confirmation is the interpersonal route of a self-fulfilling prophecy. Stereotype threat is ruled out because the women were not aware of any stereotype being applied to them.

questions.q: When low teacher expectations lead to lower student performance, this negative version of the Pygmalion effect is called what?
o: Halo effect
The halo effect is a rating bias, not performance change.
Hawthorne effect
The Hawthorne effect is behavior change because one is being observed.
Golem effect
Correct: low expectations produce poorer performance.
Placebo effect
The placebo effect is improvement from an inert treatment.
questions.x: The Pygmalion effect is when high expectations from others raise performance; the Golem effect is the negative counterpart, in which low expectations lead to poorer performance. Both are self-fulfilling prophecies operating through how the expecter treats the target. The Hawthorne effect is tempting because it also changes performance, but it results from being observed, not from others' expectations.

questions.q: Which element is required for an outcome to count as a self-fulfilling prophecy rather than an accurate prediction?
o: The expectation must be negative
Self-fulfilling prophecies can be positive or negative.
The expectation itself causes behavior that produces the outcome
Correct: the prediction must play a causal role in making itself true.
The target must know about the expectation
Targets often never learn the expectation.
The expectation must be based on a stereotype
Any expectation, stereotyped or not, can be self-fulfilling.
questions.x: A self-fulfilling prophecy requires that the expectation causally produces its own confirmation, usually by changing the expecter's behavior, which then changes the target's behavior. An accurate prediction merely forecasts what would have happened anyway. Expectations can be positive or negative, and the target need not know about them.

questions.q: A rumor that a bank is failing leads many customers to withdraw their money at once, and the bank collapses. This best illustrates what?
o: Self-fulfilling prophecy
Correct: a false belief triggered behavior that made it come true.
Stereotype threat
No one underperforms due to a group stereotype.
Just-world hypothesis
No one is judged as deserving the outcome.
Out-group homogeneity
No perception of group sameness is involved.
questions.x: Merton's classic example of a self-fulfilling prophecy is a bank run: a false belief that a bank is failing prompts mass withdrawals, which actually cause it to fail. The belief was initially untrue but became true because people acted on it. The other choices involve group judgments or performance effects, none of which describe a belief creating its own reality.

questions.q: Older adults told a memory test measures age-related decline recall fewer words than older adults told it measures general knowledge. This best illustrates what?
o: Self-serving bias
Participants are not explaining their outcomes.
Golem effect
The Golem effect requires another person's low expectations to shape behavior.
Recency effect
No order of information is manipulated.
Stereotype threat
Correct: activating the aging-memory stereotype impairs performance.
questions.x: Telling older adults that a memory test measures age-related decline makes the stereotype that aging harms memory relevant, and their recall drops. That is stereotype threat: concern about confirming a negative stereotype about one's group impairs performance. The Golem effect is tempting, but it requires another person's low expectations changing how the target is treated.

questions.q: White male math majors told that a test compares their scores with Asian students' scores perform worse than controls. What does this suggest about stereotype threat?
o: It only affects historically disadvantaged groups
This result shows a non-disadvantaged group affected.
It depends on actual differences in math ability
The groups were not shown to differ in true ability.
It only occurs on verbal tests
The test here was a math test.
It can affect any group facing an unfavorable comparison stereotype
Correct: even high-status groups are vulnerable when a relevant stereotype applies.
questions.x: Stereotype threat is not limited to historically disadvantaged groups. Highly skilled white male math students performed worse when told they were being compared with Asian students, a group stereotyped as better at math. Any group can be affected when a negative comparison stereotype becomes relevant, showing the effect is driven by the situation rather than by true ability differences.

questions.q: Non-stereotyped participants sometimes perform slightly better when a negative stereotype about an out-group is made salient. This is called what?
o: Stereotype threat
Threat lowers performance of the stereotyped group.
Social loafing
Social loafing is reduced effort in groups.
Stereotype lift
Correct: downward comparison with a stereotyped out-group boosts performance.
Golem effect
The Golem effect is lowered performance from low expectations.
questions.x: Stereotype lift is a small performance boost in members of a non-stereotyped group when a negative stereotype about an out-group is made salient, likely from favorable downward comparison. It is the mirror image of stereotype threat, which lowers the performance of the stereotyped group. Both depend on the stereotype being relevant to the task.

questions.q: A study finds that stereotype threat effects are larger among students who care strongly about the tested domain. What does this suggest?
o: Domain identification eliminates stereotype threat
It intensified, not eliminated, the effect.
Domain identification moderates stereotype threat
Correct: the effect's size depends on how much the domain matters to the person.
Caring about a domain causes the stereotype
Identification affects vulnerability, not the stereotype's existence.
Stereotype threat depends only on test difficulty
The finding points to a person-level moderator.
questions.note: A moderator changes the strength of an effect; a mediator explains how it happens.
questions.x: A moderator is a variable that changes the strength or direction of an effect. Stereotype threat is larger for students who strongly identify with the domain, because poor performance matters more to them, so domain identification moderates the effect. It does not eliminate the effect, and a moderator differs from a mediator, which explains how the effect occurs.

questions.q: Which is the best example of xenocentrism?
o: Believing products and customs from other countries are superior to one's own
Correct: xenocentrism is preferring other cultures over one's own.
Believing one's own culture is superior to all others
That is ethnocentrism.
Evaluating customs within their cultural context
That is cultural relativism.
Adopting the dominant culture after immigration
That is assimilation.
questions.x: Xenocentrism is the belief that other cultures' products, ideas or customs are superior to one's own, the reverse of ethnocentrism. An example is assuming imported goods must be better. Cultural relativism is tempting, but it is a neutral stance of understanding practices in context, not a preference for foreign cultures.

questions.q: A critic argues that strict cultural relativism makes it impossible to condemn practices that cause serious harm. Which position responds most directly to this critique?
o: Cultural relativism as a research method need not imply that all practices are morally acceptable
Correct: methodological relativism (understanding) differs from moral relativism (approval).
Ethnocentrism is the only defensible alternative
Rejecting extreme relativism does not require judging everything by one's own culture.
Harmful practices do not exist in any culture
This denies the premise rather than addressing the critique.
Cultural relativism requires adopting other cultures' practices
Relativism concerns understanding, not adoption.
questions.x: Methodological cultural relativism is a research stance: understanding a practice within its cultural context before judging it. It does not require moral relativism, the view that no practice can be judged wrong. Separating understanding from approval answers the critique without retreating to ethnocentrism, which would judge everything by one's own culture.

questions.q: Ethnocentrism is most closely linked to which group dynamic?
o: Social loafing
Social loafing concerns effort in groups, not evaluations of cultures.
Diffusion of responsibility
Diffusion of responsibility explains the bystander effect.
Social facilitation
Social facilitation concerns performance in front of others.
In-group favoritism
Correct: ethnocentrism is cultural-level preference for one's own group.
questions.x: Ethnocentrism is in-group favoritism at the cultural level: one's own culture is treated as the standard and viewed more positively than others. It reflects the same social identity processes that lead people to favor their own groups. The other choices describe group effects on effort, helping or performance, not evaluations of groups.

questions.q: A traveler insists that people in a country where eating with one's hands is customary have 'bad manners.' What would a culturally relativist view say?
o: The traveler's culture sets the correct standard
That is ethnocentric reasoning.
Both cultures should adopt utensils
That imposes one standard on both.
Eating customs should be understood within that culture's norms
Correct: relativism evaluates practices by their cultural context.
Manners are biologically determined
Eating customs are culturally learned.
questions.x: A culturally relativist view evaluates customs according to the norms and meanings of the culture in which they occur. Eating with one's hands is a well-established custom with its own etiquette, so calling it bad manners applies an outside standard. That outside standard is ethnocentrism; imposing utensils on both cultures is also an external, not a relativist, judgment.

questions.q: An in-group is best defined as what?
o: A group a person feels opposition toward
That is an out-group.
A group a person identifies with and feels part of
Correct: in-groups are groups to which one belongs and feels loyalty.
A group used as a standard for self-evaluation
That is a reference group, which may or may not be an in-group.
A temporary collection of people in one place
That is an aggregate or crowd.
questions.x: An in-group is a group a person belongs to and identifies with, feeling loyalty and a sense of 'we.' An out-group is any group one does not identify with. A reference group is tempting, but it is a group used as a standard for evaluating oneself, which may or may not be a group one belongs to.

questions.q: Researchers create two groups by assigning shirt colors at random. When one group later shares a common enemy, in-group cohesion increases. What best explains the increase?
o: Random assignment eliminated in-group feelings
In-group feelings emerged despite random assignment.
Out-group threat strengthens in-group identity
Correct: external threat increases solidarity within the group.
Group members experienced stereotype threat
Stereotype threat concerns performance in stereotyped domains.
Members showed the actor-observer bias
No self-versus-other explanation was measured.
questions.x: Even arbitrary groups develop in-group identity, and a shared external threat or common enemy strengthens cohesion and solidarity. The out-group's threat makes the group boundary more salient and increases interdependence among members. Random assignment does not eliminate in-group feelings; the minimal group studies show that arbitrary categorization is enough to create them.

questions.q: In Kelley's covariation model, consensus refers to what?
o: Whether other people behave the same way in the same situation
Correct: high consensus means most people respond similarly.
Whether the person behaves this way across many situations
That is distinctiveness (low distinctiveness if across many).
Whether the person behaves this way every time in this situation
That is consistency.
Whether observers agree on the cause of the behavior
Consensus concerns others' behavior, not observers' agreement.
questions.x: Kelley's covariation model uses three kinds of information. Consensus asks whether other people respond the same way to the same stimulus; distinctiveness asks whether this person responds this way only to this stimulus; consistency asks whether the person responds this way every time. Consensus is about other people's behavior, not about whether observers agree on a cause.

questions.q: In Kelley's covariation model, distinctiveness refers to what?
o: Whether many people act the same way
That is consensus.
Whether the behavior repeats over time
That is consistency.
Whether the behavior is socially unusual
Distinctiveness concerns the person's behavior across stimuli, not social rarity.
Whether the person acts this way only in this particular situation
Correct: high distinctiveness means the behavior is specific to this stimulus.
questions.x: Distinctiveness asks whether a person's behavior is specific to one stimulus or situation. High distinctiveness, such as laughing only at this comedian, points toward the stimulus as the cause; low distinctiveness, behaving that way everywhere, points toward the person. It does not mean the behavior is socially rare, a common confusion with the everyday meaning of the word.

questions.q: One explanation for the actor-observer bias is perceptual salience. Which finding best supports this account?
o: Actors know more about their own past behavior than observers do
That supports an informational account, not salience.
Observers make more dispositional attributions for liked targets
Liking is a motivational factor, not visual salience.
When actors watch a video of themselves from the observer's viewpoint, they make more dispositional self-attributions
Correct: changing visual perspective changes attributions, showing the role of what is salient.
Actors make more self-serving attributions after failure
That describes self-serving bias.
questions.x: The perceptual salience account says actors explain their behavior situationally because the situation fills their visual field, while observers see the actor as most salient. Storms showed that when actors watched a video from the observer's viewpoint, their self-attributions became more dispositional. The informational account, that actors know more about their own history, is a different explanation.

questions.q: Participants explain why they chose their college major and why their best friend chose theirs. They describe their own choice in terms of the program's features and their friend's in terms of personality. Which bias is shown?
o: Self-serving bias
No success-versus-failure comparison is made.
Halo effect
No single trait is spreading to unrelated judgments.
Actor-observer bias
Correct: situational explanations for self, dispositional ones for the friend.
False consensus effect
No estimate of how common their views are is made.
questions.x: Participants explain their own choice by the situation, the program's features, and their friend's identical choice by disposition, personality. That asymmetry is the actor-observer bias. Self-serving bias is tempting, but it requires explaining one's own successes and failures differently; no outcome is being evaluated here.

questions.q: In a study, participants randomly assigned to write trivia questions stumped others assigned to answer them. Observers then rated the question writers as more knowledgeable. Why is this an example of the fundamental attribution error?
o: Question writers truly knew more than answerers
Roles were randomly assigned, so knowledge should not differ systematically.
Observers ignored the role advantage of writing questions from one's own knowledge
Correct: the situation, not greater intelligence, produced the apparent difference.
Observers attributed the result to the difficulty of the questions
That would be a situational attribution, the opposite of the FAE.
Answerers credited their own failures to bad luck
That is self-serving bias, and the stem concerns observers.
questions.x: Question writers drew on their own idiosyncratic knowledge, a built-in role advantage, so their apparent superiority came from the situation. Because roles were randomly assigned, the groups did not differ in actual knowledge. Observers who rated writers as more knowledgeable attributed a situational advantage to disposition, the fundamental attribution error.

questions.q: Studies find that people with depression show a reduced or absent self-serving bias. Which description best fits their typical attributions for failure?
o: Internal, stable and global
Correct: they tend to blame themselves broadly and persistently.
External, unstable and specific
That is the self-protective pattern of nondepressed people.
External, stable and global
External attributions would protect self-esteem.
Internal, unstable and specific
Effort-like, specific causes are relatively hopeful.
questions.x: Nondepressed people typically show a self-serving bias, attributing failures to external, unstable, specific causes. People with depression show a pessimistic explanatory style, attributing failure to internal, stable and global causes, such as 'I am incompetent at everything.' Internal but unstable and specific causes, like low effort on one task, are relatively hopeful and are not typical of depression.

questions.q: Jurors who see themselves as similar to an accident victim assign the victim less blame than jurors who see themselves as dissimilar. This best illustrates what?
o: Just-world hypothesis
The just-world view predicts more victim blame, regardless of similarity.
Out-group homogeneity
No perception of group sameness is measured.
Stereotype threat
Jurors are not performing in a stereotyped domain.
Defensive attribution
Correct: blaming a similar victim would imply one could be blamed too.
questions.x: Defensive attribution is assigning blame in a way that protects oneself from the idea of being blamed or harmed in a similar situation. Jurors who see themselves as similar to the victim blame the victim less, because blaming someone like themselves would imply they could be blamed too. Just-world reasoning predicts victim blaming generally and does not explain the role of similarity.

questions.q: A physician privately believes patients with lung cancer 'brought it on themselves.' Which concept best explains this belief?
o: Stereotype lift
Stereotype lift is improved performance by non-stereotyped people.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism concerns understanding practices in context.
Recency effect
No order of information is involved.
Just-world hypothesis
Correct: assuming illness is deserved preserves a belief that the world is fair.
questions.x: The just-world hypothesis holds that people get what they deserve. Believing that patients caused their own cancer makes the illness seem earned, preserving a sense that the world is fair and that one can avoid misfortune. Stereotype lift is unrelated: it is a small performance boost for non-stereotyped people when a negative stereotype about others is salient.

questions.q: Studies of Japanese participants often find that they attribute their successes to luck or help from others and their failures to lack of effort. This pattern is best described as what?
o: A self-serving bias
Self-serving bias would credit success internally and blame failure externally.
The fundamental attribution error
The FAE concerns explaining others' behavior.
A self-effacing or modesty bias
Correct: the pattern reverses the typical self-serving bias.
Ethnocentrism
Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by one's own standards.
questions.x: The self-serving bias is weaker or reversed in many East Asian samples, where cultural norms value modesty and self-improvement. Attributing success to luck or others and failure to one's own lack of effort is a self-effacing, or modesty, bias. A self-serving bias would show the opposite pattern: internal credit for success and external blame for failure.

questions.q: American and Chinese participants view an animated fish swimming ahead of a group. Americans more often say the lead fish is leading by its own choice; Chinese participants more often say the group is pushing or chasing it. What does this best illustrate?
o: Cultural differences in visual acuity
Both groups saw the same display; interpretation differed, not acuity.
Cultural differences in emphasis on context in explaining behavior
Correct: holistic thinkers attend to the group and situation.
Stereotype threat in the Japanese participants
No stereotype about performance was activated.
A primacy effect in the American participants
No order of information was manipulated.
questions.x: Both groups saw the same display, so the difference lies in interpretation. Americans, from an individualist culture, explained the lead fish's movement by its internal dispositions; Chinese participants, from a more collectivist culture, attended to the group as a contextual cause. This parallels the weaker fundamental attribution error found in cultures that emphasize context and relationships.

questions.q: A person feels disgust and hostility toward members of a religious group without knowing any of them. This feeling is best described as what?
o: Prejudice
Correct: prejudice is a negative attitude or feeling toward a group.
Discrimination
Discrimination is behavior, and no behavior is described.
Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat affects members of the stereotyped group.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is understanding a culture on its own terms.
questions.x: Prejudice is the affective component of intergroup attitudes: a negative feeling or evaluation toward a group and its members, often formed without personal contact. Disgust and hostility are emotions, so this is prejudice. Discrimination is tempting because it often follows prejudice, but it requires behavior such as unequal treatment, and none is described.

questions.q: A manager refuses to promote qualified employees of one ethnicity. This action is best described as what?
o: Discrimination
Correct: unequal treatment based on group membership is discrimination.
Stereotyping
Stereotyping is a belief, not an action.
Ethnocentrism
Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by one's own.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is a nonjudgmental stance.
questions.x: Discrimination is the behavioral component: treating people unequally because of their group membership. Refusing promotions to qualified employees of one ethnicity is an action. Stereotyping is the cognitive belief and prejudice the feeling that may motivate such actions, but neither is itself a behavior.

questions.q: Historically, banks denied mortgages to residents of certain neighborhoods based on their racial makeup. This practice is best classified as what?
o: Individual prejudice
The practice operated through policy, not one person's attitude.
Self-stigma
Self-stigma is internalizing negative views about oneself.
Stereotype lift
Stereotype lift is a performance boost.
Institutional discrimination
Correct: policies of an institution systematically disadvantaged a group.
questions.x: Institutional discrimination is unequal treatment built into the policies and practices of organizations, such as mortgage denials based on a neighborhood's racial makeup, known as redlining. It operates through rules and systems rather than through one individual's attitudes, and its effects, like barriers to accumulating wealth, can persist for generations. Individual prejudice is a person-level attitude.

questions.q: Researchers mail identical résumés to employers, varying only whether the name is typically associated with one ethnic group or another. Callback rates differ by name. What does this design most directly measure?
o: Employers' implicit attitudes
Attitudes are not measured; only behavior is.
Applicants' stereotype threat
Applicants are fictional and perform no task.
Discrimination in hiring behavior
Correct: unequal callbacks for equal qualifications measure discriminatory behavior.
Applicants' qualifications
Qualifications were held constant.
questions.x: Audit or correspondence studies hold qualifications constant and vary only a group cue, here a name. Because the résumés are otherwise identical, any difference in callbacks measures discriminatory behavior directly. The design does not reveal employers' attitudes, implicit or explicit, because it records only their actions, not what motivated them.

questions.q: An orchestra begins auditioning musicians behind a screen so judges hear but cannot see them. The share of women advancing rises, while the applicant pool is unchanged. What does this finding most strongly suggest?
o: Women improved as musicians once screens were introduced
The screen changed what judges knew, not how well people played.
Evaluators' knowledge of gender had biased earlier decisions
Correct: removing gender cues changed outcomes for equal performances.
Screens produced stereotype threat in men
No stereotype about performance was activated in men.
Women's applications fell after screens were introduced
The stem states the applicant pool did not change, so the rise is not about who applied.
questions.x: A screen hides the performer's identity without changing the sound. If women advance more often once judges cannot see them, while the applicant pool is the same, then knowing the performer's gender was influencing earlier evaluations. This is a classic blind-evaluation logic for detecting bias. The tempting alternative, that women played better, is ruled out because the screen changes only what judges know.

questions.q: A study finds that patients from a minority group receive less pain medication than majority-group patients with identical documented pain scores. Which additional finding would best indicate the disparity reflects provider bias?
o: Minority patients report pain more often
Pain scores were already identical.
Providers with stronger implicit bias scores show larger treatment gaps
Correct: linking individual bias to the size of the gap supports a bias explanation.
Majority patients have more insurance coverage
That suggests a structural confound, not provider bias.
The hospital has a diverse staff
Staff diversity alone does not test whether bias drives the gap.
questions.x: Showing that provider bias drives a disparity requires linking a measure of bias to the outcome. If providers with stronger implicit bias show larger treatment gaps, the gap tracks the proposed cause, supporting the bias explanation. Insurance differences are tempting, but they point to a structural confound rather than to the providers' own biases.

questions.q: The stereotype content model proposes that stereotypes vary along which two dimensions?
o: Warmth and competence
Correct: groups are judged on intentions (warmth) and ability (competence).
Power and prestige
These are sources of prejudice, not the model's two dimensions.
Consensus and consistency
These are dimensions of Kelley's attribution model.
Stability and controllability
These are dimensions of Weiner's attribution model.
questions.x: The stereotype content model holds that groups are judged on warmth, whether their intentions are friendly, and competence, whether they can act on those intentions. Combinations of the two predict different emotions, such as admiration, pity, envy and contempt. Consensus and consistency are Kelley's attribution cues, and stability and controllability are Weiner's dimensions.

questions.q: According to the stereotype content model, a group seen as highly competent but low in warmth is most likely to elicit what?
o: Pity
Pity is elicited by groups seen as warm but incompetent.
Contempt
Contempt is elicited by groups seen as low on both dimensions.
Admiration
Admiration is reserved for groups high on both dimensions.
Envy
Correct: high competence and low warmth produce envious prejudice.
questions.x: In the stereotype content model, high-competence, low-warmth groups are seen as capable but cold or threatening, eliciting envy, a mix of resentment and grudging respect. Warm but incompetent groups elicit pity, groups low on both elicit contempt, and groups high on both elicit admiration. Envious prejudice can turn into hostility during social instability.

questions.q: A person opposes policies that help a minority group, claiming the group 'no longer faces barriers' and is 'asking for too much,' while denying any prejudice. This best illustrates what?
o: Old-fashioned overt racism
Overt racism openly claims group inferiority.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is understanding practices in context.
Modern (symbolic) racism
Correct: subtle prejudice expressed through abstract values and policy opposition.
Stereotype lift
Stereotype lift is a performance effect.
questions.x: Modern or symbolic racism is a subtle form of prejudice expressed through seemingly abstract values, such as claims that discrimination no longer exists and that a group demands too much. It coexists with denial of prejudice. Old-fashioned racism openly asserts group inferiority and supports overt segregation, which is not what this person expresses.

questions.q: Which personality pattern has been linked to higher levels of prejudice?
o: High openness to experience
Openness is associated with lower prejudice.
Internal locus of control
Locus of control is not a primary predictor of prejudice.
Authoritarian personality
Correct: rigid obedience to authority and intolerance of ambiguity predict prejudice.
High agreeableness
Agreeableness is associated with lower prejudice.
questions.x: The authoritarian personality, marked by rigid adherence to conventional values, submission to authority and hostility toward outsiders, has long been linked to prejudice; its modern form is right-wing authoritarianism. Social dominance orientation is another strong predictor. Openness to experience and agreeableness are linked to lower, not higher, prejudice.

questions.q: In a jigsaw classroom, each student learns one part of a lesson and must teach it to a diverse group. Why does this reduce prejudice?
o: It increases competition among students
The technique replaces competition with cooperation.
It creates interdependence and equal-status cooperation
Correct: each member's contribution is needed, meeting contact-hypothesis conditions.
It separates groups to reduce conflict
It brings groups together rather than separating them.
It lets one group lead the others
Equal status, not dominance, is the point.
questions.x: The jigsaw classroom makes each student hold a piece of the lesson that others need, creating interdependence. It satisfies the contact hypothesis conditions: equal status, cooperative goals and support from authority, here the teacher. Competition, which the method replaces, tends to increase intergroup hostility.

questions.q: Two rival departments are encouraged to see themselves as one company team. Bias between them decreases. Which model best explains this?
o: Common in-group identity model
Correct: recategorizing 'us' and 'them' as 'we' reduces intergroup bias.
Realistic conflict theory
That explains how conflict arises from competition, not how recategorization reduces it.
Frustration-aggression hypothesis
That explains scapegoating, not bias reduction.
Implicit personality theory
That concerns beliefs about which traits co-occur.
questions.x: The common in-group identity model proposes that intergroup bias decreases when members of different groups recategorize themselves into one inclusive group, turning 'us and them' into 'we.' In-group favoritism then extends to former out-group members. Realistic conflict theory is tempting because it concerns rivalry, but it explains how conflict arises rather than how recategorization reduces bias.

questions.q: People judge a likable in-group member more favorably than a similar out-group member, but judge an unlikable in-group member more harshly than a similar out-group member. This is called what?
o: Out-group homogeneity
That concerns perceived sameness of out-group members.
Ultimate attribution error
That concerns explaining out-group behavior, not punishing in-group deviants.
Group polarization
That concerns attitude extremity after discussion.
Black sheep effect
Correct: deviant in-group members are derogated to protect the group's image.
questions.x: The black sheep effect is the tendency to judge likable in-group members more favorably but unlikable in-group members more harshly than comparable out-group members. Derogating deviant in-group members protects the group's positive image, consistent with social identity theory. The ultimate attribution error concerns explaining out-group behavior, not punishing in-group deviants.

questions.q: In a resource allocation task, participants choose between giving both groups more points or giving their own group fewer points but a larger margin over the other group. Many choose the larger margin. What does this suggest?
o: Participants were motivated purely by self-interest
Self-interest would favor the higher absolute payoff.
Participants showed cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is unrelated to point allocation.
Participants were trying to be fair
Fairness would favor equal allocation.
In-group favoritism can center on relative advantage rather than absolute gain
Correct: maximizing difference matters more than maximizing the in-group's own total.
questions.x: In Tajfel's allocation matrices, many participants chose options that maximized the difference between groups even when this cost their own group points. This shows that in-group favoritism can center on relative standing rather than absolute gain, consistent with social identity theory's emphasis on positive distinctiveness. Pure self-interest would choose the option giving the in-group the most points.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes in-group favoritism from out-group derogation?
o: Favoritism is a behavior; derogation is only a belief
Both can be expressed in beliefs and behaviors.
Favoritism occurs only in minimal groups; derogation only in real groups
Both occur in many kinds of groups.
Favoritism boosts one's own group; derogation actively harms or disparages the other group
Correct: preferring 'us' differs from attacking 'them.'
They are identical terms for the same process
Research distinguishes the two processes.
questions.x: In-group favoritism means giving one's own group extra positive treatment or evaluation, while out-group derogation means actively disparaging or harming the other group. Research shows they are distinct: much intergroup bias reflects preference for 'us' rather than hostility toward 'them.' Both can appear in beliefs and in behavior, so neither is limited to one form.

questions.q: After brief 10-second silent video clips, students rate teachers in ways that closely match end-of-semester evaluations. What does this suggest about impression formation?
o: First impressions are always inaccurate
These results show notable accuracy.
Accurate impressions can form from thin slices of behavior
Correct: brief exposures often yield surprisingly accurate judgments.
Verbal content is essential for accurate impressions
The clips were silent.
Impressions require weeks of interaction
The ratings formed in seconds.
questions.x: Thin-slice research shows that people form surprisingly accurate impressions from very brief samples of behavior, such as seconds of silent video, which match judgments made after a whole semester. Nonverbal cues like expressiveness and confidence carry much information. This contradicts the claim that first impressions are always inaccurate, though thin slices are not error-free.

questions.q: When forming impressions, people tend to weigh negative information about a person more heavily than equally extreme positive information. This is called what?
o: Negativity bias
Correct: negative information has a disproportionate impact.
Positivity offset
That is a mild tendency to view neutral stimuli positively.
Halo effect
The halo effect is one positive trait coloring others.
Recency effect
No order of information is involved.
questions.x: The negativity bias is the tendency for negative information to have a greater impact than equally extreme positive information, so a single negative act can outweigh several positive ones. It may reflect the adaptive value of detecting threats. The halo effect is tempting because it shapes impressions, but it describes one positive trait coloring others, not the extra weight given to negatives.

questions.q: Participants rate essays paired with a photo of either an attractive or an unattractive author. Essays from the 'attractive' author receive higher quality ratings. Which change would best strengthen the conclusion that attractiveness caused the difference?
o: Using the same essay across photo conditions with random assignment
Correct: identical essays and random assignment isolate the photo as the cause.
Letting participants choose which essay to read
Self-selection would introduce confounds.
Using different essays for each photo
Different essays would confound quality with photo condition.
Telling participants the hypothesis beforehand
This would create demand characteristics.
questions.x: To show that the photo causes higher ratings, everything except the photo must be identical. Using the same essay in both conditions removes essay quality as a confound, and random assignment equalizes participant differences between conditions. Using different essays for each photo is the tempting error because it confounds quality with attractiveness.

questions.q: A teacher grades an essay higher because the student is usually polite and well dressed. Which bias best describes this?
o: Self-serving bias
The teacher is not explaining her own outcomes.
Stereotype threat
The student's performance is not impaired.
Out-group homogeneity
No group sameness judgment is involved.
Halo effect
Correct: unrelated positive traits color the evaluation of the essay.
questions.x: The halo effect occurs when a positive impression from one trait, here politeness and neat dress, spreads to unrelated judgments, such as essay quality. This is why blind grading improves fairness. Self-serving bias is ruled out because the teacher is not explaining her own outcomes; she is evaluating someone else's work.

questions.q: Participants are told a test showed they were good at detecting real suicide notes, then told the feedback was fake. Many still believe they are good at the task. This illustrates what?
o: Self-fulfilling prophecy
No expectation caused behavior that confirmed it.
Halo effect
No trait is spreading to unrelated judgments.
Belief perseverance
Correct: beliefs persist after their evidence is discredited.
Fundamental attribution error
No one is explaining another person's behavior.
questions.x: Belief perseverance is the persistence of beliefs even after the evidence that created them has been discredited. Once people build explanations for why they are good at a task, those explanations survive learning that the feedback was fake. A self-fulfilling prophecy is tempting, but it requires an expectation to cause behavior that makes it come true, which did not happen here.

questions.q: In a simulation, participants must quickly 'shoot' armed targets and not unarmed ones. They mistakenly shoot unarmed Black targets more often than unarmed White targets. Which conclusion is most justified?
o: Participants hold conscious hostility toward Black people
Errors under time pressure do not demonstrate conscious attitudes.
Automatic stereotypic associations can bias rapid decisions
Correct: time pressure reveals implicit associations in behavior.
Black targets held objects that looked more like weapons
Object images were controlled across target race.
The bias would increase with more time to decide
More deliberation time typically reduces such errors.
questions.x: Shooter-bias studies show that, under time pressure, participants more often mistakenly shoot unarmed Black targets than unarmed White targets. Because objects were controlled, the difference reflects automatic stereotypic associations influencing fast decisions, which appear even in people who do not hold conscious hostility. More time to deliberate usually reduces these errors, allowing controlled processing to correct the automatic response.

questions.q: Which approach has been found to reduce stereotype threat in students before an exam?
o: Writing about personally important values
Correct: self-affirmation buffers against the threat to self-integrity.
Reading about innate group differences in ability
This would increase stereotype relevance.
Reporting one's demographic group before the test
Asking for group membership first can increase threat.
Being told the test is extremely diagnostic
Diagnostic framing increases threat.
questions.x: Self-affirmation, such as writing about personally important values, reminds people of their worth beyond the threatened domain and buffers the threat to self-integrity, which can reduce stereotype threat effects. The other choices make the stereotype more salient or relevant: reporting group membership first, reading about innate group differences or emphasizing the test's diagnosticity.

questions.q: In a study, women see successful female mathematicians as role models before a math test, and their scores improve relative to controls. What is the most likely mechanism?
o: Role models increase test anxiety
Reduced anxiety, not increased, would explain improved scores.
Role models create stereotype lift for men
Men's scores were not the focus of the comparison.
Role models change the test's difficulty
Test difficulty was unchanged.
Role models counter the stereotype and reduce stereotype threat
Correct: disconfirming examples weaken the stereotype's relevance.
questions.x: Seeing successful women in mathematics provides counterstereotypic examples that undermine the stereotype that women are poor at math. This reduces stereotype threat, freeing cognitive resources and lowering worry, so performance improves. The improvement reflects reduced, not increased, anxiety, and stereotype lift is ruled out because it describes gains in the non-stereotyped group.

questions.q: A researcher claims stereotype threat lowers scores because of anxiety. In an experiment, threat lowers scores but self-reported anxiety does not differ between conditions. What is the best interpretation?
o: Stereotype threat does not exist
The threat condition still lowered scores.
Anxiety is proven to be irrelevant in every case
One null result on self-report cannot rule out anxiety universally.
Self-reported anxiety does not appear to mediate the effect in this study
Correct: the proposed mediator did not differ, so another mechanism may be at work.
The independent variable was not manipulated
Scores differed, showing the manipulation had an effect.
questions.x: A mediator explains how an independent variable affects an outcome, so it should differ between conditions and account for the effect. Here the threat lowered scores but self-reported anxiety did not differ, so self-reported anxiety does not appear to mediate the effect in this study. Other mechanisms, such as reduced working memory, may be involved, and a single null result does not rule out anxiety entirely.

questions.q: The sociologist who coined the term 'self-fulfilling prophecy' is whom?
o: Erving Goffman
Goffman is known for stigma and dramaturgy.
Émile Durkheim
Durkheim is known for anomie and studies of suicide.
Robert Merton
Correct: Merton described false definitions that evoke behavior making them true.
Max Weber
Weber is known for bureaucracy and rationalization.
questions.x: Robert Merton coined the term self-fulfilling prophecy in 1948, defining it as a false definition of a situation that evokes behavior making the original false conception come true. He illustrated it with a bank run. Goffman is the tempting distractor because he also studied social perception, but he is known for stigma and dramaturgy.

questions.q: A doctor expects a patient to be noncompliant, spends less time explaining the regimen, and the patient later fails to follow it. This best illustrates what?
o: Stereotype lift
Stereotype lift is improved performance by comparison.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
Correct: the doctor's expectation changed his behavior, producing the expected outcome.
Just-world hypothesis
No one is judged as deserving the outcome.
Cultural relativism
No cultural practice is being evaluated.
questions.x: The doctor's expectation of noncompliance led him to explain less, which made noncompliance more likely, so the expectation produced its own confirmation. That is a self-fulfilling prophecy and shows how clinicians' assumptions can affect patient outcomes. The just-world hypothesis is ruled out because no one is judged as deserving the outcome.

questions.q: An employer favors applicants from upper-class backgrounds and assumes working-class applicants lack ambition. This best illustrates prejudice rooted in what?
o: Social class
Correct: classism is prejudice based on socioeconomic status.
Religion
No religious characteristic is mentioned.
Age
No age characteristic is mentioned.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is not a basis for prejudice.
questions.x: Classism is prejudice and discrimination based on social class or socioeconomic status. Assuming working-class applicants lack ambition is a class-based stereotype that justifies favoring upper-class applicants. Class-based prejudice is a common source of bias alongside race, ethnicity, religion and gender, and none of the other characteristics is mentioned here.

questions.q: A coach who prizes physical toughness judges other people mainly on how tough they seem and pays little attention to their kindness. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: The fundamental attribution error
The FAE concerns trait versus situation explanations, not which traits are noticed.
Out-group homogeneity
No group membership comparison is involved.
Stereotype threat
No one's performance is impaired by a stereotype.
Our self-schemas shape the dimensions we use to judge others
Correct: traits central to one's self-concept guide perceptions of others.
questions.x: Self-schemas are organized beliefs about oneself, and traits central to a person's self-concept become the dimensions they use to perceive others. A coach who values toughness notices and judges others mainly on toughness while overlooking other qualities. The fundamental attribution error is tempting, but it concerns explaining behavior by traits versus situations, not which traits a perceiver attends to.

questions.q: Satisfied couples tend to attribute a partner's thoughtful gift to the partner's caring nature, and a forgotten anniversary to a busy week. This pattern is best described as what?
o: Distress-maintaining attributions
Those attribute negatives to the partner's character.
Fundamental attribution error
The FAE would attribute the forgotten anniversary to disposition.
Self-serving bias
The attributions concern the partner's behavior, not one's own outcomes.
Relationship-enhancing attributions
Correct: positives are internal and stable, negatives external and temporary.
questions.x: Happy couples tend to make relationship-enhancing attributions: a partner's positive acts are explained by internal, stable traits, while negative acts are explained by external, temporary circumstances. Distressed couples show the reverse, distress-maintaining pattern. The fundamental attribution error would predict blaming the forgotten anniversary on the partner's character, which these couples avoid.

questions.q: Students in a good mood rate a neutral stranger more positively than students in a bad mood. This best illustrates what?
o: The halo effect
The halo effect spreads one trait of the target to others.
The primacy effect
No order of information is manipulated.
Mood-congruent social judgment
Correct: the perceiver's current mood colors evaluations of others.
Stereotype threat
No one is performing in a stereotyped domain.
questions.x: Mood-congruent judgment is the tendency for a perceiver's current mood to color evaluations, so a good mood leads to more positive ratings of the same neutral person. This shows that the perceiver's state is a key component of social perception. The halo effect is tempting, but it describes one trait of the target spreading to others, not the perceiver's mood.

questions.q: Which phrase best captures cultural relativism?
o: One's own culture is the standard for judging others
That is ethnocentrism.
Practices should be understood in terms of the culture in which they occur
Correct: relativism evaluates practices within their own context.
All cultures should eventually merge into one
That describes global homogenization.
Foreign cultures are superior to one's own
That is xenocentrism.
questions.x: Cultural relativism is understanding beliefs and practices in terms of the culture in which they occur, rather than judging them by outside standards. It contrasts with ethnocentrism, which treats one's own culture as the standard, and with xenocentrism, which treats other cultures as superior. Relativism aims to understand, not to rank cultures.

questions.q: A news outlet describes a neighboring country's holidays as 'primitive' compared with its own. This most clearly reflects what?
o: Ethnocentrism
Correct: the outlet uses its own culture as the standard of judgment.
Xenocentrism
Xenocentrism would favor the foreign culture.
Cultural relativism
Relativism would avoid such judgments.
Cultural transmission
Transmission is passing culture across generations.
questions.x: Calling another country's holidays primitive judges them by one's own culture's standards, which is ethnocentrism. Ethnocentrism often frames differences as inferiority. Xenocentrism would be the reverse, viewing the foreign holidays as superior, and cultural relativism would interpret them within their own cultural meaning.

questions.q: Which statement about ethnocentrism is most accurate?
o: It can promote in-group cohesion while fostering intergroup hostility
Correct: pride in one's group can coexist with devaluing others.
It occurs only in technologically advanced societies
Ethnocentrism is found across all kinds of societies.
It is identical to cultural relativism
The two are opposing perspectives.
It always involves deliberate discrimination
Ethnocentrism is an attitude that may or may not lead to discrimination.
questions.x: Ethnocentrism can strengthen in-group cohesion, loyalty and identity while fostering negative views of and hostility toward other groups. It appears in societies of all kinds and levels of technology. Because it is an attitude, it may or may not lead to discriminatory behavior, so it does not always involve deliberate discrimination.

questions.q: An out-group is best defined as what?
o: A group a person admires and wishes to join
That describes an aspirational reference group.
A group a person identifies with
That is an in-group.
A group with no formal structure
Lack of structure does not define an out-group.
A group a person does not belong to or identify with
Correct: out-groups are groups outside one's own.
questions.x: An out-group is any group a person does not belong to or identify with, often thought of as 'them.' Out-groups can become targets of bias, homogeneity perceptions and competition. A group one admires and hopes to join is an aspirational reference group, which is a different concept even though one is not yet a member.

questions.q: Researchers find that participants show more out-group homogeneity for a rival university than for their own. Which explanation is most consistent with this finding?
o: Rival students are actually more similar to each other
No evidence suggests real differences in variability.
Participants were experiencing stereotype threat
Stereotype threat concerns performance in a stereotyped domain.
People have more varied, detailed exposure to in-group members
Correct: greater familiarity reveals in-group variability.
Participants were using cultural relativism
Relativism would reduce, not explain, such judgments.
questions.x: People usually know many varied in-group members personally and interact with them in different contexts, so they notice differences among them. Out-group members are encountered less and in narrower roles, making them seem more alike. Familiarity explains the out-group homogeneity effect without assuming that rival students are actually less varied.

questions.q: A woman completes residency and becomes a board-certified surgeon. Her status as surgeon is best described as:
o: Achieved
Correct: it was earned through her own effort and training.
Ascribed
Ascribed statuses are assigned at birth or involuntarily, such as race or age.
Master
Nothing indicates this status dominates all others in how people see her.
Primary
Primary describes a type of group, not a type of status.
questions.x: An achieved status is a position a person gains through her own effort, choices or merit, like earning a degree and board certification. An ascribed status is assigned without effort, at birth or by circumstance, such as age, race or royal birth. Master status is not a separate type of acquisition; it describes any status that dominates how others see someone, and nothing here suggests that.

questions.q: A man released from prison finds that employers focus only on his criminal record and overlook his degree and work history. His ex-offender status is functioning as a:
o: Role set
A role set is the cluster of roles tied to one status, not a dominant label.
Ascribed status
A criminal record results from his own actions, so it is not ascribed.
Reference group
