A reference group is a standard for self-evaluation, not a status.
Master status
Correct: one status overshadows all others and shapes every interaction.
questions.x: A master status is the one status that overrides all others and shapes how people interpret everything about a person. Here the ex-offender label eclipses his education and job history, so employers react to it alone. It is tempting to call it ascribed because it feels imposed, but it stems from his own actions, so it is achieved; what makes it master is its dominance, not how it was acquired.

questions.q: A professor teaches lectures, advises graduate students and serves on hiring committees. These multiple behaviors attached to her single position are called her:
o: Status set
A status set is all the statuses a person holds, not roles within one status.
Role set
Correct: a role set is all the roles linked to one status.
Role strain
Role strain is tension within a role; the stem describes no tension.
Master status
A master status dominates identity; nothing here describes domination.
questions.x: A status is a position; the bundle of roles, or expected behaviors, attached to that one position is its role set. A professor's single status brings teaching, advising and committee roles. The status set is different: it is all the statuses one person holds at once, such as professor, mother and citizen. Role strain would require tension among these roles, which the stem does not describe.

questions.q: A child born into a royal family is called a prince from birth. His royal status is:
o: Achieved
Achieved statuses require effort or choice by the person.
Instrumental
Instrumental describes goal-directed group ties, not status types.
Ascribed
Correct: he did nothing to earn it; it was assigned at birth.
Exited
Role exit refers to leaving a role, which has not occurred.
questions.x: Ascribed statuses are assigned to a person involuntarily, usually at birth, regardless of effort or ability; royal title, sex and ethnicity are classic examples. Achieved statuses, by contrast, are earned or chosen. Because the prince did nothing to obtain his title, it is ascribed, even though he will later be expected to perform the duties that come with it.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes a status from a role?
o: A status is chosen; a role is assigned at birth
Statuses can be ascribed or achieved, and roles follow from either.
A role is a position; a status is the behavior attached to it
This reverses the definitions.
A status is a social position; a role is the behavior expected of someone in it
Correct: you occupy a status and perform a role.
Statuses apply only to groups; roles apply only to individuals
Both statuses and roles are held by individuals within a social structure.
questions.x: Sociologists separate the position from the behavior: a status is a recognized social position (student, doctor, parent), and a role is the set of expectations for how someone in that position should act. You occupy a status but play a role. Reversing these is the common trap, and both statuses and roles can be either ascribed or achieved.

questions.q: A woman is a respected physician but a member of a group that faces discrimination, and patients sometimes question her authority. Which concept best captures the mismatch?
o: Status inconsistency
Correct: her statuses carry conflicting levels of prestige, producing contradictory treatment.
Role exit
She has not left any role.
Role strain
Role strain is competing demands inside one role, not unequal prestige across statuses.
Achieved master status
Her physician status is achieved, but the problem is the clash between statuses.
questions.note: Status inconsistency: a person ranks high on one status and low on another.
questions.x: Status inconsistency occurs when a person holds statuses ranked very differently in prestige, so others respond to her in contradictory ways. Her high-prestige profession clashes with a stigmatized group membership, and some patients react to the lower-ranked status. Role strain is tempting, but strain is about competing demands within one role, not mismatched prestige between two statuses.

questions.q: A nurse's daughter has a school recital at the same time as a mandatory staff meeting. The tension she feels is an example of:
o: Role strain
Role strain involves competing demands within a single status.
Role exit
She is not disengaging from either role.
Status inconsistency
Status inconsistency concerns unequal prestige, not clashing obligations.
Role conflict
Correct: demands from two different statuses (parent and nurse) clash.
questions.note: Conflict = two statuses; strain = one status.
questions.x: Role conflict arises when the expectations of two different statuses a person holds collide, here parent versus employee at the same time. Role strain is the near-miss: it describes incompatible demands inside a single status. A quick test is to count statuses; two clashing statuses means conflict, one overloaded status means strain.

questions.q: A first-year resident is told by attendings to see patients faster and by patients to spend more time with them. This is best classified as:
o: Role conflict
Role conflict requires clashing demands from two different statuses.
Role strain
Correct: both expectations attach to the single status of resident.
Role exit
Nothing suggests the resident is leaving the role.
Role reversal
Role reversal means trading positions with another person.
questions.note: Trap: multiple audiences can still create strain within one role.
questions.x: Role strain is tension among the expectations attached to one status. Speed demanded by attendings and time demanded by patients are both expectations of being a resident, so this is strain. Role conflict is tempting because two audiences are involved, but conflict requires the demands to come from two different statuses the person holds.

questions.q: In sociology, a role is best defined as:
o: The set of behaviors, rights and obligations expected of someone holding a status
Correct: roles are the expected behavior tied to a position.
A position a person occupies in society
That is the definition of a status.
A group a person uses to evaluate themselves
That defines a reference group.
A label that dominates a person's identity
That defines a master status.
questions.x: A role is the set of expected behaviors, rights and obligations that go with a status, the script a person is expected to follow. The status is the position itself. Confusing the two is the main trap; reference groups and master statuses are separate concepts about self-evaluation and identity dominance.

questions.q: According to Ebaugh's model of role exit, which stage immediately follows a person's first doubts about a role?
o: The turning point
The turning point comes after alternatives have been considered.
Creating the ex-role
Building an ex-role identity is the final stage.
Anticipatory socialization
This is a general socialization concept, not a named Ebaugh stage.
Searching for alternatives
Correct: after doubts, the person weighs other possible roles.
questions.note: Ebaugh: first doubts → alternatives → turning point → creating ex-role.
questions.x: Ebaugh described role exit as four stages: first doubts about the role, a search for alternatives, a turning point where the person decides to leave, and creating an ex-role identity. Weighing alternatives therefore comes right after the first doubts. The turning point is tempting but comes later, once alternatives have been considered and a decision is made.

questions.q: A retired firefighter still introduces himself as an "ex-firefighter" and attends reunions with former crew. This reflects which aspect of role exit?
o: Role engulfment preventing any exit
He has actually left the role, so exit occurred.
Establishing an ex-role identity that blends past and present
Correct: people often retain an identity tied to the role they left.
Role strain within his current role
There is no conflict of expectations within a single role.
Resocialization in a total institution
No total institution is described.
questions.x: In the final stage of role exit, people build an ex-role identity: they have left the role but still define themselves partly by it, as ex-firefighters, ex-nuns or ex-athletes. Former role relationships and labels often persist. Role engulfment is wrong because he clearly did exit; the point is that leaving a role does not erase it from one's identity.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a primary group?
o: A company's accounting department
Workplace departments are typically secondary, task-focused groups.
A semester-long lecture class
Classes are impersonal, temporary and goal-oriented, so secondary.
A close-knit family
Correct: primary groups are small, intimate, long-lasting and expressive.
A national professional association
Large formal associations are secondary groups.
questions.x: Primary groups are small, intimate, long-lasting and valued for the relationships themselves (expressive), with family and close friends as the model. Secondary groups are larger or impersonal, formed to accomplish tasks (instrumental), and often temporary. Departments, classes and professional associations bring people together for goals, not for intimacy, so they are secondary.

questions.q: Five students form a team for a class project and disband after the presentation. Which feature most clearly makes this a secondary group?
o: Members share emotional intimacy
Emotional intimacy is characteristic of primary groups.
It is very small
Size alone does not define primary versus secondary.
Members met in person
Face-to-face contact occurs in both group types.
It is organized around a specific task and is temporary
Correct: secondary groups are instrumental and often short-lived.
questions.x: Secondary groups are defined by an instrumental purpose and limited, often temporary, impersonal ties. A project team that forms for a task and disbands afterward fits this exactly. Small size and face-to-face contact are tempting cues for a primary group, but they appear in both group types; what defines a primary group is emotional intimacy and long-term bonds.

questions.q: Researchers randomly label participants as "overestimators" or "underestimators" of dot counts. Participants then give more money to anonymous members of their own label. This best demonstrates:
o: In-group favoritism even with trivial group criteria
Correct: the minimal group paradigm shows mere categorization produces bias.
Realistic conflict over scarce resources
Groups never competed, so conflict over resources does not explain it.
Reference group comparison
Participants were allocating rewards, not evaluating themselves.
Primary group loyalty
These arbitrary groups have no intimacy or history.
questions.x: Tajfel's minimal group paradigm showed that assigning people to groups on trivial or even random criteria is enough to produce in-group favoritism in reward allocation. No competition, history or contact was needed. Realistic conflict theory is the tempting alternative, but it explains bias through competition for scarce resources, which was absent here.

questions.q: A college junior hoping to attend medical school models her study habits after current medical students she admires. The medical students serve as her:
o: Primary group
She has no intimate, enduring relationship with them.
Out-group
An out-group is a group she does not belong to or identify with; she admires and emulates these students.
Reference group
Correct: a reference group provides standards a person uses to evaluate themselves.
Dyad
A dyad is a two-person group, not a source of standards.
questions.x: A reference group is any group whose standards a person uses to evaluate herself and guide her behavior, whether or not she belongs to it. Aspiring students often adopt the habits of the profession they hope to join, a form of anticipatory socialization. Primary group is wrong because she has no intimate, lasting tie to these students.

questions.q: According to Simmel, what is a defining feature of a dyad?
o: It allows coalitions of two against one
Coalitions require at least three members (a triad).
It ends if either member leaves
Correct: a two-person group cannot survive the loss of one member.
It is the most stable group size
Dyads are intimate but the least stable.
Members cannot form intimate ties
Dyads are often the most intimate groups.
questions.x: Simmel noted that a dyad, a two-person group, is uniquely fragile: if either member leaves, the group ceases to exist. Dyads tend to be highly intimate because attention is not divided, but they are the least stable group form. Coalitions of two against one require a third member, which is why triads behave differently.

questions.q: Two roommates who keep arguing invite a third friend to move in. Compared with the dyad, the new triad is more likely to:
o: Collapse if any one person leaves
Losing one member of a triad leaves a dyad, so the group survives.
Become more intimate
Adding members generally reduces intimacy.
Allow one member to mediate or join a coalition
Correct: a third person can act as mediator or create two-against-one alliances.
Eliminate all conflict
Triads add new conflict possibilities, such as exclusion.
questions.x: Adding a third member creates a triad, which is more stable than a dyad because it survives the loss of one person, and it introduces new dynamics. The third person can mediate disputes between the other two or join one of them in a coalition. Intimacy usually drops as attention is divided, and new conflicts such as exclusion become possible.

questions.q: A team grows from 4 members to 6. How does the number of possible one-to-one relationships change?
o: From 4 to 6
This counts members, not pairwise relationships.
From 12 to 30
Using n(n − 1) double-counts each pair.
From 8 to 12
Doubling the member count does not give the number of pairs.
From 6 to 15
Correct: n(n − 1)/2 gives 4·3/2 = 6 and 6·5/2 = 15.
questions.note: Relationships grow much faster than members: n(n − 1)/2.
questions.x: The number of possible pairwise relationships in a group of n people is n(n − 1)/2, because each person can pair with n − 1 others and each pair is counted twice. For 4 members that is 4·3/2 = 6; for 6 members it is 6·5/2 = 15. Forgetting to divide by 2 gives 12 and 30, the most tempting error.

questions.q: As a group grows larger, which change is most likely?
o: It becomes less stable and more intimate
This describes moving toward a dyad, not a larger group.
It becomes more stable but less intimate
Correct: larger groups survive member loss but have weaker individual ties.
Formal rules become less necessary
Larger groups usually need more formal structure.
Every member interacts more with each other member
Interaction is spread thinner as possible pairs multiply.
questions.x: Larger groups are more stable because losing any one member does not dissolve them, but ties between individuals weaken because interaction is spread across many more possible pairs. They also tend to need more formal rules and roles to coordinate. The dyad sits at the opposite extreme: most intimate and least stable.

questions.q: A job seeker hears about her new position through a former classmate she rarely talks to, not through close friends. This supports the idea that:
o: Weak ties bridge to new information
Correct: acquaintances link to circles with information close friends lack.
Strong ties carry the most novel information
Close friends usually share the same information as you.
Dense networks speed job searches
Dense networks circulate redundant information.
Primary groups control hiring
No primary group is involved in the referral.
questions.note: Granovetter: the strength of weak ties.
questions.x: Granovetter's strength of weak ties argument holds that acquaintances are especially valuable for new information because they connect us to social circles our close friends do not reach. Close friends tend to know the same people and hear the same news, so their information is redundant. That is why job leads often come from weak ties.

questions.q: A social network is best defined as:
o: A formal organization with written rules
That describes a bureaucracy.
A web of social ties linking individuals or groups
Correct: networks map who is connected to whom.
A group sharing a strong sense of identity
Networks can exist without shared identity.
Any group of exactly three people
That is a triad.
questions.x: A social network is the pattern of ties linking individuals or groups, mapping who is connected to whom regardless of whether they share an identity or formal rules. Network analysis looks at features like density, centrality and bridges. A bureaucracy is a type of formal organization, not a network, and a triad is simply a three-person group.

questions.q: In a hospital's communication map, one nurse is the only link between the ICU staff and the pharmacy staff. Removing her would most likely:
o: Increase the density of each cluster
Density within clusters is unaffected by removing a between-cluster link.
Have no effect because weak ties are unimportant
Bridging ties are often the most important for information flow.
Merge the two clusters into one
Removing the only connection separates rather than merges them.
Cut the flow of information between the two clusters
Correct: she is a bridge across a structural hole, so losing her disconnects the clusters.
questions.x: A bridge is a tie that is the only link between two otherwise separate clusters; it spans what network theorists call a structural hole. Removing it disconnects the clusters, so information can no longer pass between them. Density within each cluster is unchanged, which is why the density option is a distractor.

questions.q: Compared with bridging social capital, bonding social capital is best characterized by:
o: Strong ties among similar people that provide support and solidarity
Correct: bonding capital links close, homogeneous members.
Weak ties that connect diverse groups
That describes bridging social capital.
Formal rules of a bureaucracy
Social capital refers to network resources, not rules.
Ties that exist only online
Bonding capital is defined by tie strength, not medium.
questions.x: Social capital is the resources available through social ties. Bonding social capital comes from strong ties among similar people, such as family or close communities, and provides emotional support and solidarity. Bridging social capital comes from weaker ties that connect diverse groups and provides access to new information and opportunities.

questions.q: Which is a characteristic of Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy?
o: Hiring based on family connections
Weber's model calls for hiring by technical qualifications.
Flexible, informal decision-making
Bureaucracies rely on formal, standardized procedures.
A clear hierarchy of authority with written rules
Correct: Weber emphasized hierarchy, rules, division of labor and impersonality.
Emotional ties among all members
Bureaucracy stresses impersonal relationships.
questions.x: Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy has a hierarchy of authority, written rules and procedures, specialized division of labor, impersonal relationships and hiring or promotion based on technical qualifications. These features aim at efficiency and predictability. Hiring through family connections and informal, emotional decision-making are exactly what the model tries to eliminate.

questions.q: A grassroots patient-advocacy group founded on equal voting gradually comes to be run by a few long-serving leaders who control decisions. This illustrates:
o: The iron law of oligarchy
Correct: Michels argued organizations tend toward rule by a small elite.
McDonaldization
McDonaldization concerns efficiency and standardization, not elite rule.
Bureaucratic ritualism
Ritualism is rigid rule-following, not concentration of power.
The strength of weak ties
That concept concerns information flow in networks.
questions.x: Michels' iron law of oligarchy states that organizations, even democratic ones, tend to be taken over by a small group of leaders because of the need for coordination, expertise and control of communication. An egalitarian group drifting into rule by a few long-serving leaders is the textbook case. McDonaldization is about efficiency and standardization, not who holds power.

questions.q: A clinic judges physicians mainly by the number of patients seen per hour rather than by quality of care. Which dimension of McDonaldization does this reflect?
o: Predictability
Predictability means standardized, uniform experiences.
Control
Control refers to replacing human judgment with technology or rules.
Efficiency
Efficiency is the fastest means to an end, not measurement of quantity.
Calculability
Correct: calculability emphasizes quantifiable output over quality.
questions.x: Ritzer's McDonaldization has four dimensions: efficiency, calculability, predictability and control. Calculability means emphasizing what can be counted, valuing quantity over quality. Judging physicians by patients per hour rather than care quality is calculability; efficiency is tempting, but efficiency concerns the fastest method to a goal, while this stem is about measuring and valuing quantity.

questions.q: A pharmacy chain installs automated dispensing machines that limit what pharmacists can do and dictate each step. Which McDonaldization dimension is most emphasized?
o: Calculability
No emphasis on counting or quantity is described.
Predictability
Uniform outcomes may follow, but the key feature is constraining workers.
Control
Correct: nonhuman technology constrains workers' discretion.
Efficiency
Speed is not the focus; dictating worker behavior is.
questions.x: In McDonaldization, control means replacing human judgment with nonhuman technology, scripts or rules that dictate how work is done. Machines that constrain pharmacists' discretion and specify each step exemplify control. Predictability is tempting because uniform output may follow, but the stem stresses limiting workers' choices, which is the core of control.

questions.q: A national urgent-care chain uses identical décor, scripts and menus of services so patients have the same experience in every city. This reflects McDonaldization's emphasis on:
o: Calculability
Nothing is being counted or quantified.
Predictability
Correct: uniform experiences across locations define predictability.
Iron law of oligarchy
That concerns leadership concentration, not uniformity.
Role strain
Role strain is an individual tension, not an organizational feature.
questions.x: Predictability is the McDonaldization dimension that ensures customers get the same product and experience regardless of time or place. Identical décor, scripts and service menus across cities are designed for uniformity. Calculability would instead emphasize counting outputs, such as visits per hour, which the stem does not mention.

questions.q: A hospital volunteer program that people join because they value its mission is, in Etzioni's typology, a:
o: Coercive organization
Coercive organizations, like prisons, involve involuntary membership.
Normative organization
Correct: normative organizations attract members through shared values.
Utilitarian organization
Utilitarian organizations offer pay or material reward.
Primary group
A volunteer program is a formal organization, not a primary group.
questions.x: Etzioni classified formal organizations by why people join: normative (voluntary) organizations attract members who share their values or goals, coercive organizations hold members involuntarily, and utilitarian organizations offer pay or material reward. Volunteers who join for the mission and receive no pay belong to a normative organization.

questions.q: A feature that distinguishes formal organizations from other groups is that they:
o: Always involve close emotional bonds
Formal organizations are typically impersonal.
Have exactly two or three members
That describes dyads and triads.
Lack any hierarchy
Formal organizations usually have defined hierarchies.
Persist even as individual members come and go
Correct: roles and rules, not particular people, sustain formal organizations.
questions.x: Formal organizations are structured to achieve goals through defined roles, rules and hierarchies, so they continue to exist even as specific individuals join and leave. That durability comes from positions being separate from the people who fill them. Close emotional bonds describe primary groups, and the lack of hierarchy is the opposite of how formal organizations work.

questions.q: Deliberately shaping how others perceive you, such as dressing formally for an interview, is called:
o: Role exit
Role exit is leaving a role, not shaping others' perceptions.
Self-handicapping
Self-handicapping creates excuses for failure.
Impression management
Correct: impression management is conscious control of the image you present.
Deindividuation
Deindividuation is loss of self-awareness in groups.
questions.x: Impression management is the deliberate effort to control how others perceive us, through appearance, words and behavior, as in dressing formally for an interview. Goffman's dramaturgical approach frames this as a performance. Self-handicapping is a specific defensive tactic that builds in an excuse for failure, not general image shaping.

questions.q: In Goffman's dramaturgical approach, a physician's white coat, stethoscope and office décor that help convey competence are part of the:
o: Front
Correct: the front includes setting, appearance and manner that define the performance.
Back stage
Back stage is where performers relax away from the audience.
Audience
The audience is the people observing the performance.
Role set
A role set is the roles tied to a status, not props.
questions.x: Goffman's dramaturgy treats social life as theater. The front is the part of the performance that defines the situation for the audience: the setting (office décor), appearance (white coat, stethoscope) and manner. These props communicate competence. Back stage is where performers relax out of the audience's view, which is the opposite of what these props do.

questions.q: After a difficult shift, nurses joke and complain freely in a staff room patients cannot enter. In Goffman's terms, the staff room is:
o: Front stage
Front stage is where the performance is given to an audience.
Back stage
Correct: back stage is where performers drop their public role.
A reference group
A reference group is a standard of comparison, not a setting.
A total institution
A total institution controls all aspects of residents' lives.
questions.x: In Goffman's dramaturgy, front stage is where people perform for an audience according to role expectations, and back stage is where they can drop the performance and act more freely. A staff room that patients cannot enter is back stage, where nurses joke and vent. A total institution, such as a prison, controls all aspects of residents' lives and does not fit.

questions.q: Before an exam, a student tells classmates he stayed up all night at a party. If he does poorly, the excuse protects his image. This strategy is:
o: Ingratiation
Ingratiation uses flattery or favors to gain liking.
Self-promotion
Self-promotion emphasizes one's strengths and successes.
Exemplification
Exemplification portrays oneself as morally exemplary.
Self-handicapping
Correct: creating an obstacle or excuse protects self-image from failure.
questions.x: Self-handicapping is creating an obstacle or excuse before a performance so that failure can be blamed on the obstacle rather than on lack of ability, protecting self-image. Claiming an all-nighter before an exam is a classic example. Self-promotion is the opposite approach, actively highlighting one's competence rather than preparing an excuse.

questions.q: An intern repeatedly compliments her supervisor's ideas to be viewed favorably. Which impression management strategy is she using?
o: Self-handicapping
She is not creating excuses for possible failure.
Intimidation
Intimidation seeks to appear threatening.
Ingratiation
Correct: flattery to increase liking is ingratiation.
Supplication
Supplication presents oneself as weak to gain help.
questions.x: Ingratiation is an impression management strategy that uses flattery, favors or agreement to make others like you. Repeatedly praising a supervisor's ideas aims to win liking. It differs from supplication, which seeks help by appearing weak or needy, and from self-promotion, which seeks to look competent rather than likable.

questions.q: A job applicant who privately dislikes teamwork describes herself as a passionate collaborator because the company values it. Which self is she presenting?
o: Tactical self
Correct: the tactical self is who others expect us to be.
Authentic self
The authentic self is who she believes she truly is.
Ideal self
The ideal self is who she would like to become, not who the employer expects.
Looking-glass self
That is Cooley's idea of self formed from imagined judgments.
questions.x: Impression management frameworks distinguish the authentic self (who we believe we really are), the ideal self (who we want to be) and the tactical self (who we present to match others' expectations). Presenting as a passionate collaborator because the company values it is the tactical self. The ideal self is tempting, but she does not aspire to this trait; she adopts it for the audience.

questions.q: In a study, participants who score high on self-monitoring change their behavior more across different social settings than low self-monitors. The best explanation is that high self-monitors:
o: Have lower self-esteem
Self-monitoring is distinct from self-esteem.
Rely mainly on internal attitudes
That describes low self-monitors.
Lack awareness of social norms
High self-monitors are especially aware of norms.
Attend closely to situational cues and adjust their self-presentation
Correct: high self-monitors tailor behavior to fit the audience.
questions.x: Self-monitoring is the tendency to observe situational cues and adjust one's self-presentation to fit them. High self-monitors act like social chameleons, so their behavior varies across settings, while low self-monitors act more on internal attitudes and behave consistently. It is a different construct from self-esteem.

questions.q: A server who trips while carrying plates laughs and jokes about being clumsy to restore a competent image. In Goffman's terms, this is an example of:
o: Face-work after a disrupted performance
Correct: people act to repair their image when a performance breaks down.
Role exit
The server is not leaving the role.
Back-stage behavior
The repair happens in front of the audience.
Role conflict
No two statuses are making competing demands.
questions.x: Goffman described face-work as the actions people take to maintain or restore the image (face) they present when a performance is disrupted. Joking about a stumble in front of customers repairs the server's image of competence. It is not back-stage behavior, because it happens in front of the audience as part of the performance.

questions.q: An applicant lists her awards and achievements during an interview to appear competent. She is using:
o: Supplication
Supplication involves appearing needy to gain help.
Self-handicapping
She is not preparing an excuse for failure.
Self-promotion
Correct: self-promotion highlights abilities and accomplishments.
Ingratiation
Ingratiation seeks liking, typically through flattery.
questions.x: Self-promotion is an impression management strategy that highlights one's skills and accomplishments to be seen as competent. Listing awards in an interview is a direct example. Ingratiation is the tempting alternative but aims to be liked, typically through flattery, rather than to be judged capable.

questions.q: Which is an example of nonverbal communication?
o: Sending a text message
Text uses words, so it is verbal communication.
Leaning toward a speaker to show interest
Correct: posture conveys meaning without words.
Writing a letter
Written language is verbal communication.
Giving a speech
Spoken words are verbal communication.
questions.x: Nonverbal communication conveys meaning without language, through posture, gestures, facial expression, eye contact, touch and use of space. Leaning toward a speaker signals interest without words. Texts, letters and speeches all use language, so they are verbal communication even though only one of them involves speaking.

questions.q: Two Deaf colleagues discuss a project in American Sign Language. Their exchange is best classified as:
o: Nonverbal communication
Trap: verbal means using language, not using the voice.
Verbal communication
Correct: sign languages use words and grammar, so they are verbal.
Paralanguage
Paralanguage refers to vocal qualities like tone and pitch.
Animal signaling
ASL is a full human language.
questions.note: Verbal = language-based, whether spoken, written or signed.
questions.x: Verbal communication means communication through language, with words and grammar, whether spoken, written or signed. American Sign Language is a complete natural language, so a conversation in ASL is verbal. The trap is equating verbal with vocal; gestures that are not part of a language, like a shrug, are nonverbal.

questions.q: A patient says "I'm fine" in a flat, shaky voice. The listener's sense that she is not fine relies mainly on:
o: Proxemics
Proxemics concerns use of personal space.
Haptics
Haptics concerns touch.
Paralanguage
Correct: tone, pitch and rate of speech convey meaning beyond the words.
Verbal content
The words themselves say she is fine.
questions.x: Paralanguage is the vocal but nonlinguistic part of speech: tone, pitch, volume, rate and hesitations. A flat, shaky voice can contradict the literal words and reveal emotion. Proxemics concerns personal space and haptics concerns touch, and the verbal content here actually points the opposite way.

questions.q: An American visitor stands closer than his Finnish host prefers, and the host keeps stepping back. This illustrates cultural variation in:
o: Proxemics
Correct: norms for interpersonal distance differ by culture.
Paralanguage
Paralanguage involves vocal cues, not distance.
Universal facial expressions
Facial expressions are not involved.
Verbal communication
No words are described.
questions.x: Proxemics is the study of how people use interpersonal space, and comfortable conversational distance differs across cultures. When one person's norm is closer than another's, the second person tends to back away to restore comfort. Paralanguage would involve vocal cues, and no facial expressions or words are relevant here.

questions.q: Participants from two cultures watch a disgusting film alone and show similar facial expressions, but when an authority figure is present, one group masks its expressions. This best supports:
o: Facial expressions are entirely learned
The similar expressions when alone argue against purely learned expressions.
Disgust is not a basic emotion
Both groups showed disgust, consistent with a basic emotion.
Paralanguage varies by culture
The study measured faces, not vocal cues.
Universal basic expressions modified by cultural display rules
Correct: expressions are shared, but norms govern when they are shown.
questions.x: Research by Ekman and colleagues found that basic emotional expressions are largely universal, but cultural display rules govern when it is appropriate to show them. When alone, both groups showed similar expressions; with an authority present, one group masked them. The similarity when alone rules out the idea that expressions are entirely learned.

questions.q: A hand gesture meaning "OK" in one country is considered offensive in another. This shows that gestures, unlike basic facial expressions of emotion, are:
o: Universally understood
The example shows different meanings across cultures.
A form of paralanguage
Paralanguage refers to vocal qualities, not hand movements.
Largely culturally specific
Correct: many gestures have meanings learned within a culture.
Controlled by display rules for emotion
Display rules govern emotional expression, not symbolic gestures.
questions.x: Basic facial expressions of emotion are recognized fairly consistently across cultures, but gestures are largely learned symbols whose meanings vary from culture to culture. The same hand sign can mean approval in one place and be insulting in another. Display rules are tempting but they regulate when emotions are expressed, not what symbolic gestures mean.

questions.q: Researchers show participants silent video clips of people expressing emotions. On average, which finding is most consistent with prior research on gender and emotion detection?
o: Women decode nonverbal emotional cues slightly more accurately than men
Correct: studies typically find a small female advantage in decoding.
Men decode nonverbal cues far more accurately than women
This reverses the usual finding.
No one can identify emotions without sound
Facial cues alone allow above-chance recognition.
Only people from the actors' culture recognize any emotion
Basic emotions are recognized above chance across cultures.
questions.x: Studies of nonverbal decoding consistently find a small average advantage for women in reading emotional cues from faces and bodies. The effect is modest, so it describes group averages, not every individual. Facial cues alone allow above-chance emotion recognition, and basic emotions are recognized across cultures, ruling out the other options.

questions.q: A coach gives a player a pat on the back after a good play. This form of nonverbal communication is:
o: Proxemics
Proxemics is about distance, not touch.
Paralanguage
Paralanguage is vocal tone and pitch.
Kinesics of the face
The message is conveyed by touch, not facial movement.
Haptics
Correct: haptics is communication through touch.
questions.x: Haptics is the study of communication through touch, such as a pat on the back, a handshake or a hug. Touch can convey encouragement, affection or dominance. Proxemics is about distance between people and paralanguage about vocal qualities, so neither describes a message delivered by physical contact.

questions.q: A forager honeybee returns to the hive and performs a waggle dance. What information does the dance convey?
o: The presence of a predator
Alarm is signaled by pheromones, not the waggle dance.
The direction and distance of a food source
Correct: dance angle signals direction and waggle duration signals distance.
The forager's age
The dance does not encode age.
Which bee will become queen
Queen development depends on larval feeding, not dances.
questions.x: Von Frisch showed that the honeybee waggle dance communicates the location of a food source. The angle of the waggle run relative to vertical indicates direction relative to the sun, and the duration of the waggle portion indicates distance. Alarm in bee colonies is communicated chemically by pheromones, not by this dance.

questions.q: Vervet monkeys give different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and listeners respond with predator-appropriate escapes. This shows that the calls are:
o: Referential signals carrying specific information
Correct: each call refers to a specific predator type.
Pheromones
The signals are vocal, not chemical.
Random vocalizations
Distinct, consistent responses show the calls are meaningful.
Courtship displays
The calls warn of predators, not attract mates.
questions.x: Vervet monkeys produce acoustically distinct alarm calls for different predators, and listeners respond with the appropriate escape, climbing trees for leopards, looking up for eagles and scanning the ground for snakes. Because each call reliably refers to a category of external threat, the calls function as referential signals, not random noise.

questions.q: Ants lay chemical trails that lead nestmates to food. This form of communication relies on:
o: Visual displays
The trail is chemical, not visual.
Auditory alarm calls
No sound is involved.
Hormones acting within one ant
Hormones act inside an organism; pheromones act between individuals.
Pheromones
Correct: pheromones are chemical signals between members of a species.
questions.x: Pheromones are chemical signals released by one individual that affect the behavior or physiology of others of the same species. Ant trail pheromones recruit nestmates to food and are reinforced as more ants use the trail. Hormones are tempting but act within the body that produces them, not between individuals.

questions.q: Gazelles that spot a predator sometimes leap high in place (stotting), wasting energy instead of fleeing. The best evolutionary explanation is that stotting:
o: Is an accident with no function
Persistent costly behavior usually signals adaptive value.
Lures predators toward kin
This would reduce inclusive fitness.
Is a costly, honest signal that the gazelle is fit and hard to catch
Correct: only healthy animals can afford the display, so predators may abandon pursuit.
Is a pheromone release
Stotting is a visual display, not a chemical signal.
questions.note: Handicap principle: costly signals are hard to fake.
questions.x: Zahavi's handicap principle holds that signals which are costly to produce are honest, because only individuals in good condition can afford them. A stotting gazelle advertises to the predator that it is fit and would be hard to catch, so the predator does better chasing a weaker target. Calling it an accident ignores that a costly behavior persisting in a population usually has adaptive value.

questions.q: In a study of a new apartment complex, residents became friends most often with neighbors whose doors were nearest their own. Which factor best explains this?
o: Similarity of attitudes
Door location was the variable, not attitudes.
Proximity
Correct: physical closeness increases interaction and liking.
Physical attractiveness
Attractiveness was not measured.
Reciprocal altruism
This is an evolutionary helping concept, not attraction.
questions.x: Proximity, or physical closeness, is one of the strongest predictors of attraction because it creates repeated chances to interact. In Festinger's classic housing study, friendships formed most often between residents whose doors were closest. Attitude similarity also predicts liking, but the variable that differed here was physical location.

questions.q: Participants view photographs of strangers, some shown once and some shown ten times. Later they rate the frequently shown faces as more likable. This demonstrates:
o: The halo effect
The halo effect involves inferring traits from attractiveness.
The mere exposure effect
Correct: repeated exposure increases liking.
The matching hypothesis
Matching concerns partners of similar attractiveness.
Misattribution of arousal
No arousal manipulation is described.
questions.x: The mere exposure effect is the tendency to like stimuli more simply because we have encountered them repeatedly, even without any interaction. Faces seen ten times became more familiar and therefore more likable. The halo effect is a different bias, in which one positive trait such as attractiveness spills over into judgments of unrelated traits.

questions.q: Jurors rate an attractive defendant as more honest and intelligent than an unattractive one with identical evidence. This reflects:
o: The mere exposure effect
Jurors did not see either defendant more often.
In-group favoritism
No group membership is described.
The halo effect
Correct: one positive trait (attractiveness) colors judgments of others.
Self-serving bias
Self-serving bias concerns explaining one's own outcomes.
questions.x: The halo effect is the tendency for one positive characteristic, often physical attractiveness, to color judgments of a person's other traits, such as honesty and intelligence. Because the evidence was identical, only appearance can explain the jurors' ratings. Mere exposure is ruled out because neither defendant was seen more often.

questions.q: Which pair of strangers is most likely to report mutual liking after a brief conversation?
o: Two who discover they share political and religious views
Correct: attitude similarity is a strong predictor of attraction.
Two who hold opposing core values
Opposites rarely attract on core attitudes.
Two who avoid eye contact throughout
Reduced engagement typically lowers liking.
Two who learn the other dislikes them
Reciprocity of liking runs the other way.
questions.x: Similarity, especially in core attitudes and values, is one of the most reliable predictors of attraction; it validates our views and makes interaction smoother. The idea that opposites attract has little support for core attitudes. Learning that someone dislikes you lowers liking, because liking tends to be reciprocated.

questions.q: Participants who were told a partner liked them later rated the partner more favorably than participants given no such information, even though the partner's behavior was identical. This illustrates:
o: Mere exposure
Exposure time was the same in both conditions.
Proximity
Physical distance was not manipulated.
The matching hypothesis
Attractiveness levels were not compared.
Reciprocity of liking
Correct: we tend to like people who like us.
questions.x: Reciprocity of liking is the tendency to like people who we believe like us. Since the partner's behavior was identical across conditions, only the belief about being liked differed, and it raised ratings. Mere exposure and proximity are ruled out because time with the partner and physical distance were the same in both groups.

questions.q: Computer-generated composite faces created by averaging many individual faces are typically rated as:
o: Less attractive than the individual faces
Averaging tends to increase, not decrease, attractiveness ratings.
More attractive than most of the individual faces
Correct: averageness and symmetry are rated attractive.
Equally attractive regardless of how many faces are averaged
Ratings rise as more faces are averaged.
Unrecognizable as faces
Composites look like realistic faces.
questions.x: Faces created by averaging many individual faces are typically rated more attractive than most of the faces that went into them, and attractiveness rises as more faces are averaged. Averaging produces features that are typical and symmetrical, which may signal health and genetic quality. The intuition that averaging produces a bland, less attractive face is the main trap.

questions.q: Men who met a female interviewer on a high, swaying bridge were more likely to call her later than men who met her on a stable bridge. Which explanation best fits?
o: They misattributed fear-related arousal to attraction
Correct: physiological arousal from the bridge was labeled as attraction.
Mere exposure to the interviewer increased liking
Exposure time was similar in both conditions.
Proximity differed between groups
Both groups met the interviewer face to face.
The stable bridge produced more arousal
The high bridge produced more arousal.
questions.x: In the Dutton and Aron bridge study, men on the frightening suspension bridge experienced physiological arousal and misattributed it to attraction to the interviewer, making them more likely to call her. This fits the two-factor view that emotion depends on arousal plus a cognitive label. The stable bridge produced less arousal, which is why that group showed less interest.

questions.q: A mugger shoves a pedestrian in order to grab her purse. This is best classified as:
o: Hostile aggression
Hostile aggression aims to cause harm out of anger.
Relational aggression
Relational aggression damages social relationships.
Instrumental aggression
Correct: harm is a means to another goal (getting the purse).
Displaced aggression
The pedestrian is the intended target, not a substitute.
questions.x: Instrumental aggression uses harm as a means to a separate goal, such as getting money or property. The mugger shoves the pedestrian to obtain the purse, not out of anger at her. Hostile aggression is the tempting alternative, but it is driven by anger, with causing harm as the end in itself.

questions.q: A driver stuck in traffic for an hour honks and yells at other drivers. Which theory best explains the outburst?
o: Social exchange theory
This explains relationships via costs and rewards.
Mere exposure effect
Exposure increases liking, not aggression.
Kin selection
Kin selection explains helping relatives.
Frustration-aggression hypothesis
Correct: blocked goals produce frustration that can lead to aggression.
questions.x: The frustration-aggression hypothesis states that when goal-directed behavior is blocked, the resulting frustration increases the likelihood of aggression. Being stuck in traffic blocks the goal of getting somewhere, and yelling and honking follow. Later revisions note frustration produces anger that may or may not become aggression, but this is the best fit among the options.

questions.q: Children who watched an adult hit an inflatable doll later hit the doll more than children who watched a calm adult. This finding supports:
o: Catharsis reducing aggression
Watching aggression increased, not reduced, aggression.
Observational learning of aggression
Correct: children imitated the modeled behavior.
Frustration-aggression theory
No frustration manipulation produced the difference.
Instinctive aggression independent of learning
Group differences came from what children observed.
questions.x: Bandura's Bobo doll studies showed that children who watched an adult model hit an inflatable doll were more likely to imitate that aggression, demonstrating observational learning. The catharsis idea predicts the reverse, that watching aggression would drain aggressive impulses, which the data contradict. Because the groups differed only in what they saw, learning, not instinct, explains the difference.

questions.q: Which biological profile is most associated with increased impulsive aggression?
o: Low serotonin activity and reduced prefrontal cortex control
Correct: weak prefrontal inhibition and low serotonin are linked to impulsive aggression.
High serotonin and enhanced prefrontal activity
These are associated with better impulse control.
Low testosterone and a smaller amygdala response
Lower testosterone and amygdala reactivity are linked to less aggression.
High oxytocin alone
Oxytocin is mainly linked to bonding.
questions.x: Impulsive aggression is associated with low serotonin activity and weak prefrontal cortex control over emotional responses, often alongside high amygdala reactivity and higher testosterone. The prefrontal cortex normally inhibits impulses that the amygdala generates. Low testosterone and reduced amygdala response point toward less aggression, not more.

questions.q: City data show that assaults rise on hotter days. Which conclusion is best supported by these data alone?
o: Heat directly causes aggression
Correlational data cannot rule out confounds like more people outdoors.
Cold weather causes aggression
The data show the opposite pattern.
Temperature has no relation to aggression
The data show a relationship.
Temperature is associated with aggression
Correct: correlational data show an association, consistent with the heat hypothesis.
questions.x: City data showing more assaults on hotter days are correlational, so they establish an association but not causation. Confounds such as more people outdoors, more alcohol use or school vacations could explain the pattern. Concluding that heat directly causes aggression is the tempting overreach; that requires experimental evidence.

questions.q: Angered participants gave more electric shocks to a confederate when a rifle lay on a nearby table than when a badminton racket did. This best illustrates:
o: Catharsis
No venting occurred, and aggression increased.
Instrumental aggression
The shocks served no other goal.
The weapons effect, in which aggressive cues prime aggression
Correct: weapons act as cues that activate aggressive thoughts.
Social facilitation
The presence of others was not manipulated.
questions.x: Berkowitz and LePage found that angered participants delivered more shocks when a rifle was nearby than when a badminton racket was, the weapons effect. Weapons act as aggressive cues that prime aggressive thoughts and make aggression more likely in people who are already aroused. Catharsis would predict less aggression, the opposite of what occurred.

questions.q: After being criticized by her boss, a woman goes home and snaps at her roommate. This is an example of:
o: Displaced aggression
Correct: aggression is redirected to a safer target.
Instrumental aggression
She gains nothing from snapping.
Relational aggression
Relational aggression harms relationships through exclusion or rumors.
Reciprocal altruism
This is helping, not aggression.
questions.x: Displaced aggression is aggression redirected from the true source of frustration, often a powerful person like a boss, toward a safer, more available target like a roommate. The woman cannot retaliate against her boss without risk. Instrumental aggression is ruled out because snapping at her roommate gains her nothing.

questions.q: A survey finds that teens who play more violent video games report more aggressive behavior. Which additional study would best test whether the games cause aggression?
o: Surveying more teens about their gaming habits
A larger correlational sample still cannot establish causation.
Randomly assigning teens to play violent or nonviolent games and then measuring aggression
Correct: random assignment controls confounds and permits causal inference.
Asking aggressive teens why they like violent games
Self-reports of preferences cannot show causation.
Measuring parents' attitudes toward video games
This adds a variable but not experimental control.
questions.x: Correlational surveys cannot show causation because third variables or reverse causation could explain the link, for example aggressive teens choosing violent games. Randomly assigning participants to play violent or nonviolent games makes the groups equivalent on average, so a difference in aggression can be attributed to the games. Simply enlarging the survey sample does not fix the design problem.

questions.q: A group of students spreads rumors to exclude a classmate from their social circle. This behavior is best described as:
o: Instrumental aggression
Unless harm serves another goal, this is not instrumental.
Physical aggression
No physical harm occurs.
Relational aggression
Correct: harming someone through social exclusion and reputation damage.
Prosocial behavior
The behavior harms rather than helps.
questions.x: Relational aggression harms others by damaging their social relationships or status, through rumors, gossip or exclusion. Spreading rumors to push a classmate out of a social circle is a direct example. Physical aggression is ruled out because no one is hurt bodily, and the behavior is clearly harmful rather than prosocial.

questions.q: In the Strange Situation, an infant is upset when the mother leaves, greets her warmly when she returns and is quickly soothed. This infant is classified as:
o: Avoidant
Avoidant infants show little distress and ignore the caregiver on return.
Ambivalent
Ambivalent infants are hard to soothe and resist comfort.
Disorganized
Disorganized infants show confused, contradictory behavior.
Securely attached
Correct: secure infants use the caregiver as a secure base and are easily comforted.
questions.x: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation, securely attached infants use the caregiver as a secure base, show distress at separation, greet the caregiver on return and are soothed quickly. Ambivalent infants are also distressed, but they resist comfort and are hard to soothe, and avoidant infants show little distress and ignore the caregiver on reunion.

questions.q: An infant shows little distress when the caregiver leaves and turns away when she returns. Which caregiving pattern is most associated with this attachment style?
o: Consistently sensitive and responsive care
That pattern predicts secure attachment.
Inconsistent, unpredictable responsiveness
That pattern predicts ambivalent attachment.
Consistently unresponsive or rejecting care
Correct: avoidant attachment is linked to caregivers who rebuff bids for comfort.
Frightening or abusive care
That pattern predicts disorganized attachment.
questions.x: Avoidant attachment, marked by little distress at separation and avoidance at reunion, is associated with caregivers who are consistently unresponsive or rejecting of the infant's bids for comfort. The infant learns that seeking comfort does not work. Inconsistent responsiveness is the tempting choice, but it predicts ambivalent attachment instead.

questions.q: An infant becomes extremely distressed when the caregiver leaves and, upon reunion, clings to her while also pushing her away. This describes:
o: Secure attachment
Secure infants are readily comforted.
Avoidant attachment
Avoidant infants show little distress.
Disorganized attachment
Disorganized infants show freezing or confused behavior, not this pattern.
Ambivalent (resistant) attachment
Correct: seeking and resisting comfort at once is ambivalent attachment.
questions.x: Ambivalent (resistant) attachment is shown by infants who are very distressed at separation and, on reunion, both seek contact and resist it, often angrily, and are hard to soothe. It is linked to inconsistent caregiving. Disorganized attachment is tempting, but it is defined by the lack of any coherent strategy, such as freezing or contradictory approach.

questions.q: An infant freezes, approaches the caregiver while looking away, and shows no consistent strategy for seeking comfort. This pattern is most strongly associated with:
o: Secure attachment linked to sensitive care
Secure infants show a coherent comfort-seeking strategy.
Disorganized attachment linked to frightening or abusive care
Correct: disorganized attachment often follows maltreatment.
Avoidant attachment linked to rejecting care
Avoidant infants show a consistent strategy of avoidance.
Ambivalent attachment linked to inconsistent care
Ambivalent infants show a consistent, if anxious, strategy.
questions.x: Disorganized attachment is marked by contradictory, confused behavior, such as freezing or approaching while looking away, with no consistent strategy for getting comfort. It is most strongly linked to frightening or abusive caregiving, where the caregiver is both the source of fear and of comfort. Ambivalent infants, though anxious, still show a consistent strategy.

questions.q: Infant monkeys raised with a wire mother that provided milk and a cloth mother that provided none spent most of their time clinging to the cloth mother. This finding most directly challenged the idea that:
o: Attachment forms mainly because caregivers provide food
Correct: contact comfort, not feeding, drove attachment.
Infants need any contact at all
The monkeys strongly sought contact.
Attachment is influenced by touch
The results support the importance of touch.
Monkeys can form attachments
The monkeys clearly formed attachments.
questions.x: Harlow's experiments showed that infant monkeys preferred a cloth surrogate that provided contact comfort over a wire surrogate that provided milk. This challenged the view that attachment forms mainly because caregivers satisfy hunger. The results support, rather than challenge, the importance of touch in attachment.

questions.q: A toddler at a playground ventures off to explore but periodically returns to her father before exploring again. Bowlby would describe the father as functioning as a:
o: Reference group
Reference groups provide standards of comparison.
Back stage
Back stage is a dramaturgical concept.
Weak tie
Weak ties are acquaintances in a network.
Secure base
Correct: a secure base supports confident exploration.
questions.x: Bowlby and Ainsworth described the attachment figure as a secure base from which a child can explore the world, returning periodically for reassurance before exploring again. This pattern is a hallmark of secure attachment. The other options are sociological concepts about groups and networks, not attachment.

questions.q: Newly hatched goslings follow the first moving object they see during a brief period after hatching. This phenomenon demonstrates:
o: Operant conditioning
No reinforcement shapes the behavior.
Kin selection
The goslings follow any moving object, not specifically kin.
Imprinting during a critical period
Correct: the attachment forms only within a limited developmental window.
Secure attachment
Imprinting is a rapid, fixed process rather than a Strange Situation classification.
questions.x: Imprinting, studied by Lorenz, is a rapid form of learning in which young animals form an attachment to the first moving object they see, but only during a brief critical period after hatching. It does not require reinforcement, which rules out operant conditioning. Goslings will follow a person or even an object, showing the attachment is not specific to kin.

questions.q: Which is the best example of altruism?
o: Donating a kidney to a stranger with no expectation of reward
Correct: altruism benefits others at personal cost without expected return.
Helping a coworker so she will cover your shift later
Expecting repayment makes this reciprocal or self-interested.
Volunteering only to strengthen a résumé
Expected personal benefit is the motive.
Buying a gift to win a contest
This is self-interested behavior.
questions.x: Altruism is helping that benefits another at a cost to oneself, without expectation of reward or repayment. Donating a kidney to a stranger fits this definition. Helping a coworker in hopes she will cover your shift involves expected repayment, so it is reciprocal or self-interested rather than purely altruistic.

questions.q: According to Hamilton's rule (rB > C), helping a full sibling (r = 0.5) is favored by natural selection when the benefit to the sibling is:
o: Greater than the cost to the helper
This would apply only if r = 1, as in identical twins.
Greater than twice the cost to the helper
Correct: 0.5 × B > C means B > 2C.
Greater than half the cost to the helper
This reverses the relationship between r and B.
Greater than four times the cost
This corresponds to r = 0.25, such as a half sibling.
questions.note: Hamilton's rule: the more distant the relative, the larger B must be.
questions.x: Hamilton's rule says helping is favored when rB > C, where r is relatedness, B the benefit to the recipient and C the cost to the helper. For full siblings, r = 0.5, so 0.5B > C, meaning B > 2C. The more distant the relative, the larger the benefit must be; for a half sibling (r = 0.25), B must exceed 4C.

questions.q: Vampire bats regurgitate blood to roost-mates who failed to feed, and they share most often with bats that previously shared with them. This best illustrates:
o: Reciprocal altruism
Correct: helping is exchanged over time between individuals who interact repeatedly.
Kin selection only
Sharing tracks past help, not just relatedness.
Instrumental aggression
No aggression occurs.
Imprinting
Imprinting is early attachment, not food sharing.
questions.x: Reciprocal altruism, proposed by Trivers, is helping a non-relative at a cost with the expectation that the favor will be returned later; it works among individuals who interact repeatedly and can recognize each other. Vampire bats preferentially share blood with those who shared with them before. Kin selection alone cannot explain sharing that tracks past help rather than relatedness.

questions.q: Participants who felt high empathy for a struggling student helped her even when they could easily leave without helping. Low-empathy participants helped mainly when leaving was difficult. These results best support:
o: The negative-state relief model
That model predicts helping to relieve one's own distress, which easy escape would also do.
The empathy-altruism hypothesis
Correct: empathic concern produced helping even when escape was easy.
Kin selection
The student was not related to participants.
The frustration-aggression hypothesis
This explains aggression, not helping.
questions.x: Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis predicts that empathic concern produces genuinely altruistic helping, so high-empathy people help even when escape is easy. Low-empathy people help mainly when escape is hard, consistent with egoistic motives like reducing their own discomfort. The egoistic account is the tempting one, but it predicts that easy escape would reduce helping for everyone.

questions.q: In repeated prisoner's dilemma games, a strategy that cooperates on the first move and then copies the partner's previous move tends to do well. This strategy:
o: Always defects to maximize payoff
Tit-for-tat begins by cooperating.
Is the hawk strategy in hawk-dove games
Hawk always escalates, unlike tit-for-tat.
Depends on kinship to succeed
Tit-for-tat works among unrelated individuals.
Is tit-for-tat, which helps explain how reciprocal altruism can evolve
Correct: it rewards cooperation and punishes defection.
questions.x: Tit-for-tat cooperates on the first move and then copies the partner's previous move. In repeated prisoner's dilemma tournaments it performs well because it rewards cooperation, punishes defection immediately and forgives once the partner cooperates. This shows how reciprocal altruism can evolve among unrelated individuals without any reliance on kinship.

questions.q: In a hawk-dove model, a population of all doves can be invaded by a hawk mutant, and a population of all hawks can be invaded by doves. What does game theory predict?
o: All doves at equilibrium
An all-dove population is invaded by hawks.
All hawks at equilibrium
An all-hawk population is invaded by doves.
A stable mix of hawk and dove strategies
Correct: when neither pure strategy resists invasion, a mixed equilibrium is evolutionarily stable.
Extinction of both strategies
Invasion produces a mix, not extinction.
questions.x: An evolutionarily stable strategy is one that cannot be invaded by an alternative strategy. In the hawk-dove game, hawks do well in a population of doves and doves do well among hawks, so neither pure strategy is stable. The predicted outcome is a stable mixture of hawks and doves, with frequencies set by the costs of fighting and the value of the resource.

questions.q: A friend drives a patient to every chemotherapy appointment. This is an example of which type of social support?
o: Tangible (instrumental) support
Correct: practical help like rides or money is tangible support.
Emotional support
Emotional support conveys caring and empathy.
Informational support
Informational support provides advice or information.
Esteem support
Esteem support bolsters a person's sense of competence.
questions.x: Social support comes in several forms: emotional (caring and empathy), tangible or instrumental (practical help such as rides, money or chores), informational (advice and guidance) and esteem (boosting confidence). Driving someone to treatment is practical aid, so it is tangible support, even though it likely also conveys care.

questions.q: A support-group member explains to a newly diagnosed patient how to appeal an insurance denial. This is primarily:
o: Tangible support
No material aid or service is provided.
Emotional support
The help is practical guidance, not empathy.
Companionship support
Companionship involves shared activities and belonging.
Informational support
Correct: providing advice and guidance is informational support.
questions.x: Informational support is providing advice, guidance or knowledge that helps someone cope, such as explaining how to appeal an insurance denial. Tangible support would involve doing the task or providing material help directly. Emotional support conveys empathy and caring rather than practical know-how.

questions.q: Researchers find that social support predicts better health among people facing major life stressors but has little effect among people with low stress. These data best support:
o: The direct (main) effect hypothesis
A main effect would predict benefits at all stress levels.
The frustration-aggression hypothesis
This hypothesis concerns aggression, not health.
The buffering hypothesis
Correct: support protects mainly by cushioning the effects of stress.
The iron law of oligarchy
This concerns organizational power.
questions.note: Buffering = an interaction; main effect = benefit regardless of stress.
questions.x: The buffering hypothesis states that social support protects health mainly by cushioning the effects of stress, so its benefits show up chiefly among people under high stress. That is an interaction between stress and support. The direct (main) effect hypothesis instead predicts that support improves health at all stress levels, which these data contradict.

questions.q: Studies comparing perceived and received social support usually find that well-being is more strongly predicted by:
o: Received support, counted as the number of helping acts
Received support relates less consistently to well-being.
Perceived support, the belief that help is available
Correct: perceived availability shows stronger links to well-being than actual help received.
Network size alone
Size matters less than perceived quality.
The number of secondary groups a person belongs to
Group count is a weak proxy for support.
questions.x: Perceived social support, the belief that help would be available if needed, is generally a stronger and more consistent predictor of well-being than received support, the actual helping acts counted. Receiving lots of help can even signal that someone is struggling, which muddies its link to well-being. Network size and group counts are weaker proxies for quality.

questions.q: Under stress, women on average are more likely than men to seek out others and care for dependents. This pattern, linked to oxytocin, is called:
o: Tend-and-befriend
Correct: affiliating and nurturing is an alternative stress response.
Fight-or-flight
Fight-or-flight involves confronting or escaping a threat.
Learned helplessness
Learned helplessness involves passivity after uncontrollable events.
Displaced aggression
Displaced aggression redirects hostility.
questions.x: Taylor's tend-and-befriend model proposes that under stress, women on average are more likely to protect and nurture offspring and seek social affiliation, a pattern linked to oxytocin. It is presented as a complement to the fight-or-flight response, which involves confronting or escaping the threat.

questions.q: Optimal foraging theory predicts that a bird choosing between two food patches will prefer the one that:
o: Is closest regardless of food quality
Distance matters only as part of the net energy calculation.
Yields the greatest net energy per unit time
Correct: animals maximize energy gained minus energy spent, per time.
Has the largest single food item
Large items may cost too much to handle.
Other birds avoid
Avoidance by others is not the core prediction.
questions.x: Optimal foraging theory predicts that animals choose food sources that maximize net energy gain per unit time, that is, energy obtained minus energy spent searching and handling, divided by time. A nearby patch or a large item is not automatically best if it yields less net energy. The theory ties foraging decisions directly to fitness.

questions.q: In a species where one male mates with several females in a breeding season while each female mates with only him, the mating system is:
o: Polyandry
Polyandry is one female with multiple males.
Monogamy
Monogamy is one male with one female.
Promiscuity
Promiscuity involves both sexes mating with multiple partners.
Polygyny
Correct: polygyny is one male with multiple females.
questions.x: Mating systems are classified by how many partners each sex has. Polygyny is one male mating with multiple females; polyandry is one female with multiple males; monogamy is one male with one female; promiscuity is both sexes mating with multiple partners. A male with several females, each of whom mates only with him, is polygyny.

questions.q: Male elk battle each other with antlers for access to females. This is an example of:
o: Intersexual selection
Intersexual selection involves one sex choosing among the other.
Kin selection
The behavior does not help relatives.
Intrasexual selection
Correct: members of the same sex compete for mates.
Reciprocal altruism
Fighting is competition, not cooperation.
questions.x: Sexual selection has two forms. Intrasexual selection is competition among members of the same sex for access to mates, as when male elk fight with antlers. Intersexual selection is mate choice by one sex based on traits of the other, as with females choosing colorful males. Combat between rivals is clearly the intrasexual form.

questions.q: In pipefish, males carry and nourish the eggs, and females compete for males while males are choosy. This best supports which idea?
o: The sex that invests more in offspring tends to be choosier
Correct: parental investment, not biological sex itself, predicts choosiness.
Males are always the competitive sex
Pipefish show that females can be the competing sex.
Mating behavior is unrelated to parental care
The reversal tracks the reversal in care.
Females always invest more in offspring
Here males invest more.
questions.note: Trivers: higher investment → more selective.
questions.x: Trivers' parental investment theory predicts that the sex investing more in each offspring will be choosier about mates, while the sex investing less competes for access. In most species females invest more, but in pipefish males brood the eggs, and the roles reverse. This shows investment, not sex itself, drives choosiness.

questions.q: A female bird chooses a mate with bright plumage that signals parasite resistance, though he provides no food or nest. She gains:
o: Direct material benefits
Direct benefits include food, territory or care, which he does not provide.
Benefits from kin selection
Her mate is not her relative.
Indirect genetic benefits for her offspring
Correct: good genes passed to offspring are indirect benefits.
Benefits from reciprocal altruism
No exchange of favors over time is described.
questions.x: Mate choice can yield direct benefits, such as food, territory or parental care for the chooser, or indirect benefits, which are good genes passed to offspring. Bright plumage that signals parasite resistance, from a male that provides nothing else, offers only genetic quality for her young. Direct benefits are ruled out because he provides no resources.

questions.q: Prairie voles form lasting pair bonds, but blocking oxytocin and vasopressin receptors in their brains prevents bonding. This suggests that pair bonding:
o: Is purely learned
A biological manipulation altered the behavior.
Has a neurochemical basis
Correct: disrupting these hormones' signaling disrupts bonding.
Depends on testosterone alone
Oxytocin and vasopressin, not testosterone, were manipulated.
Is unrelated to brain receptors
Blocking receptors changed behavior.
questions.x: Prairie voles form lifelong pair bonds, and blocking oxytocin and vasopressin receptors in the brain prevents those bonds from forming. This shows pair bonding depends on specific neurochemical systems. A purely learned explanation is ruled out because a biological manipulation altered the behavior.

questions.q: Meerkat sentinels give alarm calls that warn the group but may draw a predator's attention. Because group members are often close relatives, this behavior is best explained by:
o: Intrasexual selection
No competition for mates is involved.
Optimal foraging
The behavior concerns predator warning, not feeding.
The halo effect
This is a human social-cognition bias.
Kin selection increasing inclusive fitness
Correct: helping relatives spreads shared genes even at personal risk.
questions.x: Kin selection explains helping relatives at a cost to oneself because relatives share genes, so aiding their survival can increase the helper's inclusive fitness. Alarm calls that risk attracting a predator but warn close kin fit this. Intrasexual selection and optimal foraging address mating competition and feeding, not warning others.

questions.q: Which best distinguishes prejudice from discrimination?
o: Prejudice is an action; discrimination is an attitude
This reverses the definitions.
Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is an action
Correct: prejudice is a negative feeling or belief; discrimination is unequal treatment.
Both are only institutional
Both can occur at the individual level.
Discrimination requires prejudice
Discrimination can occur without prejudice, such as through biased policies.
questions.x: Prejudice is an attitude, a negative belief or feeling toward a group, while discrimination is a behavior, unequal treatment of people based on group membership. The two can occur independently: someone can be prejudiced without acting on it, and discrimination can occur through policies without individual prejudice.

questions.q: A fire department requires all applicants to be at least 5′10″ tall, a rule that excludes most women regardless of ability. This is best described as:
o: Individual discrimination
No single person is acting on personal bias.
Prejudice
Prejudice is an attitude, not a policy.
Institutional discrimination
Correct: an organizational policy disadvantages a group without individual intent.
Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat concerns performance anxiety.
questions.note: Institutional: built into rules and practices.
questions.x: Institutional discrimination is unequal treatment built into an organization's rules or practices, which can disadvantage a group even when no individual intends harm. A height requirement that excludes most women regardless of ability works this way. It is not prejudice, which is an attitude, nor individual discrimination, which is one person acting on bias.

questions.q: Which scenario is an example of individual rather than institutional discrimination?
o: A manager personally skips over résumés with names suggesting a particular ethnicity
Correct: one person acts on bias in a specific decision.
A bank's lending rules deny loans in historically segregated neighborhoods
This is embedded in organizational policy.
A school funding formula tied to local property taxes
This is a structural policy.
Seniority-based layoffs that affect recently hired groups
This is a structural practice.
questions.x: Individual discrimination is a specific person treating others unequally based on group membership, such as a manager skipping résumés with certain names. Institutional discrimination is embedded in policies and structures, like lending rules, funding formulas or seniority-based layoffs, and can disadvantage groups without any individual bias.

questions.q: A participant reports no negative feelings toward older adults, but on an Implicit Association Test responds faster when pairing "old" with negative words. This result best indicates:
o: Explicit prejudice
She explicitly denies negative attitudes.
Institutional discrimination
No organizational policy is involved.
Individual discrimination
No discriminatory behavior was observed.
Implicit bias that may differ from explicit attitudes
