Correct: automatic associations can exist without consciously endorsed prejudice.
questions.x: The Implicit Association Test measures automatic associations by how quickly people pair concepts. Faster pairing of old with negative words indicates an implicit bias, even though she reports no negative feelings. Explicit and implicit attitudes can diverge, and an IAT result does not by itself show discriminatory behavior.

questions.q: A shop owner holds no personal prejudice but refuses to hire members of a minority group because he fears customers will object. In Merton's typology, he is a:
o: All-weather liberal
All-weather liberals neither hold prejudice nor discriminate.
Timid bigot
Timid bigots are prejudiced but do not discriminate.
Active bigot
Active bigots are prejudiced and discriminate.
Fair-weather liberal (unprejudiced discriminator)
Correct: he discriminates without holding prejudice, due to social pressure.
questions.x: Merton cross-classified prejudice and discrimination: the all-weather liberal is unprejudiced and does not discriminate, the fair-weather liberal is unprejudiced but discriminates under social pressure, the timid bigot is prejudiced but does not discriminate, and the active bigot is prejudiced and discriminates. The shop owner discriminates without prejudice, so he is a fair-weather liberal.

questions.q: A company that excluded women for decades now lays off workers by seniority, so women are disproportionately let go. This is best described as:
o: Past-in-present discrimination
Correct: a neutral-seeming practice perpetuates the effects of earlier discrimination.
Individual discrimination
No individual is acting on personal bias now.
Implicit bias
The disparity arises from policy, not automatic associations.
Prejudice
Prejudice is an attitude, not a layoff policy.
questions.x: Past-in-present discrimination occurs when a seemingly neutral practice carries forward the effects of earlier discrimination. Because women were excluded for decades, they have less seniority, so seniority-based layoffs hit them hardest. Individual discrimination is ruled out because no one is acting on bias now; the disparity comes from the policy.

questions.q: Groups with greater power, prestige and wealth are often better able to discriminate against others because they:
o: Hold more prejudice than other groups
Discrimination depends on power to act, not only on attitudes.
Control institutions and resources that shape opportunities
Correct: control over hiring, laws and resources lets dominant groups enact discrimination.
Are always smaller in number
Dominance depends on power, not size.
Lack any in-group bias
Dominant groups show in-group bias too.
questions.x: Discrimination requires the power to act on bias. Groups with more power, prestige and wealth control institutions such as employers, courts and lawmakers, so they can shape opportunities for others. Prejudice can exist in any group, so the key difference is power, not greater prejudice.

questions.q: A researcher visited many restaurants with a couple from a minority group and was refused service only once, yet most owners later replied by mail that they would refuse such customers. This finding best shows that:
o: Discrimination always follows prejudice
Owners expressed prejudice but mostly did not discriminate.
Institutional discrimination was absent
The study measured individual owners' behavior, not policies.
Stated prejudice does not always predict discriminatory behavior
Correct: attitudes reported by mail did not match actual treatment.
Implicit bias drove the refusals
Implicit associations were not measured.
questions.x: LaPiere's study found that restaurants and hotels almost always served a traveling couple from a minority group, yet most later said by mail that they would refuse such customers. This shows that stated attitudes do not always predict behavior. The finding contradicts the idea that discrimination always follows prejudice.

questions.q: Why do sociologists distinguish between sex and gender?
o: Sex is socially constructed; gender is fixed by chromosomes
This reverses the two terms.
The two terms are interchangeable in sociological research
Sociologists deliberately separate them because they can vary independently.
Gender refers only to legal status on official documents
Legal markers are one expression of gender, not its definition.
Sex refers to biological traits; gender refers to socially constructed roles and identities
Correct: sex is anatomical and physiological, while gender reflects cultural expectations and self-identity.
questions.note: Sex = biology; gender = social roles, norms and identity.
questions.x: Sex refers to biological attributes such as chromosomes, hormones and anatomy, while gender refers to the roles, norms and identities a society attaches to being a man or woman. Keeping them separate lets researchers see that gender expectations vary across cultures and over time even when biology does not. The tempting reversal gets it backwards: biology is the 'sex' side, culture the 'gender' side.

questions.q: Which observation most strongly supports the view that race is a social construct?
o: People of different races can have different average heights
Group averages in some traits do not show that the categories themselves are biologically defined.
Skin pigmentation is influenced by melanin production
A biological basis for skin color does not make racial categories biological.
Some diseases are more common in certain geographic ancestries
Ancestry-linked variation exists but does not map neatly onto socially defined races.
The racial categories on a national census have been redefined several times over a century
Correct: categories that shift with politics and convention reflect social, not biological, boundaries.
questions.x: A social construct is a category whose boundaries are set by human agreement rather than by nature. If census racial categories are redrawn every few decades, the categories must be tracking politics and convention, not fixed biology. Trait differences such as pigmentation or disease frequency are real biological variation, but they do not show that the racial boxes themselves are natural divisions.

questions.q: In the 19th-century United States, Irish immigrants were often described as a separate, inferior 'race,' a label later dropped as they were absorbed into the category 'white.' This illustrates:
o: Amalgamation
Amalgamation is the blending of groups into a new culture, not the assigning of racial labels.
Racialization
Correct: racial meaning was assigned to a group that had not been defined that way, then later withdrawn.
Symbolic ethnicity
Symbolic ethnicity is a voluntary, low-cost attachment to heritage, not an imposed racial label.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism means judging cultures by their own standards, unrelated to racial labeling.
questions.note: Racialization: attaching racial meaning to a group, often to justify unequal treatment.
questions.x: Racialization is the process of attaching racial meaning to a group that was not previously defined that way, usually to justify unequal treatment. Irish immigrants were labeled a separate inferior race and later folded into 'white,' showing the label was socially assigned and changeable. Amalgamation is tempting because groups mixed, but it describes cultural blending into something new, not the assignment of racial status.

questions.q: Compared with race, ethnicity is defined mainly by:
o: Perceived physical characteristics such as skin color
That describes how race is typically assigned.
Measured genetic differences between populations
Neither race nor ethnicity is defined by genetic testing.
Shared culture, language, ancestry, or national origin
Correct: ethnicity centers on cultural heritage rather than perceived physical traits.
Legal citizenship status
Citizenship is a legal status, separate from ethnic identity.
questions.x: Ethnicity rests on shared culture: language, religion, ancestry, customs and national origin. Race, by contrast, is assigned mainly on perceived physical traits such as skin color. Neither concept is defined by genetic testing, which rules out the tempting 'measured genetic differences' option, and citizenship is a legal status separate from either.

questions.q: A researcher follows everyone born in a city between 1990 and 1994 to study their employment over time. This group is best described as a:
o: Reference group
A reference group is one people compare themselves to, not a sampling unit by birth year.
Birth cohort
Correct: a cohort is a group sharing a defining event in the same time period, here birth years.
Dependent population
Dependents are people under 15 or over 64, not a group defined by birth period.
Primary group
A primary group is a small, intimate group like a family.
questions.x: A cohort is a group of people who share a defining experience during the same time period; a birth cohort shares birth years. Following a cohort over time lets researchers see how a generation's life course unfolds. A reference group is tempting only because it is also a 'group,' but it refers to whom people compare themselves with, not a sampling unit.

questions.q: A 2005 survey finds adults over 60 use social media far less than adults under 30. Following the same people to 2025, researchers find the older group's use barely changed, while the 2005 under-30 group, now middle-aged, still uses it heavily. The 2005 gap mainly reflected a(n):
o: Cohort effect
Correct: the difference tracked the generation people were born into, not their age at the time.
Age effect
If aging caused it, the 2005 younger adults would have reduced their use as they aged.
Period effect
A period effect would shift all age groups together at one point in time.
Hawthorne effect
The Hawthorne effect is behavior change from being observed, unrelated here.
questions.note: Cohort = generation; age = life stage; period = historical moment affecting everyone.
questions.x: A cohort effect is a difference rooted in when people were born, so it travels with a generation as it ages. Here each group kept its habits over 20 years, so the gap reflected generational experience, not age. An age effect would require people to change as they grow older, so the younger group would have cut back by midlife, which did not happen.

questions.q: After a severe economic recession, reported financial anxiety rose sharply among teenagers, middle-aged adults and retirees alike, then fell as the economy recovered. This pattern is best explained as a(n):
o: Cohort effect
A cohort effect would affect one generation and persist as it aged.
Period effect
Correct: one historical event shifted all age groups at the same time.
Age effect
An age effect would appear at a particular life stage regardless of the year.
Selection effect
Selection bias concerns who enters a sample, not a shared historical shift.
questions.x: A period effect is a change caused by a historical event that hits all age groups at roughly the same time, then fades or persists for everyone. A recession raising anxiety in teens, adults and retirees alike, then easing with recovery, fits exactly. A cohort effect would instead mark one generation and follow it through life, not move every age group together.

questions.q: In every generation studied, voter turnout rises as individuals move from their early 20s into their 50s. This consistent pattern is best described as a(n):
o: Age (life-course) effect
Correct: the change accompanies a life stage and repeats across cohorts.
Cohort effect
A cohort effect would distinguish generations, but here all generations follow the same path.
Period effect
A period effect would be tied to a specific year, not to age.
Ecological fallacy
That is an inference error about individuals from group data, not a temporal pattern.
questions.x: An age or life-course effect is a change tied to a life stage that repeats in every generation. Because turnout rises from the 20s to the 50s in each cohort studied, the pattern tracks aging itself, through things like settling down, owning property and community ties. A cohort effect would show generations differing from each other, which is the opposite of what is described.

questions.q: A country has 30 million people under 15, 10 million over 65 and 80 million aged 15 to 64. What is its total dependency ratio?
o: Correct: (30 + 10) / 80 × 100 = 50 dependents per 100 working-age people.
Divides dependents by the total population (40/120) instead of by working-age adults.
Uses only the youth group (30/80), omitting older dependents.
Uses only the older group (10/80), omitting youth dependents.
questions.note: Dependency ratio = (under 15 + over 64) / (15–64) × 100.
questions.x: The total dependency ratio compares people of non-working age (under 15 plus 65 and older) with the working-age population (15 to 64), expressed per 100. Here (30 + 10) / 80 × 100 = 50. The common error is dividing by the whole population (40/120 ≈ 33), but the denominator is only the working-age group that must support dependents.

questions.q: Which combination of trends most directly produces population aging?
o: Rising fertility and falling life expectancy
Both trends would make the population younger.
Rising fertility and rising life expectancy
High fertility keeps adding to the young share, offsetting aging.
Falling fertility and rising life expectancy
Correct: fewer births shrink the young share while longer lives enlarge the old share.
High infant mortality and high fertility
This is the pattern of young, pre-transition populations.
questions.x: Population aging means the older share of the population grows. Falling fertility shrinks the youngest age groups, and longer life expectancy enlarges the oldest groups, so both push the age structure upward. Rising life expectancy alone is tempting, but if fertility stays high, a large flow of births keeps the population young.

questions.q: A country records about 120 male births for every 100 female births. The most likely explanation is:
o: Higher male mortality in infancy
Higher male infant mortality would lower, not raise, the ratio of boys.
Emigration of young women
Emigration affects adult sex ratios, not the ratio at birth.
Normal biological variation in human births
Natural variation stays near 105 boys per 100 girls.
Son preference combined with sex-selective practices
Correct: the natural ratio is about 105; large excesses usually reflect sex-selective abortion or neglect.
questions.note: Sex ratio at birth ≈ 105; far above that signals sex selection.
questions.x: Human populations naturally produce about 105 male births per 100 female births. A ratio near 120 is far outside natural variation and is the signature of son preference combined with sex-selective abortion or neglect of girls. Emigration or male infant mortality are tempting, but they change sex ratios after birth, not the ratio at birth itself.

questions.q: In most countries, women outnumber men among people over 80. This mainly reflects:
o: A sex ratio at birth that favors girls
Slightly more boys than girls are born.
Higher male mortality at nearly every age
Correct: men die at higher rates across the life course, so women predominate at old ages.
Greater female immigration in late life
Late-life migration is too small to drive this pattern.
Undercounting of older women in censuses
Undercounting would hide women, not make them appear more numerous.
questions.note: Older populations are feminized because male mortality is higher.
questions.x: Although slightly more boys are born, men have higher death rates at nearly every age because of biology, riskier behavior, occupational hazards and health habits. These small differences accumulate, so women make up a growing majority at older ages. A girl-favoring birth ratio is the tempting distractor, but the birth ratio actually favors boys.

questions.q: Undocumented immigrants in a city avoid public clinics even when ill, fearing contact with authorities. This best illustrates how immigration status:
o: Shapes access to health care independent of medical need
Correct: legal status affects whether people seek available care.
Is unrelated to health outcomes
The scenario shows status directly changing care-seeking.
Primarily affects health through genetic differences
Immigration status is a legal category with no genetic basis.
Matters only for people without health insurance
Fear of authorities deters care regardless of insurance.
questions.x: Health care access depends not only on medical need and insurance but on legal and social conditions that shape whether people seek care. Fear of immigration enforcement keeps undocumented people away from clinics even when services are available. Insurance status is the tempting explanation, but the fear operates regardless of coverage, so status itself is the barrier.

questions.q: Recently arrived immigrants often have better health than native-born residents of similar income, but this advantage fades the longer they stay. This is called the:
o: Brain drain
Brain drain is the emigration of skilled workers, not a health pattern.
Demographic dividend
That is economic growth from a large working-age share.
Healthy immigrant effect
Correct: migrants are often healthier on arrival, with the edge eroding over time.
Epidemiologic transition
That is a society-wide shift from infectious to chronic disease.
questions.x: The healthy immigrant effect describes newly arrived immigrants being healthier than native-born residents of similar income, partly because healthier people are more likely to migrate and pass screening. Over time, acculturation to local diets, stress and discrimination erode the advantage. Brain drain is a migration term too, but it concerns loss of skilled workers, not health.

questions.q: A study finds that U.S.-born children of immigrants have higher obesity rates than their foreign-born parents despite higher incomes. Which explanation best fits this finding?
o: Adoption of the host country's diet and activity patterns through acculturation
Correct: acculturation to less healthy local habits can erode the first generation's health advantage.
Higher income directly causes obesity
Income generally predicts better, not worse, health; something else must explain the reversal.
Selective emigration of the least healthy parents
Migrant selection usually favors healthier people, which would not explain the children's decline.
Genetic drift between generations
One generation is far too short for genetic drift to explain a population trend.
questions.note: The 'immigrant paradox' often reverses with acculturation.
questions.x: Acculturation means adopting the host culture's practices, including diet and activity patterns. Children raised in the host country take up local eating and sedentary habits more fully than their immigrant parents, so the parents' health advantage fades despite rising income. Income is the tempting explanation, but higher income usually predicts better health, so it cannot explain a decline.

questions.q: In sociological research, sexual orientation refers to:
o: A person's internal sense of their own gender
That is gender identity, a separate concept.
The sex a person was assigned at birth
Assigned sex is a biological or medical classification.
A person's enduring pattern of romantic or sexual attraction
Correct: orientation concerns whom one is attracted to.
How a person expresses gender through clothing and behavior
That is gender expression.
questions.x: Sexual orientation describes a person's enduring pattern of romantic or sexual attraction, that is, whom they are drawn to. It is distinct from gender identity (one's internal sense of being a man, woman or another gender) and from gender expression (outward presentation). Confusing orientation with gender identity is the most common error, but they describe different dimensions.

questions.q: Lesbian, gay and bisexual adults show higher average rates of depression than heterosexual adults. The minority stress model attributes this mainly to:
o: Chronic stress from stigma, prejudice and discrimination
Correct: the model locates the cause in hostile social conditions, not orientation itself.
An inherent link between orientation and mental illness
The model explicitly rejects orientation itself as the cause.
Lower average income in all sexual-minority groups
Income may contribute, but the model centers on stigma-related stress.
Overreporting of symptoms by survey respondents
The model treats the disparity as real, not as a measurement artifact.
questions.x: The minority stress model holds that stigmatized groups face chronic, additional stressors such as discrimination, rejection, concealment and internalized stigma, and these stressors raise rates of depression and anxiety. The cause lies in hostile social conditions, not in orientation itself. Income may contribute to disparities, but the model's central mechanism is stigma-related stress.

questions.q: A qualified 62-year-old applicant is passed over because the manager assumes older workers cannot learn new software. This is an example of:
o: Sexism
Nothing in the scenario concerns sex or gender.
Institutional racism
The bias is about age, not race.
Role strain
Role strain is tension within one role's demands.
Ageism
Correct: prejudice or discrimination based on age.
questions.x: Ageism is prejudice or discrimination based on age, often rooted in stereotypes such as the belief that older people cannot learn new skills. Here the manager acts on a stereotype rather than the applicant's actual qualifications. Role strain is unrelated, describing tension among the demands of a single role a person holds.

questions.q: A researcher argues that the workplace discrimination faced by Black women cannot be understood by simply adding the effects of racism and sexism. This argument reflects:
o: Cultural capital
Cultural capital concerns non-financial assets such as education and taste.
Social reproduction
Social reproduction is the transmission of inequality across generations.
Ethnocentrism
Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by one's own standards.
Intersectionality
Correct: overlapping identities create distinct, not merely additive, experiences of disadvantage.
questions.x: Intersectionality holds that social identities such as race, gender and class combine to create distinct experiences of advantage or disadvantage that are not just the sum of each separately. A Black woman may face stereotypes that neither white women nor Black men face. Social reproduction is tempting because it concerns inequality, but it describes transmission across generations, not overlapping identities.

questions.q: Many recent immigrants from one country settle in a single neighborhood with shops, newspapers and places of worship in their native language. This neighborhood is an example of a(n):
o: Gentrified district
Gentrification is the influx of wealthier residents, not immigrant clustering.
Megalopolis
A megalopolis is a chain of merged metropolitan areas.
Ethnic enclave
Correct: a spatial concentration of an ethnic group with its own institutions.
Suburb
A suburb is a residential area outside a city center, not defined by ethnicity.
questions.x: An ethnic enclave is a neighborhood where an ethnic group is concentrated and has built its own businesses, media and institutions, often easing newcomers' adjustment. The defining features are spatial clustering plus group-specific institutions. Gentrification also changes neighborhoods, but it involves wealthier newcomers moving in and raising costs, not immigrant clustering.

questions.q: Over three generations, an immigrant family stops speaking its native language and adopts the customs of the dominant culture until its origins are no longer visible. This process is:
o: Cultural pluralism
Pluralism means groups keep distinct identities while coexisting.
Amalgamation
Amalgamation blends groups into a new culture rather than absorbing one into another.
Assimilation
Correct: a minority group is absorbed into the dominant culture, losing distinct traits.
Segregation
Segregation is physical and social separation of groups.
questions.x: Assimilation is the process by which a minority group gradually adopts the culture of the dominant group, losing its distinctive language and customs, often over several generations. The direction is one-way: A becomes like B. Amalgamation is the tempting alternative, but in amalgamation both groups blend to form a new culture rather than one being absorbed.

questions.q: A society in which several ethnic groups keep their own languages and traditions while sharing common political institutions best exemplifies:
o: Assimilation
Assimilation erases distinctions in favor of the dominant culture.
Amalgamation
Amalgamation merges groups into a single new culture.
Expulsion
Expulsion removes a group from the territory.
Cultural pluralism
Correct: distinct identities are maintained within one society.
questions.x: Cultural pluralism, or multiculturalism, describes a society in which groups retain their distinct languages and traditions while participating in shared institutions such as government and the economy. Distinctions are maintained, not erased. Assimilation is the main contrast, since it removes group differences in favor of the dominant culture.

questions.q: Two immigrant groups intermarry over generations, and their cuisines and holidays merge into a new tradition that neither group practiced before. This best illustrates:
o: Amalgamation
Correct: groups blend to form a new cultural group, the 'melting pot.'
Assimilation
In assimilation one group adopts the other's culture rather than both forming something new.
Cultural pluralism
Pluralism keeps the groups distinct.
Cultural lag
Cultural lag is the delay of non-material culture behind material change.
questions.note: Assimilation: A + B → B. Amalgamation: A + B → C. Pluralism: A + B → A + B.
questions.x: Amalgamation occurs when groups mix, often through intermarriage, and produce a new culture that differs from each original, the classic 'melting pot.' The new holiday traditions that neither group practiced before mark it as amalgamation. In assimilation one group simply adopts the other's existing culture, so nothing new is created.

questions.q: A fourth-generation Italian-American attends an annual heritage festival but otherwise sees ethnicity as having little effect on her work, friendships or neighborhood. This illustrates:
o: Racialization
Racialization imposes racial meaning on a group; nothing is imposed here.
Ethnic enclave
She does not live in an ethnic neighborhood.
Symbolic ethnicity
Correct: ethnicity is a voluntary, occasional identity with little social cost.
Segregation
There is no separation from the wider society.
questions.x: Symbolic ethnicity is a voluntary, occasional attachment to ethnic heritage, such as festivals or food, that carries little cost and little effect on daily life. It is common among later-generation descendants of European immigrants. An ethnic enclave would require living in a concentrated ethnic neighborhood, which this person does not.

questions.q: Historical U.S. laws classified anyone with any known African ancestry as Black, regardless of appearance. This 'one-drop rule' best demonstrates that:
o: Race is reliably determined by ancestry testing
No ancestry fraction biologically defines a race; the cutoff was arbitrary.
Racial categories are fixed across societies
Other societies drew the same lines quite differently.
Racial boundaries were set by social and legal convention
Correct: the rule assigned race by decree, not by any biological threshold.
Physical appearance determines racial identity
The rule ignored appearance entirely.
questions.x: The one-drop rule assigned anyone with any known African ancestry to the Black category, regardless of appearance or proportion of ancestry. Because the threshold was set by law and custom and differed from rules in other societies, it shows racial boundaries are socially constructed. It did not rely on appearance, which rules out the tempting physical-appearance option.

questions.q: Genetic studies show that most human genetic variation occurs among individuals within the same socially defined racial group rather than between groups. This finding:
o: Supports the view that racial categories are not discrete biological groupings
Correct: if most variation lies within groups, the categories capture little genetic structure.
Shows that racial groups are genetically identical
Variation within groups is large; individuals are not identical.
Proves that race has no effect on health
The finding concerns category boundaries; race can still affect health through racism and social conditions.
Shows that ethnicity is purely biological
Ethnicity is cultural, and the finding concerns race.
questions.x: Population genetics shows that most human genetic variation lies among individuals within any socially defined racial group, with relatively little separating the groups. Such categories therefore capture little genetic structure and are not discrete biological units. This does not mean people are genetically identical, nor that race is irrelevant to health, because racism and social conditions still shape health outcomes.

questions.q: A person whose gender identity differs from the sex they were assigned at birth is described as:
o: Cisgender
Cisgender means identity matches assigned sex.
Transgender
Correct: transgender describes this mismatch between identity and assigned sex.
Intersex
Intersex refers to biological sex characteristics that do not fit typical male or female categories.
Bisexual
Bisexual describes sexual orientation, not gender identity.
questions.x: Transgender describes a person whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned at birth; cisgender describes a match. Intersex is different because it concerns biological sex characteristics that do not fit typical male or female categories, not identity. Bisexual concerns sexual orientation, a separate dimension from gender identity.

questions.q: Anthropologists find that tasks considered 'women's work' in one society are considered 'men's work' in another. This most directly supports the claim that:
o: Gender roles are socially constructed
Correct: if roles reverse across cultures, they are not dictated by biology.
Sex differences are entirely cultural
Cross-cultural variation in roles says nothing about biological sex itself.
Gender roles are determined by hormones
Hormones would not produce opposite roles in different societies.
All societies divide labor equally
The finding concerns which sex does a task, not equality.
questions.x: If biology dictated which sex performs a task, the same tasks would be assigned to the same sex everywhere. Finding that 'women's work' in one society is 'men's work' in another shows that gender roles are shaped by culture. The tempting overreach is that sex differences are entirely cultural, but the evidence concerns roles, not biological sex itself.

questions.q: A sharp rise in births after a war creates a bulge on a population pyramid. Over the following decades, this bulge will:
o: Move upward through older age groups
Correct: the same large cohort ages, shifting the bulge up the pyramid.
Stay at the base of the pyramid
The base shows the newest births; the cohort leaves it as it ages.
Disappear within a single decade
A large cohort persists until its members die, many decades later.
Move downward toward younger ages
People cannot get younger; bulges only move up.
questions.x: A population pyramid stacks age groups from youngest at the bottom to oldest at the top. A baby boom adds a large cohort at the base, and as those people age, the bulge moves upward through older age bars until its members die. It cannot stay at the base, because the base always shows the most recent births.

questions.q: A country's fertility falls to replacement level, yet its population keeps growing for several more decades. The most likely reason is:
o: Replacement fertility always produces growth
Replacement fertility leads to stability once the age structure evens out.
A large young cohort is still entering its reproductive years
Correct: population momentum; many parents still produce many births even at 2.1 children each.
Mortality must be rising
Rising mortality would slow growth, not sustain it.
Crude birth rates are unaffected by age structure
Crude rates depend strongly on age structure; that is why growth continues.
questions.note: Population momentum: a young age structure keeps growth going after fertility drops.
questions.x: Population momentum is continued growth after fertility reaches replacement, because a young age structure means many people are entering childbearing ages. Even at about 2.1 children per woman, a large parent generation produces many births while deaths remain relatively few. Growth stops only once the age structure evens out over several decades.

questions.q: In populations with low mortality, replacement-level total fertility is approximately:
o: 1.0 child per woman
That would halve each generation.
2.1 children per woman
Correct: two to replace the parents, plus a little for deaths before reproductive age and the slight male excess at birth.
3.5 children per woman
That would roughly double the population per generation.
2.0 children per woman exactly
Slightly more than 2 is needed because some children die and more boys than girls are born.
questions.x: Replacement-level fertility is the average number of children per woman needed for each generation to replace itself. It is slightly above 2, about 2.1 in low-mortality populations, because some children die before reproducing and slightly more boys than girls are born. It is higher where child mortality is high, which is why exactly 2.0 is the tempting but wrong answer.

questions.q: Total fertility rate (TFR) is best defined as:
o: The number of births per 1,000 people in a year
That is the crude birth rate.
The average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime at current age-specific birth rates
Correct: TFR summarizes current fertility per woman, independent of age structure.
The number of births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 49
That is the general fertility rate.
The ratio of births to deaths in a year
That ratio is the vital index, not TFR.
questions.x: Total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have if she experienced current age-specific birth rates throughout her reproductive years. Because it is built from age-specific rates, it is not distorted by how many women are of childbearing age. The crude birth rate, births per 1,000 total population, is the tempting confusion, but it depends heavily on age structure.

questions.q: A country of 20 million people records 300,000 births in one year. What is its crude birth rate?
o: Off by a factor of 10 in converting to per 1,000.
Off by a factor of 10 in the other direction.
Divides by 10 million instead of 20 million.
questions.note: Crude rates are per 1,000 total population per year.
questions.x: The crude birth rate is births per 1,000 total population per year. Here 300,000 / 20,000,000 = 0.015, and 0.015 × 1,000 = 15 per 1,000. Most errors come from slipping a factor of 10 when converting to 'per 1,000,' so it helps to check that the answer falls in the typical range of about 8 to 45.

questions.q: A country has a crude birth rate of 25 per 1,000 and a crude death rate of 10 per 1,000, with no migration. What is its annual rate of natural increase?
o: Treats 15 per 1,000 as a percentage without dividing by 10.
Adds the birth and death rates instead of subtracting.
Ignores deaths, using only the birth rate.
questions.note: Rate of natural increase (%) = (CBR − CDR) / 10.
questions.x: The rate of natural increase is the crude birth rate minus the crude death rate, ignoring migration. Here 25 − 10 = 15 per 1,000, and because 1,000 is ten times 100, dividing by 10 gives 1.5%. The tempting error is reading 15 per 1,000 directly as 15%, which overstates growth tenfold.

questions.q: A country has a crude birth rate of 12, a crude death rate of 9 and a net migration rate of +5, all per 1,000. What is its overall annual growth rate?
o: Natural increase only; ignores net migration.
Adds all three rates instead of subtracting deaths.
Subtracts migration instead of adding it.
questions.note: Growth = births − deaths + net migration.
questions.x: Overall population growth combines natural increase with net migration: births minus deaths plus net migration. Here 12 − 9 + 5 = 8 per 1,000, which is 0.8%. Stopping at natural increase (0.3%) is the tempting error, since it ignores that net in-migration adds to the population just as births do.

questions.q: A population is growing at a steady 2% per year. Approximately how long will it take to double?
o: 50 years
Divides 100 by 2, ignoring compounding.
35 years
Correct: rule of 70; 70 / 2 = 35 years.
20 years
Too short: 20 years at 2% compounds to only about 1.5 times the original size.
140 years
Multiplies 70 by 2 instead of dividing.
questions.note: Doubling time ≈ 70 / growth rate (%).
questions.x: For steady exponential growth, doubling time is approximately 70 divided by the annual percentage growth rate, the rule of 70, which comes from ln 2 ≈ 0.69. At 2% per year, 70 / 2 = 35 years. Dividing 100 by 2 (50 years) treats growth as simple linear addition and ignores that each year's growth builds on a larger base.

questions.q: Country A has excellent health care but a higher crude death rate than Country B, which has poorer health care. The best explanation is that Country A:
o: Has an older age structure
Correct: crude rates ignore age; many elderly people raise deaths per 1,000 even with good care.
Has a higher infant mortality rate
Good health care would make high infant mortality unlikely.
Has a higher birth rate
More births add young people, which tends to lower the crude death rate.
Has more immigration of young workers
Young immigrants would lower the crude death rate.
questions.note: Compare mortality across populations with age-standardized rates.
questions.x: The crude death rate is deaths per 1,000 total population and does not adjust for age. A country with many elderly people will record many deaths per 1,000 even if its health care is excellent, while a young population records few deaths despite poorer care. That is why mortality comparisons use age-standardized rates; a higher birth rate would make the population younger and lower the crude rate.

questions.q: The infant mortality rate is defined as:
o: Deaths of children under age 5 per 1,000 population
That mixes the under-5 rate with a crude denominator.
Deaths at birth per 1,000 pregnancies
That is closer to a perinatal or stillbirth measure.
Deaths of children under age 1 per 1,000 live births
Correct: the standard measure of infant mortality.
Deaths of infants per 1,000 women of childbearing age
The denominator is live births, not women.
questions.x: The infant mortality rate counts deaths of children before their first birthday per 1,000 live births in the same year. The denominator is live births because those are the infants at risk. It is a sensitive indicator of a population's overall health and living conditions; the under-5 mortality rate is a different measure covering a wider age range.

questions.q: Historians attribute the initial decline in death rates in 18th- and 19th-century Europe mainly to:
o: Better food supply, sanitation and clean water
Correct: public health and nutrition preceded most effective medical treatments.
Widespread use of antibiotics
Antibiotics arrived in the 1940s, long after death rates began falling.
Falling birth rates
Birth rates fell later and do not directly reduce mortality.
Mass vaccination against all major diseases
Only smallpox vaccination existed early; most vaccines came much later.
questions.x: Death rates in Europe began falling in the 18th and 19th centuries, well before effective medical treatments existed. Historians credit improved nutrition and food supply, followed by sanitation and clean water, which reduced infectious disease. Antibiotics are the tempting answer, but they arrived in the 1940s, long after mortality had already declined substantially.

questions.q: In stage 2 of the demographic transition, population growth is rapid because:
o: Birth rates rise while death rates remain high
Birth rates stay high rather than rising, and death rates are falling.
Death rates fall while birth rates remain high
Correct: the widening gap between births and deaths drives fast growth.
Both birth and death rates are low
That is stage 4, with slow or no growth.
Both birth and death rates fall at the same pace
Equal declines would not create rapid growth.
questions.x: In stage 2 of the demographic transition, improvements in food, sanitation and health reduce death rates, but birth rates stay high because fertility norms change slowly. The widening gap between births and deaths produces rapid population growth. Birth rates do not rise in this stage, so the 'birth rates rise' option misstates which rate is changing.

questions.q: Which factor best explains falling birth rates in stage 3 of the demographic transition?
o: Urbanization makes children more costly and less economically useful
Correct: in cities, children are expensive dependents rather than farm labor.
Rising infant mortality
Infant mortality is falling in stage 3, not rising.
Declining access to contraception
Access to contraception expands in stage 3.
Reduced education for women
Women's education rises and is associated with lower fertility.
questions.x: In stage 3, birth rates fall as societies urbanize and industrialize. In cities, children cost more to raise and contribute less labor, while falling child mortality, women's education and contraceptive access further reduce desired family size. Each distractor reverses a real stage-3 trend: infant mortality falls, contraception spreads and women's education rises.

questions.q: Several high-income countries now record more deaths than births each year. Demographers who describe this as a fifth stage of the demographic transition are emphasizing:
o: A return to high birth and death rates
That describes stage 1, not a post-transition stage.
Rapid growth from falling mortality
That is stage 2.
Fertility below replacement leading to natural population decline
Correct: a proposed stage 5 features births falling below deaths.
Stable population with births equal to deaths
That is the classic stage 4 balance, not decline.
questions.x: The classic demographic transition ends in stage 4 with low birth and death rates and little growth. Some demographers add a stage 5 in which fertility falls well below replacement, deaths exceed births, and populations shrink without immigration. The stage 4 option is tempting, but stage 4 implies balance, while the scenario describes natural decline.

questions.q: According to Thomas Malthus, population tends to grow:
o: Arithmetically, while food supply grows geometrically
This reverses Malthus's claim.
Geometrically, while food supply grows arithmetically
Correct: population outpaces food, leading to crisis.
At the same rate as food supply
Malthus argued the two rates differ, which creates the crisis.
Only when death rates rise
Malthus saw rising death as a check on growth, not its cause.
questions.x: Malthus argued that population tends to grow geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8) while food supply grows only arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4). Population therefore eventually outstrips food, and checks such as famine and disease restore balance. The reversed version is the classic trap; the crisis depends on population growing faster than food.

questions.q: Malthus distinguished 'positive checks' from 'preventive checks' on population. Which is a positive check?
o: Delayed marriage
Delayed marriage lowers births, making it a preventive check.
Celibacy
Celibacy lowers births, a preventive check.
Smaller desired family size
This reduces fertility, a preventive check.
Famine
Correct: positive checks raise mortality (famine, disease, war).
questions.note: Positive checks raise deaths; preventive checks lower births.
questions.x: Malthus described two kinds of checks on population. Preventive checks reduce births, such as delayed marriage or celibacy; positive checks increase deaths, such as famine, disease and war. Famine raises mortality, so it is a positive check, while the other options all work by lowering fertility.

questions.q: Which development most directly undermined Malthus's prediction of mass famine in the 20th century?
o: A sharp rise in global birth rates
Higher births would support, not undermine, his fear.
The spread of infectious diseases
Disease is one of his positive checks, consistent with his theory.
Agricultural innovations that greatly increased crop yields
Correct: technology raised food output far faster than Malthus expected.
Rising world population after 1950
Fast growth without mass famine is what challenged him; growth alone does not.
questions.x: Malthus assumed food supply could grow only slowly, but agricultural technology, including mechanization, fertilizers and high-yield crop varieties, raised food output faster than population in most of the world. This broke the link he predicted between population growth and mass famine. Rising population alone does not refute him; growth without the predicted famine does.

questions.q: An environmental scientist argues that rising world population will exhaust fresh water and arable land unless birth rates are reduced. This view is best described as:
o: Demographic transition theory
Transition theory describes stages of birth and death rates, not resource collapse.
World systems theory
World systems theory concerns global economic hierarchy.
Neo-Malthusian
Correct: it updates Malthus by stressing resource limits and calling for lower fertility.
Dependency theory
Dependency theory concerns exploitation of poorer nations by wealthy ones.
questions.x: Neo-Malthusians update Malthus's argument by stressing that population growth threatens finite resources such as water, land and ecosystems, and they often call for lower fertility. The emphasis on resource limits and reducing births identifies the view. Demographic transition theory is tempting because it concerns population, but it describes stages of birth and death rates, not resource collapse.

questions.q: A population pyramid with a very wide base that narrows steadily toward the top indicates:
o: Low fertility and an aging population
That produces a narrow base, a constrictive pyramid.
Zero population growth
Stable populations have roughly vertical sides.
High fertility and a young population
Correct: an expansive pyramid, typical of stage 2 or early stage 3.
Heavy out-migration of children
Children rarely migrate alone at a scale that shapes the base.
questions.x: A pyramid with a wide base that narrows steadily upward is expansive. The wide base means many recent births from high fertility, and the rapid narrowing reflects a young population with relatively high mortality. A low-fertility aging population would show the opposite, a narrow, constrictive base.

questions.q: A population pyramid is narrower at the base than in the middle age groups. This shape suggests:
o: A recent baby boom
A boom would widen, not narrow, the base.
Very high infant mortality alone
High infant mortality typically accompanies high fertility and a wide base.
Fertility has declined in recent decades
Correct: a constrictive pyramid; recent birth cohorts are smaller than earlier ones.
Rapid population growth
Rapid growth produces a wide base.
questions.x: When the base of a pyramid is narrower than the middle, recent birth cohorts are smaller than earlier ones, so fertility has declined. This constrictive shape is typical of wealthy, aging societies. High infant mortality is tempting, but it usually accompanies high fertility and leaves a wide base.

questions.q: A population pyramid with nearly equal bar widths up to about age 60, tapering only at the oldest ages, indicates:
o: Rapid population growth
Rapid growth yields a wide base.
A sudden fertility collapse
A collapse would make the base much narrower than the middle.
High mortality at all ages
High mortality would taper the pyramid steadily from the bottom.
Low, stable birth and death rates
Correct: a stationary pyramid, with each cohort about the same size.
questions.x: A stationary pyramid has bars of roughly equal width up to older ages, then tapers where mortality rises. Equal-sized cohorts mean births have been steady at about replacement and death rates are low until late life. Rapid growth would create a wide base, while a fertility collapse would create a narrow base.

questions.q: The population pyramid of an oil-rich Gulf state shows far more men than women aged 20 to 45, while children and elderly are evenly split by sex. The best explanation is:
o: Sex-selective abortion
That would skew the youngest ages, which are balanced.
Higher female mortality in adulthood
Mortality would not produce such a sharp, age-limited gap.
Large-scale labor immigration of working-age men
Correct: migration is selective for age and sex, distorting only the working-age bars.
A baby boom 30 years ago
A boom would enlarge both sexes equally.
questions.note: Migration distorts pyramids in the working ages.
questions.x: Migration is selective: labor migrants are mostly young working-age adults, often men. Large inflows of male workers swell only the working-age male bars, leaving children and the elderly balanced by sex. Sex-selective abortion would skew the youngest ages, which are balanced here, so it cannot explain the pattern.

questions.q: A population pyramid shows an unusually narrow band for people now aged 75 to 79 in an otherwise smooth shape. The most likely cause is:
o: A recent decline in fertility
Recent declines affect the base, not people in their 70s.
A drop in births during a war or famine about 77 years earlier
Correct: a past birth deficit leaves a lasting 'notch' as that cohort ages.
High immigration of retirees
Immigration would widen, not narrow, that band.
Improved survival among the elderly
Better survival would widen older bands.
questions.x: Each pyramid bar is a cohort that ages upward over time. If births fell sharply in a particular period, such as during a war or famine, that small cohort leaves a 'notch' that moves up the pyramid. People now aged 75 to 79 were born about 77 years ago, so the notch points to a birth deficit then, not to anything recent.

questions.q: Abundant, well-paid jobs in a destination city that attract migrants are an example of a:
o: Pull factor
Correct: a pull factor draws migrants toward a destination.
Push factor
Push factors drive people out of their origin.
Intervening obstacle
Obstacles hinder migration rather than attract it.
Positive check
A Malthusian term for mortality-raising forces.
questions.x: Migration theory separates push factors, conditions that drive people out of an origin, from pull factors, attractions that draw them to a destination. Plentiful, well-paid jobs at the destination attract migrants, so they are a pull factor. A push factor would be something like unemployment or conflict at home.

questions.q: A man moves abroad because his brother, who emigrated earlier, offers housing and helps him find work. Later, the man's cousins follow. This pattern is best described as:
o: Forced migration
The moves are voluntary.
Brain drain
Nothing indicates the migrants are highly skilled professionals.
Return migration
Return migration is moving back to the origin.
Chain migration
Correct: earlier migrants create networks that lower costs for relatives and neighbors.
questions.x: Chain migration occurs when earlier migrants help relatives and friends follow by providing housing, job contacts and information. These networks lower the cost and risk of moving and create sequences of migration from the same family or village. Brain drain is tempting, but it concerns the emigration of highly skilled workers, which is not described.

questions.q: A family moves from a rural village to the capital city of the same country. This is:
o: International migration
No national border is crossed.
Emigration
Emigration means leaving one's country.
Counterurbanization
Counterurbanization is movement from cities to rural areas.
Internal migration
Correct: movement within a country's borders.
questions.x: Internal migration is movement within a country's borders, such as rural-to-urban migration. International migration requires crossing a national border, and emigration means leaving one's country. Counterurbanization is the reverse flow, from cities to rural areas, which rules out the most tempting distractor.

questions.q: Which person best fits the definition of a refugee?
o: Someone who moves abroad for a higher salary
That is an economic migrant.
Someone who flees her country due to well-founded fear of persecution and cannot safely return
Correct: refugees are forced migrants fleeing persecution across a border.
Someone who relocates to another region of his own country after a flood
He is internally displaced; he crossed no border.
Someone who studies abroad for two years
That is temporary voluntary migration.
questions.x: A refugee is a person who has crossed an international border because of a well-founded fear of persecution, such as for race, religion, nationality, political opinion or social group, and cannot safely return. Someone displaced within their own country by a disaster is an internally displaced person, not a refugee. Moving for higher pay is economic migration.

questions.q: A city of 500,000 receives 6,000 immigrants and loses 2,000 emigrants in a year. What is its net migration rate?
o: Adds immigrants and emigrants instead of subtracting.
Uses only immigrants and ignores emigration.
Off by a factor of 10 in the conversion.
questions.x: Net migration rate equals immigrants minus emigrants, divided by the population, times 1,000. Here (6,000 − 2,000) / 500,000 × 1,000 = 8 per 1,000. The tempting error is adding immigrants and emigrants (16), but emigrants leave, so they must be subtracted.

questions.q: Migrant workers abroad send part of their wages to families in their home country. The most direct effect on the origin community is:
o: Higher fertility caused by out-migration
Absence of young adults generally lowers local births.
Rapid urbanization of the origin village
Remittances do not by themselves turn villages into cities.
Elimination of push factors
Remittances help families but do not remove underlying push factors.
Higher household income from remittances
Correct: remittances are a major income source for many origin households.
questions.x: Remittances are money that migrants send home, and in many low-income countries they are a major source of household income. Their most direct effect is raising the purchasing power of origin families for food, schooling, housing and health care. They help families cope, but they do not eliminate the underlying push factors that caused migration.

questions.q: A low-income country trains many physicians, but a large share move to high-income countries for better pay. This is called:
o: Chain migration
Chain migration describes network-based migration of relatives.
Gentrification
Gentrification is neighborhood change in cities.
Healthy immigrant effect
That concerns migrant health, not skill loss.
Brain drain
Correct: the emigration of highly educated workers from their origin country.
questions.x: Brain drain is the emigration of highly educated or skilled workers, such as physicians and engineers, from lower-income to higher-income countries. The origin country loses the return on its training investment and may face shortages of professionals. Chain migration is also a migration pattern, but it is defined by family networks, not skill level.

questions.q: A farmer wants to emigrate for higher wages but cannot afford the journey and is barred by the destination country's visa rules. In Lee's model of migration, these barriers are:
o: Push factors
Push factors drive people out of the origin; these block departure instead.
Intervening obstacles
Correct: factors between origin and destination that impede moving.
Pull factors
Pull factors attract migrants to the destination.
Preventive checks
A Malthusian term for birth-lowering behaviors.
questions.note: Lee: push, pull, intervening obstacles, personal factors.
questions.x: Lee's model of migration includes factors at the origin (push), factors at the destination (pull), intervening obstacles between them, and personal factors. Travel cost and restrictive visa rules stand between the farmer's wish to leave and arrival, so they are intervening obstacles. They are not push factors, because push factors encourage leaving rather than block it.

questions.q: As fertility declines, a country temporarily has a large working-age population relative to children and elderly. Economists call the resulting growth potential the:
o: Demographic dividend
Correct: a favorable dependency ratio can boost savings and growth.
Population momentum
Momentum is continued growth after fertility falls, not an economic benefit.
Malthusian trap
That is a cycle of growth outstripping food.
Dependency burden
The point is a low burden, not a high one.
questions.x: A demographic dividend is the economic growth potential created when falling fertility produces a large working-age population relative to dependents. With fewer children to support and many workers, savings and investment can rise. It is temporary, because the large working-age cohort eventually ages into retirement and raises old-age dependency.

questions.q: Across many countries, higher female educational attainment is associated with lower fertility. Which mechanism best explains this?
o: Education reduces biological fertility
There is no biological effect of schooling on fecundity.
Education raises the opportunity cost of childbearing and delays marriage
Correct: schooling and careers raise the cost of time spent raising children.
Educated women have higher infant mortality
Maternal education is linked to lower infant mortality.
Education eliminates the desire for any children
Educated women typically still have children, just fewer and later.
questions.x: Women's education lowers fertility mainly through social and economic mechanisms. Schooling delays marriage, expands job opportunities, raises the opportunity cost of time spent raising children, and increases knowledge of and access to contraception. It does not reduce biological fecundity, and educated women usually still have children, just fewer and later.

questions.q: A cross-national study finds that countries with higher GDP per capita have lower fertility. A researcher concludes that rising income causes fertility to fall. The strongest criticism is that:
o: The sample includes too many countries
More countries strengthens, not weakens, a cross-national analysis.
Fertility cannot be measured across countries
TFR is routinely compared across countries.
Confounders such as urbanization and women's education may drive both
Correct: correlation in cross-sectional data cannot rule out third variables.
GDP and fertility are positively correlated
The finding is a negative correlation.
questions.x: A cross-sectional correlation between income and fertility cannot establish causation, because other variables such as urbanization, women's education and contraceptive access may drive both. These confounders could create the association even if income itself had no direct effect. More countries in the sample would strengthen, not weaken, the analysis, so sample size is not the problem.

questions.q: As a country develops, the leading causes of death shift from infections and malnutrition to heart disease and cancer. This shift is called the:
o: Epidemiologic transition
Correct: the change in disease patterns accompanying the demographic transition.
Demographic dividend
That concerns age structure and economic growth.
Nutrition transition
That refers to diet shifts, not causes of death overall.
Healthy immigrant effect
That concerns migrant health, not national disease patterns.
questions.x: The epidemiologic transition is the shift in leading causes of death from infectious disease and malnutrition to chronic, degenerative diseases such as heart disease and cancer. It accompanies the demographic transition because more people survive childhood and reach older ages. The nutrition transition is a narrower change in diets and body weight, not in overall causes of death.

questions.q: Life expectancy at birth in a country rose from 40 to 65 years over a few decades. The largest contributor to such a rise is usually:
o: Extending the maximum human lifespan
Maximum lifespan has barely changed.
Better treatment of cancer in the elderly
Late-life gains add relatively few years to the average at birth.
Higher fertility
Life expectancy is calculated from age-specific death rates, so the number of births does not raise it.
Reduced infant and child mortality
Correct: early deaths subtract many years, so preventing them raises the average sharply.
questions.note: Low life expectancy at birth mostly reflects high child mortality, not that adults die at 40.
questions.x: Life expectancy at birth is an average, so deaths in infancy and childhood pull it down sharply because each subtracts many potential years. Reducing infant and child mortality therefore produces the largest gains. Low life expectancy does not mean adults typically die at 40, and better late-life cancer care adds only a few years to the average.

questions.q: The process in which wealthier residents move into a lower-income urban neighborhood, raising property values and changing its character, is called:
o: Suburbanization
Suburbanization is movement out of cities to outlying areas.
Urban decay
Urban decay is decline, not renewal.
Ghettoization
That is forced or concentrated residence of a marginalized group.
Gentrification
Correct: upscale renewal of a neighborhood, often displacing existing residents.
questions.x: Gentrification occurs when higher-income residents and investment move into a lower-income urban neighborhood, raising property values, rents and changing its character. It often displaces long-time residents who can no longer afford to live there. Suburbanization is the opposite flow, from city centers outward.

questions.q: Which outcome is the most common criticism of gentrification?
o: Property values in the area fall sharply
Gentrification raises property values.
Public services in the neighborhood decline
Services usually improve with new investment.
The neighborhood population becomes poorer
Incoming residents are typically wealthier.
Long-time low-income residents are displaced by rising rents
Correct: higher housing costs can push out the original community.
questions.x: Gentrification brings investment and higher property values, but its central criticism is displacement: rising rents and taxes push out long-time low-income residents. The benefits of renewal can therefore go largely to newcomers. The other options describe the opposite of gentrification's usual effects, such as falling values or declining services.

questions.q: Urbanization refers to:
o: The total population of a country increasing
Population growth can occur without urbanization.
The movement of people from cities to suburbs
That is suburbanization.
The decline of manufacturing in cities
That is deindustrialization.
The growing proportion of a population living in cities
Correct: urbanization is a shift of population share toward urban areas.
questions.x: Urbanization is the increasing proportion of a population living in urban areas, driven by rural-to-urban migration, natural increase in cities and reclassification of growing towns. A country can grow in total population without urbanizing if growth is evenly spread. Suburbanization is a related but different process of movement from city centers to outlying areas.

questions.q: In mid-20th-century U.S. cities, many middle-class white families moved to newly built outer suburbs as minority populations in central cities grew. This pattern is known as:
o: Gentrification
Gentrification is the opposite flow, wealthier people moving into the city.
White flight
Correct: racially patterned movement from cities to suburbs.
Chain migration
Chain migration involves networks of relatives, not suburban moves.
Counterurbanization
Counterurbanization is a move to rural areas, not suburbs.
questions.x: White flight describes the mid-20th-century movement of white middle-class families from central cities to suburbs as minority populations in cities grew. It was shaped by racial attitudes and by policies such as discriminatory lending and highway building. Counterurbanization is a move to rural areas, not suburbs, and gentrification is the opposite flow into the city.

questions.q: A city in a low-income country grows so fast from rural migration that jobs, housing and sanitation cannot keep up, and informal settlements spread. This is best described as:
o: Gentrification
Gentrification involves wealthier residents moving in.
Suburbanization
The growth is at the city level, not a move to suburbs.
Overurbanization
Correct: urban growth outpaces economic and infrastructure capacity.
Deurbanization
The urban population is growing, not shrinking.
questions.x: Overurbanization occurs when a city's population grows faster than its jobs, housing and infrastructure can support, often due to rural-to-urban migration in low-income countries. The result is unemployment, informal settlements and strained sanitation. It differs from gentrification, which involves wealthier residents moving in, not poor migrants overwhelming capacity.

questions.q: Interviews show that residents who stayed in a gentrifying neighborhood enjoyed new parks and lower crime yet felt they no longer belonged as familiar shops and churches closed. Researchers would call this:
o: Cultural displacement
Correct: residents lose their sense of place even without physically moving.
Physical displacement
These residents remained in the neighborhood.
Assimilation
They are not adopting a dominant culture by choice.
Relative deprivation
That concerns perceived disadvantage driving collective action, not loss of place.
questions.x: Displacement can be physical, when residents must move out, or cultural, when residents stay but lose their sense of belonging as the shops, institutions and social networks of their community disappear. The residents in this study remained, so their loss is cultural. Physical displacement is tempting because gentrification often involves moving out, but these people did not leave.

questions.q: Globalization is best defined as:
o: The growing integration of economies, cultures and populations across national borders
Correct: globalization links societies through trade, communication and migration.
The movement of people from rural to urban areas
That is urbanization.
A country's withdrawal from international trade
That is protectionism or isolationism.
The decline of birth rates in wealthy nations
That is a demographic trend, not globalization.
questions.x: Globalization is the increasing interconnection of economies, cultures and populations across national borders through trade, investment, communication technology and migration. It links distant places so that events in one country quickly affect others. Urbanization is tempting because it is another large social process, but it concerns rural-to-urban movement within societies.

questions.q: National surveys report very different percentages of 'gay, lesbian or bisexual' people depending on whether they ask about identity, sexual behavior or attraction. The best explanation is that:
o: Sexual orientation cannot be studied scientifically
Measurement differences call for careful definitions, not abandoning research.
Respondents always answer randomly
Consistent differences by question type are not random.
Sexual orientation changes daily for most people
Orientation is generally stable; the gaps reflect what is measured.
Identity, behavior and attraction overlap but are not identical
Correct: some people report same-sex attraction or behavior without adopting an LGB identity.
questions.x: Sexual orientation has several dimensions: identity (how people label themselves), behavior (with whom they have sex) and attraction (whom they are drawn to). These overlap but do not coincide, so a person may report same-sex attraction or behavior without identifying as gay, lesbian or bisexual. Surveys that measure different dimensions therefore yield different estimates, without implying that orientation is unstable.

questions.q: According to world systems theory, core nations relate to periphery nations mainly by:
o: Sharing industrial technology equally with them
The theory emphasizes unequal, not equal, exchange.
Extracting raw materials and cheap labor while exporting high-value goods
Correct: the core benefits from an unequal exchange with the periphery.
Depending on them for advanced manufactured goods
The core produces the high-value manufactured goods.
Having no economic contact with them
The theory centers on their economic ties.
questions.x: World systems theory divides the global economy into core, semi-periphery and periphery. Core nations dominate through capital-intensive, high-value production and extract raw materials and cheap labor from periphery nations, an unequal exchange that reproduces global inequality. The core does not depend on the periphery for advanced goods; it produces them.

questions.q: A country has growing manufacturing and exports some industrial goods, but still relies on foreign investment and buys raw materials cheaply from poorer nations. In world systems theory, it is best classified as:
o: Core
Core nations dominate investment and do not depend on foreign capital in this way.
Semi-periphery
Correct: it is exploited by the core while exploiting the periphery.
Periphery
Periphery nations mainly export raw materials and lack industrial growth.
External area
External areas lie outside the world economy entirely.
questions.x: In world systems theory, semi-periphery nations sit between the core and the periphery: they have growing industry and some economic power, yet depend on core capital. They are exploited by the core while exploiting the periphery for cheap raw materials. Calling it core is tempting because it exports industrial goods, but its reliance on foreign investment marks it as semi-periphery.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that poor nations remain underdeveloped because wealthy nations structure trade and debt to their own advantage. This view is:
o: Dependency theory
Correct: underdevelopment results from exploitative ties to wealthy nations.
Modernization theory
Modernization theory blames internal traditional values and urges adopting Western institutions.
Demographic transition theory
That describes birth and death rate stages.
Malthusian theory
That concerns population outpacing food.
questions.x: Dependency theory argues that poor nations remain underdeveloped because their economies are structured to serve wealthy nations through unequal trade, debt and investment. The cause of poverty lies in external exploitative relationships. Modernization theory is the main contrast, since it blames internal factors such as traditional values and urges poor nations to adopt Western institutions.

questions.q: Teenagers in dozens of countries watch the same streaming shows, wear the same brands and use the same slang. Critics of globalization call this trend:
o: Cultural relativism
Relativism is judging cultures on their own terms.
Ethnocentrism
Ethnocentrism is judging others by one's own culture.
Cultural homogenization
Correct: local cultures converge toward a common, often Western, global culture.
Multiculturalism
Multiculturalism values distinct cultures coexisting, the opposite of convergence.
questions.x: Cultural homogenization is the convergence of local cultures toward a shared global culture, often dominated by Western media and brands, as globalization spreads the same products and practices worldwide. Critics worry it erodes local diversity. Multiculturalism is the opposite, describing distinct cultures coexisting while keeping their differences.

questions.q: A global fast-food chain offers vegetarian menus in India and rice dishes in Japan to suit local tastes. This illustrates:
o: Cultural lag
Cultural lag is non-material culture trailing material change.
Glocalization
Correct: global products are adapted to local cultures.
Brain drain
Brain drain concerns emigration of skilled workers.
Assimilation
The company adapts to locals, not the reverse.
questions.x: Glocalization is the adaptation of global products or practices to local cultures, such as a multinational chain changing its menu to fit local diets and religious norms. It shows that globalization does not simply erase local culture but interacts with it. Assimilation is tempting, but the company adjusts to local customers rather than customers adopting the company's culture.

questions.q: A factory in a high-income country closes and moves production to a lower-wage country. Which consequence of globalization does this best illustrate?
o: Gentrification of the factory town
Factory closures usually cause decline, not upscale renewal.
Population momentum
Momentum concerns age structure and growth.
Deindustrialization and job loss in high-income regions
Correct: offshoring shifts manufacturing jobs to cheaper labor markets.
Chain migration
No migration of relatives is described.
questions.x: Deindustrialization is the decline of manufacturing employment in a region, and globalization speeds it through offshoring production to countries with lower labor costs. High-income manufacturing towns lose jobs and tax revenue, while production rises elsewhere. Gentrification is a distractor, because factory closures typically cause decline, not upscale renewal.

questions.q: A newly emerging respiratory virus is detected on five continents within weeks of its first identified case. Which feature of globalization most directly explains this speed?
o: High volume of international air travel
Correct: global transportation networks move infected people across continents within hours.
Rising fertility in low-income countries
Birth rates do not determine how fast a pathogen spreads between continents.
Urban gentrification
Neighborhood change does not explain intercontinental spread.
Cultural homogenization
Shared culture does not transport pathogens.
questions.x: Globalization connects distant places through rapid transportation, especially international air travel, which can move infected people between continents within a day. That is why a new respiratory pathogen can appear worldwide within weeks of its first identified case. Cultural homogenization involves shared tastes and media, which do not physically carry pathogens.

questions.q: A social movement is best defined as:
o: A spontaneous, short-lived crowd event
That describes collective behavior such as a riot or fad.
Any change in population size
Population change is demographic, not a movement.
A government program that changes laws
Movements arise from members of society, not as state programs.
An organized, sustained collective effort to promote or resist social change
Correct: movements are organized and aim at change.
questions.x: A social movement is an organized, sustained collective effort to promote or resist social change, built from members of society rather than from the state. Its organization and duration distinguish it from collective behavior such as riots, fads or panics, which are spontaneous and short-lived. Government programs may respond to movements but are not movements themselves.

questions.q: A movement campaigns to pass laws requiring paid family leave while keeping the existing political and economic system intact. This is a:
o: Revolutionary movement
Revolutionary movements seek to replace the whole system.
Redemptive movement
Redemptive movements seek deep change in individuals.
Reactionary movement
Reactionary movements resist or reverse change.
Reform movement
Correct: it seeks specific changes within the current system.
questions.x: A reform movement seeks specific, limited changes, such as a new law, while keeping the existing social, political and economic system intact. Paid family leave legislation fits that goal. A revolutionary movement is the tempting contrast, because it seeks to replace the whole system rather than change one part of it.

questions.q: A movement that seeks to overthrow the existing government and completely restructure society is a:
o: Revolutionary movement
Correct: it seeks total societal transformation.
Reform movement
Reform movements seek limited change within the system.
Alternative movement
Alternative movements seek limited change in individuals.
Counter-movement
A counter-movement is defined by opposing another movement, not by total transformation.
questions.x: A revolutionary movement seeks a radical, total transformation of society, often including overthrowing the existing government. Its goals are broad and aimed at the whole social structure, unlike reform movements that change specific policies within the system. A counter-movement is defined by its opposition to another movement, not by the scope of its goals.

questions.q: A group organizes to repeal recent social reforms and restore the norms of an earlier era. This is best classified as a:
o: Reform movement
Reform movements push forward specific changes.
Redemptive movement
Redemptive movements seek personal transformation.
Reactionary (regressive) movement
Correct: it resists change or seeks to return to a past state.
Alternative movement
Alternative movements seek limited individual change.
questions.x: A reactionary, or regressive, movement seeks to resist recent change or restore earlier social arrangements. Repealing reforms and returning to past norms is its defining aim. A reform movement is the tempting contrast, since it also targets specific laws, but reform movements push for new change rather than reversal.

questions.q: A campaign encourages individuals to reduce their meat consumption by one meal per week, without seeking legal or institutional change. Using Aberle's typology, this is a(n):
o: Redemptive movement
Redemptive movements seek radical, total change in individuals.
Alternative movement
Correct: it targets a limited change in individual behavior.
Reform movement
Reform movements target limited change in society or law.
Revolutionary movement
Revolutionary movements seek radical change in society.
questions.note: Aberle: alternative (limited, individual), redemptive (radical, individual), reform (limited, society), revolutionary (radical, society).
questions.x: Aberle classified movements by whom they target (individuals or society) and how much change they seek (limited or radical). Asking individuals to make one modest behavioral change, without seeking institutional change, is an alternative movement. A redemptive movement also targets individuals, but it seeks a total personal transformation, such as a religious conversion.
